# Hypnotic and rhetorical devices

A reference of things a writer can do in a script. Families group devices; variants are named narrower forms; recipes are named sequences. Theory, at the end, explains why devices work and is not something to label.


## Induction

Also called: trance induction, hypnotic induction.

An induction is the opening procedure that marks the shift from ordinary talk to hypnosis and gets the listener absorbed and responding. The family groups inductions by their route in: the eyes, the body, the breath, numbers, imagery, confusion or overload, surprise, ordinary conversation, memory of an earlier trance, pretending, repetition, involuntary movement, an installed cue, arousal, or the act of reading. Waking hypnosis is the eyes-open route that uses no relaxation or sleep language. The family also holds four named recipes (Elman, Betty Erickson 5-4-3-2-1, double induction, Gateway). Work done after trance has started belongs to the deepening family; the confusion-overload and triggers-anchors families hold the general devices that several inductions apply.

**Choosing:** Choose by medium, listener and time. Recorded audio and text cannot see the listener or touch them, so use progressive relaxation, breath, counting, visualization, eye closure or sensation focus, and avoid the in-person rapid variants. For analytical or restless listeners, give the mind work (confusion, overload, 5-4-3-2-1, a concurrent task) or use tense-and-release. For experienced listeners, use revivification or a re-induction trigger and spend the saved time on suggestions. Most scripts combine two or three: a fixation or breath opening, an eye closure, then a count that hands over to a deepener.

**Not to be confused with:** Deepening (deepening intensifies a trance that has already been started; induction starts it); Induction section (the section is the place in the script; the family is the devices that fill it); Suggestibility test (a test shows responsiveness before induction and does not itself claim to start trance).

**Why it works:** Hypnotic induction, Response expectancy theory, Sociocognitive theory of hypnosis, Hypnotizability, Absorption (trait).

**Consent:** An induction should be announced and agreed to; the unannounced variants need consent negotiated beforehand.


### Eye fixation *(unit)*

Also called: fixation induction, Braid induction, staring induction, fixed-gaze induction.

The listener stares at a single spot, usually slightly above eye level, while the writer describes the ordinary effects of staring: blurring, watering, blinking, heaviness. The fatigue is real and guaranteed, so the suggestions appear to come true. The defining feature is a sustained external visual target; the suggested closing of the lids is the separate device eye-closure, which normally follows.

**How:** Name a spot the listener can find without help ('a point on the ceiling, a little above your eyeline'). Describe what staring does before it happens and confirm it as it happens. Give it enough time, one to three minutes in audio, and write the closure as permitted, not forced. It fails if the target is unclear or if the script rushes to 'your eyes are closed' before they are.

> Pick a spot on the wall, a little above eye level, and rest your eyes there. Keep them there.

> As you keep looking at that spot, it may blur a little at the edges. That's fine. Keep looking.

> The longer you look, the more your eyes want to blink, and each blink is a little slower than the last.

**Spot it by:** 'pick a spot'; 'keep your eyes on'; 'stare at' / 'gaze at' / 'look at that point'; 'a little above eye level'; description of blurring, watering or blinking tied to continued looking.

**Not to be confused with:** Eye-closure suggestion (eye-closure suggests the lids shutting; fixation is the staring that comes before); Gaze capture (gaze capture uses imagined or on-screen eyes as an attention hold, not a tiring stare at a neutral point); Narrowing attention (narrowing says everything else fades; fixation gives the eyes one physical target).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. The oldest standard induction and the opening of the Stanford scales; no good evidence it works better than other inductions, and Braid's physiological explanation is not accepted. Source: Braid, Neurypnology (1843).

**Why it works:** Hypnotic induction, Attentional tunneling, Habituation, Response expectancy theory.


#### Pendulum / pocket watch *(variant)*

Also called: pocketwatch, swinging watch, pendant, pendulum induction.

Eye fixation where the target moves in a slow, regular arc. Tracking the swing gives the eyes continuous work and adds a rhythm the voice can match. It is the stock image of hypnosis, so it also carries strong expectation.

**How:** In person, hold the object slightly above eye level so the eyes strain upward. In audio or text, have the listener imagine the watch or use a video, and time phrases to the swing ('back... and forth'). Lean on the cliche if the listener enjoys it; drop it for listeners who find it silly, because the expectation it carries then works against you.

> Follow the watch with your eyes. Back... and forth. Back... and forth. Only your eyes move.

> Each swing is a little harder to follow, and your eyelids get a little heavier each time it passes.

> Imagine a pendant swinging slowly in front of you, catching the light at the end of each swing.

**Spot it by:** 'watch' / 'pendulum' / 'pendant' with 'swing'; 'back and forth'; 'follow it with your eyes'; 'side to side'; phrases split to a two-beat swing rhythm.

**Not to be confused with:** Spiral fixation (a spiral is a rotating visual on a screen; a pendulum is a swinging object tracked side to side); Metronome / steady beat (a metronome is an audio beat; the pendulum is a visual target, real or imagined); Suggestibility test (the Chevreul pendulum is held by the listener to show ideomotor movement, not watched to tire the eyes).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. A stage and popular-culture staple; no studies show a moving target works better than a still one, and its effect is probably mostly expectation.

**Why it works:** Attentional capture, Response expectancy theory, Habituation.


#### Spiral fixation *(variant)*

Also called: hypno spiral, spiral induction, hypnodisc.

Eye fixation on a turning or animated visual, shown on screen or imagined. The motion draws the eyes to the centre and gives the writer an inward, downward image to talk over. It differs from the pendulum in that the eyes stay still while the target moves around them.

**How:** Tell the listener to look at the centre and let the edges move without following them. Tie the turning to the wanted direction: in, down, deeper. If the script is audio only, describe the spiral plainly and briefly; a long description of an unseen picture loses people. Note in the stage directions that a visual is required.

> Look into the centre of the spiral. Let the rest turn without following it.

> Round and round, and in, and down. The centre stays still while everything around it moves.

> The longer you watch it turn, the harder it is to look anywhere else.

**Spot it by:** 'spiral' / 'swirl' / 'vortex'; 'look into the centre'; 'round and round'; 'turning' / 'spinning' with 'drawn in' or 'pulled in'; stage direction for on-screen visual.

**Not to be confused with:** Pendulum / pocket watch (the pendulum swings side to side and is tracked; the spiral rotates around a fixed gaze); Visuals (that entry is the production choice to show visuals; this is the instruction to fixate on one); Descent imagery (descent imagery deepens after trance starts; the spiral is the fixation target that starts it).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Common in online hypnosis video; no controlled evidence that a spiral adds anything beyond any fixation target and the expectation attached to it.

**Why it works:** Attentional capture, Attentional tunneling, Response expectancy theory.


#### Candle / light fixation *(variant)*

Also called: flame gazing, candle induction, light fixation.

Eye fixation where the target is a flame or a bright point in a dim room. The light gives a natural single focus, darkens everything around it, and leaves an afterimage that can carry over when the eyes close.

**How:** Ask for a dim room and a steady light at a comfortable distance. Describe the flicker, the darkening edges and the urge to blink. On closure, use the afterimage: tell the listener they can still see the glow behind their lids and follow it inward. Do not write a real flame into a script that ends in sleep.

> Let your eyes rest on the flame. Watch how it moves a little, and settles.

> Everything around that small light grows dim. There is only the light.

> When your eyes close, you may still see the glow behind your eyelids. Watch it fade.

**Spot it by:** 'flame' / 'candle' / 'point of light'; 'gaze at' / 'watch the light'; 'flicker'; 'the room grows dim'; 'afterimage' / 'glow behind your eyelids'.

**Not to be confused with:** State-as-substance (light that fills the body is state-as-substance imagery; here the light is a thing to stare at); Spiral fixation (the spiral is a moving graphic; the flame is a near-still light source).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. A long-used fixation target, also found in meditation practice; nothing shows it outperforms any other target.

**Why it works:** Attentional tunneling, Habituation.


#### Eye roll *(variant)*

Also called: Spiegel eye roll, eye-roll induction, eyes up induction.

A brief induction taken from the Spiegels' procedure: look up as far as possible, hold the gaze up while slowly closing the eyelids, take a deep breath, then exhale and let the eyes relax and the body float. The upward strain tires the eyes in seconds. It is short, the same every time, and easy to teach for self-hypnosis.

**How:** Give the steps as plain numbered instructions and keep them in order: up, close, breathe, release. Tie the release of the eyes to a release of the whole body. Because it is a fixed sequence, it makes a good self-hypnosis entry that the listener can repeat alone. Follow with a deepener; alone it is very short.

> Look up, as if at a spot inside the top of your forehead. Keep looking up.

> Keep your eyes up there while your eyelids slowly close.

> Take a breath, let it out, let your eyes relax, and let your body float.

**Spot it by:** 'roll your eyes up' / 'look up toward your forehead / eyebrows'; 'keep looking up while your eyelids close'; 'let your eyes relax' following an upward gaze; 'float' right after eye release; three-step sequence: up, close, breathe out.

**Not to be confused with:** Eye fixation (the parent holds a stare for minutes at an outside point; the eye roll is a seconds-long upward strain with the lids closing over it); Eyelid lock (some eyelid-lock scripts also have the eyes rolled up; label the lock only when the text says the lids cannot open or invites a test, and the eye roll when the upward gaze is followed by closing and release with no test); Eye-closure suggestion (eye-closure suggests heaviness until the lids close; here closing is a deliberate step).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. The induction is part of the Spiegels' published Hypnotic Induction Profile and is widely taught for self-hypnosis; it has not been shown to work better than other brief inductions. The separate claim that the degree of eye roll measures hypnotizability has largely failed independent replication. Source: Spiegel & Spiegel, Trance and Treatment (1978).

**Why it works:** Hypnotic induction, Response expectancy theory, Hypnotizability.


#### Peripheral vision *(variant)*

Also called: hakalau, expanded awareness, soft focus.

The eyes stay on one point while attention spreads outward to take in everything at the sides, above and below. Practitioners report that holding wide, unfocused awareness quiets scanning and inner chatter and brings a calm, slightly detached state; this has not been tested. It is fixation plus a second step, which sets it apart from the plain stare.

**How:** Start as for eye fixation, with a point slightly above eye level. Then ask the listener to notice, without looking away, what is at the left and right edges, then above and below, then all of it at once. Keep the instruction to hold both the point and the whole field. It works with eyes open, so it suits text scripts and waking trance.

> Keep your eyes on that spot, and without moving them, start to notice what is at the edges of your vision.

> The walls on either side. The floor. The ceiling. All of it at once, while you keep looking at the one point.

> Let your attention spread wider than your eyes can look.

**Spot it by:** 'peripheral vision' / 'edges of your vision' / 'corners of your eyes'; 'without moving your eyes'; 'widen' / 'spread' / 'expand your awareness'; 'all of it at once'; 'soft focus' / 'soften your gaze'.

**Not to be confused with:** Eye fixation (the parent narrows onto the point; this keeps the point and widens to the whole field); Narrowing attention (narrowing fades everything but one thing; this takes in everything at once); Betty Erickson 5-4-3-2-1 (5-4-3-2-1 names individual seen items in turn; this holds the whole field with no naming).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Taught in NLP circles as 'hakalau' with claims about the parasympathetic nervous system that have not been tested; the calming effect is plausible but unverified.

**Why it works:** Attentional capture, Working-memory interference, Response expectancy theory.


### Eye-closure suggestion *(unit)*

Also called: heavy eyelids, eyes closing, eyelid heaviness.

A suggestion aimed at one response: the lids become heavy and shut. The closing is then named as the moment trance begins. It is the usual end of an eye fixation but stands alone too, as a direct request ('close your eyes') or a suggested, involuntary-feeling closure.

**How:** Build heaviness over several sentences before asking for closure, and tie it to blinking, which is happening anyway. Offer a fallback so no one is left with eyes open: 'and if they haven't closed yet, close them now'. Mark the closure straight away with a ratification and a drop in pace. In text scripts, where the reader must keep reading, replace it with heaviness that stops short of closing.

> Your eyelids are getting heavy. Heavier with every blink.

> So heavy now that it would feel good to let them close. Let them close.

> And as your eyes close, that comfortable feeling spreads, and you begin to drift.

**Spot it by:** 'eyelids' with 'heavy' / 'heavier'; 'let your eyes close' / 'close your eyes'; 'each blink'; 'as your eyes close' followed by a trance claim; 'so heavy they want to close'.

**Not to be confused with:** Eye fixation (fixation is the staring; eye-closure is the suggestion that the lids shut); Eyelid lock (the eyelid lock says the closed eyes cannot open and tests it; eye-closure only gets them shut); Heaviness / floating (that deepener spreads heaviness through the body; this one targets the lids and ends in closing).

**Evidence:** experimental. Eye closure is a standardized item on hypnotizability scales and most people pass it; that it marks entry to a distinct state is a convention, not a finding.

**Why it works:** Hypnotic induction, Response expectancy theory, Direct verbal suggestion.


### Progressive relaxation *(unit)*

Also called: progressive muscle relaxation, PMR, Jacobson relaxation, body relaxation induction.

The writer names body regions in sequence, usually feet to head or head to feet, and suggests each one loosening. The defining features are the ordered sweep and the instruction to relax. As used in hypnosis it is suggested relaxation; the original Jacobson method, with deliberate tensing, is the variant tension-release.

**How:** Fix a direction and keep to it. Give each region one or two sentences and a pause, and vary the verbs (loosen, soften, let go) while keeping the frame the same. Let the pace slow as you move along. It is the safest default for recordings because it needs no feedback, but it is slow; shorten it for experienced listeners and do not use it when the session needs energy.

> Start with your feet. Let the muscles there loosen, and let that looseness move up into your ankles.

> Now your shoulders. Let them drop. Let the weight go out of them.

> That comfortable, loose feeling moves up through your neck and into your scalp, until your whole body is at rest.

**Spot it by:** body parts named in anatomical order; 'relax' / 'loosen' / 'let go' repeated once per region; 'starting with your feet' / 'from the top of your head'; 'moving up into' / 'spreading down through'; 'your whole body' as the closing line.

**Not to be confused with:** Body scan (a body scan only notices sensation; progressive relaxation tells each part to relax); Sensation-focus induction (sensation focus stays on one sensation and lets it spread; this sweeps region by region); Heaviness / floating (that is a depth cue for the whole body, without an ordered tour).

**Evidence:** experimental. Muscle relaxation training is well studied for anxiety and tension; as a hypnotic induction it works about as well as others, and relaxation is not required for hypnotic responding. Source: Jacobson, Progressive Relaxation (1929).

**Why it works:** Hypnotic induction, Response expectancy theory, Habituation.


#### Tense-and-release *(variant)*

Also called: Jacobson tense-release, tense and relax, contract-relax.

Progressive relaxation with a deliberate contraction before each release. The listener does something physical on instruction, and the relaxation that follows is a real muscular after-effect, not only a suggestion. It derives from Jacobson, who used tensing to teach people to recognize tension; the short tense-hold-release cycle found in scripts is the abbreviated form developed later by behaviour therapists.

**How:** Give a clear cue to tense, a hold of about five seconds, and a clear cue to release, then a longer pause to notice the difference. Use fewer, larger muscle groups than in the plain sweep. It suits restless or sceptical listeners because they feel a result at once. Tell listeners to skip any area that hurts.

> Make a fist with both hands. Tight. Hold it... and let go. Feel the difference.

> Pull your shoulders up toward your ears. Hold them there. Now drop them, all at once.

> Notice how much looser that feels than before you tightened it.

**Spot it by:** 'tense' / 'tighten' / 'squeeze' / 'clench' followed by 'release' / 'let go'; 'hold it'; 'feel the difference' / 'notice the contrast'; a counted hold ('hold for five'); tense-release pair repeated per body region.

**Not to be confused with:** Progressive relaxation (the parent only suggests relaxing; this variant commands a contraction first); Small physical tasks (small tasks are used to build a habit of following; here the task is there for the physical contrast); Apposition of opposites (that pairs two suggested experiences in one sentence; this is a physical act followed by its release).

**Evidence:** experimental. The tense-release form of muscle relaxation has many controlled trials for tension and anxiety; its specific value as a hypnotic induction has not been separated out. Source: Jacobson, Progressive Relaxation (1929).

**Why it works:** Contrast effect, Self-perception theory.


#### Autogenic phrases *(variant)*

Also called: autogenic training, heavy and warm, autogenic formulae.

A fixed set of first-person, present-tense formulae ('my right arm is heavy') repeated several times each while the listener attends passively to the body part. The standard themes are heaviness, warmth, calm heartbeat, easy breathing, warm abdomen and cool forehead. What sets it apart from the parent is the listener's own voice and the fixed wording.

**How:** Give the phrase, then leave silence for the listener to repeat it inwardly three to six times. Keep the wording identical each time. Ask for passive attention: the listener says the phrase and waits, without trying to make it happen. Work heaviness through the limbs first, then warmth.

> Say to yourself, slowly: my right arm is heavy. My right arm is heavy.

> My arms and legs are heavy and warm.

> My breathing is calm and even. It breathes me.

**Spot it by:** first-person body statements: 'my arm is heavy', 'my legs are warm'; 'heavy and warm'; 'say to yourself' / 'repeat silently'; the same formula repeated verbatim several times; 'my heartbeat is calm' / 'my forehead is cool'.

**Not to be confused with:** Affirmations (affirmations state traits or goals; autogenic phrases state present body sensations); First-person suggestion (that is the general I-form for any suggestion; this is a fixed set of body formulae used to induce); Mantra (a mantra is one phrase repeated for its own sake; these are a sequence of formulae that move through the body).

**Evidence:** experimental. Autogenic training has controlled trials showing moderate effects on stress-related complaints; the studies vary in quality and concern weeks of practice, not a single use as an induction. Source: Schultz, Das autogene Training (1932).

**Why it works:** Self-reference effect, Response expectancy theory, Generation effect.


### Body scan *(unit)*

Also called: somatic sweep, body awareness scan.

An ordered tour of the body in which the only instruction is to notice. Nothing is commanded to change. Absorption comes from sustained inward attention, and any relaxation is left to happen by itself, which makes it hard to fail.

**How:** Use verbs of attention (notice, feel, be aware of) and avoid 'relax'. Name neutral facts the listener can check: contact with the chair, warmth, weight, the air on the skin. Accept every result, including 'nothing in particular'. It is a good choice when commands to relax make the listener try too hard.

> Bring your attention to your feet. Just notice what is there. Warm, cool, heavy, nothing in particular.

> Move your attention up to your knees. You don't need to change anything.

> Notice the places where your back meets the chair.

**Spot it by:** 'notice' / 'be aware of' / 'bring your attention to' with body parts in order; 'you don't need to change anything'; 'just notice'; lists of possible sensations offered without preference; absence of 'relax' commands in a region-by-region passage.

**Not to be confused with:** Progressive relaxation (the parent instructs each region to relax; the scan only observes); Pacing (pacing states verifiable facts in any order to build acceptance; the scan is an ordered tour of the body); Sensation-focus induction (sensation focus picks one sensation and stays with it).

**Evidence:** experimental. Studied as a mindfulness exercise with modest benefits for stress; evidence for it as a hypnotic induction specifically is thin. Source: Kabat-Zinn, Full Catastrophe Living (1990).

**Why it works:** Absorption (trait), Attentional tunneling.


### Breath-focus induction *(unit)*

Also called: breathing induction, breath pacing, breath-counting induction.

The breath is made the object of attention, either observed as it is or guided into a slower pattern. It is always present, rhythmic and partly voluntary, so it is easy to pace and easy to lead. As an induction it is the main route in; tying each exhale to going deeper once trance has begun is the deepener breath-deepener.

**How:** Start with one or two deliberate deep breaths as a clear starting signal, then let the breath return to its own rhythm and simply describe it. Do not prescribe long holds or sustained deep breathing; both cause dizziness. Time your phrases to an easy exhale, and attach the first suggestions of release to breathing out.

> Take a slow breath in... and let it go.

> You don't need to breathe in any special way. Just notice the air coming in, and going out.

> In through your nose for a count of four... and out, slowly, for six. Let your attention rest on nothing but that.

**Spot it by:** 'take a deep breath' / 'breathe in... and out' as an opening instruction; 'notice your breathing' / 'follow your breath'; counted or paced breaths ('in for four, out for six'); description of the breath itself: 'the air coming in', 'the rise and fall of your chest'; phrase rhythm following inhale and exhale before any trance claim.

**Not to be confused with:** Breath-linked deepening (a line that only attaches depth or release to each exhale is the deepener wherever it sits; label this entry when the text directs attention to the breath or sets its pace as the opening); Breathe in, breathe out (that gives the in-breath something to take in and the out-breath something to let go, at any stage; this entry attends to or paces the breath without loading it with content); Breath-synced pacing (that is a delivery choice about timing the voice, not a script instruction to attend to the breath); Small physical tasks ('take a breath for me' used as a small order is compliance building, not breath as the trance route).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Slow paced breathing has measurable calming effects; its use as a hypnotic induction is standard practice and has not been tested against other inductions in any decisive way.

**Why it works:** Hypnotic induction, Attentional tunneling, Pacing and leading.


### Counting induction *(unit)*

Also called: countdown induction, count-down, numbered induction.

A count is the spine of the induction: the writer announces what will happen by the final number, then counts with suggestions between the numbers. The numbers give a visible measure of progress and a fixed endpoint. As an induction the count takes the listener from awake to tranced; the same form used on someone already in trance is countdown-deepener.

**How:** State the contract first: 'I will count from ten to one, and at one...'. Put one or two short suggestions between numbers and slow down as the count runs. Make the final number carry a single clear command. Counts of five to ten are usual; longer counts need more varied filler or they sag.

> I'm going to count from ten down to one. With each number, you let go a little more.

> Seven... your shoulders loosening. Six... your breathing slower.

> One. All the way down. Eyes closed, body still.

**Spot it by:** 'I'm going to count from ... to ...'; descending numerals spaced through a passage; 'with each number'; 'by the time I reach one' / 'when I reach zero'; a command or state claim on the last number.

**Not to be confused with:** Countdown deepener (label the deepener when the count builds depth after trance is established; label this entry when the count brings the listener from waking attention into trance, even if other opening instructions precede it); Counted passage (there the numbers pace other content without linking each number to trance depth or naming the last as arrival; here the count itself carries the induction); Losing the numbers (there the listener counts aloud and the numbers are suggested away; here the writer counts); Count-up wake (a count upward that restores alertness ends the session).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Counting is part of standardized induction texts; nothing shows the numbers themselves do anything beyond pacing the passage and setting an expectation of arrival.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Hypnotic induction.


### Visualization induction *(unit)*

Also called: guided imagery induction, imagery induction, special place induction.

Guided imagery used as the entry procedure. The listener is walked into a place, and its features (stillness, warmth, a path, descending steps) carry the suggestions of settling and letting go. The difference from guided-imagery in general is function and position: here the scene is the induction, not the content of the session.

**How:** Leave the scene's details open so the listener builds their own: 'a place where you feel at ease'. Bring in several senses, feeling and sound as well as sight, because some listeners see little. Give time between details. Move inward or downward through the scene and let that movement hand over to the deepener. Say 'imagine' or 'get a sense of', not 'see', so poor visualizers are not shut out.

> Imagine a place where you feel completely at ease. It can be real or invented.

> Notice what is around you there. The light. The sounds. The temperature of the air on your skin.

> As you settle into this place, the room you started in seems further away.

**Spot it by:** 'imagine' / 'picture' / 'see yourself'; 'a place where'; sensory inventory of a scene (light, sound, air, ground); 'as you settle into this place'; 'it can be real or imagined'.

**Not to be confused with:** Guided imagery (guided imagery is the general device at any stage; this is its use as the induction); Safe place (safe place is a scene kept as a base to return to; an induction scene need not be about safety); Descent imagery (descent imagery maps downward movement to depth after trance has begun).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Imagery inductions are standard in clinical texts and perform like other inductions; response depends on the listener's imagery ability and absorption, and a minority report no visual imagery at all.

**Why it works:** Absorption (trait), Narrative transportation, Hypnotic induction.


### Confusion induction *(unit)*

Also called: confusional induction, confusion technique induction.

The confusion technique used as the whole induction. The writer keeps up a run of statements that sound meaningful but cannot be followed, built on time, direction, negation or word-play. When the listener gives up tracking, a simple suggestion such as 'close your eyes and drop' is taken as relief. Both parts are needed: the tangle and the clear exit.

**How:** Keep sentences grammatical and coherent enough to invite interpretation. Follow the confusing passage with one short, clear instruction, changing pace to mark the turn. A release line such as 'you don't have to work any of that out' can mark the exit. If the listener disengages before that turn, or the exit remains confusing, the intended transition may not occur.

> You can forget to remember what you were trying not to think about, or remember to forget it, and either way it is not something you need to know now.

> Your left hand is the one that is not your right, and the right one is the one that is left when the other has gone.

> And you don't have to work any of that out. Just close your eyes.

**Spot it by:** dense alternation of opposites (left/right, remember/forget, now/then, know/no); long grammatical sentences that do not resolve; stacked negatives; a short plain imperative right after a tangled passage; 'you don't need to follow' / 'it doesn't matter'.

**Not to be confused with:** Confusion technique (the general device at any stage; this entry is its use as the induction); Overload induction (overload gives too many items to track at once; confusion gives one stream that cannot be made sense of); Rapid induction (a rapid induction uses a sudden interruption of seconds, not a sustained verbal tangle).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Rests on Erickson's case reports; the related disrupt-then-reframe effect has experimental support for compliance, but the confusion induction itself has no controlled test. Source: Erickson, 'The confusion technique in hypnosis', American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1964).

**Why it works:** Ericksonian confusion technique, Confusion-restructuring, Cognitive load, Distraction-induced persuasion.

**Consent:** It works by wearing down the listener's evaluation, so use it only where the listener has agreed to be hypnotized.


### Overload induction *(unit)*

Also called: 7 plus or minus 2, sensory overload, cognitive overload induction.

Cognitive overload used as the induction. The writer stacks simultaneous demands: feel this, count that, listen for something else, keep an image in mind. Unlike confusion, each instruction is clear; there are simply too many. When tracking fails, the writer supplies the one thing left to do.

**How:** Add tasks one at a time and never remove one. Mix channels: a count, a body sensation, an outside sound, an image. Four or five running tasks are enough. When the listener is plainly stretched, tell them to let it all go and give one simple instruction. In audio, a second voice or a concurrent counting task does the same job.

> Feel your left foot on the floor, and keep that while you listen for the quietest sound in the room.

> Now count backward from three hundred by threes, still feeling that foot, still listening, and notice your breathing as well.

> And when that is too much to hold, let all of it go at once.

**Spot it by:** several concurrent attention instructions in one passage; 'while' / 'at the same time' / 'and also' / 'still' chains; a hard counting task ('backward by threes', 'by sevens'); 'let it all go' / 'drop all of it' after the stack; explicit mention of too much to hold or track.

**Not to be confused with:** Cognitive overload (the general device at any stage; this entry is its use as the induction); Confusion induction (confusion makes one stream senseless; overload makes several clear streams too many); Betty Erickson 5-4-3-2-1 (5-4-3-2-1 lists sense items one after another in a set pattern, not all at once).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Working-memory limits are well established and distraction can reduce counter-arguing, but the claim that overflowing '7 plus or minus 2' items produces trance is an NLP teaching, not a tested result.

**Why it works:** Cognitive load, Working-memory interference, Distraction-induced persuasion.

**Consent:** It works by crowding out evaluation, so use it only where the listener has agreed to be hypnotized.


### Rapid induction *(unit)*

Also called: instant induction, shock induction, snap induction, speed induction.

An induction that takes a few seconds. It has three parts: a setup that fixes attention and expectation, a sudden interruption or mild startle, and a short command delivered in the blank moment that follows. It is normally followed at once by a deepener, because the first response is brief. Most forms are done in person with physical contact.

**How:** Do the work in the pre-talk: the listener must expect it to happen and agree to be touched. Deliver the command at the instant of the interruption, not after, and go straight into deepening. Support the head and body; people slump. In audio and text only the weak form is possible: build up, cut off mid-sentence or use a sudden sound, then 'sleep' or 'drop'. Do not use it on anyone with neck, shoulder or back problems.

> [Stage direction: on the word, guide the head gently forward.] Sleep. All the way down. Deeper with every breath.

> In a moment I'll snap my fingers, and when I do, you simply let go. [snap] Drop.

> Look at my hand, follow it up, and... sleep.

**Spot it by:** 'sleep!' / 'drop' as a one-word command; stage direction for a snap, pull, drop or interrupted gesture; sentence broken off before the command; immediate 'deeper' language after the command; 'in a moment I will...' setup followed by a sudden cue.

**Not to be confused with:** Re-induction trigger (a re-induction trigger fires a cue installed earlier; a rapid induction needs no earlier installation); Pattern interrupt (the interrupt is the single break in an automatic sequence; rapid induction is the interrupt plus a trance command); Shock / surprise (a startle alone is that unit; here it is used to open a moment for 'sleep').

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Widely used in stage and street hypnosis; a few small studies suggest brief inductions do about as well as long ones on suggestibility scores, but the startle-gap explanation is untested and subjects are usually preselected.

**Why it works:** Pattern interruption, Expectation violation, Orienting response, Response expectancy theory, Demand characteristics.

**Consent:** Involves surprise and usually touch; get agreement to both beforehand and screen for injury risk.


#### Handshake interrupt *(variant)*

Also called: Erickson handshake, Bandler handshake, handshake induction.

A rapid induction built on the handshake, which runs automatically once begun. The operator starts the shake and then does something else: lets go slowly with ambiguous touches (Erickson's form) or lifts the hand in front of the listener's face and tells them to look at it (the NLP form). The hand is left suspended and suggestions are given during the pause.

**How:** This is an in-person procedure and cannot be done by recording. Offer the hand normally so the automatic response starts. Interrupt before the shake completes, keep your own manner calm, and speak at once: direct attention to the hand, then to eye closure. In a script, it appears only as stage directions or as a scene described to the listener.

> [Stage direction: offer hand; as they take it, lift their wrist to eye level and release.] Look at your hand. Notice the lines in it. And as your eyes close, it can lower only as fast as you go into trance.

> [Stage direction: begin handshake, loosen grip gradually, trail fingers away.] That's right... and you don't need to do anything about that hand at all.

**Spot it by:** stage direction mentioning handshake or offered hand; 'look at your hand' immediately after a greeting; hand left raised or suspended; 'only as fast as' linking the hand lowering to trance; narrated scene of a handshake that does not finish.

**Not to be confused with:** Arm levitation (levitation suggests the hand rising by itself over minutes; here the operator places it and it stays); Rigid arm (the rigid-arm convincer is a tested proof; the suspended hand here is a by-product of the interrupt); Hand drop (the hand drop removes a support the listener is pressing on; the handshake breaks a social routine).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Known from Erickson's own descriptions and NLP demonstrations; no controlled study, and reports come from settings where the subject expected hypnosis. Source: Erickson, Rossi & Rossi, Hypnotic Realities (1976).

**Why it works:** Pattern interruption, Automaticity, Expectation violation, Demand characteristics.

**Consent:** Done without warning it is touch and hypnosis without consent; use only with someone who has agreed to be hypnotized by you.


#### Hand drop *(variant)*

Also called: hand press induction, eight-word induction, hand-press drop.

A rapid induction in which the listener pushes down on the operator's upturned palm while staring at a point or at the operator's eyes. The operator removes the hand without warning. The listener's hand falls, there is a brief startle, and the command is given in that instant.

**How:** In-person only. Give simple, fast instructions that keep the listener busy: press down, harder, look here, close your eyes. Remove your hand while they are pressing and say 'sleep' at the same moment, guiding the shoulder or head so they do not pitch forward. Deepen immediately. A script can only describe it as stage direction, or imitate it with a self-administered version in which the listener drops their own hand.

> Press down on my hand. Harder. Eyes on mine. Now close your eyes... [remove hand] sleep.

> [Self-directed version] Hold one hand up. When I say the word, let it fall into your lap, and let yourself fall with it. Drop.

**Spot it by:** 'press down on my hand'; 'press harder'; stage direction to remove or drop the hand; 'sleep' straight after a pressing instruction; 'let your hand fall' paired with 'and go down with it'.

**Not to be confused with:** Physical drop deepener (the arm-drop deepener lifts and drops a limp limb in trance; this drop starts the trance); Arm pull (the arm pull is a tug toward the operator; the hand drop is a support taken away); Handshake interrupt (the handshake leaves the hand suspended; here it falls).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. A stage and street-hypnosis standard with no controlled testing; it is usually shown on volunteers already selected for responsiveness.

**Why it works:** Expectation violation, Orienting response, Response expectancy theory, Demand characteristics.

**Consent:** Involves touch, startle and a risk of slumping; agree it beforehand and support the listener.


#### Arm pull *(variant)*

Also called: arm jerk induction, arm-pull sleep.

A rapid induction in which the operator holds the listener's hand or wrist, fixes their attention, and gives a short, light tug toward themselves while saying 'sleep'. The tug is the startle. It is the form with the highest injury risk and is the one most often shown badly.

**How:** In-person only, and only by someone trained. The tug is small and along the line of the arm, never a yank, and the other hand supports the neck or shoulder. Ask about neck, shoulder and back problems first and choose another induction if there are any. A recorded script should not ask a listener to do this to themselves or to another person.

> [Stage direction: hold wrist, free hand behind shoulder; slight tug on the command.] Look at me. Take a breath in... sleep. Loose and limp, all the way down.

> [Narrated] She took his wrist, waited for him to breathe out, and with one small tug and one word he folded forward.

**Spot it by:** stage direction with 'tug' / 'pull' / 'jerk' on the arm or wrist; 'sleep' simultaneous with a pull; 'loose and limp' immediately after; instruction to support head or shoulder.

**Not to be confused with:** Hand drop (the hand drop removes a support; the arm pull adds a tug); Handshake interrupt (the handshake interrupt breaks a social routine without any pull); Physical drop deepener (the deepener drops a relaxed limb; the pull is the inducing startle).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Stage practice with no controlled testing; hypnosis trainers themselves warn about neck and shoulder injury.

**Why it works:** Expectation violation, Orienting response, Demand characteristics, Response expectancy theory.

**Consent:** Physical risk and surprise touch: explicit prior agreement and injury screening are required.


### Conversational induction *(unit)*

Also called: naturalistic induction, Ericksonian induction, indirect induction.

There is no 'close your eyes' and no count. The writer talks, apparently about something else, while pacing the listener's present experience, telling absorbing stories and scattering indirect suggestions of comfort and inward attention. Trance is allowed to develop and is ratified when signs appear. The listener may know hypnosis is intended; the form, not the secrecy, defines it.

**How:** Open with plain verifiable statements about what the listener is doing now. Slide into a topic that absorbs: a memory of learning something, a drive, a story about someone else. Thread in permissive suggestions and embedded commands, slow down gradually, and comment on changes as they show. It needs feedback, so it is strongest live; in a recording, write the pacing statements to be true of anyone listening.

> You're sitting there, listening to me, and you've probably had the experience of reading a book and not hearing someone say your name.

> I don't know whether you'll notice your breathing slow down first, or whether it will be the feeling in your hands.

> A friend of mine says the easiest way to relax is to stop trying to. He just lets his eyes rest and waits.

**Spot it by:** no announced induction, count or 'close your eyes' before trance language appears; run of pacing statements about the present moment; 'you've probably had the experience of'; 'I wonder' / 'I don't know whether' followed by a trance response; anecdote about someone else relaxing or drifting; gradual shift from chat register to slow permissive suggestions.

**Not to be confused with:** Unannounced induction (covert means the listener has not been told an induction is happening; conversational is about the form and can be fully announced); Pacing and leading (that is one building block; the conversational induction is a whole opening made from several); Indirect suggestion (an indirect suggestion is a single phrasing; this is an induction built from many).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Central to Ericksonian practice, but controlled studies have not found indirect or naturalistic approaches more effective than direct ones, and what counts as trance here is poorly defined. Source: Erickson, Rossi & Rossi, Hypnotic Realities (1976).

**Why it works:** Conversational hypnosis, Pacing and leading, Utilization, Indirect suggestion, Absorption (trait).

**Consent:** Because nothing marks the start, make sure the listener has agreed to hypnosis before the conversation begins.


### Unannounced induction *(unit)*

Also called: covert induction, disguised induction, stealth induction.

The listener is not told that an induction is taking place. The procedure is given a different label ('a quick focus exercise', 'let me tell you a story') and trance language is introduced under that cover. What separates it from its parent is the false or missing frame, not the technique.

**How:** In consensual work it belongs inside an agreement made earlier: the listener has said 'you may hypnotize me without warning', or has picked a file described as containing a surprise induction. State that in the description. Then write a plausible cover activity whose steps are the induction's steps (attend, breathe, imagine, follow). Outside such an agreement, do not write it.

> Before we start, let's just do a quick exercise to help you concentrate. Look at one spot and breathe slowly.

> This isn't hypnosis, it's only a story, so you can simply listen and picture it.

> I'll tell you how I relax after work, and you can try each step with me as I go.

**Spot it by:** explicit denial: 'this isn't hypnosis' / 'not a trance'; 'just a story' / 'just an exercise' / 'a quick relaxation tip' followed by induction language; 'before we start' preceding what is already the induction; trance vocabulary appearing only after the cover activity is under way; mismatch between the stated purpose and the suggestions given.

**Not to be confused with:** Conversational induction (the parent may be openly agreed hypnosis; this variant hides or mislabels it); Fiction frame (a fiction frame openly says the content is a story or play; covert induction hides what the procedure is); My friend John (that delivers suggestions through a described third person, with or without concealment).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Claims that people can be hypnotized without knowing are sold widely and supported poorly; hypnotic responding depends heavily on the listener expecting and accepting hypnosis.

**Why it works:** Persuasion Knowledge Model, Epistemic vigilance, Narrative transportation, Conversational hypnosis.

**Consent:** Works by the listener not knowing; legitimate only under prior, specific agreement to surprise inductions, and never on someone who has not consented to hypnosis.


### Revivification induction *(unit)*

Also called: recall a previous trance, re-induction by memory, trance recall induction.

Revivification used to induce. The listener is asked to remember the last time they were in trance, or an everyday absorbed state, and to go through it in sensory detail: where they were, how the body felt, what they heard. Remembering the state closely enough brings it back. It needs no installed cue, which separates it from a re-induction trigger.

**How:** Ask for a specific occasion, not trance in general. Question the senses one at a time and move from past tense into present tense as you go: 'you were sitting... and you can feel...'. For first-time listeners, use an everyday absorbed state such as falling asleep or being lost in a film. It is quick and works best with people who have had a good previous experience.

> Think back to the last time you went deeply into trance. Where were you sitting?

> Remember how your arms felt just as you began to go. How your breathing changed.

> And as you remember that feeling, you can feel it now, coming back the same way.

**Spot it by:** 'remember the last time you' / 'think back to a time when'; 'a time you were deeply relaxed / in trance'; sensory questions about a memory; tense shift from past to present inside the passage; 'and as you remember it, you can feel it now'.

**Not to be confused with:** Revivification (the general device relives any memory for its state; this is its use to start trance); Re-induction trigger (a trigger fires an installed cue at once; this rebuilds the state through detailed recall); Everyday trance (that compares trance to everyday absorption to normalize it, without reliving a specific memory).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Taught in Ericksonian and NLP training; recalling a state does partly reinstate it, but this induction has not been tested against others.

**Why it works:** State-dependent memory, Response expectancy theory, Absorption (trait).


### Pretend / as-if induction *(unit)*

Also called: act as if, fake it till you make it induction, pretend game.

The listener is asked to behave as a deeply hypnotized person would: go limp, close the eyes, pretend the eyes will not open. Because nothing is claimed, there is nothing to resist or fail. Sustained pretending produces the same behaviour and often the same experience. Elman's instruction to pretend the eyelids will not work is the best-known use.

**How:** Remove the stakes openly: 'you don't have to be hypnotized, just pretend'. Ask for specific behaviours to act out, not a vague state. Then stop mentioning pretending and speak as though the response were real. It suits anxious, sceptical or over-trying listeners. Do not later use the pretending as a trick against them; say plainly afterwards that this is how it works.

> You don't need to be hypnotized. Just pretend, as well as you can, that you are.

> Act as if your eyelids were so relaxed that they simply won't work, and keep pretending while you test them.

> And you can keep pretending so well that you forget you are pretending.

**Spot it by:** 'pretend' / 'act as if' / 'make believe' applied to trance or a trance response; 'just imagine what it would be like to be hypnotized'; 'you don't have to be hypnotized'; 'as long as you keep pretending'; 'forget that you are pretending'.

**Not to be confused with:** As-if frame (the as-if frame explores any imagined outcome; this applies pretending to being hypnotized, to induce); Fiction frame (a fiction frame labels the whole content as play; here only the listener's own trance behaviour is pretended); Eyelid lock (the eyelid lock is the tested convincer; pretending is one way of setting it up).

**Evidence:** experimental. Task-motivated and imagination instructions produce much of the response that hypnotic inductions do, which supports the method; whether pretending 'becomes' real trance depends on what trance is taken to be.

**Why it works:** Sociocognitive theory of hypnosis, Response expectancy theory, Self-perception theory, Demand characteristics.


### Repetition induction *(unit)*

Also called: mantra induction, loop induction.

The induction is sustained repetition and little else. One line, or a loop of three or four, is said over and over in an even rhythm, by the speaker or by the listener. Attention locks to the loop, the words lose novelty, and vigilance drops. Unlike a mantra used as a suggestion, the content of the phrase matters less than its regularity.

**How:** Choose a short phrase with an easy beat and keep the wording fixed. Keep the rhythm even and the voice level. Run it well past the point where it feels long on the page; in audio that means minutes, not lines. Small variations at long intervals stop the listener tuning out altogether. Hand over to suggestions by changing one word in the loop.

> Listen and drift. Listen and drift. Listen and drift. Listen and drift.

> Breathe in. Let go. Sink down. Breathe in. Let go. Sink down.

> Say it with me, silently, each time you breathe out: calm and quiet. Calm and quiet.

**Spot it by:** same phrase repeated verbatim four or more times in a row; short loop of lines cycling in fixed order; 'again' / 'once more' / 'keep repeating'; stage direction 'repeat for N minutes' or 'loop'; very low vocabulary variety across an opening passage.

**Not to be confused with:** Mantra (same surface form, and mantra is always a correct label for the repeated block; add this label only when that block is the script's opening and nothing else induces before the first trance claim); Deeper and deeper (that repeats depth words after trance has begun); Monotony (monotony is uneventful delivery of any content; this is literal repetition of one phrase).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Repetitive focus is common to meditation and hypnosis and plausibly reduces vigilance through habituation; as a named induction it has not been tested.

**Why it works:** Habituation, Attentional tunneling, Processing fluency, Mere-exposure effect.


### Ideomotor induction *(unit)*

Also called: motor induction, ideomotor movement induction.

The listener holds a posture and attends to it while the writer suggests a movement: a hand lifting, fingers closing, hands drifting together. Thinking about the movement produces small real muscle action, which is felt as involuntary. That experience both absorbs attention and convinces. Trance is tied to the movement's progress or completion.

**How:** Set up a starting position where the movement is mechanically easy. Describe the first tiny signs and ratify whatever happens. Link the movement to trance with a contingent suggestion: 'as it moves, you go deeper'. Allow plenty of time, and include a fallback for listeners whose hands do not move, such as letting the hand rest and using its heaviness. Recordings cannot see the response, so keep the wording open.

> Hold your hands out in front of you and just watch them. You may notice one of them wanting to move.

> You're not doing it. It is simply happening, a little at a time.

> And the more it moves, the further you drift.

**Spot it by:** 'by itself' / 'on its own' / 'without you doing it' about a movement; 'you may notice a small twitch / movement'; a movement tied to trance: 'as it moves, you go deeper'; instructions to hold out a hand or hands and watch; 'just let it happen'.

**Not to be confused with:** Ideomotor signal (a signal is a small movement used as a yes/no answer, not as the route into trance); Suggestibility test (the same movements used before induction as a demonstration, without a trance claim, are a test); Puppeteering (puppeteering says the speaker moves the body as proof of control; here the movement is the entry procedure).

**Evidence:** experimental. The ideomotor effect is well demonstrated and motor suggestions are the easiest items on hypnotizability scales; their advantage as an induction over other methods is not established.

**Why it works:** Ideomotor effect, Cold control theory, Response expectancy theory, Automaticity.


#### Arm levitation *(variant)*

Also called: hand levitation, Erickson arm levitation, floating arm.

An ideomotor induction in which one hand, resting on the thigh, is suggested to become light and float upward in small jerky steps. Lightness is suggested, not lifting. The rise is tied to trance, and contact with the face, or the hand's slow return to the lap, is set as the moment of going fully under.

**How:** Begin with attention to sensations in the hands and wait for the first finger twitch; ratify it. Use lightness images (a balloon at the wrist) and time 'lifting' to the in-breath, when the body rises anyway. Offer choices that all presuppose movement: which hand, which finger first. It is slow, often ten minutes or more, and a fair share of listeners get no lift; have the fallback ready.

> Notice which hand feels lighter. One of them does.

> Perhaps a finger lifts first, or the whole hand at once, a tiny bit with every breath in.

> And when your hand touches your face, your eyes can close and you can go all the way down.

**Spot it by:** 'lighter and lighter'; 'lifting' / 'floating up' / 'rising' about a hand or arm; 'balloon' / 'string at the wrist'; 'which hand will lift first'; 'when it touches your face'; 'all by itself'.

**Not to be confused with:** Book and balloon (book and balloon contrasts a heavy arm with a light one as a quick test or convincer); Rigid arm (catalepsy suggests a rigid arm that cannot bend; levitation suggests a light arm that moves); Magnetic hands (magnetic hands draws two hands together sideways; levitation lifts one hand).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. A standard clinical induction and a scale item; a substantial minority do not respond, and no study shows it gives a better trance than simpler methods. Source: Erickson, 'Historical note on the hand levitation and other ideomotor techniques', American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1961).

**Why it works:** Ideomotor effect, Cold control theory, Response expectancy theory.


#### Magnetic hands *(variant)*

Also called: magnetic fingers, magnetic palms, hands together.

An ideomotor induction in which the listener holds the palms a little apart, or the index fingers apart with the other fingers clasped, and the writer suggests a growing pull between them. With the fingers version, muscle fatigue makes the result close to certain. Touching is set as the cue to close the eyes and drop.

**How:** Give exact positioning instructions. Describe the pull as already starting and growing. Announce in advance what happens when they touch, then deliver the command at contact, or 'whenever they touch' in a recording. It is fast, reliable and playful, and works well as a first experience. Often used as a test first and then again as the induction.

> Hold your hands out, palms facing, a few inches apart. Imagine a strong magnet in each palm.

> Feel them drawing together. Closer. You're not pushing them, they're being pulled.

> And the moment they touch, your eyes close and your hands drop to your lap.

**Spot it by:** 'magnet' / 'magnets' / 'magnetic'; 'palms facing' / 'fingers apart'; 'pulling together' / 'drawn together' / 'closer and closer'; 'the moment they touch'; 'you're not doing it'.

**Not to be confused with:** Suggestibility test (the same exercise used before induction with no trance claim at contact is a test); Stuck (stuck suggests the hands cannot come apart; this suggests they come together); Arm levitation (levitation lifts one hand slowly; this draws two together quickly).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. The movement itself is a reliable ideomotor and fatigue effect; its use as an induction is stage and street practice without controlled testing.

**Why it works:** Ideomotor effect, Response expectancy theory, Self-perception theory.


### Elman induction *(recipe)*

Also called: Dave Elman induction, Elman rapid induction, three-minute induction.

A fixed sequence of about three to four minutes devised by Dave Elman for medical and dental use. Each step is a small test the listener passes: eyes that will not open, deeper relaxation each time the eyes reclose, an arm that drops limp, and numbers that disappear. The sequence is direct and brisk, and each success is used as proof for the next step.

**How:** Follow the order and keep the pace up; it is meant to be quick. Phrase the eyelid lock as something the listener does ('relax them so much they won't work'), and stop the test the moment it succeeds. In a recording, replace the lifted arm with the listener lifting and dropping their own, and write the number loss so that either silence or stumbling counts. Do not pad it with long relaxation passages.

1. Take a deep breath, let it out, and close the eyes. (Eye-closure suggestion)
1. Relax the eyelids until they will not work; test briefly, then stop testing. (Eyelid lock)
1. Send that same relaxation from the eyelids down to the toes in one wave. (Progressive relaxation)
1. Open and close the eyes several times, with each closing going much deeper. (Fractionation)
1. Lift a hand by the wrist and drop it; it falls limp and the drop sends the listener deeper. (Physical drop deepener)
1. Count backward aloud from one hundred, relaxing the numbers away until they are gone. (Losing the numbers)

> Relax your eyelids so completely that they just won't work. When you're sure they won't, test them. Good. Stop testing.

> In a moment I'll ask you to open and close your eyes, and each time you close them you'll go ten times deeper.

> Start counting backward from one hundred, out loud. With each number, let them fade, until after a few numbers they're simply gone.

**Spot it by:** 'relax your eyelids to the point where they won't work'; 'test them' followed by 'stop testing'; 'open your eyes... close your eyes' repeated with 'deeper' each time; arm lifted and dropped 'like a wet dishcloth' / 'limp'; 'count backward from one hundred' with 'let the numbers go' / 'all gone?'; 'ten times deeper' / 'twice as deep'.

**Not to be confused with:** Rapid induction (rapid inductions take seconds and use a startle; Elman takes minutes and uses a chain of passed tests); Progressive relaxation (Elman relaxes in two or three quick waves, not a slow region-by-region tour); Losing the numbers (losing the numbers is the final step on its own; the recipe is the whole sequence).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Among the most widely taught inductions in lay and clinical training; Elman's claims about reaching defined depths such as 'somnambulism' are his own framework and are not validated. Source: Elman, Hypnotherapy (1964).

**Why it works:** Critical faculty (Elman), Response expectancy theory, Self-perception theory, Hypnotic induction.


### Betty Erickson 5-4-3-2-1 *(recipe)*

Also called: 3-2-1 induction, 5-4-3-2-1, sensory countdown, Betty Erickson self-hypnosis.

A self-hypnosis induction attributed to Elizabeth (Betty) Erickson. The listener states a number of things they see, then hear, then feel, and repeats the cycle with one fewer each round. Every statement is true, so it paces present experience, and keeping count occupies working memory. In the full version the eyes close partway and the items shift from external facts to internal images.

**How:** State the rule once and start. Use a fixed sentence frame: 'now I am aware that I see...'. Let items repeat; it does not matter. Tell the listener that losing count is a sign it is working and that they can simply drift from there. Add a purpose and a time limit beforehand if it is taught for self-hypnosis. Shorter versions start at three.

1. Name five things seen, five heard and five felt in the room, each as a plain true statement. (Pacing)
1. Repeat the see-hear-feel cycle with four items, then three, two, one. (Counted passage)
1. Let the eyes close when they want to, usually within the first rounds. (Eye-closure suggestion)
1. Continue the rounds with imagined sights, sounds and feelings in place of external ones. (Turning attention inward)
1. Keeping count occupies the mind; when the count is lost, stop and drift. (Occupying the conscious mind)

> Notice five things you can see. Name each one to yourself. Then five things you can hear. Then five things you can feel.

> Now four things you see. Four you hear. Four you feel. It's fine if some are the same.

> And if you lose track of the count somewhere along the way, just let it go and drift.

**Spot it by:** 'five things you can see' (or hear / feel); see-hear-feel triplets with a falling number; 'now I am aware that I see / hear / feel'; 'it's fine if you repeat one'; 'if you lose count'; shift from external items to imagined ones.

**Not to be confused with:** Counting induction (there the writer counts down with suggestions; here the listener lists sense items in shrinking sets); Overload induction (overload stacks tasks simultaneously; this is one orderly task done in rounds); Pacing (pacing is any verifiable statement; this is a fixed pattern of them used as a whole induction).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Passed down through NLP and Ericksonian teaching and credited to Betty Erickson; no controlled study, though a similar 5-4-3-2-1 exercise is widely used informally as an anxiety grounding technique.

**Why it works:** Pacing and leading, Working-memory interference, Attentional tunneling.


### Double induction *(recipe)*

Also called: dual induction, two-voice induction, dual-voice induction.

Two speakers, or two recorded tracks, deliver different induction text simultaneously, usually panned left and right. Each track is clear alone; together they exceed what can be followed. Often one voice is direct and the other indirect or story-based, and at chosen moments they converge on the same word.

**How:** Write two complete tracks with different rhythms so they interleave, and mark the sync points where both say the key word. Keep each track simple; the overlap supplies the difficulty. Tell the listener not to try to follow. Pan the voices apart and require headphones. In a script, lay it out in two columns or labelled tracks.

1. Tell the listener two voices will speak and that they need not follow either. (Expectation setting)
1. Start two different induction tracks at once. (Layered voices)
1. Place one voice in each ear. (Panning)
1. Keep both streams running so that neither can be tracked fully. (Cognitive overload)
1. Bring both voices together on a single clear word or command. (Direct suggestion)

> [Left] Follow my voice and let your body grow heavy... [Right] ...and you might listen to the other voice instead, or to neither...

> [Left] Ten. Sinking. Nine. Looser. [Right] There was once a river that knew its own way down to the sea...

> [Both] ...deeper.

**Spot it by:** two labelled voices or tracks in parallel ('Left / Right', 'Voice A / Voice B'); two-column script layout; stage direction: 'simultaneous', 'overlapping', 'pan left/right'; 'you can't follow both' / 'don't try to follow'; marked sync words spoken by both voices.

**Not to be confused with:** Layered voices (layering is the production choice at any stage; double induction is the induction built on it); Overload induction (overload can be done by one voice stacking tasks; this needs two concurrent speech streams); Subliminal track (a subliminal track is mixed below easy hearing; both voices here are fully audible).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Listeners cannot follow two speech streams at once, which is well established; claims that the unattended voice 'reaches the unconscious' or that the two ears address separate brain hemispheres are not supported.

**Why it works:** Cognitive load, Working-memory interference, Distraction-induced persuasion.

**Consent:** The listener cannot fully monitor either track, so describe the content of both in the file description.


### Sensation-focus induction *(unit)*

Also called: kinesthetic induction, somatic induction, single-sensation focus.

One real sensation is chosen: the weight of a hand, warmth in the palms, a tingle in the fingertips. The listener studies it closely, and the writer then suggests it intensifying and spreading. It differs from progressive relaxation in staying with one starting point, and from a body scan in suggesting change.

**How:** Pick a sensation that is certainly there, such as contact, weight or warmth, and have the listener describe it to themselves in detail. Stay with it longer than seems necessary. Then suggest it grows, and only then that it moves outward. Offer alternatives (warm, heavy, tingling) so that whatever they feel fits.

> Put all your attention into your right hand. Just the feeling of it resting there.

> Notice its weight. Notice exactly where it touches your leg. The longer you attend to it, the clearer it gets.

> Stay with that hand a little longer. And as the feeling grows, let it spread up your arm, and let yourself settle with it.

**Spot it by:** 'put all your attention into your [body part]'; one sensation word repeated: 'warmth', 'weight', 'tingling'; 'the more you notice it, the stronger it gets'; 'let it spread'; sustained passage on a single body part before any other is named.

**Not to be confused with:** Progressive relaxation (that tours regions in order and tells each to relax; this stays with one sensation and lets it spread); Suggested sensation (that is a single suggested feeling at any stage, often offered as proof; label this entry only for a sustained opening passage that stays on one sensation and ties its growth to going into trance); Travelling sensation (there the movement of the sensation through the body, region by region, is the whole device; here the spread is the last step after a long stay in one place); Arousal-focus induction (arousal focus is this same method with arousal as the sensation).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Focusing on a body sensation is a common element of clinical inductions and of autogenic and mindfulness practice; it has not been evaluated as a distinct induction.

**Why it works:** Attentional tunneling, Absorption (trait), Response expectancy theory.


#### Arousal-focus induction *(variant)*

Also called: erotic induction, pleasure induction, arousal induction.

A sensation-focus induction in which the chosen sensation is arousal. The writer directs attention to it, builds it, and ties its growth to narrowing focus and letting go. It reverses the usual relaxation route: the body is activated, not calmed, and absorption comes from wanting, not from rest.

**How:** Use only in content the listener has chosen as erotic. Start by pacing the arousal that is already there, then link its increase to focus on the voice and to dropping. Keep instructions simple, since evaluation falls as arousal rises. Relaxation language can sit alongside it, but do not expect a still, sleepy trance. Say in the description that the file uses arousal in this way.

> Notice that warm feeling starting, and let your attention settle on it.

> The more it builds, the less room there is for any other thought.

> Let that feeling pull you in and down, until it is the only thing you notice.

**Spot it by:** 'arousal' / 'that warm feeling' / 'pleasure' as the object of 'focus on' / 'notice'; 'the more aroused... the deeper / the less you think'; arousal language preceding any relaxation or eye-closure language; 'let it pull you down'; build-up verbs: 'growing', 'building', 'rising' applied to the sensation.

**Not to be confused with:** Pleasure as deepener (the deepener ties pleasure to depth once trance exists; this uses arousal to start it); The more... the more (leverage uses arousal to get a suggestion accepted; this uses it as the fixation for induction); Sensation-focus induction (same method with a neutral sensation such as warmth or weight).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Common in erotic hypnosis recordings with no formal study; sexual arousal is known to narrow attention and weaken risk judgement, which fits the practice and is also the reason for care.

**Why it works:** Attentional tunneling, Absorption (trait).

**Consent:** Arousal lowers judgement, so agree the content and its limits beforehand, not once the listener is aroused.


### Re-induction trigger *(unit)*

Also called: instant re-induction, drop trigger, sleep trigger, re-induction cue.

The firing, as an induction, of a posthypnotic cue for trance: a word, phrase, snap or gesture that was set up in an earlier session or earlier in the same one. The cue stands in for the whole induction. It works only for listeners who have the cue, and it is distinct from installing the cue, which is trigger installation.

**How:** Name or briefly remind the listener of the cue before firing it, and say who it works for; a file that opens with an unexplained 'drop' does nothing for a new listener and startles them. Fire it once, clearly, and follow with a short deepener. Keep the cue's wording exactly as installed. State its limits in the installing session: who may use it, and that it does not work when the listener needs to be alert.

> You know the word, and you know what happens when you hear it. Deep sleep.

> If you've listened before, the next sound takes you straight back down. [snap]

> And... drop. All the way back to where you were last time.

**Spot it by:** a short cue phrase standing alone: 'deep sleep', 'drop', 'sleep now'; 'you know what happens when' / 'you remember this word'; 'back to where you were last time'; 'if you have listened before'; snap or tone stage direction followed by depth language with no induction passage before it.

**Not to be confused with:** Trigger installation (installation states the cue and its response for future use; this is the cue being used to induce); Rapid induction (a rapid induction needs no prior cue and relies on a startle or interrupt); Next-time-deeper suggestion (the seed is a general suggestion before waking that future sessions go faster, with no specific cue); Trigger test (a trigger test fires any trigger in-session to prove it; this fires the trance cue as the session's opening).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Cued re-induction is a standard clinical convenience and responsive subjects do respond quickly; this is best explained by expectation and practice, and there is no evidence a cue can force trance on an unwilling person.

**Why it works:** Posthypnotic suggestion, Response expectancy theory, Classical conditioning, Automaticity.

**Consent:** The cue persists after the session; agree who may use it and under what conditions, and never fire it on someone who has not agreed in the present moment.


### Text induction *(unit)*

Also called: reading induction, written induction, text-based induction.

An induction for written scripts that makes the reader's own reading the object of attention. The text describes what the reader is doing right now: eyes moving along the line, the words sounding in the head, the screen holding the gaze. Every statement is true as it is read. The eyes must stay open, so the target is an eyes-open, absorbed state.

**How:** Address the reader directly and in the present tense. Pace the reading: the eyes moving, the next line, the voice in the head. Then lead: that voice slowing, the edges of the page fading, each line easier to follow than to stop. Control speed with layout, using short lines, white space and ellipses. Never tell the reader to close their eyes unless you also tell them when to open them and read on.

> You are reading these words, one after another, and your eyes are moving along the line without you having to think about it.

> Notice the voice in your head that is saying this. Notice that it has slowed down.

> Each line is a little easier to follow.

A little harder to look away from.

**Spot it by:** 'as you read' / 'reading these words'; 'your eyes move along the line' / 'down the page'; 'the voice in your head reading this'; 'each line' / 'the next word'; 'screen' / 'page' named as the focus; progressively shorter lines with more white space.

**Not to be confused with:** Eye fixation (fixation holds a still point until the eyes close; reading keeps the eyes moving and open); Inner-voice suggestion (inner-voice suggestion says the speaker's words become the listener's thoughts as a lasting change; here the reading voice is only the attention target); Naming the technique (naming the technique is commentary on method; this describes the reader's act of reading in order to pace it).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. A convention of online text hypnosis with no formal study; absorption in reading is real and well described, but whether it amounts to hypnosis has not been tested.

**Why it works:** Pacing and leading, Absorption (trait), Narrative transportation, Self-reference effect.


### Waking hypnosis *(unit)*

Also called: waking trance, eyes-open hypnosis, alert induction, active-alert hypnosis, alert hypnosis, waking suggestion.

An induction that narrows attention and builds responsiveness while the listener stays upright, eyes open and wide awake. It keeps what inductions share (an announced procedure, fixed attention, suggestions accepted in sequence) and drops eye closure, 'sleep', heaviness and relaxation; some versions suggest rising alertness and energy in their place. What marks it off from its neighbours is the starting point: a partial wake reaches an eyes-open state by coming up from a conventional trance, and a conversational induction is defined by sounding like ordinary talk, eyes open or not. Waking hypnosis is announced, direct and never goes down first.

**How:** Say at the start that the eyes stay open and that no relaxation is needed, so the listener does not wait for drowsiness as the sign. Fix attention on one thing (a point, the voice, a hand) and give a short run of direct suggestions that can be checked at once, such as hands that stick together or a foot that will not lift; each success is the deepener. Keep the voice firm and the pace brisk, and use words of focus, clarity and energy instead of depth words. It suits listeners who fall asleep in relaxation scripts, text and screen formats where the eyes must stay open, and sessions aimed at study, sport or performance. End it properly all the same: cancel the tested suggestions and state that ordinary attention is back.

> Keep your eyes open and stay wide awake. You don't need to relax for this. Just look at this one point and listen.

> With every breath you feel more alert and more focused, and the sharper your focus gets, the more easily each thing I say simply happens.

> Eyes open, fully awake, press your palms together. They are locking tight, tighter with each word, and in a moment you will find they stay that way.

**Spot it by:** 'keep your eyes open', 'eyes open the whole time', 'you don't need to close your eyes'; 'wide awake', 'fully alert', 'more alert', 'more energy' used in the induction, not at the wake; explicit denial of relaxation or sleep: 'you don't need to relax', 'this is not sleep'; direct suggestions and tests (lock, stick, cannot lift) appearing with no eye closure, countdown or depth language before them; focus vocabulary in place of depth vocabulary: 'sharper', 'clearer', 'locked on', 'focused'; no 'sleep', 'drowsy', 'heavy', 'deeper' anywhere in the induction span.

**Not to be confused with:** Partial wake (that opens the eyes after a conventional trance and declares it ongoing; waking hypnosis starts eyes-open and never suggests sleep or depth); Conversational induction (that is defined by sounding like ordinary talk with no announced procedure; waking hypnosis is announced and usually direct); Suggestibility test (a test before the induction claims no trance; here the same exercises are the induction and are followed by working suggestions).

**Evidence:** experimental. Controlled comparisons, beginning with Banyai and Hilgard's active-alert induction in 1976, find alert eyes-open inductions raise suggestibility about as much as relaxation inductions, so relaxation is not required; whether 'waking hypnosis' is a state or simply suggestion given to an attentive person is unsettled. Source: Wells, 'Experiments in waking hypnosis for instructional purposes', Journal of Abnormal Psychology and Social Psychology (1924).

**Why it works:** Hypnotic induction, Nonhypnotic suggestibility, Response expectancy theory, Sociocognitive theory of hypnosis, Attentional tunneling.
