**Why it works:** Self-reference effect, Generation effect, Illusory truth effect, Counterarguing, Response expectancy theory.


### Breathe in, breathe out *(unit)*

Also called: inhale X, exhale Y, breath substitution, breathing in calm, breathing out tension, in with the good, out with the bad.

A two-part suggestion laid over one breath cycle: the inhale brings in a wanted quality and the exhale releases an unwanted one. What makes it this entry is the pairing of opposite directions, in and out, with opposite contents, gain and loss. A breath-linked deepener ties only the exhale to depth, and a breath-focus induction directs attention to breathing without loading it with content.

**How:** Name one thing to take in and one thing to let go, and keep both to a word or two so they fit inside a breath. Put the wanted quality on the inhale and the release on the exhale; the body already loosens on the way out, so that half is confirmed by itself. Repeat the pair for three or more breaths, then either leave it running ('with every breath') or swap in a new pair. It fails when the lines are longer than a breath or when the script's rhythm fights the listener's own breathing.

> Breathe in calm. Breathe out tension. In with the calm, and out with whatever you no longer need.

> Each breath in brings a little more focus. Each breath out carries a little more of the day away.

> Breathe in my words. Breathe out your own thoughts. In, and they settle. Out, and there is more room.

**Spot it by:** 'breathe in X ... breathe out Y' with two different objects; 'inhale' and 'exhale' each followed by an abstract noun (calm, tension, doubt, confidence); 'in with the ..., out with the ...'; 'each breath in brings ...' paired with 'each breath out takes / carries away ...'; bare 'In, ... Out, ...' lines alternating a gain and a release; the pair repeated over several consecutive breaths.

**Not to be confused with:** Breath-linked deepening (the deepener ties each exhale to going deeper and gives the inhale no content; this entry loads both halves with paired contents); Breath-focus induction (the induction makes breathing the object of attention or guides its pace; it need not attach anything to the breath); Apposition of opposites (apposition sets two opposite experiences side by side in any wording; here the opposites are mapped onto the two halves of the breath).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Routine in relaxation, meditation and clinical hypnosis scripts; slow breathing itself lowers arousal, but whether attaching paired contents to the two halves of the breath adds anything has not been tested.

**Why it works:** Pacing and leading, Response expectancy theory, Classical conditioning.


### Presupposition and implication

Also called: background suggestion, assumed content, not-at-issue suggestion.

Every sentence has a main point and things it takes for granted. Listeners weigh the main point and usually let the rest through, because rejecting background content means stopping the conversation to object. This family covers the ways a writer moves the target claim into that background: by grammar (presupposition), by a question (loaded question), by inference (implication), by a gap in an argument (unstated premise), or by treating it as already agreed (assumed common ground). It differs from direct suggestion, which asserts the claim, and from artful vagueness, which leaves content empty instead of smuggling specific content in.

**Choosing:** Choose by where the claim hides. If a grammatical trigger carries it and it survives negation, use Presupposition and pick the variant by trigger: time clause, ordinal, awareness verb, adverb, change-of-state verb, already-happened framing, or 'or'. If the carrier is a question the listener must answer, use Loaded question. If the listener has to work the claim out and could be told 'I never said that', use Implication, or If-then implication when a voluntary act is made to stand for agreement. If an argument is missing a step, use Unstated premise. If the claim is flagged as shared knowledge ('of course', 'as you know'), use Assumed common ground. Presuppose only what is plausible or about to be true; a presupposition the listener can plainly see is false gets noticed and costs trust.

**Not to be confused with:** Direct suggestion (asserts the response as the main point instead of taking it for granted); Artful vagueness (leaves content unspecified for the listener to fill; this family slips specific content in); Binds and choices (binds are about the choice offered; the presupposition is the grammar that makes every option assume the outcome).

**Why it works:** Presupposition, Presupposition accommodation, Common ground, Projective content, Conversational implicature, Counterarguing.

**Consent:** The whole family works by keeping a claim out of the listener's direct view, so use it only for outcomes the listener has already agreed to pursue.


#### Presupposition *(unit)*

Also called: presuppositional framing, linguistic presupposition, presupposition install, assumption built into the sentence.

A presupposition is what a sentence takes for granted in order to mean anything. It is carried by a specific word or construction (the trigger) and it survives negation and questioning: 'you will notice the heaviness' and 'you won't notice the heaviness yet' both assume heaviness. That survival test separates it from implication, which can be cancelled, and from direct suggestion, which puts the claim up for judgment.

**How:** Decide the claim you want accepted, then write a sentence about something else that needs it: its timing, its degree, its order, or the listener's awareness of it. Put the open question on a detail that does not matter (when, how easily, which first). Keep the presupposed claim plausible at that moment; use it after pacing or just as the response is starting, not cold. Do not stack several large presuppositions in one sentence, because one visible false assumption makes the listener re-read all of them.

> The heaviness in your hands can spread at its own pace.

> It's the quiet part of your mind that does the listening now.

> Your trance can take whatever shape suits you today.

**Spot it by:** target response sits in a subordinate clause or noun phrase, not the main verb; the claim survives if the sentence is negated or turned into a question; definite or possessive noun phrase for a state not yet established: 'the heaviness', 'your trance', 'that calm'; cleft or pseudo-cleft: 'it's the ... that ...', 'what you'll find is ...'; no variant trigger carries the claim; if before/after/when, first/another/again, notice/realize, already/still/easily, begin/continue/stop or 'or' does, label the variant; a direct question (with a question mark) that carries the assumption is a loaded question, not this unit.

**Not to be confused with:** Implication (an implication is inferred and can be denied; a presupposition is required by the grammar and survives negation); Direct suggestion (direct suggestion states the response as the main point); Loaded question (when the assumption rides on a direct question the listener is expected to answer, label loaded question; this unit covers statements); Embedded question ('I wonder how/when/which' is the embedded question; add a presupposition label only for the trigger inside it, by variant); Double bind (a bind is the offer of options; presupposition is the mechanism that makes each option assume the outcome).

**Evidence:** experimental. Experiments on question wording and memory show presupposed content is accepted and later recalled as fact; no controlled work shows it raises hypnotic responding over plain suggestion. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Presupposition, Presupposition accommodation, Projective content, Common ground, Misinformation effect, Counterarguing.

**Consent:** It works because the listener does not stop to evaluate the assumed claim, so presuppose only responses the listener has agreed to.


##### Time-clause presupposition *(variant)*

Also called: subordinate clause of time, temporal clause, before/after/while/when presupposition.

A time clause locates one event relative to another and takes the event in the clause as given. 'Before you go deeper, take a breath' is about the breath; going deeper is assumed. The trigger is the time conjunction. It differs from a contingent suggestion, where the clause holds something already true and the suggestion sits in the main clause.

**How:** Put the response you want in a time clause and an easy instruction or observation in the main clause. 'After', 'once', 'while' and 'since' can present the response as a temporal landmark, but a future clause does not guarantee it will occur. 'Before' is especially weak: 'stop before you fall' is coherent even if no fall occurs. 'When' and 'as' can sound like predictions or descriptions. Use these clauses where the response is plausible, and keep the main clause something the listener can do or verify at once. Avoid claiming a response the listener clearly is not having.

> Before you drift all the way down, notice the weight of your hands.

> After your eyes close, the sounds in the room can fade into the background.

> While that calm spreads through your chest, your shoulders can drop a little.

**Spot it by:** 'before you ...'; 'after you ...' / 'once you have ...'; 'while you ...' / 'during ...'; 'when you ...' / 'as you ...' followed by a response not yet established; 'until you ...' / 'since you began ...'; wanted response in the time clause, minor instruction in the main clause.

**Not to be confused with:** Contingent suggestion (there the clause holds a fact already true and the main clause is the suggestion; here the suggestion is in the clause); Time bind (a time bind offers a choice of when; a time clause offers no choice); Implied directive (an implied directive adds an internal response and a signal that it has happened).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Time clauses are established presupposition triggers in linguistics and standard in Ericksonian texts; their specific effect on hypnotic response has not been tested on its own. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Presupposition, Presupposition accommodation, Projective content.

**Consent:** The assumed response passes without being offered for agreement, so keep it within what the listener signed up for.


##### Ordinal presupposition *(variant)*

Also called: ordinal numeral, first/next/another, repetitive presupposition, again/another presupposition.

An ordinal or repetition word places an item in a sequence and takes the rest of the sequence as given. 'The first thing you'll notice' assumes there will be several things noticed; 'another wave of calm' assumes an earlier wave; 'again' assumes it happened before. The open question is the order or the identity of the item, never whether the series exists.

**How:** Use 'first' at the start of a phase to promise more to come, and 'another', 'again' or 'once more' when one response has shown, so it reads as one of many. Pair it with uncertainty about which item comes first ('I don't know which hand will feel it first'); the not-knowing draws attention away from the assumption. Do not say 'again' or 'another' about something that has not happened once in the session; the listener can check, and describing an earlier occasion that never took place is suggested memory, with its own cautions.

> The first thing you might notice is a change in your breathing.

> I wonder which hand will begin to feel heavy first.

> And here comes another wave of that calm, moving down through you again.

**Spot it by:** 'the first thing you'll notice'; 'which ... first' in a question or 'I wonder' clause; 'next', 'the next time', 'second', 'last'; 'another', 'again', 'once more', 'one more'; 'also', 'too', 'as well' adding a response to one already named.

**Not to be confused with:** Adverb / adjective presupposition ('still', 'already' and 'even more' comment on one response in progress; 'first', 'another' and 'again' count it as one of a series); Double bind ('which first, left or right' adds listed alternatives; label both when alternatives are named); Suggested memory ('again' alone stays here; label suggested memory when the script goes on to describe an earlier occasion that did not happen).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Ordinals and repetition words are recognized presupposition triggers in linguistics; the claim that they increase hypnotic response comes from NLP teaching and is untested. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Presupposition, Presupposition accommodation.

**Consent:** It works by the listener not questioning the assumed series, so use it only for responses the listener has agreed to.


##### Awareness predicate *(variant)*

Also called: awareness verb, factive presupposition, factive verb, notice/realize/discover pattern.

Awareness verbs such as notice, realize, discover and be aware are factive: they can only be used of something true. 'Notice how heavy your arms are' therefore takes the heaviness as fact and makes the instruction about attention. This differs from pacing trance signs, which asserts the sign directly as evidence, and from mind reading, which claims to know what the listener is thinking.

**How:** Write the response as the object of an awareness verb: 'notice how ...', 'you may realize that ...', 'become aware of the ...'. It suits responses that are faint, ambiguous or just beginning, because a listener who goes looking for a sensation usually finds something to count. Soften with 'may', 'might' or 'not yet' so a listener who feels nothing concludes they have not noticed yet, not that it is absent. Avoid it for gross, checkable claims (an arm that is plainly not lifting).

> Notice how heavy your arms have become.

> You may be surprised to discover how easy it is to let that thought go.

> At some point you'll realize your breathing slowed down a while ago.

**Spot it by:** 'notice how/that ...'; 'realize', 'discover', 'find that', 'recognize'; 'be aware of', 'become aware that', 'are you aware'; 'you may not have noticed yet ...'; 'know that', 'remember that', 'it's nice to know that' followed by the target claim; awareness verb in the main clause, target response in its object clause.

**Not to be confused with:** Pacing trance signs (that names an observable sign and calls it evidence; this assumes the response and asks only for attention); Mind reading (mind reading claims knowledge of the listener's thoughts; this directs their attention to an assumed fact); Embedded question ('I wonder whether you notice' is an embedded question; label both when the object is an assumed response).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Factive presupposition is well established in linguistics and the pattern is standard in clinical scripts; its effect on hypnotic response has not been isolated experimentally. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Factive presupposition, Presupposition accommodation, Response expectancy theory, Confirmation bias.

**Consent:** The listener is led to search for and confirm a state without being asked whether it exists, so use it for agreed outcomes only.


##### Adverb / adjective presupposition *(variant)*

Also called: commentary adverb, commentary adjective, adverbial presupposition, easily/deeply/already/still.

A sentence that asks or comments on how a response happens takes for granted that it happens. 'How easily you relax' assumes relaxing and leaves only its ease open; 'fortunately, you don't need to try' assumes the not-needing and comments on its luck. Three groups do this work: manner and degree words when they are the open element of a question or 'how' clause (how easily, how deeply), phase words (already, still, yet, even more), and commentary words that give the speaker's attitude to a clause taken as fact (fortunately, luckily, curiously). A manner adverb in a plain statement ('you relax easily') asserts the response and is not this variant.

**How:** Write the response as a plain verb or clause, then add the modifier and make the modifier the point of the sentence: 'I wonder how quickly ...', 'it's interesting how deeply ...'. Choose modifiers the listener would be glad to accept (easily, comfortably), since accepting the adverb accepts the verb. 'Already' and 'still' are the strongest and the easiest to falsify; use them once there is something to point at. Too many adverbs in a row reads as padding and weakens each one.

> I wonder how easily you can let your shoulders drop.

> Fortunately, you don't have to do anything for this to work.

> You're still relaxing, even more deeply now.

**Spot it by:** 'how easily / quickly / deeply / completely you ...'; 'already', 'still', 'yet', 'anymore' with a response verb; 'even more', 'even deeper', 'so much more'; sentence-opening evaluative word: 'fortunately', 'luckily', 'happily', 'curiously', 'interestingly'; 'it's interesting / nice / surprising how ...'; question or wonder-clause whose only open element is a manner or degree word.

**Not to be confused with:** Comparative deletion ('more relaxed' with no standard is comparative deletion; it need not assume a response is under way); Lost performative ('it's good to let go' is a value judgment with no judge; it does not assume the letting go is happening); Already-happened framing ('already' alone overlaps; label already-happened framing when the whole clause reports the effect as done).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Phase words (already, still) and commentary adverbs are recognized triggers in linguistics. Manner and degree adverbs background the verb only when they are the open element of a question or 'how' clause; in a plain statement the verb is asserted. The claim that any of these improves hypnotic response is NLP teaching without independent tests. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Presupposition, Presupposition accommodation, Conventional implicature.

**Consent:** The response is assumed while attention goes to its quality, so use it only for responses the listener has agreed to.


##### Change-of-state verb *(variant)*

Also called: change-of-time verb, aspectual verb, begin/continue/stop pattern, phase verb.

Verbs of starting, continuing and stopping take a prior state for granted. 'Continue to relax' assumes relaxing is under way; 'stop holding on' assumes the listener was holding on; 'begin to notice' assumes they were not noticing and now will. The trigger is the phase verb, and what it presupposes is a state before the moment of speaking, where already-happened framing reports the effect itself as present or done.

**How:** Use 'begin' and 'start' to open a response gently: the listener only has to accept a beginning, which is hard to disprove. Switch to 'continue', 'keep' and 'go on' once any sign has appeared; these turn one small response into a process in motion. Use 'stop' and 'no longer' to assume an effort or tension the listener can now drop. Avoid 'continue' as the first mention of a response; with nothing before it, the false assumption is easy to hear.

> You can begin to notice the weight of your eyelids.

> And just continue relaxing, the way you have been.

> You can stop trying to follow every word now.

**Spot it by:** 'begin to', 'start to', 'starting to'; 'continue to', 'keep', 'keep on', 'go on', 'carry on'; 'stop', 'quit', 'no longer', 'not anymore'; 'return to', 'go back to', 'resume'; 'become', 'change into', 'turn into' with a state.

**Not to be confused with:** Already-happened framing (that reports the effect itself as present or finished; a phase verb assumes only the state before it); Direct suggestion ('relax' asserts; 'continue to relax' assumes relaxing and instructs only its continuation); Present tense and progressive (progressive tense is a tense choice; this needs a phase verb).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Phase verbs are textbook presupposition triggers and routine in clinical scripts; no study isolates their effect on hypnotic response. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Presupposition, Presupposition accommodation, Projective content.

**Consent:** The prior state is assumed, not offered for agreement, so keep it to responses the listener has consented to.


#### Already-happened framing *(unit)*

Also called: fait accompli, done deal, it has already begun, presupposed completion, perfect-tense framing.

The writer uses past or perfect tense, 'already', or a result state to report the response as an accomplished fact: 'something has already shifted'. Nothing is requested, so nothing can be refused; the listener is left checking for evidence. It differs from a change-of-state verb, which assumes only a prior state, and from inevitability framing, which predicts a future outcome instead of reporting a present one.

**How:** Place it right after a stretch where some response is likely to have occurred (a long exhale, a silence, a deepener), then report the response as done and send attention to finding it. Keep the claimed effect internal and hard to check: 'something has shifted', 'part of you has already decided'. Follow with an awareness predicate or ratification so the listener confirms it. Do not claim completed effects that are visibly absent, and do not use it in place of the work; it harvests a response, it does not create one from nothing.

> It has already begun, and you don't need to do anything to help it along.

> Somewhere in the last few breaths, your body decided to let go.

> That change is made now. All that's left is to notice it.

**Spot it by:** 'already' with perfect or past tense: 'has already begun', 'you've already'; 'it's done', 'that's settled', 'the decision is made', 'that change is made'; 'all that's left is to ...', 'the only thing left is ...'; past or perfect tense for a response the script never requested; 'somewhere back there', 'at some point', 'in the last few breaths' locating the effect in the session's past; 'by the time you notice, it has ...'.

**Not to be confused with:** Direct suggestion (direct suggestion states the response in the present or future ('your eyes are closing', 'you will relax'); this reports it in the past or perfect and leaves only noticing it); Change-of-state verb ('continue' assumes a prior state; this states the effect itself as accomplished); Inevitability (inevitability says it will happen; this says it has); It was always so (retroactive framing says the trait was always true, across the listener's life; this covers the session's recent past); Future progression (future progression moves the listener to a later date to look back; this stays in the present).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Common in Ericksonian and clinical scripts and consistent with expectancy research, but not tested as a separate technique.

**Why it works:** Presupposition accommodation, Response expectancy theory, Self-perception theory, Confirmation bias.

**Consent:** It removes the moment at which the listener could decline, so use it only for effects agreed before the session.


#### Loaded question *(unit)*

Also called: complex question, many questions, fallacy of many questions, trick question.

A loaded question carries a claim the listener has not agreed to, and every direct answer grants it. 'How long have you wanted to let go?' assumes the wanting whatever number comes back. It is the question form of presupposition, set apart because the listener must respond, and responding is what commits them. A leading question pushes toward one answer; a loaded question makes all answers concede the same thing.

**How:** State the claim you want conceded, then ask about one of its details: how long, how much, when it started, what it feels like. Open questions (how, when, what) load better than yes/no questions. In recorded scripts, leave a pause so the listener answers inwardly; the inner answer is the concession. It is more exposed than a statement, because a question invites a reply and 'I don't' is an available one; keep the assumption close to something the listener has already shown or said.

> How long have you been needing a rest like this?

> What made you decide to come back tonight?

> When did you first realize you were good at this?

**Spot it by:** direct wh-question ('how long', 'when did', 'what is it about', 'why do you') with a question mark; what it assumes is a wish, need, motive, history or trait of the listener, not a sensation they can check right now; 'how much do you want ...', 'why do you keep coming back to ...'; 'do you still ...', 'have you stopped ...'; no direct answer denies the assumption; denying it takes 'I don't' or 'it isn't'.

**Not to be confused with:** Question as suggestion (label that when the question directs attention to a present sensation or response ('which hand feels warmer?'); label this when it assumes a wish, motive, history or trait); Presupposition (the same assumption in a statement is presupposition; loaded question needs a direct question the listener is expected to answer); Embedded question ('I wonder how long you've wanted this' owes no answer; label embedded question, with the presupposition variant for its trigger); Double bind (a direct 'X or Y?' that offers two versions of the response is a bind, or a time bind when only timing differs; the or-presupposition variant covers alternatives inside a statement); Tag question (a tag asks for agreement with a stated claim; a loaded question leaves the assumed claim unstated); Rhetorical question (a rhetorical question makes a point without seeking an answer; a loaded question solicits an answer that concedes its assumption).

**Evidence:** experimental. Studies of leading questions show that wording which presupposes a detail changes answers and later memory; whether an inward answer during trance commits the listener the same way is untested.

**Why it works:** Loaded question, Presupposition accommodation, Misinformation effect, Commitment and consistency, Begging the question.

**Consent:** Answering concedes something the listener was never asked to agree to, and can alter what they later remember wanting, so load only what they have told you is true.


#### Implication *(unit)*

Also called: conversational implicature, implied suggestion, psychological implication, suggestion by inference.

An implication is content a sentence does not state or grammatically require, but which a listener can infer from its wording and context. 'You can keep your eyes open for the first minute or two' suggests that closing them later is expected, without saying that it will happen. The inference can be cancelled without contradiction. Indirect suggestion is the broad style; implication is the particular inference left for the listener to draw. When the target response itself is negated ('you don't have to close your eyes yet'), label negative suggestion.

**How:** Write down the conclusion you want, then write a sentence that is only worth saying if that conclusion is true, and stop. Useful levers: a limit that implies what lies past it ('for now', 'only as fast as', 'for the first minute'), a mention that implies relevance ('some people find their hands tingle first'), and emphasis that implies a contrast ('your conscious mind can keep listening'). Leave a beat afterwards; the inference needs time. If the inference takes more than one step, most listeners will not make it, and spelling it out afterwards turns it into a direct suggestion.

> You can keep your eyes open for the first minute or two.

> Most people find their eyelids start to feel it somewhere around the third breath.

> You can keep that steady, ordinary breathing for now.

**Spot it by:** a limit on a permission or description: 'for now', 'so far', 'at first', 'for the first minute or two'; a ceiling that only makes sense if the response is coming: 'only as deep as', 'no faster than'; one statement about other people or about one option, with the application to the listener left unsaid; target response never stated as instruction or fact, and not named under 'don't' or 'not', anywhere in the span; the inferred claim can be named in a sentence and could be denied without contradiction ('I didn't say that').

**Not to be confused with:** Presupposition (a presupposition is required by the grammar and survives negation; an implication is inferred and can be cancelled); Negative suggestion (when the target response is named under 'don't', 'not' or 'won't', label negative suggestion, even with 'yet' or 'until'; implication covers inferences from sentences that do not negate the target); Unstated premise (one statement with its application left open is implication; an unstated premise needs two stated parts (a rule and a case, or a reason and 'so') with the last step missing); Indirect suggestion (indirect suggestion is the general style, covering story and possibility; implication is one specific inference left to the listener).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Memory research shows listeners often recall pragmatic inferences as if they had been stated; studies comparing indirect with direct hypnotic suggestion have found no reliable advantage for indirect wording. Source: Erickson, Rossi & Rossi, Hypnotic Realities (1976).

**Why it works:** Conversational implicature, Pragmatic enrichment, Generation effect, Psychological reactance, Indirect suggestion.

**Consent:** The listener experiences the conclusion as their own and the writer keeps deniability, so imply only what you would be willing to say outright.


##### If-then implication *(variant)*

Also called: conditional implication, if-then suggestion, conditional contingency.

The writer ties a response to a simple voluntary act with 'if ... then'. The conditional is stated; what is implied is that by performing the act the listener has agreed to the consequence. It differs from a contingent suggestion, whose first half is already happening or certain to happen, so no act of acceptance is involved. Here the listener's own move closes the deal.

**How:** Choose an 'if' the listener is about to do anyway or can do with no effort: sit back, close the eyes, take a breath, keep listening. State the 'then' as the response you want, with 'can' or 'will'. Say it before the act, and ratify the act when it comes. It works best early, as the listener settles, and at decision points. If the act and the response have no plausible connection, say so lightly or build one; an arbitrary link is noticed.

> If you settle back in the chair, that is your signal to let this begin.

> If you close your eyes now, you're telling yourself you're ready to go deeper.

> If you take one more slow breath, that breath is your signal to release the tension.

**Spot it by:** 'if you [simple voluntary act], (then) you will / can [response]'; the 'if' clause names something the listener does on purpose, not something happening to them; the act has not been done yet; the sentence comes before it; the act is one the listener is about to do anyway: sit back, close the eyes, take a breath; ratification ('that's right', 'good') in the lines right after.

**Not to be confused with:** Contingent suggestion (its first half is already true or inevitable ('as you breathe out'); here the first half is a choice whose taking signals agreement); Implied directive (an implied directive has the internal response first and a behavioral signal after; here the act comes first and the response follows); Complex equivalence ('X means Y' asserts the meaning outright; label both when a conditional also says what the act means); Your actions prove it (that points back at something already done; this sets the meaning before the act).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Described in Ericksonian texts and consistent with commitment research, but not tested as a distinct technique. Source: Erickson, Rossi & Rossi, Hypnotic Realities (1976).

**Why it works:** Conversational implicature, Commitment and consistency, Self-perception theory, Response expectancy theory.

**Consent:** It converts an ordinary act into consent without asking for consent, so do not treat the act as agreement to anything the listener has not been told about.


#### Unstated premise *(unit)*

Also called: enthymeme, truncated syllogism, listener completes the argument, missing premise.

An enthymeme is an argument in which a premise or the conclusion is not stated. The listener fills the gap to make the reasoning hold, and in doing so adopts the missing piece without examining it. It needs argument structure, a 'so', 'because' or 'which means' linking a reason to a claim, which separates it from implication. The unstated part is usually the general rule that would be the weakest point if said aloud.

**How:** Write the full argument first: general rule, particular case, conclusion. Then delete the rule if it is the contestable part, or delete the conclusion if you want the listener to reach it and own it. Keep the gap one step wide. State the remaining parts plainly and join them with a connective so the listener knows an argument is being made. Check the deleted premise yourself: if it is false or you would not defend it, the device is doing dishonest work.

> Tense muscles can't hold on once the breathing slows. And your breathing slowed a while ago.

> People who can imagine vividly respond well to this. And you pictured that room in detail.

> You came back to listen again, which tells you something.

**Spot it by:** general statement followed by a particular case, conclusion left unsaid; 'which tells you something', 'and you know what that means', 'you can work out the rest'; two stated parts of an argument (rule and case, or fact and pointer) with the last step missing from the text; a pause or line break where the conclusion would go; if the reason and the claim are both stated and joined by 'so' or 'because', label giving a reason.

**Not to be confused with:** Giving a reason (when the reason and the claim are both on the page, label giving a reason; label this only when a step, usually the conclusion, is visibly left for the listener); Implication (implication is one statement with an inference left open; this needs two stated parts of an argument with a step missing); Your actions prove it (when the stated fact is the listener's own act and the point is what they want or are, label your-actions-prove-it; add this label only if the conclusion is left unsaid); Unfinished sentence (an unfinished sentence breaks off the grammar; here the sentences are whole and the logic has the gap); Cause-effect link (a cause-effect link asserts that X causes Y; this argues from X to Y through an unspoken rule).

**Evidence:** rhetorical-tradition. A classical figure. Persuasion studies comparing stated and unstated conclusions do not establish an advantage for leaving the conclusion unsaid; the result varies with the message and audience. Source: Aristotle, Rhetoric.

**Why it works:** Enthymeme, Enthymematic persuasion, Generation effect, Pragmatic enrichment.

**Consent:** The listener adopts a premise they never heard stated, so leave out only premises you could state and defend.


#### Assumed common ground *(unit)*

Also called: as we both know, of course, taken-for-granted framing, shared-knowledge marker, as you know.

The writer attaches a marker of shared knowledge ('of course', 'as you know', 'we both know', 'obviously') to a claim the listener has not agreed to. The claim is stated in the open, which separates this from grammatical presupposition; what is slipped in is its status as settled. Objecting now means denying something one supposedly already knows, which costs more than doubting a fresh claim.

**How:** Use it on a claim that is close to true for the listener or that they would like to be true, and say it lightly, in passing, on the way to another point. Put the marker at the start or as an aside, then move on without pausing for agreement. It is strongest after real common ground has been built by pacing or earlier sessions. Overuse or use on a clearly new claim reads as pressure and invites the reply 'no, I don't know that'.

> As you already know, your body remembers how to do this.

> Of course, the body does most of this by itself.

> We both know you do this better when you stop trying.

**Spot it by:** 'as you know', 'as you already know', 'as we both know', 'we both know'; 'of course', 'obviously', 'naturally', 'clearly', 'needless to say'; 'between us', 'as we agreed', 'you and I both know' presenting a claim as shared; 'remember, ...' introducing something not said earlier in the script; 'after all', 'as always', 'as we agreed' with no earlier agreement in the text; marker is an aside or sentence opener, or invokes shared agreement; the claim itself is stated in full.

**Not to be confused with:** Truism (a truism really is undeniable; this dresses a contestable claim as already agreed); Awareness predicate ('you know / realize that X' with the claim as the verb's object is the awareness predicate; label this entry for an aside or opener ('as you know', 'of course') or a 'we' subject ('we both know')); Mind reading (mind reading claims knowledge of what the listener thinks or feels now; this claims they already hold a belief in common with the speaker); Social proof (social proof cites what other people do; this cites agreement between speaker and listener).

**Evidence:** rhetorical-tradition. Common ground and accommodation are well described in pragmatics, and discourse studies document these markers in persuasive talk; their effect on acceptance has little direct experimental testing.

**Why it works:** Common ground, Common-ground manipulation, Presupposition accommodation, Epistemic vigilance, Illusory truth effect.

**Consent:** It tells the listener they already agreed to something they did not, which shades into rewriting their history; use it only for things actually established with them.


### Artful vagueness

Also called: Milton model, Milton-model language, artfully vague language, inverse meta model.

A group of sentence-level patterns, catalogued by Bandler and Grinder from Erickson's speech, that remove or blur information: who, what, how, compared with what, according to whom. The listener has to complete the sentence to understand it, and completes it with material that fits them. The family covers three kinds of pattern: deletions (missing content), unsupported links and generalizations (cause-effect, equivalence, mind reading, quantifiers, modals), and ambiguities (one wording, two readings). It differs from presupposition, which smuggles a specific claim into the background; vagueness leaves the claim open.

**Choosing:** Use deletions (nominalization, unspecified verb, unspecified referent, comparative deletion, simple deletion, lost performative) when you write for many listeners and cannot know their details; they keep statements unfalsifiable. Use the linking patterns (cause-effect link, complex equivalence, mind reading) when you need to connect something observable to the response you want. Use universal quantifiers and modal operators to set how certain or how permitted a response is. Use the ambiguities (sound-alike, syntactic, scope, run-on, double meaning) sparingly, as a light second channel; they are the weakest-supported members. Vagueness suits induction and general suggestion; switch to specific wording for triggers, safety statements and anything the listener must carry out exactly. Presupposition patterns are a separate nested family (presupposition), and the remaining Milton-model items live elsewhere: tag-question, conversational-postulate, embedded-command, embedded-question, quoted-suggestion, double-bind, pacing, utilization.

**Not to be confused with:** Presupposition and implication (presupposition builds in a specific claim; vagueness leaves the content open for the listener to fill); Indirect suggestion (indirect suggestion is the broader stance of not commanding; these are the specific wording patterns often used to do it); Confusion technique (confusion makes the sentence hard to process on purpose; vague language is easy to process and simply under-specified).

**Why it works:** Milton Model, Meta Model, Pragmatic enrichment, Self-reference effect, Generation effect.

**Consent:** Vague wording makes statements hard to disagree with; do not use it to blur what a session will do or what the listener is agreeing to.


#### Nominalization *(unit)*

Also called: abstract nouns, process as thing, process noun.

A verb or adjective turned into a noun: relaxing becomes relaxation, learning becomes a learning, being comfortable becomes comfort. The noun drops who does it, how, and to what, so it cannot be checked against the listener's actual experience. The standard test: it is a noun, but you could not put it in a wheelbarrow. It differs from an unspecified verb in that the process is frozen into a thing the listener can have, find or go into.

**How:** Use nominalizations where you need a statement every listener can accept: early in an induction, in general suggestions, and when naming resources ('your own understanding'). Pair them with verbs of having, finding or allowing. A long run of them reads as empty; follow with concrete sensory language when you want a specific experience.

> You can find a certain comfort in this stillness.

> Let that relaxation bring with it a new understanding.

> There is a learning here, and it belongs to you.

**Spot it by:** abstract nouns ending in -tion, -ment, -ness, -ance, -ity (relaxation, awareness, surrender, clarity); noun forms of state or process words: comfort, peace, focus, trust, change, learning, understanding, control; 'a certain ...', 'a sense of ...', 'a feeling of ...', 'that ...' before an abstract noun; abstract noun as object of have, find, discover, allow, enjoy; the noun could be replaced by a verb phrase ('your relaxation' = 'you relaxing').

**Not to be confused with:** Unspecified verb (there the process stays a verb with its manner left out; here it has become a noun); State-as-substance (that gives the state a physical substance (fog, warmth); a nominalization stays abstract); Naming the state (that tells the listener what their present state is called; a nominalization only refers to a state loosely).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Nominalization is a standard linguistic category, but no controlled study shows that abstract nouns produce stronger hypnotic response than concrete wording. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Milton Model, Meta Model, Pragmatic enrichment, Self-reference effect.


#### Unspecified verb *(unit)*

Also called: vague verb, process verb.

A verb that names an internal process but gives no manner or mechanism: change, learn, experience, notice, let go, allow, drift. The listener must supply the how, and any way they do it counts. It differs from nominalization because the process stays a verb, something the listener does or undergoes.

**How:** Use it when the exact route does not matter or when you cannot know what will work for this listener. Give the direction and leave the method to them: 'let go' instead of 'unclench your jaw'. When you need a particular physical or imagined act, name it specifically instead. Vague verbs combine well with permissive modals ('you can begin to change').

> You can simply let go now.

> Something is beginning to change as you listen.

> Allow yourself to experience this in your own way.

**Spot it by:** process verbs with no manner or means: change, learn, experience, discover, understand, sense, become, allow, let go, drift, shift, settle; 'in your own way', 'however it happens', 'somehow' following the verb; 'begin to ...', 'allow yourself to ...', 'let yourself ...' plus a vague verb; no 'by ...' or 'with ...' phrase saying how the action is done.

**Not to be confused with:** Nominalization (that turns the process into a noun; this keeps the verb and omits the manner); Not doing / not knowing (that states outright that the listener need not know how; this just leaves the how unsaid); Deletion (deletion removes an object or topic from the sentence; here the verb itself is under-specified).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Listed in every Milton-model catalogue; its specific contribution to response has not been tested apart from permissive wording in general. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Milton Model, Meta Model, Pragmatic enrichment.


#### Unspecified referent *(unit)*

Also called: lack of referential index, unspecified referential index, generalized referential index, people can, one can.

A noun phrase that does not pick out a specific person or thing: people, someone, one, a person, it, that feeling, certain things. Because the sentence is not about the listener by name, it draws no resistance, yet the listener is the only person present to apply it to. It differs from direct address, which says 'you', and from social proof, which cites others as evidence.

**How:** Use it to offer a suggestion without directing it at the listener: say what 'a person can' do and let them take it up. It works best just before or after a 'you' statement on the same topic, so the transfer is easy. Demonstratives ('that feeling', 'this place') let the listener choose which feeling or place you mean. Overuse makes the script sound evasive.

> A person can relax more quickly than they expect.

> One can listen and drift at the same time.

> And that feeling can begin to spread.

**Spot it by:** generic subject plus 'can' or 'may' plus a response verb: 'a person can', 'people can', 'one may', 'someone could'; 'that feeling', 'this sensation', 'certain things', 'something' with no antecedent; 'it' or 'this' with nothing earlier in the text to point to; a generic statement sitting between sentences addressed to 'you'; the sentence states a possibility, not a count or report of what others actually do.

**Not to be confused with:** Social proof (social proof reports what others actually do or feel ('most people find') as a reason to follow; here the generic subject is a stand-in for the listener and the sentence states a possibility); Truism (a truism is an undeniable general fact that asks for nothing ('everyone has felt tired'); this offers the wanted response under a generic subject ('a person can let go')); Normalizing (normalizing states that the response is ordinary and expected; this only leaves the subject open); My friend John (that describes a specific third person responding in detail; this names no one).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. That listeners apply generic statements to themselves is plausible and consistent with self-reference research, but the pattern itself has not been tested as a hypnotic device. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Milton Model, Self-reference effect, Pragmatic enrichment, Indirect suggestion.


#### Comparative deletion *(unit)*

Also called: unspecified comparison, deleted comparison, deeper than what.

A comparative or superlative word with no stated standard. 'Deeper' does not say deeper than what, so any state at all can count as the baseline and any small change confirms the statement. It differs from the more-the-more form, which ties two increasing things to each other; here there is one quantity and a missing reference point.

**How:** Use comparatives to suggest movement without claiming a level: 'more comfortable' is always safer than 'completely comfortable'. Repeat across a passage to build a sense of steady increase. Do not supply the standard unless you want it measured. It fits deepening passages and ratification ('that's better').

> You are becoming more relaxed.

> And it feels better now.

> This is the easiest way to rest.

**Spot it by:** comparatives with no 'than' clause: deeper, more relaxed, easier, heavier, calmer, better, further; 'more and more', 'even more', 'more deeply', 'less and less'; superlatives with no stated set: 'the best way', 'the deepest level'; 'more' or '-er' adjective directly after become, feel, grow, get, go.

**Not to be confused with:** The more... the more (that yokes two increases to each other; this is a single comparison with the standard missing); Deeper and deeper (that is depth words restated across a passage; this is one comparative with no standard, on any quality. A run of 'deeper... deeper and deeper' takes the passage-level label, and a lone 'more comfortable' takes this one); Adverb / adjective presupposition ('even more' and 'still deeper' also presuppose a prior amount; label that when the point is the assumed earlier state, this when the point is the open standard).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Ubiquitous in hypnotic scripts and plainly unfalsifiable by design; no study isolates its effect. Source: Bandler & Grinder, The Structure of Magic, Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Milton Model, Meta Model, Pragmatic enrichment.


#### Lost performative *(unit)*

Also called: value judgment without a judge, it's good to, unattributed judgment.

An evaluation with the evaluator removed: 'it's good to let go' instead of 'I think it's good for you to let go'. With no judge named there is no one to disagree with, so the judgment reads as a general truth. It differs from a truism, which is verifiably true, and from authority, which names the source.

**How:** Use it to give approval to a response without making it your personal opinion: 'it's good to...', 'it's important to...', 'the best thing is...'. Keep the judgment mild and easy to accept; a strong or contestable value stated this way invites the question 'says who?'. It works well just before a suggestion the listener may be holding back from. If you only mean that the response is allowed, that is permission, not a judgment.

> It's good to take this time for yourself.

> And it's important to rest as deeply as you need.

> The best thing to do with a busy mind is to leave it alone.

**Spot it by:** 'it's good to', 'it's right to', 'it's important to', 'it's best to', 'it's wise to', 'it's wrong to'; evaluative adjective of worth or correctness (good, right, wrong, best, important, wise, natural) in an impersonal 'it is ... to/that' frame; 'the best way to ...', 'the right thing is ...' with no one named as holding the view; no 'I think', 'for me', 'according to' attached to the judgment; the judged thing is a response or attitude the script wants, not a checkable fact.

**Not to be confused with:** Permission ('it's okay / all right / fine to' says the response is allowed and is permission-giving; label lost performative when the adjective asserts worth or correctness (good, right, best, important, wrong)); Ratification (a free-standing 'that's right' or 'good' after a response confirms that it happened; a lost performative is a full sentence judging a response or attitude in general); Truism (a truism can be checked and is undeniable; this is an opinion presented as fact); Normalizing (normalizing says the response is common; this says it is good or right).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. The pattern is a real grammatical form; whether dropping the judge makes a value more readily accepted has not been tested in hypnosis. Source: Bandler & Grinder, The Structure of Magic, Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Milton Model, Meta Model, Common ground.

**Consent:** Because the judge is hidden, the listener may take the writer's values as general fact; keep such judgments to ones the listener would endorse awake.


#### Mind reading *(unit)*

Also called: I know you're wondering, claimed insight.

A claim about the listener's inner experience with no stated basis: 'I know you're wondering', 'part of you is curious'. Kept general, it is likely to be true, and a correct guess makes the speaker seem attuned. It differs from pacing, which states what is outwardly verifiable (sitting, hearing, breathing), and from desire attribution, which specifically assigns the wish for the outcome.

**How:** Claim only inner events that are near-universal in the situation: curiosity, wondering, some doubt, wanting to relax. Hedge the content, not the knowing ('you may be wondering just how...'). Use it early to build rapport and as a bridge into a suggestion. A specific wrong guess breaks rapport, so stay general or cover both sides.

> I know you're wondering how deep you can go.

> Part of you is already curious about what comes next.

> You may be thinking this is easier than you expected.

**Spot it by:** 'I know you ...', 'I can tell you ...', 'I know that you ...' plus a mental verb; 'you're wondering', 'you're thinking', 'you're curious', 'you're starting to feel'; 'part of you ...' plus a thought or wish; second-person mental-state claim with no evidence given; 'you might be asking yourself'.

**Not to be confused with:** Pacing (pacing states what the listener can verify externally right now; mind reading asserts unobservable thoughts or feelings); It's what you want (that attributes wanting the suggested outcome; mind reading covers any claimed thought or feeling); Preempting objections (that names a likely objection in order to answer it; mind reading need not answer anything).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. People do rate general statements about themselves as accurate, which explains why it seems to work, but its effect on hypnotic response is untested. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Milton Model, Meta Model, Response expectancy theory, Rapport matching.

**Consent:** Telling a listener what they think or want can replace their own report of it; do not use it to override a stated limit or doubt.


#### Cause-effect link *(unit)*

Also called: causal linkage, X makes you Y, implied causation, cause and effect.

An unsupported assertion that X produces Y: 'the sound of my voice makes you relax'. The stated cause is normally something present or certain, so the effect seems to follow from it. This entry is the explicit causal claim (makes, causes, because, so); the looser time-linked forms (as, while, when) are contingent suggestions. It differs from complex equivalence, which says X means Y, not X produces Y.

**How:** Pick a cause the listener cannot deny is happening (breathing, hearing, sitting) and attach the response with a causal verb. The link does not need to be logical, but it lands better when it feels natural, such as breathing out and loosening. Start with weak links ('and', 'as') early in a script and move to strong ones ('makes', 'causes') once responses are coming.

> Each breath out makes your shoulders drop a little further.

> Listening to these words causes your mind to grow quiet.

> Because you are sitting still, calm comes easily.

**Spot it by:** 'makes you', 'causes you to', 'forces', 'brings', 'sends you', 'takes you' linking a present event to a response; 'because', 'so', 'and so', 'that is why' joining a present fact to an involuntary response, not to an instruction; 'X will make Y happen' where X is the voice, breath, a sound or a count; a verifiable clause followed by a causal verb and an unverifiable response.

**Not to be confused with:** Contingent suggestion (that links by timing ('as', 'while', 'when', 'with every'); this asserts causation outright); Complex equivalence (that says X means or shows Y; this says X produces Y); Giving a reason (there the 'because' clause gives grounds for doing or accepting what is asked; here a present event is said to produce a response that just happens. If the main clause is an instruction or a 'you can', it is reason-giving).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Stated causal expectations do shape response (expectancy research), but the specific NLP grading of weak to strong linkage is untested. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Milton Model, Meta Model, Response expectancy theory.


#### Complex equivalence *(unit)*

Also called: X means Y, equivalence claim, that means.

An assertion that two different things are the same or that one is evidence of the other: 'your eyes closing means you're ready'. It gives an ordinary event a meaning chosen by the writer. It differs from a cause-effect link (X produces Y) and from reframing, which changes the meaning of something the listener already has a meaning for.

**How:** Take something that is happening or about to happen and state what it means, using 'means', 'shows', 'is a sign that', or plain 'is'. Choose an X that is certain to be true, such as hearing the voice, sitting still or the room being quiet. Two common uses have their own entries: declaring relaxation signs to be evidence of trance (ratifying-trance-signs) and declaring the listener's actions to be proof of what they want (self-perception-proof).

> Being still means being safe.

> Hearing my voice means it is time to rest.

> A quiet room is a sign that nothing is needed from you.

**Spot it by:** 'means', 'means that', 'which means'; 'shows that', 'proves', 'tells you', 'is a sign that', 'is how you know'; 'the fact that ... means ...'; 'X is Y' or 'X-ing is Y-ing' where X is an observable event or condition and Y is a state, meaning or trait; two unlike things joined by 'is just another way of', 'is the same as', 'is what ... looks like'.

**Not to be confused with:** Cause-effect link (that says X brings Y about; this says X is, or is evidence of, Y); Pacing trance signs (when X is an ordinary bodily sign of relaxation and Y is trance, label that narrower entry; this is the general X-means-Y form); Relabeling sensation (that is the narrower case of giving a felt body sensation a new cause or meaning; label it when X is a sensation being renamed); Your actions prove it (when X is something the listener voluntarily did and Y is what they want or are, label that; this covers the remaining X-means-Y claims).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Interpreting ambiguous sensations as evidence of hypnosis is consistent with expectancy and misattribution research; the NLP pattern as such has no direct tests.

**Why it works:** Milton Model, Meta Model, Response expectancy theory, Misattribution of arousal, Self-perception theory.

**Consent:** The listener is handed a meaning for their own reactions; avoid equivalences that turn hesitation or discomfort into agreement.


#### Universal quantifier *(unit)*

Also called: always, every, all, never, generalization.

A word that generalizes a statement to all instances, times or things: every breath, all of your attention, always, never, nothing, everyone. It removes exceptions, so a suggestion applies each time and to the whole of the listener. It differs from inevitability framing, which claims an outcome is certain, and from hyperbole, which exaggerates for effect and is not meant literally.

**How:** Attach the quantifier to something recurring (each breath, every word, every time you hear this) to spread a suggestion across the session or across future occasions. Use 'all' and 'completely' for totality, 'never' and 'nothing' to rule out interference. One exception the listener notices breaks an absolute, so pair it with responses that are easy or self-confirming. Limit the scope of lasting suggestions explicitly.

> All of your attention rests here.

> Nothing needs doing now.

> Every part of you knows how to rest.

**Spot it by:** all, every, each, any, always, never, none, nothing, no one, everyone, everything, everywhere; 'every time', 'each and every', 'with every ...', 'all of your ...', 'every part of you'; 'whenever', 'wherever', 'no matter what / where / when'; quantifier attached to a recurring event (breath, word, sound, count).

**Not to be confused with:** Contingent suggestion ('with every breath, ...' and 'each time ..., ...' are contingent suggestions (breath-deepener when tied to depth); label the quantifier separately only where no such linking form already covers it); Inevitability (that asserts the outcome cannot be avoided; a quantifier only removes exceptions from a statement); Hyperbole (hyperbole is overstatement not meant literally; the quantifier is meant to hold in every case); Truism (a truism with 'everyone' is offered as plain fact to be agreed with; the quantifier label is for a suggestion made exceptionless); Everything deepens (that specifically says any stimulus deepens trance; label that narrower device when the quantifier ranges over stimuli linked to deepening).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. A basic feature of language used throughout hypnotic scripts; no study isolates the effect of universal wording on response. Source: Bandler & Grinder, The Structure of Magic, Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Milton Model, Meta Model.

**Consent:** Words like always, never and everywhere extend a suggestion beyond the session; bound them with scope limits when the effect is meant to last.


#### Modal operator *(unit)*

Also called: modal operator of necessity, modal operator of possibility, must, can, have to, need to.

A modal verb or equivalent that sets the status of an action: possibility (can, may, might, could, able to), certainty (will), necessity (must, have to, need to, should) or impossibility (can't, unable). The same suggestion changes force with the modal alone. Possibility modals are the working words of permissive suggestion; this entry is the word-level choice, whatever style it serves.

**How:** Pick the modal to match how sure you are of the response and how far in the listener is. 'Can' and 'may' are almost never false and suit the start; 'will' commits you; 'must' and 'have to' suit an authoritarian style or a well-established response. A common build moves from possibility to certainty to necessity across a passage. 'Can't' is used for challenges and for removing an unwanted option.

> You can relax. You will relax. In a moment you must relax.

> You have to let that breath go sooner or later.

> You simply cannot hold on to that tension any longer.

**Spot it by:** possibility: can, could, may, might, able to, it's possible to; necessity: must, have to, need to, should, got to, it's necessary; impossibility: can't, cannot, unable to, impossible to, won't be able to; 'you' plus a modal plus a response verb; modals strengthening across a passage (can, then will, then must).

**Not to be confused with:** Permissive suggestion (a suggestion offered with 'can', 'may' or 'might' is permissive-suggestion and needs no modal label; label the modal here only when it is one of necessity, certainty or impossibility, or when the passage shifts from one modal to another); Conversational postulate (that is a modal question ('can you...?') working as a request; this is a modal in a statement); Challenge suggestion (that invites a test of a suggested inability; 'can't' alone, with no invited attempt, is just the modal); Inevitability (that asserts the outcome is certain as its whole point; a bare 'will' or 'must' inside another suggestion is the modal).

**Evidence:** contested. Permissive versus authoritarian wording has been compared in controlled studies with generally small or no differences in response; the NLP claims for particular modals go beyond that. Source: Bandler & Grinder, The Structure of Magic, Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Milton Model, Meta Model, Psychological reactance, Illocutionary force.


#### Deletion *(unit)*

Also called: simple deletion, missing object, unspecified object.

A sentence with a required piece of information missing, usually the object of an adjective or verb: 'you are ready', 'you're becoming aware', 'you already know'. The listener completes it with whatever is on their mind. It differs from comparative deletion (a missing standard of comparison) and from an unfinished sentence, which is visibly broken off; a deletion is grammatically complete.

**How:** Use state words that normally take a complement (ready, aware, curious, sure, open, willing) and stop before the complement. Place it where the context already points toward the response, so the listener's fill-in is the one you want. If the fill-in matters, such as what exactly they are agreeing to, state it instead.

> You are ready now.

> And you're becoming aware.

> You already know, don't you.

**Spot it by:** ready, aware, curious, sure, willing, open, certain, prepared with no 'for', 'of', 'about' or 'to' phrase; know, understand, notice, remember, learn with no object; short 'you are / you feel' plus adjective sentence ending at the adjective; the question 'ready for what?' or 'know what?' has no answer in the surrounding sentences.

**Not to be confused with:** Comparative deletion (that omits the standard of a comparison; this omits an object or topic); Unfinished sentence (that breaks off mid-sentence so the gap is felt; a deletion sounds complete); Unspecified referent (there a noun is present but picks out no one in particular; here the element is absent altogether).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Listeners routinely fill missing arguments from context (a well-studied pragmatic fact); no evidence shows the deletion itself increases suggestibility. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Milton Model, Meta Model, Pragmatic enrichment, Generation effect.


#### Sound-alike ambiguity *(unit)*

Also called: phonological ambiguity, homophone, your/you're, by now/buy now, here/hear.

A homophone or near-homophone placed so that the spoken sentence carries a second reading: here/hear, know/no, your/you're, two/too/to, by now/buy now. The written sentence makes ordinary sense; the alternate reading exists only in sound. It differs from double meaning, where one word has two senses under the same spelling, and from circular wordplay, which piles sound-alikes up to confuse.

**How:** Write the sentence so the surface meaning is natural and the sound-alike falls where the hidden reading forms a short command or statement. It needs audio; in text it only works if the reader sounds it out. The voice can mark it with a slight pause or drop in tone. Use one at a time; several in a row turn into confusion or comedy.

> Now, you can rest.

> Here, you can let your shoulders settle.

> Now, your breathing can slow.

**Spot it by:** homophone pairs near a suggestion: here/hear, know/no, your/you're, to/two/too, by/buy, write/right, weight/wait, whole/hole; a deliberate 'misspelling' in a script that swaps one homophone for another; stage direction or emphasis mark on a homophone; the same sound repeated in both senses in one sentence ('you know... no need to').

**Not to be confused with:** Double meaning (that is one word with two senses; this is two different words that sound alike); Circular wordplay (that loops sound-alikes to overload sense-making; this is a single quiet second reading); Embedded command (an embedded command is plainly present in the wording; here the command exists only in the alternate hearing).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Both senses of an ambiguous word are briefly activated in comprehension, but there is no evidence that the unintended sense acts as an instruction. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Milton Model, Equivocation, Spreading activation, Priming.

**Consent:** It is meant to pass unnoticed; the hidden reading should say nothing the listener has not agreed to hear openly.


#### Syntactic ambiguity *(unit)*

Also called: structural ambiguity, hypnotizing hypnotists.

A phrase with two possible grammatical structures, classically an -ing word plus a noun: 'relaxing voices' can be voices that relax you or the act of relaxing them. The words are unambiguous; the roles are not. It differs from scope ambiguity, where the structure is clear but the reach of one modifier is not, and from double meaning, which rests on one word's two senses.

**How:** Build it from a transitive verb in -ing form placed before a noun, or from a phrase that can attach to either of two parts of the sentence. Put it in a low-stakes descriptive line; the listener may take either reading and both should serve you. It is a decorative pattern: use rarely and never where the instruction must be clear.

> Relaxing muscles can be a pleasure.

> Calming thoughts can be very easy.

> You may enjoy quieting voices.

**Spot it by:** transitive verb in -ing form directly before a plural noun ('relaxing muscles', 'calming thoughts', 'deepening feelings'); '-ing noun can be ...' as sentence subject; a phrase that could attach to either the subject or the object ('watching you relax with ease'); sentence gives two sensible answers to 'who is doing the -ing?'.

**Not to be confused with:** Scope ambiguity (there the parse is clear and only the reach of a modifier is open; here the grammatical roles themselves are open); Run-on ambiguity (that fuses two sentences on a shared word; this is one well-formed phrase with two parses); Double meaning (that depends on one word's two senses, not on grammar).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Structural ambiguity is well studied in psycholinguistics as a processing cost; no evidence supports a hypnotic effect. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Milton Model, Equivocation, Cognitive load.


#### Scope ambiguity *(unit)*

Also called: modifier scope ambiguity.

A sentence in which an adjective, adverb or verb could apply to only the next item or to everything that follows. In 'your heavy arms and legs', heavy may cover only the arms or the legs too; in 'I wonder if you know that you are relaxing and going deeper', the going deeper may be inside the wondering or stated as fact. It differs from syntactic ambiguity because the grammatical roles are clear; only the reach is open.

**How:** Put a modifier or a soft opening verb ('I wonder if', 'you may notice that') before a coordinated list joined by 'and'. The first item clearly falls under it; later items can be heard either as covered or as free-standing assertions. Use it to let a statement drift from tentative to factual, or to spread one quality across several things.

> Feel your heavy arms and legs.

> I wonder if you know that you are relaxing and going deeper now.

> Speaking to you as someone who relaxes easily and learns quickly.

**Spot it by:** adjective or adverb before two or more nouns or verbs joined by 'and'; 'I wonder if / I don't know whether / you may notice that' followed by clauses joined with 'and'; a long sentence where a late clause could be inside or outside an earlier hedge; 'as' or 'when' clause followed by coordinated items.

**Not to be confused with:** Syntactic ambiguity (there the phrase has two different parses of who does what; here only the reach of a modifier is unclear); Compound suggestion (that joins a fact and a suggestion with 'and' to transfer acceptance; label scope ambiguity only when an earlier modifier may or may not cover the second part); Embedded question ('I wonder if' alone is an embedded question; this entry needs the trailing 'and' clause whose coverage is open).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. A recognized linguistic phenomenon; its use as a hypnotic device is untested and it is the least used of the Milton-model ambiguities. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Milton Model, Equivocation.


#### Run-on ambiguity *(unit)*

Also called: punctuation ambiguity, overlapping sentences, pivot word, run-on sentence ambiguity.

Two sentences fused on a shared word or phrase with no break between them: 'you can feel your hand me the glass', 'notice how you can relax now is the time'. The pivot word belongs to both, so the listener cannot tell where one sentence ended. It differs from an unfinished sentence, which stops and leaves a gap, and from polysyndeton, which links complete clauses with conjunctions.

**How:** Choose a pivot that ends the first thought and starts the second, often a word like 'now', 'deeply', 'relax' or a noun that doubles as a verb. Deliver or punctuate it with no pause at the join. The second sentence is usually the suggestion. Use sparingly; it produces a brief stumble, and repeated stumbles become confusion technique.

> You can begin to relax now is the time to let go.

> Listening to my voice carries you down into comfort grows with every breath.

> As you look at your watch how quickly your eyes grow tired.

**Spot it by:** a sentence that is ungrammatical as a whole but splits into two good sentences sharing one word; 'now', 'here', 'deeply', 'relax', 'down' sitting at a join with no punctuation; missing full stop or comma where a sentence boundary is expected; a noun that immediately serves as a verb (watch, hand, rest, feel, sink); script note such as 'no pause' at a sentence boundary.

**Not to be confused with:** Unfinished sentence (that breaks off and leaves the thought hanging; this continues straight into a second sentence); And... and... and (that joins whole clauses with repeated conjunctions; here a shared word belongs to both sentences); Non sequitur (that drops in an irrelevant statement; here the join, not the content, is what is odd).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Bandler and Grinder describe this overlapping-sentence technique in Erickson's speech; evidence that it makes the second clause more acceptable is lacking. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Milton Model, Prediction error, Cognitive load, Expectation violation.


#### Attributing feeling to things *(unit)*

Also called: selectional restriction violation, the chair can relax, displaced referent.

A sentence that gives an inanimate thing a human experience: 'the chair can relax', 'the room is growing sleepy'. Since objects cannot feel, the listener makes sense of the sentence by moving the feeling to the only available feeler, themselves. It is a single displaced predicate, not a sustained image; a thing given its own will or voice over a passage is personification, and a full parallel story is metaphor.

**How:** Name something in the listener's surroundings or in the imagined scene and give it the state you want them to have. Keep it to a sentence or two and do not explain it. It suits indirect styles and listeners who push back on being told what they feel. Follow it with a statement about the listener so the transfer has somewhere to land.

> The chair beneath you knows how to rest completely.

> Even the walls seem to be letting go of the day.

> The lamp beside you feels no need to hurry.

**Spot it by:** inanimate subject (chair, room, bed, tree, stone, candle) with a verb of feeling, knowing or intending; 'the ... knows how to', 'the ... can relax', 'the ... feels', 'the ... is content to'; an object described with the target state shortly before 'you' is given the same state; one or two sentences only, with no developed story.

**Not to be confused with:** Personification (personification gives the listener's own body parts or states a will ('your eyelids know'), or addresses the thing; label this entry when an outside object is given the feeling the listener is meant to have); Metaphor (a metaphor is a story or image with parallel structure; this is one predicate on the wrong kind of subject); Unspecified referent (that uses a generic human subject; this uses a non-human one).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Derived from Erickson's indirect work (for example speaking about a plant's comfort); the claimed mapping onto the self is plausible but untested. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Volume 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Milton Model, Metaphorical suggestion, Indirect suggestion, Pragmatic enrichment.


#### Double meaning *(unit)*

Also called: pun, double entendre, semantic ambiguity, lexical ambiguity.

A single word or phrase that has two established meanings, placed so each fits: 'going down', 'let it sink in', 'falling' asleep, 'light'. One sense belongs to the surface topic and the other to the trance or the suggestion. It differs from sound-alike ambiguity (two different words) and from metaphor (a developed comparison); the work is done by one word.

**How:** Look for ordinary words that have both a literal and a state meaning: down, deep, drop, sink, fall, under, light, open, follow, absorbed. Put them in a sentence about the surface topic (stairs, water, a story) so the state meaning rides along. Works in text and audio. Too obvious a pun pulls the listener out to appreciate the joke.

> Let that idea sink in as you sink into the chair.

> Step by step, you are going down.

> It's so easy to follow where this voice leads.

**Spot it by:** words with a literal and a trance sense: down, deep, under, drop, sink, fall, light, open, absorbed, follow, lost, blank; the same word used twice in one sentence in two senses; an idiom whose literal reading also fits the scene ('sink in', 'let go', 'drift off', 'fall for'); a direction or position word in a scene that matches a depth word in the trance.

**Not to be confused with:** Sound-alike ambiguity (that uses two different words that sound the same; this uses one word with two senses); Metaphor (metaphor develops a parallel image or story; a double meaning rests on a single word); Interspersal (interspersal scatters suggestion words through unrelated narrative; label double meaning when one word is doing two jobs at once).

**Evidence:** rhetorical-tradition. Both senses of an ambiguous word are briefly active during comprehension, which is well established; that the second sense works as a suggestion is not.

**Why it works:** Equivocation, Spreading activation, Priming.

**Consent:** The second sense is meant to pass without comment; it should carry nothing the listener has not agreed to hear said plainly.


## Pacing and utilization

Also called: pacing and utilisation, meeting the listener where they are, accept and use.

This family groups devices that work by agreement with the listener's present reality instead of by instruction against it. Pacing devices describe what is already so (pacing, pacing trance signs, matching, normalizing, permission). Utilization devices take what the listener brings or what the setting throws up and assign it a role (utilization, incorporation of distractions, using the listener's own material). Pacing and leading is the bridge: it spends the credit that pacing earns.
