The family has no nested families; its nearest neighbours are the suggestion forms (truism, ratification, contingent suggestion) and resistance handling.

**Choosing:** Use pacing when you need agreement before you have earned it: the opening of a pretalk or induction. Use pacing and leading when you are ready to move the listener somewhere new. Use utilization and its variants when something could compete with the script: noise, restlessness, doubt, a wandering mind, the listener's own habits. Use normalizing and permission when the obstacle is worry about doing it wrong or shame about responding. Use pacing trance signs once the listener has had time to settle, so the signs you name are probably there. In a recording you cannot see the listener, so pace only what is true for nearly everyone, and write utilization as incorporation in advance.

**Not to be confused with:** Suggestion forms (that family is about how one suggestion is phrased; this one is about anchoring the script to the listener's actual situation); Resistance handling (resistance handling deals with opposition specifically; utilization takes anything the listener brings, opposition included).

**Why it works:** Pacing and leading, Utilization, Response expectancy theory, Common ground, Psychological reactance.


### Pacing *(unit)*

Also called: pacing current experience, verifiable statements, pacing statements, pacing ongoing experience.

Pacing is describing the listener's present experience in terms they can check at once: what they are doing, hearing, seeing or physically feeling at this moment. Each statement can be verified on the spot, so each one earns a small silent yes. It differs from a truism in that it is about this listener now, not a general fact about people; from mind reading in that it keeps to what can be checked and makes no claim about what the listener thinks or wants; and from pacing and leading in that it stops before any suggestion is added.

**How:** Open with it, before you ask for anything. In a recording, pace only what is true for almost every listener: they are hearing a voice, breathing, sitting or lying somewhere, reading or listening to these words. Keep each statement plain and neutral; any adjective the listener could dispute ("comfortable", "relaxed") turns a pace into a lead. Vary the sense channel (hearing, sight, body) so the run does not read as a list. A statement about what the listener is thinking is a guess; it is mind reading, not a pace. One wrong pace costs more than several right ones gain, so hedge with "perhaps" when unsure.

> You're listening to the sound of my voice. You're breathing in, and breathing out.

> You can feel the weight of your body where it rests, and the temperature of the air on your skin.

> You've set this time aside. You're reading these words, one after another.

**Spot it by:** second-person present-tense statements about the immediate situation: 'you are sitting', 'you can hear', 'you're breathing'; sensory verbs with neutral objects: hear the sounds, feel the chair, see the screen; references to the act of listening or reading itself: 'my voice', 'these words'; no evaluative or state words in the statement (no 'relaxed', 'deeper', 'calm'); typically at the opening of a script or section.

**Not to be confused with:** Truism (a truism is a general undeniable fact ('everyone has drifted off in a lecture'); pacing describes this listener's experience right now); Mind reading (mind reading claims what the listener is thinking, wondering or wanting, which they cannot check against the senses; pacing names only what they can verify (sitting, hearing, breathing, reading)); Pacing and leading (pacing and leading adds a suggested statement after the verifiable ones; pacing alone suggests nothing); Pacing trance signs (that entry paces specific signs and claims they mean trance; plain pacing attaches no meaning).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Taught in most clinical and Ericksonian texts; that accurate statements build agreement is plausible and consistent with acquiescence research, but pacing as a hypnotic device has not been isolated in controlled studies. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Vol. 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Pacing and leading, Common ground, Mere-agreement effect / acquiescence, Processing fluency, Epistemic trust.


### Pacing and leading *(unit)*

Also called: pace and lead, pace pace lead, pacing and leading statements, pace-lead.

A run of pacing statements is followed, in the same tone and grammar, by a statement that is not yet verifiable: the lead. The lead is delivered as if it were one more observation, so it tends to be accepted along with the rest. What marks it from plain pacing is the shift from fact to suggestion; what marks it from a yes set is that it is built from statements about present experience, not questions seeking an answer.

**How:** Start with more paces than leads (three to one is the usual teaching ratio) and reverse the ratio as the session goes on. Join pace to lead with 'and', 'as' or 'which means' so there is no seam. Keep the first leads small and close to what is likely anyway (a slower breath, a little more comfort) so they come true and become paces for the next round. It fails when a pace is false for the listener or when the lead jumps too far from the paces.

> You're sitting there, hearing my voice, feeling the chair beneath you, and you can begin to feel a little more settled.

> You're breathing in, and out. You're reading each word. Your shoulders are starting to soften.

> You've closed your eyes. You can hear the room around you. You can feel your hands resting. And something in you is beginning to slow down.

**Spot it by:** two or more verifiable present-tense statements followed by a state or change claim in the same sentence or the next; linkers between fact and suggestion: 'and', 'as', 'while', 'and that means'; final clause introduces a state word absent from the earlier clauses: relax, deeper, heavy, calm, drift; softeners on the last clause: 'you can begin to', 'you may notice'; ratio shifts over the passage: fewer verifiable statements per suggestion later on.

**Not to be confused with:** Yes set (a yes set seeks explicit or inner yes answers, often to questions and on any topic; pace and lead uses statements about present experience); Compound suggestion (compound suggestion is the single 'fact and suggestion' sentence form; pace and lead is the wider pattern of several paces and a shifting ratio); Contingent suggestion (contingent suggestion makes the response depend on a specific event ('as X, then Y'); here the paces only lend credibility).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. The pattern is taught everywhere and is plausible on acquiescence and fluency grounds, but the specific claims (ratios, that accepted paces transfer to the lead) have not been tested in controlled hypnosis studies. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Vol. 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Pacing and leading, Mere-agreement effect / acquiescence, Processing fluency, Common ground, Counterarguing.

**Consent:** The lead is meant to pass as one more observation; use it for responses the listener has agreed to pursue.


### Utilization *(unit)*

Also called: Ericksonian utilization, accept and use, utilization approach, utilisation.

Utilization treats any behavior, feeling, belief or event as usable: it is accepted as it is and then described as helping, or as the very route to the wanted response. Nothing is corrected or fought. It differs from reframing in that the thing is not only given a new meaning but put to work, and from resistance utilization in that it covers everything the listener brings, not only opposition.

**How:** Name the thing as it is, without judgment, then link it to the direction you want: 'and that can...'. Live, you use what you observe. In a recording, write for the common cases: fidgeting, a busy mind, doubt, an itch, laughing, wanting to open the eyes. Keep the link plausible; restlessness can 'settle on its own once it has moved enough', but claiming it is relaxation will not be believed. Use it early, so the listener learns that nothing they do is wrong.

> If your mind is busy, good. Let it stay busy. A busy mind can keep itself occupied while the rest of you settles.

> If you need to shift or scratch, go ahead, and notice how much easier it is to be still afterwards.

> If you feel like smiling or laughing, let it happen. Each laugh lets a little more tension out, and you can settle further once it has passed.

**Spot it by:** conditional naming of a listener behavior followed by acceptance: 'if you ... , that's fine', 'good', 'let it'; a behavior that would normally interfere (fidgeting, thinking, doubting, opening the eyes) described as useful; link phrases: 'and that can help you', 'use that', 'that is exactly what'; no instruction to stop or correct the behavior; 'whatever you ... is right' followed by a specific use, not only reassurance.

**Not to be confused with:** Using resistance (that entry covers the special case where the thing used is opposition or a contrary response); Reframing (reframing only changes what something means; utilization assigns it a function in the procedure); No-fail framing (no-fail framing declares every outcome a success; utilization takes one specific behavior and puts it to use).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. A core principle of Ericksonian practice supported by case reports; there are no controlled comparisons showing that utilization raises responsiveness beyond standard procedures. Source: Erickson, Further clinical techniques of hypnosis: Utilization techniques (1959).

**Why it works:** Utilization, Psychological reactance, Reframing, Response expectancy theory, Sociocognitive theory of hypnosis.


#### Incorporation of distractions *(variant)*

Also called: noise incorporation, incorporating sounds, utilizing distractions.

Incorporation is utilization applied to events in the environment: traffic, voices, a phone, a creak in the building. The script names them before or as they happen and says they belong to the experience, are unimportant, or help. It is narrower than utilization, which also covers what the listener does, feels and believes (a cough, an itch, a doubt), and it differs from 'everything deepens' in that its purpose is to stop a noise from breaking the state, not to turn all stimuli into deepeners.

**How:** Place it early in the induction, before the first interruption is likely. Name the category ('any sounds around you'), not a specific noise that may not occur. Offer one of three treatments: the sound fades into the background, the sound is a sign that all is well, or the sound helps. Pair it with an emergency clause so real alarms still get through. One or two sentences is enough; repeating it draws attention to the noises.

> Any sounds you hear around you, a car, a door, a voice in another room, are just the ordinary sounds of the world carrying on, and they can help you settle.

> If something makes a noise, you can notice it, let it go, and come back to my voice even more easily than before.

> The hum in the room can become part of this, a steady background that lets you rest.

**Spot it by:** 'any sounds', 'noises around you', 'outside sounds', 'whatever you hear'; a list of everyday interruptions: traffic, doors, phones, voices, a clock; outcome clauses: 'fade into the background', 'won't disturb you', 'only help you', 'part of the experience'; exception clause for emergencies nearby ('unless it needs your attention'); placed in the first minutes of an induction.

**Not to be confused with:** Everything deepens (that deepener declares every stimulus sends the listener deeper; incorporation only neutralizes or absorbs interruptions); Narrowing attention (narrowing attention makes everything but one thing fade; incorporation lets the distraction stay and gives it a place); Emergency wake (the emergency clause that often follows is a separate safety device).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Routine in clinical and recorded scripts; no controlled study isolates whether naming distractions in advance protects the state better than saying nothing.

**Why it works:** Utilization, Response expectancy theory, Habituation, Orienting response.


#### Using the listener's own material *(variant)*

Also called: subject-material utilization, using their words, using their interests, utilizing the listener's frame, symptom utilization.

This is utilization applied to content the listener supplied: their vocabulary for the state, their hobby, their job, their habitual way of doing things, or the problem itself. The suggestion is expressed in that material so that it reads as an extension of what they already think and do. It differs from matching, which copies style and tempo, in that it borrows subject matter and puts it to work as the vehicle of the suggestion.

**How:** Collect the material first: an intake question, a custom-script brief, or a line in the script that asks the listener to supply it ('think of the thing you do that absorbs you completely'). Then use their terms unchanged; a paraphrase loses the effect. Map the wanted response onto a skill or pattern they already have (a runner already knows how to find a rhythm and stop thinking). For general-audience recordings, leave a slot the listener fills inwardly, or write for a named audience whose shared interests you know.

> You told me that when you paint, hours go by without your noticing. You already know how to do this. Let it be like that now.

> Think of the word you would use for that settled feeling. Your word, not mine. Say it to yourself, and let it name what is happening.

> You said you can't switch your mind off. So don't. Give that busy mind the job of counting each breath out, the way you would check a list.

**Spot it by:** attribution to the listener: 'you told me', 'you said', 'as you described', 'your word for it'; a prompt for the listener to supply content, then reuse of it: 'think of a place you know... that place'; the listener's occupation, hobby or habit used as the model for the response ('the way you do when you ...'); quoted or unusual vocabulary repeated verbatim from an earlier listener statement; the presenting problem recast as a skill ('the same persistence that keeps you worrying').

**Not to be confused with:** Matching (matching mirrors tempo, breathing or sensory vocabulary for rapport; this entry builds the suggestion out of the listener's content); Analogy (an analogy can use any familiar thing; here the comparison is taken from what this listener supplied); Linking to values (values linking ties a suggestion to what the listener cares about as a reason; this uses their material as the form of the suggestion).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Rests on Erickson's case reports and later clinical teaching; tailored messages and self-relevant material are better remembered in general research, but this hypnotic use has not been tested directly. Source: Erickson & Rossi, Hypnotherapy: An Exploratory Casebook (1979).

**Why it works:** Utilization, Self-reference effect, Generation effect, Processing fluency, Rapport matching.


#### Using resistance *(variant)*

Also called: utilizing resistance, polarity response, resistance utilization.

The writer accepts the resistance and assigns it a role whose performance is the wanted response: hold the eyes open (so they tire), keep the hand down (so the effort becomes the focus), stay alert (so the alertness is watched). It differs from reverse psychology, which instructs the opposite of what is wanted, and from resistance as participation, which only re-describes resistance without giving it work to do.

**How:** Name the likely resistance without judgment, then hand it a specific job that ends in the response you want. Choose a job the listener can do fully, so success at resisting still lands in trance. Ratify whatever happens. It fails when the assigned task is something the listener can do indefinitely with no cost.

> Part of you wants to stay alert, and that part can keep watch, carefully, while the rest of you rests.

> Go ahead and keep those eyes open as long as you can. Really work at keeping them open.

> Hold on to that doubt tightly, so tightly that your hands begin to feel how much effort it takes.

**Spot it by:** acknowledgment of resistance followed by a task for it ('that part can...', 'let it...'); 'keep (doing X) as long as you can'; 'part of you wants to... and that part can...'; instructions to try harder at the resisted behavior.

**Not to be confused with:** Reverse psychology (reverse psychology tells the listener to do the opposite; using resistance assigns the resistance a task); Resistance as participation (resistance as participation re-describes resistance; using resistance gives it work); Reverse-set double bind (a reverse-set bind offers choices built for a contrary listener; using resistance needs no choice).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Standard in Ericksonian clinical teaching; there are no controlled studies of resistance utilization as a separate technique. Source: Erickson & Rossi, Hypnotherapy: An Exploratory Casebook (1979).

**Why it works:** Utilization, Psychological reactance, Therapeutic double bind, Ironic process theory.


### Normalizing *(unit)*

Also called: everyone does, it's natural, natural-state framing, normalization, it's perfectly normal.

Normalizing tells the listener that what they are experiencing, or are about to experience, is common and unremarkable. It removes the worry that a response is strange, a failure or a loss of control. It differs from social proof in that it describes the response as natural to people in general without citing what specific others did, and from myth correction in that it reassures without arguing against a stated false belief.

**How:** Place it in the pretalk and again wherever a response might alarm or embarrass: a wandering mind, twitching, tears, time slipping, not feeling much. State the experience, call it normal, and move on; one sentence is enough. Normalize a range ('some people feel heavy, some light, some notice very little at first') so no listener is left out. Do not use it to wave away real discomfort; that needs a safety or stop instruction, not reassurance.

> If your mind wanders, that's perfectly normal. Minds wander. It doesn't mean this isn't working.

> It's natural for the body to twitch or shift a little as it lets go.

> Some people feel heavy, some feel light, and some don't notice much the first time. All of that is ordinary.

**Spot it by:** verdict words applied to a response: 'normal', 'natural', 'perfectly normal', 'ordinary', 'common', 'to be expected'; reassurance clause: 'it doesn't mean anything is wrong', 'it doesn't mean this isn't working', 'nothing unusual'; 'it's natural to' or 'it's only natural that' followed by a response; a generic statement such as 'minds wander' followed by reassurance that this is ordinary or harmless; range statements ('some people ..., others ...') closed by a verdict that all of them are fine or ordinary.

**Not to be confused with:** Social proof (social proof reports what other people do or feel so the listener will expect or do the same ('most people find their hands get heavy first'); normalizing passes a verdict of normal, natural or nothing-wrong on something the listener might worry about. If the sentence carries that verdict, label normalizing even when it mentions other people; if it only reports what others do, label social proof); Truism (a truism is a bare undeniable fact used to build acceptance ('minds wander'); normalizing attaches the reassurance ('so it doesn't mean this isn't working')); Myth correction (myth correction names and rebuts a false belief about hypnosis; normalizing reassures about an experience); Permission (permission says the listener is allowed to respond; normalizing says the response is common).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Standard in clinical pretalks; reducing fear and raising positive expectancy are known to improve response, and descriptive norms influence behavior, but normalizing phrases themselves have not been tested alone.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Descriptive norms, Informational social influence, Sociocognitive theory of hypnosis, Metacognitive monitoring.


#### Everyday trance *(variant)*

Also called: highway hypnosis, you've done this before, common everyday trance, trance is natural.

The writer names familiar absorbed states (driving a known route without remembering it, losing track of time in a film or book, daydreaming, the moment before sleep) and says trance is the same kind of thing. This normalizes trance specifically, and gives the listener a memory to work from. It is a variant of normalizing because the claim is 'you have already done this many times'.

**How:** Use it in the pretalk or as the first move of a conversational induction. Give two or three examples so at least one fits; describe each with a concrete detail so the listener starts to recall it. Then draw the conclusion: this is the same, you already know how. If you go on to have the listener relive one example in detail, you have moved into revivification. Present it as a comparison, not as settled science; whether these states are the same as hypnosis is disputed.

> You've driven a familiar road and arrived with no memory of the last few miles. That was a kind of trance, and you did it without trying.

> It's like being so caught up in a film that you forget the room around you. You already know how to do that.

> You go through something like this every night in the moments before sleep. This is the same doorway, taken on purpose.

**Spot it by:** stock examples: driving and missing the exit, lost in a book or film, daydreaming, staring out of a window, just before sleep; 'you've done this before', 'you already know how', 'many times a day'; 'it's just like', 'the same as', 'a kind of trance'; the phrases 'everyday trance', 'natural state', 'highway hypnosis'; past-experience framing with 'you have' or 'remember a time when' followed by an equation to trance.

**Not to be confused with:** Revivification induction (that induction has the listener relive a past absorbed state in detail until it returns; this only cites such states as a likeness); Myth correction (myth correction rebuts a false belief ('hypnosis is not sleep'); this offers a positive comparison); Analogy (analogy is the general device of explaining by likeness; this is its specific use to make trance familiar).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. A standard pretalk move; trait absorption correlates modestly with hypnotizability, but whether everyday absorption is the same state as hypnosis is disputed, and the comparison works mainly by lowering fear and raising expectancy. Source: Erickson, Rossi & Rossi, Hypnotic Realities (1976).

**Why it works:** Absorption (trait), Response expectancy theory, Familiarity heuristic, Sociocognitive theory of hypnosis.


### Permission *(unit)*

Also called: it's okay to, comfort permission, permission giving, you're allowed to, giving permission.

Permission addresses a response that is already available but inhibited by politeness, self-consciousness, duty or fear of doing it wrong: letting go, moving, feeling something, not paying attention, enjoying it. The writer says outright that it is allowed. It differs from a permissive suggestion, which is a soft phrasing for introducing a new response, in that permission removes a restraint on one the listener is already close to.

**How:** Identify what this listener is likely to be holding back at this point, and name it plainly: 'it's okay to ...'. Place it just before the response is wanted, or right after normalizing it. Say who is granting it when that matters (the speaker, or the listener to themselves). Permission to do less (not listen, not try, not understand) is often the most useful. It fails when it permits something the listener has no pull toward; then it is only a weak suggestion.

> It's okay to stop paying attention to my words. You don't have to follow every one.

> You have permission to let your shoulders drop. Nobody needs anything from you right now.

> You're allowed to enjoy this. There's nothing you have to do to earn it.

**Spot it by:** 'it's okay to', 'it's all right to', 'it's fine to'; 'you're allowed to', 'you have permission to', 'I give you permission', 'give yourself permission'; an explicit option to release, rest, feel, move, or stop listening without disapproval; 'you don't have to' when it grants a specific choice ('you don't have to keep your eyes closed; you can open them'); generic instructions to stop trying or doing belong to not-doing-not-knowing; often follows a normalizing statement.

**Not to be confused with:** Permissive suggestion (permissive suggestion is the 'you may / you can' phrasing used to offer any response; permission lifts a restraint on a response the listener is holding back); Not doing / not knowing (that form says no effort or knowledge is needed so the response feels automatic; permission says the response is allowed); Asking permission (there the listener asks the speaker for permission; here the speaker grants it unasked).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Common in clinical and permissive-style scripts; it fits findings that autonomy-supportive wording reduces reactance, but explicit permission statements have not been tested as a separate hypnotic device.

**Why it works:** Psychological reactance, Self-determination theory, Response expectancy theory, Illocutionary force.

**Consent:** Permission can release things the listener was holding back for good reason; permit only what falls inside what they agreed to.


## Binds and choices

Also called: binds, choice patterns.

Devices in this family work on the listener's sense of choosing. Either the writer offers alternatives that all contain the target response (double bind and its variants), or the writer claims that only two options exist (false dilemma), or the writer makes the listener pick from a closed list (forced choice). What separates the family from presupposition in general is that a choice is explicitly on the table. Citing a choice the listener already made as proof of wanting the result is a different move and is filed under compliance as you-chose-this.

**Choosing:** Use a double bind when every offered alternative includes the agreed response. Choose illusion of choice for an inconsequential concrete detail, time bind for when the response happens, conscious-unconscious bind when conscious alternatives leave the unconscious response fixed, reverse-set bind for a listener whose opposition is established, and non-sequitur bind for an illogical choice. Use forced choice to require a pick from substantively different options, and false dilemma to claim that only two paths exist. To draw a conclusion from a choice already made, use you-chose-this under compliance. Keep the options acceptable to the listener, and leave the real choice to refuse or stop clear. The family has no nested families.

**Not to be confused with:** Presupposition and implication (presupposition builds a claim into any sentence; binds do it specifically through an offered or cited choice); Compliance and commitment (compliance devices build agreement over a series of steps; a bind works within one offer).

**Why it works:** Therapeutic double bind, Presupposition, Psychological reactance, Self-determination theory.

**Consent:** Binds give the feeling of choice without the substance, so the real choice (to take part at all, and to stop) must be offered plainly somewhere outside the bind.


### Double bind *(unit)*

Also called: therapeutic double bind, Ericksonian double bind, no-lose bind, bind, Or presupposition, whether-or, either-or presupposition, alternative question, disjunctive presupposition.

A double bind is an offer of alternatives in which the target response is common to every option. The listener's attention goes to choosing between the options, and the shared outcome is not put up for decision. Erickson and Rossi separated the bind (a choice between comparable alternatives that the listener makes consciously) from the double bind proper (where the response is assigned to something outside conscious choice); in common practitioner use, and here, the unit covers both and the variants carry the distinctions. It differs from an or-presupposition in that the alternatives are a real offer the listener is expected to take up, not just a clause in passing.

**How:** Decide the response you want, then find a detail of it that does not matter to you: speed, timing, side, manner, which part of the mind does it. Offer that detail as the choice, with 'or' between the options, and make both options easy and pleasant. Place it where the listener is already cooperating, usually late induction through suggestion; early in a pre-talk it reads as a sales trick. Follow it by accepting whichever happens ('that's right') and do not stack several binds in a row, which makes the pattern obvious.

> You can drift down slowly, or you can let go all at once. I don't mind which.

> Maybe the calm starts in your shoulders, or maybe in your hands. Find out which.

> Your eyes may close by themselves, or you may decide to close them. Either is fine.

**Spot it by:** 'X or Y' where both X and Y entail the same response; 'either ... or ...', 'whether ... or ...'; 'I don't know if ... or ...', 'I wonder whether ... or ...'; 'which', 'which one', 'find out which' applied to a detail of the response; disclaimer of preference after the offer: 'it doesn't matter which', 'whichever you prefer'.

**Not to be confused with:** False dilemma (a false dilemma offers two different outcomes and hides the others; a double bind offers alternatives that share the target outcome); Covering all possibilities (that lists every possible response including none; a bind offers a short set that all include the target); Forced choice (forced choice requires a pick from substantively different options; a double bind offers alternatives that share the target outcome, whether or not the listener is asked to pick one).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Standard in Ericksonian clinical texts; the presupposition it rests on is well studied, but the claim that binds outperform direct suggestion has no controlled support. Source: Erickson & Rossi, Varieties of Double Bind (1975).

**Why it works:** Therapeutic double bind, Presupposition accommodation, Presupposition, Psychological reactance, Indirect suggestion.

**Consent:** The listener is not offered the option of not responding, so use it only for responses they have already agreed to seek.


#### Illusion of choice *(variant)*

Also called: bind of comparable alternatives, alternative choice close, this chair or that, simple bind.

The plainest bind: the listener really does choose, and can say which they chose, but both options are versions of the same act. Erickson and Rossi called this a bind of comparable alternatives and treated it as the simple case, because the choice is made consciously and nothing is assigned to the unconscious. The salesperson's alternative-choice close has the same shape.

**How:** Offer two options that are concrete, equally acceptable and visibly trivial: which hand, which chair, eyes open or closed, this breath or the next. Use it early, in pre-talk and the first lines of induction, where an easy real choice starts cooperation. It fails when one option is plainly worse, or when the listener wanted neither, so do not use it to slip in something they have not agreed to.

> Would you like to go into trance sitting up or lying back?

> You can rest your hands in your lap or by your sides.

> Pick a spot to look at: one on the wall, or one on the ceiling.

**Spot it by:** 'would you like to ... or ...?', 'do you want to ... or ...?'; two concrete, physical or procedural options joined by 'or' (which hand, which chair, eyes open or closed); 'you can X or Y' where X and Y are both ways of doing the same thing; 'whichever is more comfortable', 'whichever you prefer', 'your choice'; question about manner or position placed before the main instruction; nothing later in the script depends on which option was taken.

**Not to be confused with:** Forced choice (forced choice demands a pick from options that differ in substance and uses the pick as commitment; here the options are equivalent); Time bind (label time bind when the only thing that varies is when); Double bind (that is an 'or' inside a sentence that moves on; here the listener is asked to actually choose).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Providing even trivial choice raises motivation and lowers reactance in experiments; that the hypnotic form increases response to the underlying suggestion is untested. Source: Erickson & Rossi, Varieties of Double Bind (1975).

**Why it works:** Presupposition accommodation, Psychological reactance, Self-determination theory, Commitment and consistency.

**Consent:** The choice offered is real but small; it does not stand in for asking whether the listener wants the session.


#### Conscious-unconscious double bind *(variant)*

Also called: conscious-unconscious bind, conscious/unconscious double bind, unconscious bind.

A double bind whose alternatives are assigned to two parts of the mind. Whatever the conscious mind does (listens, wanders, doubts, forgets) is allowed, and the response is given to the unconscious, which the listener cannot inspect or veto. Erickson and Rossi counted it among the double binds proper, because the response is placed outside conscious choice.

**How:** Write two clauses, usually joined by 'while', 'and' or 'or': the first releases the conscious mind from any task, the second states what the unconscious does. Make the conscious half something the listener is probably doing anyway, so it works as pacing. Use it once the idea of an unconscious mind has been introduced, and keep the unconscious task simple and checkable later (a hand lifting, a feeling arriving). It falls flat for listeners who reject the conscious/unconscious model, so introduce that model first or use a time bind instead.

> Your conscious mind can listen to my words, or wander off somewhere else, while your unconscious mind takes in everything it needs.

> Whether or not you consciously notice it happening, your unconscious has already begun to slow your breathing.

> If your unconscious is ready to relax further, one hand will start to feel lighter. If it wants a little longer, the other one will.

**Spot it by:** two or more options for the conscious mind joined by 'or' ('can listen, or wander') followed by a fixed statement about what the unconscious does; 'whether or not you consciously ...' followed by a response assigned to the unconscious in either case; 'you may or may not consciously notice/remember' followed by what the unconscious does regardless; paired 'if' branches in which the unconscious produces or directs a response in both branches; 'it doesn't matter whether your conscious mind X or Y' followed by a fixed unconscious response.

**Not to be confused with:** Conscious / unconscious split (the split addresses the unconscious as a separate listener and offers no alternatives; label the bind only when the span states alternatives ('or', 'whether or not', paired 'if' branches) and the response is assigned to the unconscious in all of them. A plain 'your conscious mind can wander while your unconscious listens' is the split); Not doing / not knowing (that only releases the listener from effort; the bind also assigns the response to the unconscious); Implied directive (an implied directive adds a time clause and a signal that the inner response has happened; it can contain this bind).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. A staple of Ericksonian texts; the 'unconscious mind' it addresses is a working metaphor, and no controlled study shows the bind itself adds to response beyond the expectancy it sets. Source: Erickson & Rossi, Varieties of Double Bind (1975).

**Why it works:** Therapeutic double bind, Neodissociation theory, Response expectancy theory, Cold control theory, Automaticity.

**Consent:** It tells the listener the response is outside their conscious say, so pair it with a clear statement elsewhere that they can stop at any time.


#### Time bind *(variant)*

Also called: time double bind, now or in a moment, now or later bind.

A double bind whose alternatives are points or spans of time. Every option is a time at which the response occurs, so the only open question is its timing. It is the easiest bind to write and the hardest to fail, because one of the offered times always arrives.

**How:** Name two or three times for the response: now or in a moment, on this breath or the next, before I finish counting or after. Include a slow option so that a listener who has not responded yet is still inside the suggestion. It suits eye closure, deepening and posthypnotic responses. Keep the window short enough that the listener notices the response within it; 'today or sometime this week' is too loose to feel like anything.

> Your eyes can close now, or in a few more breaths.

> I don't know whether you'll feel that calm settle in before I reach one, or just after.

> You might notice the change tonight, or it might be tomorrow morning.

**Spot it by:** 'now or in a moment', 'now or later', 'right away or in a little while'; 'on this breath or the next'; 'before ... or after ...' with the same response in both; 'I don't know whether ... now or ...', 'I wonder if it will be ... or ...' naming two or more times; 'today or tomorrow', 'tonight or in the morning' attached to a stated response; two or more named times or counts joined by 'or', with no option in which the response does not occur.

**Not to be confused with:** Time-clause presupposition (a time clause ('before you go deeper') presupposes the response with no choice offered; a time bind offers alternative times); Self-paced wake (that hands over the timing of waking as a courtesy, not as a way to secure a response); Illusion of choice (label illusion of choice when the options differ in manner or place, not time).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Described in Ericksonian texts and widely used; no controlled comparison with a plain timed suggestion exists. Source: Erickson & Rossi, Varieties of Double Bind (1975).

**Why it works:** Therapeutic double bind, Presupposition accommodation, Response expectancy theory.

**Consent:** When the response is one that lasts past the session, the bind removes 'never' as an option, so the listener should have agreed to that response beforehand.


#### Non-sequitur double bind *(variant)*

Also called: non-sequitur bind, illogical bind.

A double bind in which the options sound alike in content but do not follow from one another, or the link between option and outcome is absent. The sentence has the form of a choice or a conditional, so the listener starts working out the logic, finds none, and is left with the one thing both halves share: the response. It combines a bind with a small dose of confusion.

**How:** Keep the grammar clean and the delivery matter-of-fact; the illogic must be in the content only. Both halves should mention or lead to the same response in similar words. Use it sparingly, with listeners who over-analyze or as a light confusion beat before a direct suggestion, and follow it at once with a plain instruction. Used on someone who is simply listening it is noise, and several in a row sound like a mistake.

> Do you want to settle into that chair before you relax, or relax while you settle into that chair?

> You can go into trance with your eyes closed, or close your eyes as you go into trance.

> Will your left hand feel lighter while the chair remembers your name, or will the chair remember your name while your left hand feels lighter? Now, notice that hand.

**Spot it by:** 'or' joining two clauses that restate each other with the order of terms swapped; 'either ... or ...' or 'would you rather ... or ...' where the second option shares words with the first but is not an alternative to it; same response word in both halves of an offered choice; question form that cannot be answered by picking a side; plain direct instruction immediately after an illogical choice.

**Not to be confused with:** Non sequitur (a non sequitur is any irrelevant statement used to confuse; label the bind only when it is framed as alternatives that share an outcome); Confusion technique (confusion technique is sustained disorientation over a passage; this is a single choice-shaped sentence); Chiasmus (chiasmus is the ABBA word order as style; here the reversal is offered as a choice between two things).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Named and illustrated by Erickson and Rossi from case material; it has not been studied on its own, and its effect cannot be separated from ordinary confusion. Source: Erickson & Rossi, Varieties of Double Bind (1975).

**Why it works:** Therapeutic double bind, Ericksonian confusion technique, Cognitive load, Expectation violation.

**Consent:** It works by the listener failing to track the logic, so it belongs only in sessions where confusion methods were agreed to or are expected.


#### Reverse-set double bind *(variant)*

Also called: reverse-set bind, polarity bind, you won't until, reverse set.

A double bind built for a listener who is in the habit of opposing. The writer forbids, doubts or delays the wanted response, so that defying the writer means producing it, while obeying the writer is also acceptable (usually it just postpones it). In Erickson's version a run of statements first establishes the habit of contradicting, and the key statement is then delivered in reversed form.

**How:** Use it only where opposition is real or expected: a listener who says 'that won't work on me', or a script that has invited resistance. State the wanted response as something they will not, cannot or should not do yet, and make the compliant reading harmless: 'you won't go under until you're ready' is fine whether they wait or not. Do not use it on a cooperative listener, who will simply do what the words say and hold back. It is weaker in recordings, where you cannot see whether the listener is opposing.

> You won't go all the way down until you're completely sure you want to.

> You're not comfortable yet. You don't want to close your eyes. And you certainly can't go into trance sitting in that chair.

> You probably can't let your eyes close yet, and that's fine. They can stay open and get heavier, or close anyway.

**Spot it by:** 'you won't ... until ...' where the text also offers a route to the wanted response after the wait; a negated or doubted wanted response paired with explicit alternatives that both lead toward it: 'stay open and grow heavier, or close anyway'; 'either way' after the two reactions, followed by the shared wanted response; a run of negative statements that visibly establishes the listener's contradiction before the wanted response is stated in reverse form; 'I doubt you can ... yet' followed by an explicit account of what happens if the listener waits and if they prove the speaker wrong.

**Not to be confused with:** Reverse psychology (a bare opposite instruction pays off if defied; label a reverse-set bind when the text establishes a pattern of the listener contradicting the speaker and then reverses the wanted response, or when it explicitly gives both compliance and defiance paths to the wanted response. An 'until' clause alone only postpones it); Negative suggestion (that names the response under a negation; it can co-occur, but negation alone does not establish opposition or a bind); Challenge suggestion (a challenge invites an attempt expected to fail as proof; this uses established opposition or explicitly covers both reactions).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Rests on Erickson's case reports; reactance, the tendency it exploits, is well established, but the bind itself has not been tested and depends on correctly judging that the listener is opposing. Source: Erickson & Rossi, Varieties of Double Bind (1975).

**Why it works:** Psychological reactance, Therapeutic double bind, Ironic process theory, Utilization.

**Consent:** It turns the listener's refusal into the response, so it must not be used to override an actual wish to stop; a real 'no' ends the session.


### False dilemma *(unit)*

Also called: false dichotomy, either-or fallacy, black-and-white framing, false choice.

A false dilemma narrows a situation to two outcomes that really are different, and leaves out the rest. Usually one option is made unattractive so the other wins by elimination. Unlike a double bind, the two options do not lead to the same place: the device works by what is hidden, not by what is shared.

**How:** State the two options in strong, parallel terms and make the contrast feel complete: hold on or let go, think or feel, the old way or this one. Put it at a decision point, in pre-talk or just before a key suggestion, and let the listener reject the bad option themselves. It lands when the missing middle is not obvious and fails the moment the listener thinks of a third option, so it suits absorbed listeners and short passages. In copy it is an argument; say less and move on.

> You can keep carrying all that tension, or you can put it down. There isn't a third thing.

> Either you're thinking, or you're relaxing. You can't do both.

> There are two kinds of listeners: the ones who analyze every word, and the ones who let it work.

**Spot it by:** 'either ... or ...' with two different outcomes, one clearly worse; 'there are only two ...', 'two kinds of ...', 'you have two choices'; 'you can't do both', 'there is no middle', 'no third option'; 'if you're not X, you're Y'; 'the only alternative is ...', 'it's this or ...'.

**Not to be confused with:** Double bind (in a double bind both options give the same outcome; here they differ and the other possibilities are hidden); Antithesis (antithesis sets two opposed ideas side by side for style without claiming they are the only options); Forced choice (forced choice asks the listener to pick; a false dilemma is a claim about what options exist and may ask for nothing).

**Evidence:** rhetorical-tradition. A long-catalogued informal fallacy; framing research shows that restricting the options offered shapes choices, but the figure as such is described, not measured.

**Why it works:** False dilemma, Framing effect, Agenda-setting, Contrast effect.

**Consent:** It works by the listener not noticing the omitted options; do not use it to frame stopping or leaving as one of two bad choices.


### Forced choice *(unit)*

Also called: closed choice, which do you choose, choice point, pick one.

A forced choice is a demand to select one of a closed set of options, with a pause for the listener to do it. The options differ in substance, and the act of choosing is the point: the listener has done something and now owns the result. It differs from a double bind in that the options need not lead to the same place, and from a false dilemma in that the listener is made to answer.

**How:** Give two or three clearly worded options, tell the listener to choose, and leave a real pause. Say how to answer: aloud, with a nod, or silently. Then refer back to the choice as theirs and carry on from it; in branching scripts each option leads to its own section, in linear ones the follow-up must fit any pick. It fails without the pause, with more than three options, or when the options are so alike that choosing means nothing. For a detail that does not matter, use illusion of choice instead.

> Choose now: do you want to go deeper, or stay right where you are? Say it in your mind.

> Three doors. Rest, focus, or confidence. Pick one, and only one.

> Calm or energy: which do you want from tonight? Nod once for calm, twice for energy. ... Good.

**Spot it by:** imperatives of choosing: 'choose', 'pick', 'decide', 'select'; 'which do you choose?', 'which is it?', 'which one?'; an enumerated or lettered list of options followed by a pause marker; 'only one', 'you have to pick', 'you can't have both'; instruction on how to answer: 'say it aloud', 'nod', 'answer in your mind'.

**Not to be confused with:** Illusion of choice (there the options are equivalent ways to do the same thing; here they differ in substance and the listener is required to select one); You chose this (that is the later reference back to a choice as proof of wanting ('you chose this'); forced choice covers only the options and the demand to pick); Asking for a yes (that asks for a yes to one proposal; forced choice asks for a selection among several); Consent check (a consent check offers stopping as a real, unpenalized option; a forced choice restricts the listener to the writer's list).

**Evidence:** experimental. Choosing among options reliably raises liking for and commitment to the chosen one in laboratory studies; whether a silent choice made while listening to a script has the same effect has not been tested.

**Why it works:** Commitment and consistency, Cognitive dissonance, Self-perception theory, Generation effect, Agenda-setting.

**Consent:** If none of the listed options is acceptable the listener has no stated way out, so a session using it should offer a real exit elsewhere and must not treat a forced pick as consent.


## Confusion and overload

Also called: confusion techniques, overload techniques, disruption techniques.

A family of devices that interfere with the listener's running evaluation of what is said. Some break meaning (confusion technique, paradox, non sequitur), some break sequence (pattern interrupt, shock, unfinished sentence), some exceed capacity (cognitive overload, concurrent task, rapid delivery), and some under-feed attention until it lapses (monotony). What unites them is the second half: a plain, easy suggestion placed at the moment of disruption. Without that follow-up the listener is only confused or annoyed.

**Choosing:** Choose by what you want to disturb. To break meaning, use confusion-technique or one of its variants, paradox for a single contradiction, or semantic-satiation to wear one word down to sound; to break an expected sequence, use pattern-interrupt, shock-surprise or incomplete-sentence; to exceed or divert capacity, use cognitive-overload, dual-task, distraction-of-conscious-mind or fast-speech; to let vigilance run down, use boredom-monotony. Write the clear instruction that follows, and keep the disruption short enough that the listener can still follow it. The induction family holds the full-induction forms (confusion-induction, overload-induction, rapid-induction, double-induction); disrupt-then-reframe in the compliance family is the sales-research version.

**Not to be confused with:** Artful vagueness (vagueness leaves content open for the listener to fill in; this family blocks or overworks the filling-in); Resistance handling (resistance handling addresses doubt by naming or using it; this family goes around evaluation without addressing it); Attention and absorption (absorption narrows attention onto one thing; this family splits, jams or drains it).

**Why it works:** Cognitive load, Working-memory interference, Distraction-induced persuasion, Counterarguing, Ericksonian confusion technique, Pattern interruption.

**Consent:** These devices work by reducing the listener's ability to evaluate what follows, so what follows should be something the listener agreed to beforehand.


### Confusion technique *(unit)*

Also called: Ericksonian confusion, confusion-restructuring, confusional language.

Wording that sounds as if it should make sense but resists being worked out, followed at once by a clear, easy suggestion. The confusion can be a passage or a brief non sequitur. It is built from ordinary words and correct-seeming grammar, so the listener may keep trying to follow. It differs from cognitive overload, which adds more to track, and from paradox, which presents a contradiction: here the meaning keeps slipping.

**How:** Start from true, simple statements so the listener commits to following, then tangle one dimension (time, direction, negation, sound-alikes) for two to five sentences. Deliver it seriously and at an even pace, as if it were perfectly clear. End with a short, plain suggestion in a different rhythm: this is the part that matters. It fails when it is so obviously nonsense that the listener stops trying, or when no clear suggestion follows.

> You can know that you don't know what you already knew before you knew you were relaxing, and you don't need to know. Just let go.

> Part of you is listening to the part that isn't listening, and it doesn't matter which part is which. Close your eyes.

> The thought you were about to think is not the thought you think it was, and as it slips away, you can simply rest.

**Spot it by:** one word repeated in shifting senses within a sentence (know, think, part, right); long sentence with nested clauses that does not resolve to a clear claim; short plain imperative directly after a dense passage; 'it doesn't matter', 'you don't need to work it out', 'just let ...' closing the passage; mixed tenses, directions or negations in one sentence.

**Not to be confused with:** Cognitive overload (overload is too much to track; confusion is content that will not resolve); Confusion induction (that is a whole induction built on this device; this is the device wherever it appears); Disrupt then reframe (that is one odd phrase plus a reframe in a request; this is a sustained passage plus a suggestion).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Standard in Ericksonian texts and supported by case reports; controlled comparisons with plain inductions are few and do not show an advantage. Source: Erickson, 'The Confusion Technique in Hypnosis', American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1964).

**Why it works:** Ericksonian confusion technique, Confusion-restructuring, Cognitive load, Processing fluency, Counterarguing.

**Consent:** It works by making the following suggestion harder to weigh, so use it only to deliver what the listener came for.


#### Time confusion *(variant)*

Also called: today tomorrow yesterday, temporal confusion, time disorientation.

A confusion passage built from time words: days, tenses and before/after relations are stacked so each clause is true but the whole cannot be held. It is the confusion technique with time as the tangled dimension. It differs from time distortion, which plainly suggests that time feels slow or fast, and from temporal presupposition, which uses one clear time clause.

**How:** Begin with an obvious truth about today, then restate it from the viewpoint of yesterday and tomorrow, shifting tense each clause. Keep every clause defensible; the listener should feel that it would make sense with enough effort. Close with a present-tense suggestion, or use the loosened sense of time to lead into regression or future progression.

> Today is the tomorrow you thought about yesterday, and tomorrow, today will be the yesterday you can hardly remember. So right now is the only time to relax.

> Before you had started, you had not yet finished what you will have begun later, and by then it won't matter when it was.

> Last week's next week is this week, and next week this week will be last week, and all that time you can go on resting.

**Spot it by:** 'yesterday', 'today', 'tomorrow' (or last/this/next) recombined in one sentence; three or more tense shifts in one sentence; future perfect and past perfect close together ('will have', 'had not yet'); 'before ... after ... before' stacked; ends by resolving to 'now' or 'right now'.

**Not to be confused with:** Time distortion (that states that time stretches or shrinks; this scrambles time references without claiming anything); Time-clause presupposition (one clear time clause that presupposes; nothing is tangled); Age regression (regression sends the listener to a specific earlier time; time confusion may precede it but is only the scrambling).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Described by Erickson as a lead-in to regression; known from case reports, not controlled tests. Source: Erickson, 'The Confusion Technique in Hypnosis', American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1964).

**Why it works:** Ericksonian confusion technique, Cognitive load, Working-memory interference.


#### Left-right confusion *(variant)*

Also called: here-there confusion, directional confusion, spatial confusion, this-that confusion.

A confusion passage built from direction and pointing words. It leans on the two meanings of 'right' and 'left' (direction; correct; remaining) and on words whose reference shifts with viewpoint. It is the confusion technique with space or the body as the tangled dimension, and it often feeds straight into a hand or arm suggestion.

**How:** Direct attention to the hands first so the listener has something to track. Then swap the labels quickly, using 'right' as correct and 'left' as remaining alongside their directional senses. Finish with a simple physical suggestion (one hand lifts, both rest, eyes close). In audio the listener cannot re-read, so two or three sentences are enough; in text, readers can parse it, so keep it moving.

> Your right hand is the one that's left when the left hand isn't right, and that's right, isn't it? Let whichever one is left grow heavy.

> What's here for you is there for me, and what's there is here once you go there, so wherever here is, settle into it.

> This hand, not that hand, unless that one is this one, can start to feel lighter now.

**Spot it by:** 'right' and 'left' several times in one sentence, in more than one sense; 'here' and 'there', or 'this' and 'that', swapped within a sentence; 'that's right' placed inside a left/right passage; 'whichever', 'the one that's left', 'the other one'; followed by a hand, arm or eye suggestion.

**Not to be confused with:** Circular wordplay (wordplay loops on any sound-alike; this is specifically direction and place words); Apposition of opposites (that pairs two opposed experiences clearly (one rises, one sinks); here the labels are scrambled); Double meaning (a single pun that serves the suggestion, not a pile-up meant to confuse).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. A common worked example in Ericksonian and NLP training; no controlled tests of the variant itself.

**Why it works:** Ericksonian confusion technique, Cognitive load, Working-memory interference, Equivocation.


#### Stacked negation *(variant)*

Also called: double negatives, you can't not, multiple negation, triple negative.

A sentence with two, three or more negatives whose net meaning takes effort to compute. The usual net meaning is the suggestion itself, so the listener either works it out and arrives at the suggestion or gives up and takes the named response. It differs from negative suggestion, which uses one negation to name a response.

**How:** Decide the net meaning first, then wrap it in negatives: 'can't not', 'don't have to not', 'never fail to'. Two negatives read as emphasis; three or more start to confuse. Use one or two such sentences and follow with a positive, simple statement of the same suggestion. Check the arithmetic, because an odd count reverses the meaning.

> You can't not notice that you don't have to not relax.

> There's no reason you shouldn't fail to stay tense, and nothing you need to not do about it. So let the shoulders drop.

> You don't have to not listen, and you can't fail to not hold on. So let go.

**Spot it by:** 'can't not', 'won't not', 'don't not'; three or more of not / n't / never / no / nothing / un- in one sentence; negated failure verbs: 'never fail to', 'not unable to', 'can't avoid not'; 'no reason you shouldn't', 'nothing you need to not do'; plain positive restatement in the next sentence.

**Not to be confused with:** Negative suggestion (one negation that names the response; meaning is clear); Reverse psychology (a clear instruction to do the opposite, not a meaning that must be computed); Not doing / not knowing (a clear statement that no effort is needed; negation is not stacked).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Negated sentences are reliably slower to process and more error-prone; that this helps a suggestion land is practitioner claim.

**Why it works:** Cognitive load, Processing fluency, Ironic process theory, Ericksonian confusion technique.


#### Non sequitur *(variant)*

Also called: irrelevancy, out-of-context remark, illogical statement.

A statement that has no connection to what came before, or that draws a conclusion that does not follow, spoken in the same tone as the rest. The listener searches for the link and finds none. It is a confusion device made of one sentence, where the main confusion technique is a sustained passage.

**How:** Place it mid-passage, between two normal sentences, and do not mark it with a pause or a change of voice. Make it grammatical and concrete, not random word salad. Follow it immediately with a clear suggestion, while the listener is still looking for the connection. One per passage is usually enough; several in a row become comedy.

> Your breathing is slowing, and the chairs in a waiting room are always the same colour, so you can let your eyes close.

> Because Tuesday comes after rain, your shoulders already know how to drop.

> You're doing well. A door only has two sides. Now go deeper.

**Spot it by:** sentence with no topical link to its neighbours; 'so', 'because', 'which means' joining unrelated clauses; concrete everyday fact (weather, furniture, weekdays) inside a trance passage; imperative or suggestion directly after the odd sentence; no acknowledgement that anything odd was said.

**Not to be confused with:** Non-sequitur double bind (a bind offers two unlinked alternatives as a choice; this is a statement, not a choice); Cause-effect link (a causal link the listener can accept as plausible; a non sequitur is meant not to connect); Shock / surprise (shock relies on suddenness or intensity; a non sequitur is flat and only fails to follow).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Erickson described out-of-context remarks as a core of his confusion method; the nearest controlled work is on disrupt-then-reframe, a sales setting. Source: Erickson, 'The Confusion Technique in Hypnosis', American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1964).

**Why it works:** Expectation violation, Prediction error, Ericksonian confusion technique, Narrative coherence.


#### Circular wordplay *(variant)*

Also called: know/no, mind your mind, homophone loop, looping wordplay.

A confusion passage built by repeating one word, its other senses and its homophones (know/no, here/hear, mind as noun and verb, right/write) in a circular sentence. The device is the pile-up: each use alone is clear. It differs from a single sound-alike ambiguity or pun, which carries a second meaning without trying to confuse.

**How:** Pick a word that has a homophone or works as both noun and verb, and that suits the suggestion (know, mind, hear, feel, right). Write one or two sentences that return to it five or more times, changing sense each time. It is strongest heard, since spelling disambiguates homophones on the page. End on a short clear line.

> You know there's no need to know what you know, and no one knows that better than you. So let it go.

> You can mind your mind, or never mind your mind, and your mind won't mind either way.

> Hear what's here, and here is where you hear it, and you don't have to be anywhere but here.

**Spot it by:** one word or homophone pair five or more times in one or two sentences; know/no, here/hear, right/write, mind (noun)/mind (verb), there/their; sentence that ends on the word it began with; same word as noun and verb in one clause; release line after the loop ('let it go', 'never mind').

**Not to be confused with:** Left-right confusion (when the looped words are direction or pointing words (right, left, here, there, this, that) used about the body or the room, label left-right confusion; label this for any other looped word); Semantic satiation (the same word in the same sense repeated back to back until it is only sound; here the word changes sense or spelling at each return and sits in a grammatical sentence); Sound-alike ambiguity (one sound-alike carrying a hidden instruction, not a loop built to confuse); Double meaning (a single pun where both senses serve the suggestion).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Widely taught in Ericksonian and NLP training; no independent test of its effect.

**Why it works:** Equivocation, Cognitive load, Ericksonian confusion technique.


### Pattern interrupt *(unit)*

Also called: pattern interruption, interrupt, interrupted routine.

A familiar, automatic sequence (a handshake, a count, a stock phrase, a breathing rhythm the script has set up) is stopped before its expected next step. For a moment the listener has no prepared response, and a suggestion placed there meets less evaluation. It differs from shock, which needs no established pattern, and from an unfinished sentence, which is left hanging with no instruction replacing the missing part.

**How:** The pattern must be automatic before you break it: use one the listener already has (counting, the alphabet, a common saying) or build one by repeating it several times in the script. Break it at the point of strongest expectation and put the instruction immediately after, with no pause to explain. In recorded audio the physical forms are unavailable, so interrupt counts, rhythms, refrains and sentence frames. It fails when the pattern was not established or when the instruction comes late.

> Five... four... three... sleep.

> Breathe in... and out. In... and out. In... and hold it. Now drop.

> A, B, C, D, and you've already stopped thinking about the next letter. Rest.

**Spot it by:** a count, list or alphabet that stops before its end; a repeated frame or refrain broken on its fourth or later repetition; 'sleep', 'drop', 'stop', 'now' at the break point; a stock saying cut off and replaced by an instruction; stage direction for a sudden stop or change mid-sequence.

**Not to be confused with:** Shock / surprise (shock needs no prior pattern; an interrupt depends on one being under way); Unfinished sentence (that leaves the gap open for the listener; here the gap is filled with an instruction); Rapid induction (that is an induction that uses an interrupt plus a sleep command; this is the interrupt wherever it occurs).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Unexpected events do capture attention and briefly halt ongoing action; that this opens a window of raised suggestibility is practitioner claim, not an established finding.

**Why it works:** Pattern interruption, Prediction error, Orienting response, Expectation violation, Automaticity.

**Consent:** It is built to land an instruction before the listener can weigh it, so the instruction should be one they have already agreed to receive.


### Cognitive overload *(unit)*

Also called: overload, working-memory overload, attention overload.

Several simultaneous demands on attention: multiple sensations to monitor, a task to perform, more than one voice or stream. Each item is clear by itself; the quantity is what defeats tracking. It differs from the confusion technique, where a single stream will not make sense, and from sensory immersion, where many details build one coherent scene.

**How:** Add items one at a time and tell the listener to keep all of them going: this breath, that hand, a sound, a count. Four or five concurrent items is usually past what people hold. Then offer the release, either by giving one simple thing to do or by permitting them to let everything go. Unlike confusion, this works on listeners who would dismiss nonsense, because every instruction is reasonable.

> Keep feeling your left foot, and the air at your nostrils, and count your breaths, and listen to the sounds outside the room, and notice your right thumb, all at once.

> Hold the number in mind, keep following my voice, feel both hands, and watch the colour behind your eyelids. When it's too much, let all of it go.

> Track the breath, the heartbeat, the weight of your legs and every third word I say. Or just stop keeping track.

**Spot it by:** 'at the same time', 'all at once', 'while also', 'and keep ...'; list of four or more concurrent objects of attention; 'keep track of', 'hold in mind', 'don't lose'; release line: 'let it all go', 'too much to follow', 'stop keeping track'; stage direction for two voices or streams at once.

**Not to be confused with:** Confusion technique (confusion is one stream that will not resolve; overload is many clear streams); Overload induction (that is a full induction built on overload; this is the device at any point in a script); Sensory immersion (dense detail that builds one scene to absorb the listener, not competing items to track).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Working-memory limits and reduced counterarguing under load are well established; overload as a way to produce hypnotic response has not been independently tested, and Miller's 'seven plus or minus two' is routinely over-applied.

**Why it works:** Cognitive load, Working-memory interference, Distraction-induced persuasion, Counterarguing, Dual-process theory.

**Consent:** Suggestions given under load are harder for the listener to assess, so keep them within what was agreed.


### Shock / surprise *(unit)*

Also called: startle, unexpected statement, surprise technique, shock technique.

A single unexpected event: a sharp sound, a sudden change of volume, or a statement the listener did not see coming. It needs no pattern set up beforehand, which separates it from the pattern interrupt. It is brief and intense, which separates it from the non sequitur, whose oddness is flat.

**How:** Set a calm, even baseline first, since surprise is measured against what came before. Use the shock once, at a chosen point, and follow it within a second with a short suggestion. For a verbal shock, a blunt true statement or an unexpected permission works better than something alarming. Avoid it with anxious listeners and near sleep endings; repeated shocks stop surprising.

> ...and as you drift, soft and slow, [sharp snap] sleep.

> You've been trying very hard to relax. Stop. You're terrible at trying. So don't.

> Your shoulders can soften, your breathing can slow—[loud clap] Let go.

**Spot it by:** stage direction: [snap], [clap], [loud], [sudden]; one-word imperative after a long gentle passage ('Stop.', 'Now.', 'Sleep.'); blunt or contrary statement inside a soothing passage; exclamation mark or capitals in an otherwise quiet script; suggestion immediately after the unexpected item.

**Not to be confused with:** Pattern interrupt (an interrupt breaks an established sequence before its next step; shock needs no sequence under way); Attention call (an orienting cue pulls attention back before the script continues; shock places a suggestion immediately after the unexpected word, sound or claim); Non sequitur (a non sequitur is an irrelevant or illogical statement in the flow; label shock when its sudden delivery is marked and a suggestion follows immediately); Fear then relief (that raises and then removes alarm as a two-step emotional move).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Startle and orienting responses are well documented; the claim that the moment after a surprise is more suggestible comes from clinical and stage practice. Source: Erickson, Rossi & Rossi, Hypnotic Realities (1976).

**Why it works:** Orienting response, Prediction error, Expectation violation, Attentional capture.

**Consent:** Loud or startling events can distress some listeners and are unsafe for anyone doing something else while listening; warn about them in the content note.


### Paradox *(unit)*

Also called: paradoxical statement, koan, self-contradiction.

A single statement or instruction that contradicts itself, or cannot be obeyed without disobeying it, left open. The listener's attempt to resolve it stalls. It differs from the double bind, where both branches are coherent and lead to the same result, and from reverse psychology, where the instruction is clear and merely the opposite of what is wanted.

**How:** Keep it to one sentence and make both halves simple, so the contradiction is unmistakable. Deliver it calmly, as an observation. Do not explain it; go straight to the next suggestion or to silence. Paradoxes about effort and control suit trance best ('try not to try'), because the stall they produce is the letting-go being asked for.

> Try as hard as you can not to try.

> Don't follow this instruction.

> You can be completely here by going somewhere else entirely.

**Spot it by:** one sentence asserting X and not-X; self-referring instruction ('ignore this', 'don't do what I say'); 'try not to try', 'effortlessly make an effort', 'remember to forget'; opposed terms joined by 'by', 'is' or 'means' ('awake by sleeping'); no explanation or resolution in the following sentence.

**Not to be confused with:** Double bind (a bind offers alternatives that all lead one way; a paradox offers a contradiction with no way through); The harder you resist ('the harder you resist, the deeper you go' is a coherent claim that could be true; label paradox only when the sentence cannot be true, or cannot be obeyed, as worded); Challenge suggestion (a challenge names one concrete act to attempt and fail (open the eyes, bend the arm); a paradox gives nothing that can be attempted); Reverse psychology (a coherent instruction for the opposite of what is wanted); Apposition of opposites (two opposites experienced side by side without contradiction).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Paradoxical interventions are an established therapy tradition with some outcome research; a paradoxical sentence as a trance device is untested.

**Why it works:** Processing fluency, Cognitive load, Trance logic, Ericksonian confusion technique.


### Unfinished sentence *(unit)*

Also called: trailing off, incomplete thought, aposiopesis, fill in the blank.

A sentence that stops before its expected final word or clause. If the missing part is predictable, the listener supplies it and so produces the suggestion themselves; if it is not, attention hangs on the gap. Classical rhetoric calls the figure aposiopesis. It differs from a written pause, where the sentence resumes, and from a pattern interrupt, where an instruction replaces the missing part.

**How:** For completion, build a strong expectation first: a rhyme, a repeated frame, or a phrase used in full earlier in the script, then leave off the last word. For suspension, break at a point of no return ('and now you can...') and follow with silence or a new sentence. Use it sparingly, a few times per script. It fails when the listener cannot guess the ending and nothing is done with the gap.

> And with every breath out, you go deeper and...

> Down, and down, and all the way...

> You already know what happens when I count to...

**Spot it by:** sentence ending in an ellipsis or dash with the grammar incomplete; final word missing from a phrase given in full earlier; line ending on 'and', 'to', 'the', 'so', 'because', 'you can'; next sentence starts a new thought and does not resume; stage direction for a pause or silence after the break.

**Not to be confused with:** Written pause (a pause inside a sentence that then continues to its end); Pattern interrupt (the break is filled at once with an instruction); Unstated premise (an argument with a missing premise; the sentences themselves are complete); Curiosity hook (a complete promise or question whose answer is delayed for minutes, not a broken sentence).

**Evidence:** rhetorical-tradition. A classical figure; self-generated material is better remembered than supplied material, but the hypnotic use is untested and the Zeigarnik effect it is often credited to has a mixed replication record.

**Why it works:** Generation effect, Zeigarnik effect, Narrative closure, Prediction error.


### Monotony *(unit)*

Also called: boredom induction, droning, monotonous delivery, boring the listener into trance.

A sustained stretch in which nothing new happens: same rhythm, same sentence shape, same small set of words, low stakes. With nothing to evaluate, vigilance lapses and attention drifts inward. It works by under-feeding attention where the rest of this family over-feeds or jams it. It differs from repetition used to drive in one suggestion, where the repeated content is the point.

**How:** Write long runs of near-identical sentences about something neutral and true (breathing, the chair, the count), with no jokes, questions or new images. Ask for an even voice and steady pace. Let it run longer than feels comfortable to write; a few sentences are not monotony. Then place suggestions once responsiveness has dropped, or let it carry into a sleep ending. It fails with listeners who came for intensity and switch off.

> And the breath goes in. And the breath goes out. And the breath goes in. And the breath goes out. And nothing else needs to happen.

> The next number is forty-one. Nothing happens on forty-one. The next number is forty. Nothing happens on forty.

> [flat, even] The same chair. The same room. The same slow voice saying the same slow thing.

**Spot it by:** five or more consecutive sentences with the same structure and near-identical words; neutral, low-information content (breath, counting, 'the same'); 'nothing to do', 'nothing happens', 'nothing new'; stage directions: [monotone], [flat], [even], [droning]; long passage with no questions, images or new vocabulary.

**Not to be confused with:** Repetition induction (repeats one suggestion or mantra to absorb the listener; here the content is deliberately uneventful); Deeper and deeper (repeats depth words to deepen trance, rather than keeping the delivery uneventful); Semantic satiation (repeats one word until it loses meaning; monotony uses sustained, uneventful phrasing or delivery); Parallelism (repeats a sentence shape while varying the content; monotony requires sustained sameness of content or delivery as well); Wearing down (outlasts active resistance by length; monotony keeps the material uneventful).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Monotonous stimulation reliably lowers alertness and induces drowsiness; drowsiness is not the same as hypnotic responsiveness, and research finds relaxation is not required for hypnosis.

**Why it works:** Habituation, Cognitive ease, Processing fluency, Epistemic vigilance.


### Occupying the conscious mind *(unit)*

Also called: decoy focus, give the conscious mind a job, distracting the conscious mind, busy work for the critic.

An explicit assignment of something for the 'conscious mind' to attend to or think about (watch a spot, follow the breath, wonder about a question, analyse the voice) so that it is not monitoring the suggestions. The job is a decoy and its content does not matter.
