> People who are good at focusing usually find their hands get heavy first.

**Spot it by:** 'most people', 'many people', 'everyone', 'thousands of listeners'; 'people like you', 'others who', 'listeners often'; a statistic or count about other people's responses; third-person plural subject followed by the response the script wants; 'you're not alone', 'just like everyone else who'.

**Not to be confused with:** Normalizing (normalizing reassures that a response the listener has, or fears having, is ordinary ('that's normal', 'nothing is wrong'); social proof reports what others do or feel so the listener does the same. If the line predicts or invites a response, label social proof; if it excuses one, label normalizing); Modeling (modeling shows one person performing the response and what it earned them; social proof reports what many do, with no scene and no reward); Unspecified referent ('people can relax' states a possibility about a vague subject; social proof reports what others actually do); Authority (authority rests on one expert or powerful source, not on the number of peers).

**Evidence:** experimental. Conformity and descriptive-norm effects are well replicated; whether a line of social proof inside a recording changes hypnotic response has not been tested directly. Source: Cialdini, Influence (1984).

**Why it works:** Social proof, Informational social influence, Descriptive norms, Normative social influence, Argument from consensus, Response expectancy theory.

**Consent:** Claims about what others do should be true or clearly generic; invented numbers are deception.


#### Testimonial *(variant)*

Also called: listener stories, others report, case story, review.

A testimonial is social proof carried by one specific case instead of a count. It describes, or quotes, an individual who went through the process and what happened to them. The single vivid case is what separates it from general social proof; the fact that the person is presented as real and reporting separates it from My friend John, where the third person is a vehicle for live suggestions.

**How:** Place it in the pre-talk or the description. Give one or two concrete details of the person's doubt before and their experience after; the doubt is what lets a skeptical listener identify. Keep it short and specific, and let the reported experience match what the script will suggest next. It fails when it reads as advertising or when the reported result is too large to believe.

> One listener wrote to say she was sure it wouldn't work on her. She says she lost track of the room about four minutes in.

> Someone told me last week that the first thing he noticed was his shoulders, and then nothing else for quite a while.

> A man who had tried three other recordings told me afterwards, 'I didn't think I was under until I tried to move.'

**Spot it by:** 'one listener', 'someone told me', 'a client of mine', 'a woman who wrote to me'; reported speech or a quoted remark from one past listener; before-and-after story about a third person ('she was sure it wouldn't work... then'); 'they said', 'he described it as', 'she reported', 'told me afterwards'; past-tense report of a finished session, not a scene narrated as it happens.

**Not to be confused with:** Modeling (modeling shows someone performing a response and its consequence; a testimonial reports an earlier person's completed experience as evidence, whether quoted or described by the speaker); My friend John (My friend John delivers live suggestions through the third person; a testimonial reports a finished result); Vicarious deepening (vicarious deepening narrates someone going under in the present for the listener to follow); Borrowed authority (borrowed authority cites an expert or science, not a peer's experience).

**Evidence:** experimental. Single cases can shift judgment, and base rates are often underused, but studies comparing narrative with statistical evidence give mixed results; no controlled work shows testimonials inside a script raise hypnotic response.

**Why it works:** Social proof, Narrative persuasion, Availability heuristic, Social learning theory, Response expectancy theory, Character identification.

**Consent:** Invented testimonials presented as real are deception; composite or illustrative cases should be worded as such.


#### Manufactured consensus *(variant)*

Also called: chorus, staged agreement, crowd effect, astroturfing.

Manufactured consensus is social proof that is shown instead of claimed. The script or production supplies the crowd: a chorus repeating the line, background voices saying yes, a scene where every character complies. It differs from plain social proof, which only asserts what others do, and from layered voices, which is the audio technique and need not carry agreement.

**How:** Write the agreeing voices as stage directions or as characters in the scene, and have them respond just before the listener is asked to. Keep the chorus lines short and identical so they read as unanimity. It works best inside a fiction frame, where the listener knows the crowd is part of the scene. It fails when one dissenting or awkward voice breaks the unanimity, or when the staging is so heavy it draws attention to itself.

> [Several voices, together:] Yes. We listen. We relax.

> All around you the others have already closed their eyes. Every one of them. You can hear them breathing slowly.

> [Background murmur of agreement] And everyone in the room nods, so you nod too.

**Spot it by:** stage directions for a chorus, crowd, murmur or multiple voices saying the same line; 'we' lines spoken by a group voice that is not the main speaker; scene description in which every other character has already complied; 'all of them', 'every one of them', 'the whole room'; the same short line repeated by different named or numbered voices.

**Not to be confused with:** Social proof (plain social proof asserts what others do; this stages the others so the listener seems to witness it); Layered voices (layered voices is the audio technique of overlapping tracks, whatever they say); Vicarious deepening (vicarious deepening follows one person going under; this shows a unanimous group).

**Evidence:** experimental. Conformity to a unanimous group and effects of staged audience reactions are established in the lab; their use in recorded hypnosis is untested practice.

**Why it works:** Manufactured consensus, Social proof, Normative social influence, Informational social influence, Argument from consensus.

**Consent:** Outside an acknowledged fiction frame the crowd is fake evidence; do not present staged voices or invented agreement as real listeners.


### Authority *(unit)*

Also called: expertise, prestige suggestion, credentials, authority positioning.

Authority is any statement or stance that sets up the speaker's standing: training, experience, track record, role or plain assurance. The claim is about the speaker, not about the technique or the recording. That separates it from the potency claim, which praises the method, and from borrowed authority, where the standing belongs to someone else.

**How:** Establish it early, in the pre-talk, in one or two factual lines; then show it through certainty and plain instructions instead of repeating the claim. Experience stated as numbers or years is more credible than adjectives. Match the kind of authority to the script: clinical competence for self-help, command and role for dominance. It fails when it is overclaimed, defended at length, or contradicted by hesitant wording later.

> I've guided people into trance for fifteen years, and I'll tell you exactly what to do at each step.

> You don't need to work anything out. That's my job. Yours is to follow.

> I know how this goes. I've watched it happen many hundreds of times.

**Spot it by:** first-person statements of training, years, numbers of clients or sessions; 'trust me', 'I know', 'leave that to me', 'that's my job'; titles or roles the speaker claims (doctor, hypnotist, teacher, a dominant title); explicit division of roles: 'I lead, you follow'; unhedged declaratives about what will happen, attributed to the speaker's experience.

**Not to be confused with:** Borrowed authority (borrowed authority cites an outside source; authority is the speaker's own standing); Potency claim (the potency claim is about how strong the recording or technique is, not who the speaker is); Role assignment (role assignment tells the listener what they are and how that role behaves; authority states the speaker's standing or right to direct. 'I lead' is authority; 'you are my student' is role assignment); Direct suggestion (a direct suggestion is the command itself; authority is the standing that makes commands acceptable).

**Evidence:** experimental. Obedience to authority and source-credibility effects are well documented; perceived prestige of the hypnotist raises expectancy, but its separate effect on hypnotic response is modest and mixed. Source: Cialdini, Influence (1984).

**Why it works:** Authority principle, Response expectancy theory, Epistemic trust, Sociocognitive theory of hypnosis, Demand characteristics.

**Consent:** False credentials are deception, and claimed clinical authority carries a duty of care the script must be able to meet.


#### Borrowed authority *(variant)*

Also called: science says, studies show, appeal to tradition, appeal to authority, expert citation.

Borrowed authority supports a claim by pointing to a source outside the speaker: research, medicine, an old practice, a named figure. The source does the persuading; the speaker only reports it. It differs from authority, where the standing is the speaker's own, and from giving a reason, where any 'because' clause will do whether or not a source is named.

**How:** Use one citation, in the pre-talk, attached to the specific response you are about to ask for. Be accurate and proportionate: 'relaxation slows the heart rate' can be said plainly; claims about the unconscious mind cannot. A vague 'studies show' is weaker than a concrete, true statement and is easy for a skeptical listener to dismiss. Avoid it in deep trance, where citations invite analysis.

> Slow breathing like this is known to lower your heart rate. That part is just physiology.

> People have used a steady point of focus to quiet the mind for centuries. You're doing something very old.

> Researchers who study attention say it narrows when you give it one thing to hold. So give it my voice.

**Spot it by:** 'studies show', 'research shows', 'science tells us', 'it's been proven'; 'doctors', 'psychologists', 'researchers', 'experts' as the subject of a claim; 'for centuries', 'ancient', 'traditional', 'monks have long'; a named expert, school or institution cited in support; technical vocabulary (brainwaves, neurons, the nervous system) used as backing.

**Not to be confused with:** Authority (authority is the speaker's own expertise or role, not an outside source); Giving a reason (reason-giving attaches any 'because'; borrowed authority needs a cited source); Social proof (social proof cites many ordinary peers, not an expert or a body of knowledge).

**Evidence:** experimental. Credible sources raise acceptance of a message in persuasion research; many 'science says' lines in hypnosis scripts cite findings that do not exist or do not say what is claimed.

**Why it works:** Authority principle, Epistemic trust, Response expectancy theory, Placebo effect, Elaboration likelihood model.

**Consent:** Citing science or experts that do not support the claim is deception; cite only what is true.


### Liking *(unit)*

Also called: rapport, warmth, similarity, compliments.

Liking covers what the speaker says to be liked: friendliness, stated similarity, compliments, humor, care for the listener. People agree more readily with those they like. It differs from praise, which rewards a specific response just made, and from matching, which copies the listener's tempo or language instead of expressing warmth.

**How:** Open with it and keep it going in small doses. State a real point of common ground, compliment something the listener actually did (showing up, making time), and speak as one person to another. Keep compliments specific and modest; flattery that the listener cannot believe lowers trust. Warmth in the pre-talk also makes later firm instructions easier to take.

> I'm glad you made time for this. It's not easy to stop in the middle of a day.

> I'm the same way. My mind takes a while to quiet down too, so we'll go at an easy pace.

> I like people who are curious enough to try something like this. I think we'll get on well.

**Spot it by:** 'I'm glad you're here', 'it's good to have you', greetings with warmth; 'I'm like that too', 'just like you, I' - stated similarity; compliments not tied to a response just performed; 'I like', 'I enjoy', 'I care about' with the listener as object; light humor shared with the listener; a personal admission by the speaker (label the self-disclosure variant, which also counts as liking).

**Not to be confused with:** Praise (praise follows a specific response as its reward; liking builds affection before or apart from any response); Matching (matching mirrors the listener's pace or words; liking is expressed warmth and similarity); Affection flooding (affection flooding is intense, sustained and out of proportion; liking is ordinary warmth).

**Evidence:** experimental. Similarity, compliments and familiarity reliably raise liking and compliance; rapport is held essential in clinical hypnosis but its measured contribution to hypnotic response is small. Source: Cialdini, Influence (1984).

**Why it works:** Liking principle, Rapport matching, Epistemic trust, Mere-exposure effect, Source derogation.


#### Parasocial intimacy *(variant)*

Also called: girlfriend experience, just us, personal attention, simulated closeness.

Parasocial intimacy simulates a personal relationship in a one-way medium. The speaker talks as if alone with this listener, remembers them, missed them, and is paying attention only to them. It differs from ordinary liking in claiming a relationship, not just showing warmth, and from direct address, which is only the use of 'you'.

**How:** Write as to one person in a private room: refer to shared history ('last time'), to the present moment between you, and to your attention being on them. Keep details general enough to fit any listener. Close-mic or whispered delivery supports it. Be clear in the description that this is a recording and a role; it fails, and can hurt, when a listener takes the relationship as real and it is not answered.

> It's just you and me now. Nobody else is here, and I'm not going anywhere.

> I was hoping you'd come back tonight. I remember how well you settled last time.

> I'm right here with you, paying attention to you and nothing else.

**Spot it by:** 'just us', 'just you and me', 'nobody else', 'alone together'; 'I missed you', 'I was thinking about you', 'I'm glad you came back'; references to shared history: 'last time', 'like we always do'; 'I'm right here', 'I'm watching you', 'I can see you' in a recording; pet names and terms of endearment; stage directions for whispering or close-mic delivery.

**Not to be confused with:** Liking (liking shows warmth and similarity; parasocial intimacy claims a private ongoing relationship); Isolation (isolation runs down or replaces the listener's other people ('they wouldn't understand'); intimacy says only that speaker and listener are alone together now, with no claim about anyone else); Affection flooding (affection flooding is overwhelming approval used to bind; this is the simulated one-to-one frame at any intensity); Direct address (direct address is second-person wording; intimacy adds the claim of closeness); Mind reading (mind reading claims to know the listener's inner state; this claims presence and relationship).

**Evidence:** experimental. Parasocial relationships are well documented and can raise a source's persuasive pull; nothing shows they raise hypnotic response, and effects on lonely listeners are a known concern. Source: Horton & Wohl, 'Mass Communication and Para-Social Interaction: Observations on Intimacy at a Distance' (1956).

**Why it works:** Parasocial interaction, Liking principle, Attachment theory, Epistemic trust, Self-reference effect.

**Consent:** The closeness is simulated and one-way; say so outside the session, and do not use it to build dependency or to press for money or more listening.


#### Self-disclosure *(variant)*

Also called: stepping out of role, speaker vulnerability, personal aside, admitting a flaw.

A first-person statement about the speaker's own inner life or imperfection that is not needed to carry out the session: a nervousness, a habit, a mistake, what they enjoy about this work. It is the form of liking that works by showing something of oneself, as opposed to complimenting the listener or claiming similarity. In a persona-driven script it often appears as a brief step out of role, where the speaker drops the character's voice to say something as themselves.

**How:** Keep it small, relevant and brief: one or two sentences, then return to the listener. Place it in the pre-talk, or at a turn where trust matters, such as just before asking for something harder or just after intense content. A minor flaw from a speaker who is otherwise competent raises liking; a large one, or one that bears on their ability to run the session, lowers confidence. Do not let it become the subject: disclosure that asks the listener to look after the speaker reverses the roles. If the disclosure is written for a character, it should still be true of the person voicing it or be clearly inside the fiction.

> I'll admit I still get a little nervous before recording these. I want it to be good for you.

> My own mind is a noisy one. It took me a long time to learn to do what I'm about to show you.

> Let me step out of the role for a moment. I enjoy this part more than I probably should.

**Spot it by:** 'I'll admit', 'I have to confess', 'to be honest with you', 'between us' followed by a statement about the speaker; first-person feeling or flaw statements: 'I get nervous', 'I used to struggle with', 'I'm not good at'; 'stepping out of character', 'speaking as myself for a moment', 'out of role'; a short passage whose subject is 'I' in a script otherwise addressed to 'you'; the speaker naming their own enjoyment, doubt or mistake.

**Not to be confused with:** Confession (confession has the listener disclose private material to the speaker; here the speaker discloses to the listener); Parasocial intimacy (that claims a private ongoing relationship with the listener; a disclosure is one revealed fact about the speaker and claims no relationship); Naming the technique (naming the technique tells the listener what is being done to them; self-disclosure tells them something about the speaker).

**Evidence:** experimental. Disclosure raises liking for the discloser and invites disclosure in return in controlled studies, and a small blunder can make a competent person more likeable; the scripted, one-way version in a recording has not been tested. Source: Collins & Miller, 'Self-disclosure and liking: a meta-analytic review' (1994).

**Why it works:** Liking principle, Reciprocity principle, Parasocial interaction, Epistemic trust, Persuasion Knowledge Model.

**Consent:** A disclosure invented to win trust works only while the listener takes it as real; do not fabricate vulnerability, and do not use a real one to draw a matching disclosure the listener would not otherwise give.


### Reciprocity *(unit)*

Also called: gift, favor, I gave you this, give first.

Reciprocity uses the felt obligation to repay. The script provides a benefit (rest, pleasure, attention, a free session), marks it as a gift from the speaker, and then makes a request. Both halves must be present: the gift and the ask. It differs from positive reinforcement, where the reward comes after the response, and from door in the face, where the 'gift' is a concession on a refused request.

**How:** Deliver something the listener actually feels before the ask: a good stretch of relaxation is enough. Name it briefly as something you gave, then ask once, for something proportionate. The closer the ask follows the gift, the stronger the pull. It fails when the gift is not felt, and it sours when the debt is pressed or when the return asked is far larger than what was given.

> I've given you this quiet, and all this time to rest. Now do one small thing for me: listen again tomorrow.

> That calm is my gift to you. In return, give me your full attention for the next few minutes.

> I took care of you just now. So let me ask something of you.

**Spot it by:** 'I gave you', 'my gift to you', 'I've done this for you'; 'in return', 'in exchange', 'now do something for me'; 'you owe', 'the least you can do', 'it's only fair'; a benefit described as coming from the speaker, followed within a few lines by a request; 'free', 'at no cost' attached to the session, followed by an ask.

**Not to be confused with:** Positive reinforcement (reinforcement rewards after the response; reciprocity gives before the ask); Door in the face (door in the face trades a concession on a refused large request, not a prior gift); Thanking (thanking has the listener express gratitude; reciprocity asks for repayment); That's not all (that's-not-all adds extras to an offer still on the table, before any answer).

**Evidence:** experimental. An unrequested favor raises later compliance in controlled studies; the effect of a 'gift' that is itself only suggested has not been tested. Source: Cialdini, Influence (1984).

**Why it works:** Reciprocity principle, Equity theory, Injunctive norms.

**Consent:** Using a felt debt to extract money, escalation or continued listening the listener did not sign up for is manipulative; keep the ask proportionate and refusable.


### Scarcity *(unit)*

Also called: limited, rare opportunity, limited time, urgency.

Scarcity states that the opportunity is rare, short-lived or about to be lost. Things that are harder to get are judged more valuable, and a possible loss moves people more than an equal gain. It concerns the availability of the offer; the exclusivity variant narrows it to who is allowed. It differs from deprivation, which actually withholds something to raise its value, where scarcity only describes the limit.

**How:** State the limit concretely: this session, this moment, these few minutes. Put it where a decision is needed, typically the description, the pre-talk or the point of commitment. One clear limit works better than repeated urgency. False limits are quickly discounted on a recording that can be replayed, so prefer limits that are true: a state that will pass, a moment of depth that will not last unless used.

> You won't get many moments in a day as quiet as this one. Use it.

> This depth doesn't last long. While it's here, take in what I say next.

> There are only a few minutes left in this session, and they are the ones that matter.

**Spot it by:** 'limited', 'rare', 'just this once', 'only a few' applied to the session, the moment or the offer; 'while it lasts', 'before it's gone', 'this moment won't come again'; deadlines and counts: 'only a few minutes left', 'the last chance'; 'don't miss', 'don't waste', loss wording attached to the present opportunity; 'now or never', 'it won't be here later'.

**Not to be confused with:** Deprivation (deprivation actually withholds something; scarcity describes the offer as limited); Gain / loss framing (loss framing recasts an outcome as an avoided loss without claiming limited supply); Warning as lure (a warning-as-lure forbids or cautions; scarcity says supply or time is short).

**Evidence:** experimental. Scarce items are rated more valuable in controlled studies, with effect size depending on context; no evidence shows scarcity wording changes hypnotic response. Source: Cialdini, Influence (1984).

**Why it works:** Scarcity principle, Psychological reactance, Framing effect.

**Consent:** Invented deadlines or shortages are deception and pressure the listener to skip their own judgment.


#### Exclusivity *(variant)*

Also called: only for you, chosen, special, not for everyone, selective access.

Exclusivity is scarcity of access: what is limited is who may have it. The listener is told they were chosen, qualify, or are among the few who can do this. It differs from plain scarcity, which limits time or quantity for everyone, and from labeling, which assigns a trait in order to ask for behavior that fits it.

**How:** Give a reason the listener qualifies, tied to something true of them: they came back, they listened this far, they respond well. Then describe what follows as reserved for people who did that. One statement is enough. On a public recording an unqualified 'only for you' is plainly false, so tie it to a condition the listener has met.

> Not everyone gets this far. This next part is only for the ones who do.

> I don't say this to most people. I'm saying it to you because you kept listening.

> This is for the few who can stay this still. You're one of them.

**Spot it by:** 'only for you', 'just for you', 'not for everyone', 'not everyone can'; 'chosen', 'selected', 'singled out', 'special'; 'the few who', 'most people never', 'I don't tell most people'; access wording: 'reserved', 'invitation', 'members only', 'you've earned'; a qualifying condition followed by privileged content.

**Not to be confused with:** Scarcity (plain scarcity limits time or supply for everyone; exclusivity limits who is allowed); Unity (unity says speaker and listener share an identity ('we', 'one of us'); exclusivity says the listener was admitted to something others are not, and needs no shared 'we'); Labeling (labeling assigns a trait to get matching behavior; exclusivity raises the value of what is offered); Isolation (isolation devalues everyone outside the speaker; exclusivity flatters the listener's selection without running anyone down); Parasocial intimacy (parasocial intimacy simulates a one-to-one relationship; exclusivity only says the listener was selected).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. It follows from scarcity research and is standard in sales copy, but being 'chosen' by a mass recording has no direct test.

**Why it works:** Scarcity principle, Self-reference effect, Labeling effect.

**Consent:** Telling every listener they alone were chosen is a false claim; tie it to a condition the listener really met.


### Unity *(unit)*

Also called: shared identity, we, one of us, belonging.

Unity invokes a shared identity: speaker and listener, or listener and a community, are 'we'. The appeal is membership, not resemblance: liking says 'I am like you', unity says 'we are the same kind'. It differs from social proof, which reports what a group does, by placing the listener inside the group.

**How:** Name the group and what makes the listener part of it, then phrase what follows with 'we' and 'us'. Use an identity the listener already holds or has just earned (people who practice, those who have listened before). It suits series and communities more than a single cold recording. It fails when the group is one the listener does not recognize, or when 'we' appears with nothing behind it.

> We're the kind of people who take the time to do this properly, you and I.

> You're one of us now. Everyone who has done this session shares what you're feeling.

> This is what we do. We slow down, we listen, and we let go together.

**Spot it by:** 'one of us', 'you belong', 'part of', 'our kind'; a named group or collective noun the listener is placed in; 'we' or 'us' as subject of a statement about what the group is or does ('we're the kind of people who', 'this is what we do'), not 'we' for a shared task; family or kin terms used for a non-family group; 'people like us' followed by a norm of the group.

**Not to be confused with:** Liking (liking is similarity and warmth between two individuals; unity is membership in one group); Social proof (social proof cites what others do; unity makes the listener one of them); Labeling (labeling gives the listener alone a trait and then asks for behavior that fits; unity puts speaker and listener, or listener and a group, in one category); Exclusivity (exclusivity says the listener was let in to something restricted; unity says the listener and the speaker are the same kind); Pronoun shift (pronoun shift is the change of pronoun as a device; unity is the membership claim, whatever the pronoun).

**Evidence:** experimental. In-group favoritism and greater influence from in-group sources are well established; unity as a distinct principle is Cialdini's later synthesis and is untested in hypnosis. Source: Cialdini, Pre-Suasion (2016).

**Why it works:** Unity principle, Normative social influence, Injunctive norms, Epistemic trust.

**Consent:** Belonging offered on condition of compliance, or set against outsiders, shades into the coercive family.


#### In-group language *(variant)*

Also called: shared jargon, insider terms, group vocabulary, shibboleth.

In-group language is unity carried by vocabulary. The script uses terms of art, nicknames for states, or set phrases that an outsider would not know and a member would. Recognizing the term signals belonging. It differs from loaded language, where the special terms carry a built-in judgment and close down thought; in-group terms only mark membership.

**How:** Introduce a term once with a plain gloss, then use it without explanation so the listener has the experience of knowing it. Keep the set small and consistent across a series. Words for states the listener has just felt work best, since the term then names a shared experience. It fails when too many terms arrive at once, or when a new listener is left unable to follow.

> Those of us who do this call it 'the hush', that moment when the room goes quiet inside. You know the one.

> You've reached what regulars here call the floor. Rest on it.

> Welcome back. You already know what we mean when we say 'settle'.

**Spot it by:** 'we call it', 'what we call', 'regulars call', 'those of us who'; a coined or capitalized term for a state or practice, used without explanation; scare quotes or italics around a term presented as the group's word; 'you know what that means', 'you know the one'; the same coined term recurring across files in a series.

**Not to be confused with:** Loaded language (loaded language builds a verdict into the term and narrows thought; in-group terms only mark membership); Naming the state (naming the state tells the listener what a state is called; in-group language presents the name as the group's own); Trigger word / phrase (a trigger word is installed to produce a response; an in-group term only signals belonging).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Shared vocabulary as a marker of group membership is documented in sociolinguistics; its effect on acceptance of suggestions has not been tested.

**Why it works:** Unity principle, Common ground, Processing fluency.

**Consent:** A private vocabulary that outsiders cannot follow can make the listener harder to reach for people outside the group; keep terms explainable in plain words.


### Modeling *(unit)*

Also called: vicarious learning, observational learning, demonstration, vicarious reinforcement, showing a model.

The script presents a model: one person who performs the response, and what they get for it. The listener is given no instruction; they watch, and the shown consequence does the persuading. It differs from social proof, which reports that many people do something, in showing one performance and its outcome. It differs from My friend John, where the third person is a channel for live suggestions the listener carries out as they are given. Modeling here is the social-learning sense; the NLP use of the word, copying an expert's strategy, is a different thing.

**How:** Choose a model the listener can see themselves in, close to them in age, doubts and starting point. Show the response in concrete steps, including a moment of hesitation that the model gets past, then show the reward clearly and at once. Leave out 'and you will too'; the comparison is the listener's to make. A model who succeeds too easily or is too unlike the listener is dismissed. In video or live work the model is an actual demonstration; in a script it is a described person.

> The woman before you sat in that same chair, sure it wouldn't work for her. She let her shoulders drop anyway, and I watched the worry leave her face.

> He answered without stopping to think, and she smiled at him. 'That's it,' she said. 'That's exactly right.' He had not felt that pleased with himself in weeks.

> Watch how she does it. One slow breath, her hands open, and she is already calmer than she was a moment ago.

**Spot it by:** a third person (he, she, a named character, 'the last person who sat here') performing the target response; the model's reward stated right after the act: praise received, relief, pleasure, approval; 'watch how...', 'notice what happens when she...', 'I once worked with someone who...'; no imperative addressed to the listener within the passage; the model's initial doubt or hesitation described, then overcome.

**Not to be confused with:** Social proof (social proof reports what many people do as a norm; modeling shows one person doing it and what it earned them); My friend John (there the third person receives live suggestions step by step for the listener to carry out; a model is only watched); Vicarious deepening (that is the narrower use where the listener follows a described person down into trance; label it when depth is the response shown); Testimonial (a testimonial is an earlier listener's report of a finished result, offered as evidence; a model is shown in the act).

**Evidence:** experimental. Observational learning and vicarious reinforcement are well established, and watching a responsive model raises hypnotic responding in controlled studies; a model who is only described in a recording has not been tested separately. Source: Bandura, Social Learning Theory (1977).

**Why it works:** Social learning theory, Character identification, Response expectancy theory, Descriptive norms.

**Consent:** The listener is not told that the model is there to be copied; a model presented as a real past listener should be one.


## Expectation and framing

Also called: framing, expectation management, meaning-making.

Framing devices do not ask for a response directly; they shape the expectation or meaning that a response will be read through. Some act before the experience (expectation setting, seeding, title priming, myth correction), some reinterpret it as it happens or after (reframing and its variants, naming the state, redefinition). The family is distinct from presupposition, which builds a claim into sentence grammar, and from suggestion forms, which phrase the request itself.

**Choosing:** Choose by timing and target. Before the experience, use expectation setting, seeding, myth correction, objection preemption or title priming to decide what the listener will look for. During it, use naming the state, reframing or no-fail framing to decide what what they notice means. Use gain/loss framing, reference points and redefinition when the job is to change how a single outcome or word is judged; use inevitability or the as-if frame when the job is to change how certain or how real the outcome feels. Fiction frame and naming the technique set the overall contract with the listener and should be chosen early, since they change how everything after is evaluated.

**Not to be confused with:** Presupposition and implication (presupposition hides the claim inside sentence grammar; framing states or shapes the interpretation openly); Suggestion forms (suggestion forms phrase the request itself; framing sets how the request and its result are read).

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Framing effect, Conversational framing.


### Contrast *(unit)*

Also called: perceptual contrast, compared with, contrast effect.

Contrast sets up a comparison whose only job is to shift how the next item is judged. A large effort is described first so the actual request feels small; tension is described so the calm feels deeper. It differs from antithesis, which is a balanced phrasing of opposites for style, and from the numeric reference point, which sets a number that later estimates adjust from.

**How:** Give the extreme comparison first, briefly, then the real item straight after. The two must be on the same dimension (effort, time, intensity). Use it before a request that might seem large or before a state you want felt as strong. It fails when the comparison is so far-fetched it is ignored, or when too much time passes between the two.

> You spent the whole day holding everything together. All I'm asking for is ten minutes of doing nothing.

> Compared with how tight your shoulders were when you sat down, notice how loose they feel now.

> I could ask you to clear your whole mind. I won't. Just let go of one thought.

**Spot it by:** 'compared with', 'compared to', 'next to', 'after all that' linking the target to something more extreme; 'all I'm asking', 'just', 'only' directly after a larger effort or request has been described; a harder or more extreme alternative named and then set aside by the speaker ('I could ask... I won't'); 'so much easier than', 'nothing like as', comparatives with the standard stated; an earlier, worse state named so the present one is judged against it ('compared with how tight they were').

**Not to be confused with:** Door in the face (door in the face puts a large request to the listener, voices refusal or reluctance, then retreats to a smaller request; contrast may merely mention and set aside the larger option); Reference point (a reference point supplies a number before inviting a judgment of the same quantity; contrast compares experiences or requests to change how one is judged, even when their descriptions include numbers); Antithesis (antithesis is a balanced figure of opposed ideas; contrast is a comparison meant to shift a judgment); Apposition of opposites (apposition pairs two simultaneous opposed experiences as a suggestion; contrast compares to change how one is judged); That's not all (that's-not-all improves an offer before the listener answers; contrast compares the target with a separate, more extreme option or experience).

**Evidence:** experimental. Contrast effects in perception and judgment are well established; their size in spoken persuasion varies and is unmeasured in hypnosis. Source: Cialdini, Influence (1984).

**Why it works:** Contrast effect, Anchoring effect (judgment), Framing effect.


### Expectation setting *(unit)*

Also called: here's what will happen, setting expectations, expectancy, previewing the session.

A plain forward-looking statement of what the session will feel like or do. It works by giving the listener a template to match their experience against. It differs from seeding, which mentions an idea casually without announcing it as the plan, and from direct suggestion, which asks for the response now.

**How:** Put it in the pre-talk or at the start of each section. Describe likely, achievable experiences in concrete sensory terms (heaviness, a slowing breath, sounds becoming distant). Set ranges, not single outcomes, so that whatever happens fits. Overpromising dramatic effects backfires when they do not arrive.

> In a few minutes you will probably notice your arms getting heavier, and your breathing slowing on its own.

> Some people feel a pleasant tingling, some feel very still. You will find out which it is for you.

> First your breathing will slow, then your body will start to feel heavy, and after that your thoughts will get quiet.

**Spot it by:** you will notice; you'll probably find; here's what will happen; in a few minutes; some people feel ... others feel; future tense description of sensations before they are suggested.

**Not to be confused with:** Seeding (seeding drops the idea casually without presenting it as the plan); Direct suggestion (direct suggestion asks for the response now; expectation setting predicts it for later); Normalizing (normalizing says a response is ordinary so the listener stops worrying about it; expectation setting forecasts what will be felt).

**Evidence:** experimental. Expectancy reliably predicts hypnotic response in controlled studies, though it explains only part of the variance in suggestibility.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Placebo effect, Sociocognitive theory of hypnosis.


#### Potency claim *(variant)*

Also called: this is powerful, warning: strong, hype, prestige framing.

Expectation setting aimed at magnitude rather than content: the listener is told the effect will be strong, fast or hard to resist. It raises expectancy without describing what will be felt. It is distinct from authority, which builds the speaker's standing, though the two often appear together.

**How:** Place it in the title, description or opening lines. A short, specific claim (this file is designed to work quickly) lands better than piled superlatives. If the claim far outruns what the listener then feels, it turns into evidence that the file failed, so pair it with a no-fail frame.

> This is one of the strongest inductions I have recorded, so make sure you are somewhere you can rest.

> This one works fast. It is built to take hold before the introduction is over.

**Spot it by:** strongest; most powerful; intense; warning: this file; takes hold within; superlatives about the file or technique.

**Not to be confused with:** Warning as lure (a warning-as-lure frames the strength as a reason not to listen, inviting defiance); Authority (authority is about the speaker's standing, not the file's strength).

**Evidence:** experimental. Labelling a procedure as hypnosis or as powerful raises response in studies of expectancy, but the gain is modest and depends on the claim being believed.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Placebo effect.


#### Warning as lure *(variant)*

Also called: do not listen unless, forbidden fruit, you've been warned.

A caution phrased to raise curiosity and appeal rather than to inform. It combines a potency claim with a touch of prohibition, so listening becomes a dare. It differs from a content note, whose aim is informed choice, and from reverse psychology, which instructs the opposite of the wanted act within the session.

**How:** Put it at the top of the description or pre-talk. Name an effect and tell the listener not to proceed unless they want it. It works on listeners who enjoy defying a limit; it can read as a gimmick to others. If the warning is also meant to protect, keep a separate, plain content note.

> Do not listen to this file unless you are ready to stop thinking for a while.

> Fair warning: people who finish this one tend to come back for more.

**Spot it by:** do not listen unless; fair warning; you have been warned; only if you're ready; warning followed by an effect presented as desirable.

**Not to be confused with:** Content note (a content note informs so the listener can decline; a lure is built to make declining less likely); Listening conditions (listening conditions name a real hazard (driving, operating machinery); a lure names the file's wanted effect as the danger); Reverse psychology (reverse psychology instructs the opposite of a wanted in-session response; the lure is about whether to listen at all); Potency claim (a plain potency claim has no prohibition or dare in it).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Forbidden-content labels can raise interest in some studies of reactance, but there is no direct study of this device in hypnosis audio.

**Why it works:** Psychological reactance, Scarcity principle.

**Consent:** Because it is built to look like a warning while discouraging refusal, it should not replace an honest content note.


### Seeding *(unit)*

Also called: priming, foreshadowing, pre-suasion, seeding an idea.

An early, low-key reference to a later target response, made without asking for it. The later suggestion then lands on prepared ground. It differs from interspersal, which scatters suggestion words through the same passage, and from expectation setting, which openly announces what will happen.

**How:** Put the seed in the pre-talk or induction, well before the target. Mention the idea in an unrelated context (a remark about how hands sometimes feel light on a warm day before an arm levitation). Keep it casual; a seed that is stressed reads as a suggestion and loses its point. Make the later suggestion echo the seed's words so the link is felt.

> Funny how on a warm afternoon your hands can feel almost weightless resting in your lap.

> Some mornings you wake before the alarm and have no idea how long you have been lying there.

> I once watched a cat fall asleep in a sunbeam, completely still, without deciding to.

**Spot it by:** an image, word or sensation mentioned in passing in the pre-talk or induction that returns later as a suggestion; asides and anecdotes: 'funny how', 'you know how', 'I once', 'some mornings'; nothing is asked of the listener in the sentence and nothing is predicted for the session; the later suggestion repeats the seed's key word or image.

**Not to be confused with:** Interspersal (interspersal scatters suggestion words through a passage; seeding plants the idea ahead of time); Expectation setting (expectation setting states the plan openly); Curiosity hook (a curiosity hook opens a question to hold attention; a seed is not meant to be noticed).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Semantic priming is well established in the lab, but whether a seed made minutes earlier measurably raises response to a later hypnotic suggestion is untested.

**Why it works:** Priming, Spreading activation, Pre-suasion, Processing fluency.

**Consent:** A seed is meant to pass unnoticed, so seed only responses the listener has already agreed to in the description or pre-talk.


### Reframing *(unit)*

Also called: reframe, meaning reframe, context reframe, positive connotation.

The facts stay the same; what they mean is changed. A meaning reframe says what X really signifies; a context reframe names a setting where X is useful. It differs from redefinition, which changes the meaning of a word, and from complex equivalence, which is the grammatical form 'X means Y' that a reframe often uses.

**How:** Start from something the listener is actually experiencing or doing, ideally something they see as a problem. Offer the new meaning as a plain statement, then build on it at once so it is used rather than argued. A reframe lands when it fits the facts at least as well as the old meaning; a reframe the listener can easily refute invites counterargument.

> That restlessness is just your body using up the last of the day's energy before it settles.

> A wandering mind is not a problem here. It means you have stopped forcing things.

> Being stubborn is exactly what you want once you have decided to stay relaxed no matter what.

**Spot it by:** that just means; what that really is; is not a problem, it's; another way to see it; is exactly what you want when; an unwanted experience or trait is named, then given a favorable meaning or a setting where it is useful.

**Not to be confused with:** Redefinition (redefinition changes a word's meaning, not an experience's); Complex equivalence (complex equivalence is the 'X means Y' sentence form given to any event; label reframing when the listener already holds a meaning (usually negative) that is being replaced); Utilization (utilization gives what the listener brings a job in the process; reframing only changes what it means); Positive intention (positive intention addresses a part and credits it with a purpose; reframing needs no part).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Reframing is standard in family therapy and clinical hypnosis, and cognitive reappraisal has experimental support; the NLP six-step form is not independently validated. Source: Watzlawick, Weakland & Fisch, Change: Principles of Problem Formation and Problem Resolution (1974).

**Why it works:** Reframing, Framing effect, Moral reframing.


#### Relabeling sensation *(variant)*

Also called: that tingle means, arousal relabeling, misattribution, sensation reinterpretation.

A reframe applied to a physical sensation the listener already has: a tingle, warmth, heartbeat or flutter is given a specific new cause or meaning, such as the speaker's influence, a particular suggestion taking hold, or a different emotion. It borrows the sensation's reality to make the claim feel confirmed. When the meaning given is simply that trance or relaxation is occurring, the span is pacing trance signs. It differs from suggested sensation, which creates the feeling.

**How:** Pick sensations that are likely anyway (warmth in the hands, a faster heartbeat, tingling in the fingertips, eyelid flutter). Name the sensation, then attach the meaning in the same sentence. Keep the meaning tied to the suggestion's goal. It is weak if the listener does not have the sensation, so hedge with 'if you notice'.

> That flutter in your stomach isn't nerves. It's your body getting ready to enjoy this.

> That quickening in your chest is your attention locking onto my voice.

> If you notice warmth in your hands, that's the word 'calm' starting to do its work.

**Spot it by:** that tingling is; that warmth means; if you notice ... that's; that feeling in your ... is the; a named body sensation followed by its meaning.

**Not to be confused with:** Suggested sensation (suggested sensation creates the feeling; relabeling reinterprets one already there); Pacing trance signs (if the meaning given is 'you are going into trance' or 'you are relaxing', label pacing trance signs; relabeling assigns any other cause or meaning); Complex equivalence (complex equivalence is the general 'X means Y' form; use this label when X is a felt body sensation).

**Evidence:** experimental. Misattribution of arousal and reappraisal of bodily arousal have experimental support, though some classic misattribution findings replicate weakly.

**Why it works:** Misattribution of arousal, Reframing.


#### No-fail framing *(variant)*

Also called: whatever happens is right, fail-safe, there's no wrong way.

A reframe that removes failure as a category: not going deep, staying alert or not feeling anything is defined as correct or as part of the process. It is applied to the whole session or a phase. It differs from open-ended suggestion, which phrases one suggestion so all responses fit, and from doubt-as-a-sign, which reframes doubt specifically.

**How:** Put a short version in the pre-talk and repeat it after any demanding suggestion. Name the likely disappointing outcomes explicitly (staying aware, hearing every word) and say each is right. It lowers performance anxiety; overdone, it can make the listener feel nothing is expected.

> There is no wrong way to do this. If you hear every word, that is fine; if you drift and miss some, that is fine too.

> Whatever you notice, or don't notice, is just right for today.

**Spot it by:** there's no wrong way; whatever happens is right; you can't do this wrong; even if you ... that's fine; if you don't feel anything, that's.

**Not to be confused with:** Open-ended suggestion (open-ended suggestion phrases one suggestion to accept all responses; no-fail framing redefines outcomes across the session); Doubt as a sign (doubt-as-a-sign reframes the listener's doubt, not their outcome); Covering all possibilities (covering all possibilities lists the classes of response for one suggestion).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Common in clinical and Ericksonian practice for reducing performance anxiety; no controlled study isolates its effect.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Reframing.


#### Surrender as freedom *(variant)*

Also called: giving up control as relief, letting go is freedom, obedience as release.

A reframe of yielding: what might be read as giving something up is described as being freed from effort, decisions or self-monitoring. It targets one specific meaning, the cost of compliance. It differs from comfort and safety, which reassure without reinterpreting control, and from desire attribution, which claims the listener wants it.

**How:** Name the burden first (deciding, holding on, keeping track), then present letting go as putting it down. Keep the reframe tied to concrete relief the listener can feel, such as shoulders dropping. Used without consent framing, it shades into pressure, so pair it with an explicit freedom to stop.

> You don't have to decide anything for a while. That's the freedom of just following along.

> Handing over the steering isn't losing anything. It's finally getting to rest.

**Spot it by:** the freedom of following along; such a relief to let go; letting go feels like relief; free from having to decide; handing over control means you can rest; a relief or freedom word predicated of yielding, following or obeying.

**Not to be confused with:** Safety and comfort (comfort and safety reassure without reframing control as gain); It's what you want (desire attribution says the listener wants it, not that it frees them); Not doing / not knowing (not doing tells the listener effort is unneeded; it does not claim release as the meaning).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. No direct study; the general effect of reframing is supported, this specific frame is not.

**Why it works:** Reframing, Framing effect.

**Consent:** Because it makes yielding feel like a benefit, it should sit inside a session that also states the listener can stop.


#### Resistance as participation *(variant)*

Also called: your resistance helps, resisting is part of it, every push takes you in.

A reframe that removes the opposition between resisting and responding: the act of resisting is defined as engagement, effort or evidence of involvement. It does not claim resistance strengthens the effect (that is 'the harder you resist') or give it a task (using resistance).

**How:** Name resistance plainly when it is likely, then state that it is part of how this works. Follow with a suggestion the resisting listener can still accept. Keep it calm and unworried; a frame that sounds defensive confirms there is a contest.

> If part of you wants to hold on, that's fine. Holding on is just another way of paying attention.

> Even the part of you that pushes back is listening closely right now.

**Spot it by:** resisting is just; even the part of you that pushes back; holding on is another way; your resistance is part of; resistance described as attention or participation.

**Not to be confused with:** The harder you resist ('the harder you resist' claims resistance strengthens the effect); Using resistance (using resistance gives resistance a job; this only redefines it); Doubt as a sign (doubt-as-a-sign targets doubt, not active resistance).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Part of Ericksonian handling of resistance; not independently tested.

**Why it works:** Reframing, Utilization, Psychological reactance.


#### Doubt as a sign *(variant)*

Also called: doubt means it's working, skepticism as evidence, the doubt is part of it.

A reframe applied to doubt: the listener's 'this isn't working' becomes evidence that it is. Typical forms are 'the part of you wondering if it works is the part that's going under' and 'people who doubt often go deepest'. It differs from resistance as participation, which calls active resistance useful, and from no-fail framing, which covers every outcome rather than doubt in particular.

**How:** Place it in the pre-talk or right where doubt is likely, such as after the first convincer. Name the doubt in words the listener would use, then state what it means. Tie it to a sign they can check (wondering, analysing, noticing). It fails if it sounds like a trick; say it calmly and move on.

> If you're wondering whether this is working, that wondering is a very good sign.

> Many people who doubt at first go deepest, because they're paying such close attention.

> That little voice asking 'am I hypnotized?' only shows up once something has changed.

**Spot it by:** 'if you're wondering whether..., that's a sign'; 'doubt/skepticism means...' or 'is a sign that...'; 'people who doubt often go deepest'; doubt or questioning named, followed by a complex equivalence.

**Not to be confused with:** Resistance as participation (resistance as participation re-labels active resistance; this re-labels doubt); No-fail framing (no-fail framing makes every outcome success; this targets doubt only); Complex equivalence (the general X-means-Y form; this is the case where X is doubt).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Widely used by hypnotists to handle 'I wasn't hypnotized'; it has not been tested separately, though expectancy effects on hypnotic response are well documented.

**Why it works:** Reframing, Response expectancy theory, Misattribution of arousal.


### Fiction frame *(unit)*

Also called: it's just a story, pretend, roleplay frame, play frame.

An explicit statement that what follows is a story, game or roleplay. It lowers the stakes of accepting claims, since nothing is being asserted as real. It differs from the as-if frame, which asks the listener to imagine an outcome as true, and from the story frame structure, which is the scene itself rather than the statement about it.

**How:** State the frame once, early and plainly, then stay inside it. It lets a script use stronger language than the listener would accept as fact. It also lowers effect for listeners who discount 'just a story', so it suits entertainment more than change work. Close the frame at the end if any suggestions are meant to persist.

> This is only a story, so you can let yourself enjoy it without deciding whether any of it is true.

> Let's play a game for the next twenty minutes. In this game, my voice is the only thing that matters.

**Spot it by:** just a story; let's pretend; let's play a game; in this story; none of this has to be real; for the next ... minutes, in this game.

**Not to be confused with:** As-if frame (the as-if frame asks the listener to suppose the outcome true and explore it); Story frame (the story frame structure is the scene the session is built on; this is the statement declaring it fiction); Fantasy boundary (a fantasy boundary states that claims end with the session, a safety move).

**Evidence:** contested. In transportation studies, labelling a narrative fiction or fact made little difference to how much it shifted beliefs, so fiction-framed content still persuades, but there is no clear evidence that the label itself lowers scrutiny. Source: Bateson, A Theory of Play and Fantasy (1955).

**Why it works:** Suspension of disbelief, Narrative transportation, Entertainment Overcoming Resistance Model, Cognitive decoupling.

**Consent:** If suggestions inside a fiction frame are meant to persist after the session, say so plainly, since the frame implies they will not.


### Naming the technique *(unit)*

Also called: transparent narration, telling you what I'm doing, open technique, meta-commentary.

The speaker names or explains the device while using it (notice I keep saying 'deeper'; that repetition is deliberate). What is disclosed is the method, not what the listener will feel. Done honestly, it builds trust and turns the device into a shared game. It differs from expectation setting, which describes the listener's coming experience, and from myth correction, which addresses beliefs about hypnosis in general.

**How:** Use it where the listener is likely to notice the device anyway, or where knowing makes the experience more fun. Name the device, then use it immediately. Transparency can reduce reactance in skeptical listeners; it can also break absorption, so keep it brief once trance has begun.

> I'm going to use a little trick now: I'll say a word softly, and you'll hear it a little louder in your mind.

> You might notice I keep starting sentences with 'and'. That's on purpose. It helps everything run together.

**Spot it by:** I'm going to use; this is a technique called; notice how I; that's on purpose; what I'm doing now is; names a device by name or describes its mechanism.

**Not to be confused with:** Expectation setting (expectation setting predicts the experience, not the method); Myth correction (myth correction addresses beliefs about hypnosis in general); Naming the state (naming the state names the listener's experience, not the speaker's technique).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Forewarning of persuasive intent usually reduces persuasion in the lab, so the claim that disclosure raises response is unsupported in general; it may help through trust and play.

**Why it works:** Persuasion Knowledge Model, Forewarning effect, Psychological reactance.


### Myth correction *(unit)*

Also called: hypnosis isn't sleep, you stay in control, misconceptions talk, dispelling myths.

A pre-talk move that names common misconceptions (you will be unconscious, you can be made to do anything, you might get stuck) and replaces them with accurate statements. It removes fear and false benchmarks. It differs from objection preemption, which answers this listener's likely objection to this session, and from no-fail framing, which redefines outcomes.

**How:** Put it in the pre-talk, before any induction. Pick two or three myths that matter for this listener and correct each in a sentence. Replace the myth with something they can expect, such as remaining aware and able to hear. Corrections should be accurate; a reassuring false claim is not myth correction.

> Hypnosis isn't sleep. You'll hear everything I say, and you can open your eyes whenever you choose.

> Nobody gets stuck in trance. If you stopped listening right now, you would simply drift back to normal.

**Spot it by:** hypnosis isn't; you won't be unconscious; you can't get stuck; contrary to what you may have seen; a lot of people think; you stay in control.

**Not to be confused with:** Preempting objections (objection preemption answers this listener's likely objection, not general misconceptions); No-fail framing (no-fail framing redefines outcomes; myth correction fixes false beliefs about hypnosis); Protected core (protected core claims suggestions against one's values will be rejected, a specific assurance that may itself be inaccurate).

**Evidence:** experimental. Favourable pre-hypnotic information raises responsiveness in controlled studies, but the gain from information alone is modest; the larger effects come from programmes that add attitude change and practice.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Sociocognitive theory of hypnosis.


### Preempting objections *(unit)*

Also called: you might think, answering the objection first, prolepsis, procatalepsis.

The speaker voices the doubt or counterargument the listener is likely to have, then disposes of it. Hearing it named and answered first makes it feel already handled. It differs from myth correction, which addresses general beliefs about hypnosis, and from doubt-as-a-sign, which reinterprets doubt rather than answering it.

**How:** Phrase the objection in the listener's own words, fairly, and answer it briefly with a reason or reassurance. One or two objections are enough; listing many plants doubts the listener did not have. Place it before the request the objection would block.

> You might be thinking this won't work for you because you've never been hypnotized. That's actually ideal; you have no habits to unlearn.

> Some of you will say you can't relax on command. You don't have to. You only have to follow one breath at a time.

**Spot it by:** you might be thinking; maybe you're wondering; some of you will say; I know what you're thinking; you may feel that ... but.

**Not to be confused with:** Myth correction (myth correction targets general misconceptions about hypnosis); Doubt as a sign (doubt-as-a-sign reinterprets doubt as progress instead of answering it); Mind reading (mind reading claims to know the listener's inner state; preemption uses that claim to raise and answer an objection).

**Evidence:** experimental. Two-sided messages that refute counterarguments and inoculation by weakened counterarguments both have experimental support in persuasion research.

**Why it works:** Inoculation theory, Counterarguing, Forewarning effect.


### Naming the state *(unit)*

Also called: this is trance, this feeling is, labeling the state, state naming.

A label applied to the listener's present experience (this is trance, this is what deep focus feels like). It turns an ambiguous feeling into a named, recognized state the listener can return to. It differs from pacing trance signs, which cites observable signs as evidence, and from relabeling sensation, which assigns a meaning to one bodily feeling.

**How:** Name the state after enough induction that the listener is feeling something. Use a short, confident declarative and pause. Keep the label stable across the script and across sessions so it becomes a cue. If the label promises more than the listener feels, soften it ('this is the beginning of trance').

> This, right here, is what trance feels like.

> That calm, heavy, quiet feeling has a name. It's called being under.

**Spot it by:** this is what ... feels like; this is trance; that feeling has a name; this is called; right here is.

**Not to be confused with:** Pacing trance signs (pacing trance signs lists observable signs as evidence; naming the state gives the whole state a label); Relabeling sensation (relabeling sensation gives one bodily feeling a meaning); Labeling (labeling assigns a trait to the person, not a name to the present state).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Labelling ambiguous states shapes how they are experienced in emotion research, but naming trance has not been tested on its own.

**Why it works:** Labeling effect, Misattribution of arousal, Sociocognitive theory of hypnosis.


### Gain / loss framing *(unit)*

Also called: framing effect, attribute framing, goal framing.

The outcome is fixed; only its description changes, as a benefit gained by acting or a cost suffered by not acting. Losses often weigh more than equal gains in choices, but that does not mean loss-framed messages are generally more persuasive. Message-framing studies find a small, variable gain-frame advantage for prevention behaviors and no reliable overall loss-frame advantage for detection behaviors. It differs from reframing, which changes what an experience means, not which side of the ledger it is described from.

**How:** Decide what you want the listener to do, then describe it as what they keep or gain by doing it, or what they miss by not. Loss frames add urgency but can feel like pressure; gain frames feel warmer. Stay consistent within a passage; switching frames dilutes both.

> Every minute you spend relaxing tonight is a minute of rest you get to keep tomorrow.

> If you rush through this, you miss the best part, the quiet at the bottom.

**Spot it by:** you'll miss; you get to keep; don't lose; what you gain; what it costs you to; same outcome described as gain or loss.

**Not to be confused with:** Reframing (reframing changes an experience's meaning; gain/loss framing changes only its valence description); Scarcity (scarcity claims the opportunity is limited; a loss frame need not).

**Evidence:** experimental. Framing effects on choice are robust; effects of gain versus loss frames on persuasion are smaller and depend on topic. Source: Tversky & Kahneman, The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice (1981).

**Why it works:** Framing effect, Attribute salience.


### Reference point *(unit)*

Also called: numeric anchoring, anchoring effect, reference value, anchor number.

A specific value stated just before the listener judges how deep, how long, how heavy or how strong something is: a typical figure, a benchmark or an extreme. The offered value may influence the listener's estimate. It differs from the depth scale, which gives depth its own numbered dial; from stepwise doubling, which ties a multiplier to each count as an instruction to go further; and from NLP anchoring, which ties a state to a cue.

**How:** State a reference value before asking the listener to estimate a felt quantity. Present it as a typical figure or benchmark, then invite the listener to make their own judgment. A conspicuously implausible number may be less credible as a benchmark. A numbered dial or scale belongs to depth scale instead.

> Most people need about three minutes to go all the way down. See how long it takes you.

> A really heavy arm can feel like it weighs fifty pounds. How heavy is yours right now?

**Spot it by:** a specific figure for a felt quantity: 'about three minutes', 'around fifty pounds'; 'most people take about', 'usually around', 'as much as' + a number; the figure is followed by a question or invitation to estimate: 'how heavy is yours', 'how long do you think'; 'take a guess', 'see how long', 'see how far'; no count, dial or scale attached to the number.

**Not to be confused with:** Stepwise doubling ('twice as deep' or 'ten times deeper' tied to a count or breath is an instruction to increase, not a value to judge against); Depth scale (a depth scale is a numbered dial or scale for depth; a reference point is one value offered before an estimate); Contrast (contrast sets two experiences side by side; a reference point is a number); Anchoring (NLP anchoring links a state to a cue; this sets a number for judgment).

**Evidence:** experimental. Numeric anchoring of judgment is well replicated; whether it changes felt depth, rather than reported depth, is unknown. Source: Tversky & Kahneman, Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases (1974).

**Why it works:** Anchoring effect (judgment), Contrast effect.


### Redefinition *(unit)*

Also called: persuasive definition, what X really means, stipulative definition.

The speaker declares what a word truly means (real strength is letting go; relaxing is a skill) and then relies on the new sense. The listener's positive or negative feeling about the word carries over to the new content. It differs from reframing, which changes the meaning of an experience, and from loaded language, which is a group's whole stock of judgment-laden terms.

**How:** Pick a word the listener already values or fears. State the new definition as a plain truth, then use the word several times in its new sense so it sticks. It works best when the new sense is a plausible stretch of the old one; a definition that is obviously false invites pushback.

> Real focus isn't straining. Real focus is letting everything else go quiet.

> Control doesn't mean holding on. Control means choosing where your attention goes.

**Spot it by:** real ... is; true ... means; what ... really means; ... is just another word for; a valued word followed by 'is' and an unusual definition.

**Not to be confused with:** Reframing (reframing changes what an experience means, not what a word means); Complex equivalence (in complex equivalence X is an event or behavior that is said to show Y; in redefinition X is a word or value term (often marked 'real', 'true', 'really') whose sense is being replaced); Loaded language (loaded language is a group's whole vocabulary of judgment-laden terms).

**Evidence:** rhetorical-tradition. Persuasive definition is a long-recognized rhetorical and argumentation figure; its persuasive effect is not directly measured. Source: Stevenson, Persuasive definitions (1938).

**Why it works:** Equivocation, Metalinguistic negotiation, Framing effect.


### Inevitability *(unit)*

Also called: it's going to happen, you can't help it, resistance is futile, only a matter of time.

Open assertion that the response will happen whatever the listener does. It removes the question of whether. It differs from presupposition (already-happened framing), which builds the outcome into the grammar rather than asserting it, and from the permanence claim, which concerns how long the change lasts.

**How:** Use calm, certain language: will, is going to, sooner or later. Pair with a time or manner choice so the listener has something to do with the certainty. Delivered as threat it raises reactance; delivered as a quiet fact it lowers effort.

> Sooner or later your eyes are going to close. It might be now, it might be in a minute.

> You can't stop the relaxation from spreading. You can only notice where it goes next.

**Spot it by:** sooner or later; it's only a matter of time; you can't help; you can't stop; inevitably; no matter what you do.

**Not to be confused with:** Direct suggestion (a plain 'you will' states the response; label inevitability only when the wording says it will happen whatever the listener does); It happens by itself ('it happens by itself' is about who is doing it; inevitability is about whether it can fail to happen); Already-happened framing (already-happened framing treats the result as done via grammar instead of asserting it will come); Time bind (a time bind offers a choice of when; inevitability may stand without any choice).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Confident framing raises expectancy, which predicts response, but strong inevitability language can also trigger reactance; no direct study.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Psychological reactance.

**Consent:** Inevitability language aimed at outcomes after the session should be balanced by a stated way to stop or undo them.


### As-if frame *(unit)*

Also called: suppose, what would it be like if, act as if, imagine it were true.

An invitation to imagine a hypothetical as real and to elaborate it from the inside. The listener generates the details, which makes the outcome feel more possible and more their own. It differs from the fiction frame, which declares the whole content to be play, and from mental rehearsal, which runs a specific future behavior step by step.

**How:** Phrase it as a question or a 'suppose': what would it be like if...? Then give room (a pause, follow-up questions) for the listener to fill it in. It works best on outcomes the listener wants but doubts. Follow it with a suggestion that some of what they imagined can stay.

> Suppose, just for a moment, that you were already completely calm. What would you notice first?

> What would it be like if your mind were quiet right now? How would your breathing change?

**Spot it by:** suppose the outcome had already happened; what would it be like if; imagine that you already; just for a moment, pretend that you; act as though you already; a hypothetical outcome followed by a question about what the listener notices.

**Not to be confused with:** Fiction frame (the fiction frame declares the whole content to be play); Mental rehearsal (mental rehearsal walks through a specific future behavior); Pretend / as-if induction (the pretend induction asks the listener to act hypnotized as the route into trance).

**Evidence:** experimental. Imagining an outcome raises its judged likelihood and can inflate belief that it happened; the NLP 'as if frame' itself is not independently tested.

**Why it works:** Imagination inflation, Generation effect, Self-perception theory.


### Title and description priming *(unit)*

Also called: paratext, tags, file description, packaging.

Framing carried in the material around the script rather than in it: the file name, summary, tags, listed effects and length. It decides what the listener comes in expecting and so what they look for. It differs from expectation setting, which happens inside the session, and from a content note, whose aim is informed choice.

**How:** Write the title and description as part of the script. Name the experience and the main effect clearly; tags and effect lists act as a promise. Keep claims consistent with what the file delivers, or the gap becomes evidence of failure. Put safety and content information here too, separately from the hook.

> Title: Heavy and Still. Description: A slow, gentle induction for deep physical rest. Effects: relaxation, heavy limbs, easy sleep.

> Tags: induction, deepener, sleep, no wakener.

**Spot it by:** Title:; Description:; Tags:; Effects:; text outside the spoken script that names effects or style.

**Not to be confused with:** Expectation setting (expectation setting is spoken inside the session); Content note (a content note states what the file contains so the listener can decide; it may share the description but has a different job); Potency claim (a potency claim may appear in a title but asserts strength, not content).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Prior labels shape expectancy and experience in placebo and expectancy studies; the effect of file paratext on hypnosis audio is untested.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Priming, Pre-suasion.


## Convincers and tests

Also called: convincers, trance ratifiers, hypnotic phenomena, tests, challenges.

This family holds the phenomena a script suggests in order to be noticed: locked eyelids, a rigid arm, numbness, a hallucinated sound, a forgotten number, a finger that lifts by itself. What unites them is purpose, not mechanism: each one gives the listener a felt experience they did not consciously produce, and the script then treats that experience as evidence. It differs from ratification, which comments on what already happened, and from the convincer section, which is the place in the script where these devices sit.

**Choosing:** Pick by what the listener can check alone with a recording. Body challenges (eyelid lock, rigid arm, stuck hand, freeze) give a clear pass or fail and suit a first session; sensation and numbness are gentler and almost always succeed partly; hallucinations and amnesia are harder and should come after easier items have worked. Use a suggestibility test before the induction, a convincer after deepening, and an after-the-fact proof after waking. Always ratify the result whatever it was, and prefer items that cannot visibly fail when you cannot see the listener.

**Not to be confused with:** Convincer section (the section is the place in the script; the family is the set of devices used there); Ratification (ratification interprets a response as proof; a convincer is the suggestion that produces the response); Challenge suggestion (the challenge is the 'try and you can't' wording; convincers are the phenomena it is often attached to).

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Self-perception theory, Hypnotic suggestibility, Ideomotor effect.

**Consent:** Convincers can be used to persuade a listener they are under more control than they are; a script should not use them to imply the listener cannot stop or leave.


### Convincer *(unit)*

Also called: trance ratifier, proof, trance test, hypnotic challenge item.

A convincer is a suggested effect staged to be checked: the script names an effect, usually an inability, has the listener test it, and treats the result as proof of trance or of the speaker's influence. Its point is the check, not the effect.
