Label the whole passage, from build-up to release, with the named variant where one fits (eyelid lock, rigid arm, stuck, freeze, speech lock, name or number amnesia) and with this generic label only where none does, such as a limb too heavy to lift. The 'try and you can't' sentence inside the passage is also a challenge suggestion, and the comment that follows the result is ratification.

**How:** Place it after induction and some deepening, when the listener is settled. Build the effect first with several sentences of direct suggestion, then give a short, permissive test ('try, and notice'), then stop the test quickly and release the effect explicitly. Ratify the outcome either way: a pass is proof, a partial pass is 'already beginning'. Do not run a long test, which gives effort time to win.

> Your right arm is so heavy it will not lift from your lap; try lifting it, then notice how that shows the suggestion took hold.

> That word has slipped from your mind; try saying it now, and notice how the gap shows something has changed.

> Feel your left hand grow lighter than your right; lift both and compare them, then notice the difference as proof that you responded.

**Spot it by:** 'try to ...' after a run of suggestions about the same body part; 'and you can't', 'it won't', 'the harder you try the more'; 'stop trying', 'let it go now', 'back to normal' right after the test; 'that's how you know', 'proof', 'see how deep you are'.

**Not to be confused with:** Challenge suggestion (the challenge is the single 'try and you can't' sentence; the convincer is the whole staged passage from build-up to release. Label the sentence as the challenge and the passage as the convincer; both apply); Ratification (ratification is the short comment on a result ('that's right'); the convincer is the suggestion and test that produce the result); Suggestibility test (a suggestibility test is run awake before the induction and framed as imagination; a convincer is run in trance and framed as proof); Trigger test (a trigger test fires an installed cue to show the cue works; a convincer checks an effect suggested just now).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Challenge items behave reliably on susceptibility scales, but the clinical claim that a passed convincer deepens trance or improves outcomes has not been tested directly.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Self-perception theory, Ideomotor effect, Sociocognitive theory of hypnosis.

**Consent:** A convincer persuades by producing an experience the listener did not choose; release every inability explicitly before the session ends.


#### Eyelid lock *(variant)*

Also called: eye catalepsy, eyes glued shut, eye lock, eyelid catalepsy.

The eyelid form of the convincer: suggest that the eyes cannot open and invite the listener to try opening them. Practitioners often use it as an early challenge. It differs from eye closure, which asks only that the eyes close, by the added attempt to open them.

**How:** Use it once the eyes are closed and the listener has relaxed the small muscles around them. Frame the lock as relaxation ('so relaxed they won't work') rather than force, which makes trying feel like breaking the relaxation. Keep the test to a second or two, then tell them to stop trying and relax further. In self-hypnosis or recordings, phrase it so trying is optional.

> Relax the muscles around your eyes so completely that they just won't work.

> When you're sure they won't open, test them. Try. That's right, stop trying now and go deeper.

**Spot it by:** 'eyelids', 'eyes' with 'glued', 'stuck', 'sealed', 'locked', 'won't open'; 'relax them so much they won't work'; 'test them', 'try to open them' after eye-closure suggestions; 'stop testing', 'stop trying' immediately after.

**Not to be confused with:** Eye-closure suggestion (closure only asks the eyes to close; the lock adds a test of opening); Eye roll (eye-roll uses the eyes as a fixation start; the lock tests them after closure).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Eye catalepsy is an item on standard group and individual scales and is passed by roughly half of participants in normative samples; its use as a gateway to deeper trance is clinical convention.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Ideomotor effect.


#### Rigid arm *(variant)*

Also called: arm catalepsy, stiff arm, iron bar arm, arm rigidity.

The arm form of the convincer: an outstretched arm is suggested to be stiff and unbendable, and the listener is invited to try bending it. It differs from a stuck convincer, where the limb is fixed to something, and from arm levitation, where the arm moves instead of locking. The listener tenses the arm under the suggestion, so the effect is partly genuine effort reframed as involuntary. 'Arm catalepsy' in Ericksonian writing also means a lifted arm that simply stays where it is put, with no stiffness; label that here only when the script goes on to test it.

**How:** Have the listener extend an arm and make a fist first. Build rigidity with imagery (steel, a bar, a board) and with time, then invite one bend attempt. Release it clearly, arm loose and resting, before moving on. Skip it for listeners who may have shoulder problems or who are lying down with nowhere to hold the arm.

> Stretch your arm out in front of you and make a fist. Feel it becoming straight and stiff, like a bar of steel.

> So stiff that it won't bend. Try to bend it, and find it stays straight.

> Now let it go loose, and rest it down.

**Spot it by:** 'arm' with 'stiff', 'rigid', 'steel', 'bar', 'board', 'locked'; 'stretch your arm out', 'make a fist' before the lock; 'try to bend it'; 'let it go loose', 'soft again' afterward.

**Not to be confused with:** Stuck (stuck fixes a part to a surface; rigid arm fixes the joint itself); Arm levitation (levitation produces movement; rigidity prevents it); Freeze (freeze locks the whole body, not one limb).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Arm rigidity is a standard item on susceptibility scales; it is also one of the items most easily produced by plain voluntary tension.

**Why it works:** Ideomotor effect, Response expectancy theory.


#### Stuck *(variant)*

Also called: hand stuck, stuck to the chair, frozen feet, hand lock, glued hand.

A convincer that fixes a body part to something outside it: hand to the table, hands clasped together, back to the chair, feet to the floor. The fixation is to a surface or another body part, which separates it from rigid arm (a joint locks) and freeze (the whole body stops).

**How:** Name the surface concretely and give it a property: glue, a magnet, cement. Pressing down first helps, since the listener's own pressure becomes the 'stick'. Test once, briefly. Release with an equally concrete unsticking ('the glue dissolves') so nothing is left ambiguous after the session.

> Press your hand flat on your leg. Feel it sticking there, as if glued.

> The more you try to lift it, the more firmly it stays.

> Now the glue melts away, and your hand lifts easily.

**Spot it by:** 'stuck to', 'glued to', 'stuck fast', 'magnet'; 'hands locked together', 'fingers interlocked and stuck'; 'try to lift', 'try to pull apart', 'try to stand'; 'the glue dissolves', 'unstuck', 'free again'.

**Not to be confused with:** Rigid arm (rigid arm locks the joint; stuck fixes the limb to a surface or to another body part); Freeze (freeze stops all movement; stuck fixes one contact point); Suggestibility test (a hand clasp done awake before the induction and framed as imagination is a suggestibility test; the same lock in trance, framed as proof, is this); Magnetic hands (magnetic hands suggests the hands come together; stuck suggests they cannot come apart).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Hand-lock and hands-stuck-together items appear on standard scales; stage forms (stuck to the chair) are stage practice without separate study.

**Why it works:** Ideomotor effect, Response expectancy theory.


#### Name / number amnesia *(variant)*

Also called: forget your name, forget a number, number block, missing number, lost seven.

A convincer that tests memory instead of muscle: one well-known item is suggested away, and a routine task (counting fingers, saying their name) reveals the gap. It differs from amnesia suggestion in its narrow target and built-in test, and from speech lock, where the word is known but cannot be said.

**How:** Choose one item the listener uses without thinking, often a number between one and ten. Suggest it fades, is removed, or is simply not there, then give a quick task that passes through it. Treat hesitation as success. Restore the item explicitly and test that it is back before moving on or waking.

> The number seven is drifting away now, out of your mind, gone.

> Count your fingers for me. One, two, three... and notice what happens.

> Now the number comes back, exactly where it belongs.

**Spot it by:** 'forget the number', 'the number ... is gone'; 'you can't remember your name', 'your name slips away'; 'count your fingers', 'tell me your name' right after; 'it comes back now', 'remember it again'.

**Not to be confused with:** Amnesia suggestion (amnesia suggestion targets events or content of the session; this removes one known item and checks at once that it is missing); Losing the numbers (in losing the numbers the listener counts down a long run and all the numbers fade as a route to depth; here one item is removed and a short task shows the gap); Speech lock (speech lock blocks saying a word that is still known ('you can't say it'); here the item is suggested as unknown ('it's gone', 'you can't remember it')).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. A stage and clinical staple; suggested amnesia in general is well studied, but the single-number form is not studied separately and responses vary widely.

**Why it works:** Hypnotic amnesia, Response expectancy theory, Sociocognitive theory of hypnosis.

**Consent:** Always restore the item explicitly and check it before the session ends.


#### Speech lock *(variant)*

Also called: can't speak, mute, verbal inhibition, only one word, word lock.

A convincer that blocks or narrows speech. The listener keeps knowing what they want to say; the suggestion targets the saying. A narrowed form allows only a chosen word, often used in erotic and stage scripts. It differs from name amnesia, which removes the knowledge itself.

**How:** Build the effect on the throat, jaw or voice ('your voice is resting'), then invite a single attempt, such as trying to say their name. In the narrowed form, name the one allowed word and invite them to try any other. Release with a clear statement that full speech is back, and never leave it running when the listener might need to call for help.

> Your voice is resting now, so quiet that no words come out. Try to say your name.

> The only word you can say is 'yes'. Try to say anything else.

> Your voice comes back now, clear and easy.

**Spot it by:** 'can't speak', 'can't say', 'no words come out'; 'the only word you can say is'; 'voice is resting', 'throat is quiet', 'mouth won't open'; 'your voice comes back'.

**Not to be confused with:** Name / number amnesia (amnesia removes the item from memory; speech lock blocks saying it); Freeze (freeze locks the whole body; speech lock targets the voice); Repeat after me (repeat-after-me asks for speech; a one-word lock forbids everything else).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Verbal inhibition is a recognized challenge item in hypnosis testing and stage work; it has not been studied as a separate effect.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Sociocognitive theory of hypnosis, Cold control theory.

**Consent:** A speech lock can stop a listener using a safeword; keep it short, never cover the safeword, and release it explicitly.


#### Freeze *(variant)*

Also called: paralysis, statue, body lock, total catalepsy, frozen.

The whole-body form of the convincer: every limb stops at once. Scripts use it as a dramatic proof and, in dominance contexts, as a show of control. It differs from stuck and rigid arm by scope, and from relaxation deepeners that describe heaviness without testing movement.

**How:** Lead up through a part (eyes, then arms) before claiming the whole body. Keep breathing and blinking explicitly free. Test with one small, named movement, release fully and promptly, and invite a stretch afterward to confirm the release. Avoid it in files meant for sleep, where the release may be missed.

> Your whole body is still now, like a statue. Only your breath moves.

> Try to move a finger, and find everything stays exactly as it is.

> And now you're free. Stretch, and feel everything moving easily.

**Spot it by:** 'can't move', 'frozen', 'statue', 'paralysed', 'locked in place'; 'whole body', 'every muscle' with an inability; 'try to move' after a body-wide stillness suggestion; 'free to move again', 'stretch' as a release.

**Not to be confused with:** Stuck (stuck fixes one contact point; freeze stops the whole body); Heaviness / floating (heaviness describes weight without testing movement); Physical drop deepener (a deepener uses the body to go deeper; freeze stages a test of control).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. A stage and community staple; full-body immobility is not a standard scale item and has not been studied apart from single-limb challenges.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Ideomotor effect.

**Consent:** A freeze implies the listener cannot act; keep it short, leave breathing and safewords free, and release it clearly.


### Ideomotor signal *(unit)*

Also called: finger signals, yes finger, no finger, ideomotor response, nod, head signal.

A small movement assigned a meaning (yes, no, ready) and requested from 'the unconscious' rather than the listener. Because it often comes slowly and jerkily, the listener experiences it as involuntary, which makes it both an answer and a convincer. It differs from a deliberate response request in that the script frames the movement as not chosen, and from ideomotor induction, where movement is used to deepen rather than to answer.

**How:** Set the signals first: name which finger means yes and which means no, and ask for them to be tested. Then ask questions and wait, describing the finger as lifting 'by itself'. Accept any movement, even a twitch. In recorded scripts, where no one can see the answer, use the signal as a self-check ('when you are ready, your finger lifts') rather than as a question needing a reply.

> Let your unconscious answer yes by lifting your index finger; is this the right time to continue? Wait for that finger to move.

> Let one finger mean yes and another mean no; ask whether you are ready to go deeper, and allow one finger to answer.

> Let a small nod mean yes; ask your unconscious whether it wants to pause, and notice whether the nod comes.

**Spot it by:** 'yes finger', 'no finger', 'I don't know finger'; a movement assigned a meaning: 'this finger means yes', 'a nod for yes'; 'let your unconscious answer', 'let the finger answer'; a yes/no question followed by a pause or a wait for movement; 'lift on its own', 'by itself' said of the assigned finger or the head.

**Not to be confused with:** Implied directive (the implied directive is the sentence 'when X has happened inside, your finger will lift'; the signal is a movement given a meaning and used to answer. Label setting up the signal and asking it questions here; label a 'when ..., your finger lifts' sentence as the implied directive, and add this label only if the finger was set up as a signal); Ideomotor induction (ideomotor induction uses a movement as the route into trance; the signal uses it to answer); It happens by itself (automaticity framing words any response as happening by itself; the signal is one movement assigned a meaning); Conscious / unconscious split (the split is the address to 'your unconscious' as a separate listener; the signal is the channel it is asked to answer through).

**Evidence:** contested. The ideomotor effect itself is well established; the clinical claim that finger signals give reliable access to unconscious knowledge is not supported and risks producing false answers. Source: Cheek & LeCron, Clinical Hypnotherapy (1968).

**Why it works:** Ideomotor effect, Dissociated control theory, Cold control theory.

**Consent:** Do not treat finger answers as revealing hidden facts, especially about memories; they follow expectation.


### Suggested sensation *(unit)*

Also called: kinesthetic hallucination, phantom touch, tingling, warmth, suggested feeling.

A suggestion for something felt in the body that nothing outside is causing. It is the gentlest convincer, since attention alone produces mild tingling or warmth in most people, and the script can claim it. It differs from positive hallucination, which covers sight, sound, taste and smell, and from sensation relabeling, which renames a feeling already there.

**How:** Name a body part and one sensation, and describe it in small specific terms: where it starts, how it spreads. Choose sensations attention tends to produce (tingling in fingertips, warmth in the hands) for early convincers, and harder ones (cold, a touch on the shoulder) later. Pace any real sensation first. Ask the listener to notice it rather than to feel it, so a faint response counts.

> Notice a gentle tingling starting in the tips of your fingers.

> A warmth gathering in the palm of your right hand, spreading slowly to the wrist.

> Perhaps a light pressure on your shoulder, like a hand resting there.

**Spot it by:** 'tingling', 'warmth', 'coolness', 'pressure', 'buzzing' tied to a named body part; 'notice a sensation', 'you may begin to feel'; 'as if a hand', 'like a touch', 'a breath on your skin'; a sensation stated with no outside cause and no instruction to imagine a scene.

**Not to be confused with:** Positive hallucination (positive hallucination is perception of an absent sight, sound, smell or taste; suggested sensation is a feeling in the body); Relabeling sensation (relabeling renames a feeling already there; this creates one); Heaviness / floating (heaviness or floating is a whole-body weight feeling tied to depth; this is a local feeling in a named place with no depth claim); Pleasure as reward (a sensation stated as the result of the listener's response is a reward; one simply suggested is this); Sensory language (sensory language describes a scene in sense terms; a suggested sensation tells the listener they feel it in their own body now).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Suggested warmth and tingling are routine in clinical scripts and autogenic training; attention alone produces mild versions, so success says little about trance.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Placebo effect, Hypnotic suggestibility.


#### Numbness *(variant)*

Also called: glove anesthesia, analgesia, hypnotic analgesia, numbing, anesthesia.

A suggested loss of feeling in a named area. Glove anesthesia, the classic form, numbs one hand so it can be tested and later transferred. It is the most studied convincer: suggested analgesia reduces reported pain in controlled studies. It differs from negative hallucination, which removes an outside perception, and from body dissociation, which separates the listener from the body rather than numbing it.

**How:** Start with cold or heaviness, which are easier, and build toward numbness: 'like wearing a thick glove', 'like after the dentist'. Name the borders of the area. Test with something mild the listener can do alone, such as pinching the back of the hand, and compare it with the other hand. Restore normal feeling explicitly before the session ends, unless the numbness is a clinical goal.

> Your right hand is growing cool, then numb, as if it were wrapped in a thick winter glove.

> Pinch the back of that hand gently, then the other, and notice the difference.

> Now feeling returns to your hand, normal and comfortable.

**Spot it by:** 'numb', 'no feeling', 'can't feel', 'like the dentist'; 'glove', 'wrapped', 'wooden', 'cold' leading into numbness; 'pinch', 'press' as a test, 'compare with the other hand'; 'feeling returns', 'normal sensation' as a release.

**Not to be confused with:** Negative hallucination (negative hallucination blocks an outside percept; numbness blocks body feeling); Body detachment (dissociation detaches from the body; numbness removes feeling in it); Sensation transfer (transfer moves an established numbness; this creates it).

**Evidence:** experimental. Suggested analgesia reliably reduces reported pain in controlled laboratory and clinical studies, more so in high scorers. That evidence concerns pain relief; the use of a numb hand as proof of trance has not been studied separately. Source: Hilgard & Hilgard, Hypnosis in the Relief of Pain (1975).

**Why it works:** Hypnotic suggestibility, Neodissociation theory, Response expectancy theory, Placebo effect.

**Consent:** Restore normal feeling explicitly unless pain relief is the agreed goal; numbness can hide injury.


#### Sensation transfer *(variant)*

Also called: transfer of anesthesia, moving the feeling, glove transfer, spreading the numbness.

A variant that moves an existing suggested sensation instead of building a new one. The classic form transfers glove anesthesia from the hand to the face or another area by touch. It differs from numbness or suggested sensation by depending on one that has already worked, which lets the script reuse a proven response.

**How:** Only use it after the first sensation has been tested and ratified. Give a physical carrier: touching the target area, stroking, or imagery of the feeling flowing. Say the source area returns to normal as the feeling leaves, so nothing is left behind. Test the new area the same way as the old one, then restore it.

> Now place that numb hand on your cheek, and let the numbness pass from your hand into your cheek.

> Press your warm palm against your other hand and feel the warmth move from the palm into the other hand.

> Touch your knee with the warm hand, and feel the warmth pass into the knee as the hand cools to normal.

**Spot it by:** 'let the feeling flow into', 'transfer', 'move the numbness to'; 'place your hand on' after a sensation in that hand; 'as it leaves your hand, your hand returns to normal'; earlier established sensation named again with a new location.

**Not to be confused with:** Travelling sensation (a travelling sensation is described moving through successive body regions; transfer moves an established sensation from one named area to another); Numbness (numbness suggests a loss of feeling; transfer moves an established feeling from one area to another); Everything deepens (linkage ties a stimulus or response to going deeper; transfer moves an established sensation to a new place).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Glove anesthesia transfer is standard in clinical pain-control scripts; the transfer step itself has not been studied apart from hypnotic analgesia in general.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Hypnotic suggestibility.

**Consent:** Restore normal feeling to every area that received the transfer before the session ends.


#### Travelling sensation *(variant)*

Also called: wave of relaxation, warmth spreading, moving through the body, spreading sensation, flowing feeling.

The form of suggested sensation in which a single feeling (warmth, heaviness, tingling, a wave) is given a starting point, a path and an effect: it begins in one place, moves through named regions in order, and changes each one as it arrives. The moving sensation, not an instruction, does the work in each region. It differs from progressive relaxation, which tells each region to relax, and from sensation transfer, which declares an established sensation to have jumped from one place to another.

**How:** Pick one sensation and stay with it; start it where it is easiest to feel, usually the hands, feet or the top of the head. Name the regions in anatomical order and give the sensation a motion verb at each one (spreads, flows, rises, rolls). Say at least once what it does on arrival ('and everything it touches lets go'), then let later regions inherit that. Pace it slowly enough to follow, and end with the whole body or with the place you want the effect to settle. Skipping around the body, or changing the sensation midway, breaks the track.

> A warmth begins in the palms of your hands. It moves up through the wrists, into the forearms, and everything it reaches grows loose and heavy.

> Feel a slow wave start at the top of your head. It rolls down over your face, your neck, your shoulders, and wherever it passes, the muscles let go.

> That tingling in your fingertips starts to travel. Up the arms. Across the chest. Down the spine. And it leaves quiet behind it.

**Spot it by:** one sensation noun as the subject of motion verbs: 'spreads', 'flows', 'moves', 'travels', 'rolls', 'rises', 'washes'; 'a wave of ...' followed by body regions; body regions named in order with path prepositions: 'up through', 'down into', 'across', 'all the way to'; a start point: 'begins in', 'starting at'; an arrival effect: 'wherever it goes', 'everything it touches', 'as it reaches', 'it leaves ... behind'; the same sensation carried through three or more regions.

**Not to be confused with:** Progressive relaxation (progressive relaxation instructs each region in turn to relax; here a sensation travels and the regions change because it arrives); Sensation transfer (transfer declares an established sensation moved from one area to another, usually by touch; a travelling sensation is described moving continuously along a path); State-as-substance (state-as-substance describes the state itself as a material (fog, honey, light); a travelling sensation is a literal bodily feeling with no substance image).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Spreading warmth and waves of relaxation are routine in clinical relaxation scripts; attention to a body part produces mild sensation in most people, and no study separates the travelling form from plain region-by-region relaxation.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Attentional tunneling, Absorption (trait), Hypnotic suggestibility.


### Positive hallucination *(unit)*

Also called: see what isn't there, hallucinated sound, hallucinated taste, hallucinated smell, sensory hallucination.

A suggestion to perceive an absent thing with the outer senses: a sound in the room, a scent, a taste, a colour on a real object. It differs from guided imagery, which asks the listener to imagine and knows it is imagining, by claiming the thing is actually perceived; and from suggested sensation, which covers body feeling.

**How:** Pick a sense and an object the listener knows well, often a smell or taste for audio work. Build it by detail and lead in from imagery ('imagine, and then notice it becoming real'). Ask for noticing, not certainty, and ratify faint responses. End by removing it explicitly. Full visual hallucination with open eyes is rare; do not stake the session on it.

> Notice now the smell of fresh coffee, faint at first, then clearer.

> There's a taste of lemon on your tongue, sharp and bright.

> And you can hear a soft hum somewhere in the room.

**Spot it by:** 'you can smell', 'you can taste', 'you can hear' with an absent source; 'now you notice', 'becoming real', 'really there'; named smells and tastes (coffee, lemon, flowers) without a scene to imagine; 'and now it fades' as a removal.

**Not to be confused with:** Guided imagery (imagery asks the listener to picture; hallucination claims they perceive); Suggested sensation (body feeling belongs there; this covers sight, sound, smell and taste); Imagined substance (imagined substance is a fictional object whose effects are suggested; here the percept itself is the proof).

**Evidence:** experimental. Hallucination items are on standard scales and pass mainly in high scorers; imaging studies show suggested colour changes alter brain activity, but most listeners report vivid imagery rather than true perception. Source: Weitzenhoffer & Hilgard, Stanford Hypnotic Susceptibility Scale, Form C (1962).

**Why it works:** Hypnotic suggestibility, Response expectancy theory, Absorption (trait).


### Negative hallucination *(unit)*

Also called: can't see, invisible, can't hear, anosmia, selective blindness.

A suggestion to not perceive a real object, sound or person. It is one of the harder phenomena and mainly a stage and test item. It differs from numbness, which removes body feeling, and from attention-narrowing, which tells the listener to ignore things rather than claiming they are not there.

**How:** Pick one specific target the listener can check: a sound in the recording, an object in the room, a smell. State that it is gone or invisible, then invite them to look or listen. In recordings, use a planned sound you can name and remove, since you cannot know what is in the room. Restore perception explicitly.

> In a moment the ticking you hear will fade until there is no ticking at all.

> Open your eyes and look at the chair across from you. Notice the empty space where it was.

> Now everything is back exactly as it should be.

**Spot it by:** 'you can't see', 'you can't hear', 'invisible', 'not there'; 'fades until there is no', 'disappears from your awareness'; 'look at ... and notice it's gone'; 'it's back now', 'you can see it again'.

**Not to be confused with:** Positive hallucination (adds a percept; negative removes one); Narrowing attention (narrowing says ignore; negative hallucination says it is not there); Numbness (numbness removes body feeling, not outside percepts).

**Evidence:** experimental. Negative hallucination items are among the hardest on standard scales and pass in a minority of participants; studies show changes in report and some brain response, not true blindness. Source: Weitzenhoffer & Hilgard, Stanford Hypnotic Susceptibility Scale, Form C (1962).

**Why it works:** Hypnotic suggestibility, Neodissociation theory, Response expectancy theory.

**Consent:** Do not suggest that a person or something the listener needs to see for safety is invisible, and restore perception before waking.


### Suggestibility test *(unit)*

Also called: lemon test, postural sway, Chevreul pendulum, finger magnets, hand clasp, imagination test.

A brief exercise done awake, before formal trance, to show the listener they respond to words. Typical forms: imagined lemon making the mouth water, swaying backward, magnet fingers drawing together, a pendulum swinging in the hand. It differs from a convincer by placement and stakes: it comes before the induction and is framed as a game about imagination, not proof of trance.

**How:** Present it as a test of imagination, never of whether they can be hypnotized. Choose one that nearly everyone passes (lemon, finger magnets) for recordings. Give clear setup, thirty seconds of vivid suggestion, then ask what they noticed. Ratify any response as the skill the session will use, and move straight into the induction while expectancy is high.

> Hold your hands together with the two index fingers apart, and imagine magnets in the tips pulling them closer.

> Picture a cut lemon. Bring it to your mouth and bite into it.

> Whatever you noticed, that's the same ability we'll use in a moment.

**Spot it by:** 'imagine a lemon', 'bite into it'; 'fingers' with 'magnets', 'pulling together'; 'sway', 'falling backward', 'pendulum'; 'this is just a test of imagination', 'before we begin'.

**Not to be confused with:** Convincer (a convincer is run in trance and framed as proof; a suggestibility test is run awake before the induction and framed as imagination); Magnetic hands (the same magnet exercise is an induction when contact is tied to closing the eyes or going under; with no trance claim at contact it is this test); Book and balloon (book and balloon is one named form of this test; use its label when the two-arm weight and balloon exercise appears); Expectation setting (expectation-setting tells the listener what will happen; the test has them do an exercise and notice a response).

**Evidence:** experimental. Responses to such tests correlate with formal hypnotizability scores, and the waking items share much with nonhypnotic suggestibility; that a pass improves later trance is assumed rather than shown.

**Why it works:** Nonhypnotic suggestibility, Ideomotor effect, Response expectancy theory, Hypnotizability.


#### Book and balloon *(variant)*

Also called: heavy arm light arm, bucket and balloon, dictionary and balloon, hand heaviness and lightness.

A convincer built from two opposite imagined sensations at once, ending with the listener seeing the result. Unlike other convincers it does not test an inability; it makes movement the listener can measure, so even a small response produces visible proof. It is used mostly before or at the start of an induction as a suggestibility screen.

**How:** Have the listener hold both arms straight out, palms opposite ways, eyes closed. Build the heavy side and the light side in alternation with vivid detail, adding weight and adding balloons, for thirty seconds or more. Then ask them to open their eyes and look at their hands. Treat any gap as success and say so; do not mention a lack of gap.

> Hold both arms out in front of you. In your right hand, a heavy book. Tied to your left wrist, a big balloon.

> Another book on top, heavier, pulling down. More balloons, lifting up, up.

> Open your eyes and look at where your hands are now.

**Spot it by:** 'one arm' / 'the other arm' with 'heavy' and 'light' in alternation; 'book', 'bucket', 'dictionary', 'weight' paired with 'balloon', 'helium'; 'open your eyes and look at your hands'; 'notice the distance between them'.

**Not to be confused with:** Apposition of opposites (apposition pairs opposite experiences in a sentence; book and balloon is the two-arm exercise ending with a visible comparison, and both labels may apply to their respective spans); Heaviness / floating (heaviness-lightness suggests a weight feeling as a depth cue; book and balloon contrasts the two arms and asks the listener to see the gap); Arm levitation (levitation ties one arm's rise to induction or depth; here the two arms diverge and the gap is shown as a test); Suggestibility test (suggestibility test is the general waking exercise before induction; use book and balloon for this named two-arm form, whether it occurs before or after induction).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Widely used in stage and clinical pre-talks; the related hand-lowering and hands-moving items are validated scale items, but this particular test has not been studied on its own.

**Why it works:** Ideomotor effect, Response expectancy theory, Nonhypnotic suggestibility.


### Puppeteering *(unit)*

Also called: body control, involuntary movement, puppet, remote control, puppet strings.

A suggestion that the speaker directs specific movements (a hand lifts, the head nods, fingers curl) while the listener only watches. It differs from ideomotor signal, where the unconscious answers through movement, and from obedience task, where the listener chooses to act on a command; here the framing is that the body moves without them.

**How:** Begin with movements the body makes easily and slowly (a finger lifting, a hand drifting) and describe them in present progressive as already happening. Use strings, wires or a remote as an image if wanted. Give the listener an observer frame ('just watch it'). Return control explicitly at the end of the segment.

> Watch your right hand. I'm lifting it now, as if I held a string tied to your wrist.

> Now I turn your head slowly to the left. You are only watching it happen.

> I draw your hand toward your shoulder with my words; when I release it, control returns to you.

**Spot it by:** first-person verb with the listener's body part as object: 'I lift your', 'I'm moving your', 'I turn your'; 'puppet', 'pulling the strings', 'my strings', 'remote control'; 'my words move you', 'your body follows my voice, not you'; 'just watch it move' paired with the speaker as the cause; 'control returns to you', 'I give your body back'.

**Not to be confused with:** It happens by itself (automaticity framing says the movement happens by itself and names no mover; puppeteering names the speaker as the one moving the body); Ideomotor signal (the signal is a movement given a meaning and used as an answer; puppeteering is a movement the speaker claims to drive); Task assignment (a task asks the listener to choose to act on an instruction; here the movement is framed as not chosen); Arm levitation (levitation suggests lightness and ties trance to the hand's rise; puppeteering claims the speaker is moving the limb as a show of control).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Built on the established ideomotor effect; as a named device it comes from stage and community practice and has no separate study.

**Why it works:** Ideomotor effect, Cold control theory, Response expectancy theory.

**Consent:** Framing the body as controlled by the speaker works by the listener not owning the action; agree to it beforehand and return control explicitly.


### Suggested arousal / orgasm *(unit)*

Also called: HFO, hands-free orgasm, cum command, arousal on command, hands-free.

A suggested bodily response of arousal and release, built in steps and tied to a cue. It is used both as a convincer (proof of the speaker's influence) and as the goal of a file. It differs from suggested sensation by its build-and-release shape and cue, and from pleasure pairing, which attaches a feeling to something else rather than producing a peak.

**How:** Build gradually with sensation language, a rising count and reinforcement of each increase, and name the cue for release well before giving it. Hold and release only on the cue. Ratify any response, including a partial one, so the listener does not read a weaker response as failure. Keep the build and cue separate from triggers meant to fire outside sessions unless that is agreed.

> With every number the warmth builds a little more. One. Two.

> Hold it there, right at the edge, until you hear the word.

> Now. Let it all go.

**Spot it by:** 'on my count', 'when I say the word', 'not until I say'; rising count paired with 'building', 'higher', 'closer', 'edge'; 'hands-free', 'without touching'; 'let go', 'release', 'now' as a single-word cue after a hold.

**Not to be confused with:** Countdown finale (the finale is the session-level shape of ending on a counted release of any kind; this is the suggested build and climax itself. Label the section as the finale and the build-and-release passage as this); Tease and denial (tease-and-denial withholds the peak; this delivers it on a cue); Suggested sensation (a plain sensation has no build, hold or release cue); Pleasure pairing (pairing attaches pleasure to a word or idea; this produces the peak itself).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Orgasm from imagery alone, without touch, has been recorded physiologically in a small laboratory sample of women (Whipple, Ogden & Komisaruk, 1992). No controlled study of the suggested, cue-released form used in hypnosis is known, and success rates claimed online are anecdotal.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Misattribution of arousal, Classical conditioning.

**Consent:** Sexual content needs explicit adult consent before the session; a release cue meant to work after the session is a persistent trigger and must be disclosed.


### After-the-fact proof *(unit)*

Also called: time check, notice the time, look how long that was, lingering heaviness, post-hypnotic proof.

A convincer placed after emergence. The script asks the listener to check something they can verify on waking, usually the clock, and interprets the result as proof of trance. It differs from time distortion, which suggests the altered sense of time, and from ratification during trance, which comments on responses as they happen.

**How:** Set it up earlier if possible: suggest during trance that time will feel shorter, then after waking ask them to check the clock. Other checks: a hand still slightly heavy, a gap in what they remember. Phrase it as noticing ('you may be surprised'), not a claim, since you cannot know the result. Keep it brief so the wake stays clean.

> Before you do anything else, check the time, and notice how much longer you were away than it felt.

> You may find your hands still feel a little heavy for a minute or two.

> Try to remember everything I said in the middle, and notice what's simply not there.

**Spot it by:** 'check the time', 'look at the clock'; 'longer than it felt', 'where did the time go'; 'still a little heavy', 'lingering' after the count-up; 'try to remember' after waking.

**Not to be confused with:** Time distortion (time distortion is the suggestion that time feels different, given during trance; this is the check of the clock after waking); Amnesia on waking (amnesia on waking suggests the forgetting; this invites the listener, once awake, to look for the gap); Ratification (ratification confirms a response at the moment it happens in the session; this comes after the wake and points at something the listener can check for themselves); Your actions prove it (that cites a voluntary act (still listening, came back) as proof of wanting; this cites after-effects of the session as proof of trance).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Time underestimation after hypnosis is commonly reported and was observed in early studies, but expectation explains much of it; as a deliberate script device it is practitioner convention.

**Why it works:** Self-perception theory, Response expectancy theory, Confirmation bias.


## Memory and time

Also called: memory play, time play.

Devices that act on memory or on the listener's sense of when they are: forgetting, unusually clear remembering, returning to the past, stepping into the future, recasting a new trait as old, suggesting events that did not happen, and seeding later dreams. They differ from time distortion (attention-absorption), which changes how long the session feels, not which time the listener is in or what they recall.

**Choosing:** Pick by what the suggestion should do to memory or time. To make material fade, use amnesia suggestion or one of its variants: on waking (tied to the exit), structured (bracketing the trance with one resumed topic), source (the idea stays, its origin goes) or distraction (an abrupt change of subject). To recover a resource or state from the past, use revivification; to suggest the listener is a younger age, use age regression. To make a change feel finished, use future progression; to make it feel like it was always there, use 'it was always so'. Suggested memory adds an event that did not happen and needs the strongest consent framing. Dream suggestion carries content into sleep; memory enhancement suggests clearer recall of named material. Related devices live elsewhere: name amnesia (convincers), losing the numbers (deepening), time distortion and trance time expansion (felt duration), time confusion (confusion), future pacing (imagery-story) and revivification induction (induction).

**Not to be confused with:** Time distortion (changes felt duration of the session, not which time the listener is in or what they remember).

**Why it works:** Hypnotic amnesia, Posthypnotic suggestion, Source-monitoring error, Misinformation effect, State-dependent memory.

**Consent:** Devices in this family can leave effects the listener does not notice or that persist after the session; say in the pretalk what will be forgotten, revisited or suggested about the past.


### Amnesia suggestion *(unit)*

Also called: forgetting suggestion, posthypnotic amnesia, suggested amnesia, forget.

A suggestion whose content is forgetting: of the whole session, of one section, or of a word, number or event. It is often permissive ('you may find it easy to forget') so that remembering does not count as failure. Label this unit itself only where forgetting is stated in the text. Its variants narrow it: amnesia on waking ties the forgetting to the exit, source amnesia keeps the content and removes its origin, and structured and distraction amnesia aim at the same result by arrangement, with no forgetting stated. It differs from name amnesia, a short in-trance convincer with a built-in test, and from losing the numbers, where the fading of a count is the route to depth.

**How:** Say what will be forgotten and when, ideally tied to emergence or to a cue. Permissive or ambiguous wording ('you might remember, or you might simply let it drift away') lands better than a flat command, because partial recall still fits the suggestion. Pair it with a reason (it is not needed, the unconscious keeps it) and avoid asking the listener to check whether they remember, which brings the material back. It fails when it is stated once with no frame and the listener is invited to recall right after.

> That last part can slip to the back of your mind now, the way a stranger's name does a minute after you hear it.

> You don't need to remember any of this. Your unconscious keeps what matters, and the rest can simply go.

> Whether you forget all of it or only most of it doesn't matter at all.

**Spot it by:** forget / forgetting / forgotten; you don't need to remember; drift away / fade like a dream; remember to forget; whether you remember or forget; the harder you try to remember.

**Not to be confused with:** Name / number amnesia (a brief in-trance convincer: one familiar item is suggested away and tested at once so the listener notices the gap); Losing the numbers (the listener's own count is relaxed away as a deepener; the fading is the route to depth, not a suggestion about recalling the session); Negative hallucination (suppresses perception of something present, not memory of something past); Capacity suggestion (changes the ability to remember in general ('your memory gets foggy'); amnesia names particular material to be forgotten).

**Evidence:** experimental. Posthypnotic amnesia is a standard item on hypnotic susceptibility scales and is reliably produced in highly suggestible people, but it is usually partial and reversible on a cue.

**Why it works:** Hypnotic amnesia, Posthypnotic suggestion, Hypnotic suggestibility, Ironic process theory.

**Consent:** Forgetting removes the listener's ability to review what was suggested; tell them beforehand what kind of material will be forgotten and keep it reversible.


#### Amnesia on waking *(variant)*

Also called: forget on waking, posthypnotic amnesia at emergence, wake and forget, it fades like a dream.

An amnesia suggestion delivered at the exit and tied to the moment of waking: the higher the count or the wider the eyes, the less is recalled. It may cover the whole session, the wording only, or named parts, and often leaves the effects in place while removing the memory of their source. It is the general amnesia suggestion specialized by position and by its link to the wake.

**How:** State the scope exactly: what is forgotten, what is kept, and whether effects remain. Tie the forgetting to the wake steps or to a familiar model of forgetting such as a dream fading on waking. Follow the wake with a change of subject, which helps more than insisting. Expect partial results; most listeners keep a gist. Include a reversal condition (a cue, a time, or 'you can remember whenever you need to') and say in the description that the file suggests forgetting.

> As I count you up, the words of this session slip away like a dream on waking. The calm stays.

> By five, you remember feeling relaxed and very little else, and that is fine.

> You can leave the details here, and recall them later whenever you need to.

**Spot it by:** 'forget', 'won't remember', 'slips away', 'fades', 'out of reach' inside or just before the wake passage; 'when you wake', 'as you wake', 'once your eyes open' governing a forgetting clause; 'like a dream', 'the harder you try to remember'; contrast of memory and effect ('the words fade, the feeling stays'); a release clause ('until I say', 'you will remember when').

**Not to be confused with:** Amnesia suggestion (the general device, usable anywhere; this row is its use tied to the wake); Forgetting where it came from (that keeps the idea and removes only where it came from); Distraction amnesia (that gets forgetting from an abrupt topic change, with no forgetting suggestion in the text).

**Evidence:** experimental. Suggested posthypnotic amnesia is a standard, measured scale item: it is a temporary recall failure that reverses on a cue, occurs fully in a minority of highly responsive people, and does not erase the memory. Source: Weitzenhoffer & Hilgard, Stanford Hypnotic Susceptibility Scale, Form C (1962).

**Why it works:** Hypnotic amnesia, Response expectancy theory, Demand characteristics, Source-monitoring error, State-dependent memory.

**Consent:** It works against the listener's later ability to review what was suggested, so it must be disclosed beforehand and paired with a way to recover the memory.


#### Structured amnesia *(variant)*

Also called: bracketing, resume the earlier topic, bracketed amnesia.

An amnesia move done by structure, not by instruction. The speaker stops mid-sentence or mid-topic before the induction and resumes that same sentence or topic immediately after emergence, so the trance sits between two halves of one continuous thread and tends to be skipped in recall. No forgetting is suggested aloud.

**How:** Before the induction, start a concrete, mundane sentence or topic and break off at a clear point. After emergence, resume with the exact words or the same topic, as if nothing happened. Keep the resumed line identical or close to identical; any comment on the trance ('how was that?') breaks the bracket. In audio scripts it works best when the opening topic is distinctive and the emergence is short.

> [Pretalk] ...and the thing about rainy afternoons is that the light goes soft and grey and— well, let's begin. [Emergence] ...the light goes soft and grey, and everything slows down.

> [Before induction] So, as I was saying about the train timetable— [After waking] —about the train timetable, the 8:15 is always late.

**Spot it by:** a sentence broken off just before the induction and resumed word for word after emergence; as I was saying (directly after emergence); same topic in the last pretalk line and the first post-emergence line; no mention of the trance between the resumed lines.

**Not to be confused with:** Distraction amnesia (changes to a new subject after the material; structured amnesia returns to the old one); Amnesia on waking (states the forgetting aloud; structured amnesia never mentions it); Nested loops (opens and closes stories inside the session around the suggestions; structured amnesia brackets the whole trance with one piece of ordinary talk begun before the induction and resumed after the wake); Unfinished sentence (breaks a sentence off and never resumes it; here the same sentence is picked up again after emergence).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Described in Ericksonian clinical literature and consistent with event-boundary effects on memory; no controlled test of the scripted form. Source: Erickson & Rossi, Varieties of hypnotic amnesia, American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1974).

**Why it works:** Hypnotic amnesia, Event segmentation theory, Indirect suggestion.

**Consent:** Works without the listener noticing; disclose in advance if the script uses it.


#### Forgetting where it came from *(variant)*

Also called: source amnesia, it feels like your own idea, own-idea framing.

A suggestion about where a suggested idea will seem to have come from. The content stays and its origin is removed, in one of two ways a labeler can see: the script says the listener will not remember where the idea came from, or it says the idea, urge or behavior will later feel like their own decision. Both forms point forward from a suggestion just given. It differs from plain amnesia suggestion, which removes the content; from retroactive framing, which says the trait was always there; and from 'it's what you want', which claims a wish the listener has now and makes no statement about how a suggested idea will be experienced later.

**How:** State the content first, then attach the source-forgetting: 'you'll simply find yourself ... and it will feel like your own idea'. Phrase it around ownership and naturalness, not concealment. It is stronger when the change is small and plausible. Do not combine it with checking questions that remind the listener of the session.

> Tomorrow you'll reach for water instead of coffee, and it will just feel like something you decided.

> You won't remember where this idea came from. It will simply be yours.

> Later, the thought will arrive on its own, as if you'd always meant to think it.

**Spot it by:** 'feel like your own idea', 'your own choice', 'your own thought' said of a suggestion just given; 'you won't remember where the idea came from', 'you won't remember being told it'; 'as if you decided it yourself' said of a decision the script has just suggested; a prediction that the listener will later attribute the suggested thought or action to themselves rather than to the speaker.

**Not to be confused with:** It was always so (says the trait was always there; source amnesia says a newly suggested idea will lose its origin or seem self-made); Amnesia suggestion (removes the content itself, not only its source); It's what you want (claims the listener wants the response now or already; source amnesia predicts how a suggested idea will be experienced later); You chose this (cites a choice the listener has already made as proof of wanting; source amnesia makes no appeal to a past choice); Inner-voice suggestion (suggests the speaker's voice becomes the listener's thinking voice from now on; source amnesia concerns the origin of one suggested idea).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Posthypnotic source amnesia for facts learned during hypnosis has been demonstrated experimentally. That does not establish that a scripted suggestion can make a newly suggested idea feel self-generated. Source: Evans & Thorn, Two types of posthypnotic amnesia: recall amnesia and source amnesia (1966).

**Why it works:** Source-monitoring error, Hypnotic amnesia, Sleeper effect.

**Consent:** Designed to hide its own influence; the listener should know beforehand that suggestions may later feel self-generated.


#### Distraction amnesia *(variant)*

Also called: change the subject on waking, amnesia by distraction.

Amnesia produced by denying rehearsal: the speaker moves attention away immediately after the key material, usually at emergence, with an unrelated question, task or topic. Nothing about forgetting is said. It differs from structured amnesia, which returns to a pre-trance topic, and from a pattern interrupt, which breaks a state rather than following key content.

**How:** Place the shift directly after the suggestion or the emergence count, with no pause and no recap. Use something concrete and attention-grabbing (a simple question, a small task, a sensory detail in the room). Avoid summarizing the session afterwards; that undoes it.

> ...three, two, one, eyes open. Now, quick question: what did you have for breakfast today?

> ...and that's settled. By the way, did you ever find out who left that umbrella by the door?

**Spot it by:** unrelated question or task immediately after emergence; abrupt topic change after a key suggestion; quick question / by the way (right after waking); no recap or reference to the session after waking.

**Not to be confused with:** Structured amnesia (returns to the pre-trance topic rather than switching to a new one); Reorientation check (directs attention to body feeling, the room, or alertness after trance; distraction amnesia switches to unrelated content to draw attention away from the preceding material); Attention call (uses a change of sound, voice, or topic to capture attention; distraction amnesia uses a topic switch after material to reduce rehearsal of it); Pattern interrupt (breaks an ongoing sequence rather than shifting away from material after it has ended).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Used in Ericksonian practice; consistent with research showing interference after encoding reduces later recall, but the scripted technique itself is not separately tested. Source: Erickson & Rossi, Varieties of hypnotic amnesia, American Journal of Clinical Hypnosis (1974).

**Why it works:** Working-memory interference, Hypnotic amnesia, Attentional capture.

**Consent:** Works without the listener noticing; disclose in advance if the script uses it.


### Age regression *(unit)*

Also called: regression, going back, hypnotic age regression.

A suggestion that moves the listener's sense of self to an earlier age, often by counting back through years or walking back through rooms or calendars. It covers both 'remembering as an adult' and 'being younger now'. It differs from revivification, which relives one specific memory and its state, and from suggested memory, which adds events that did not happen.

**How:** Give a clear path back (counting years down, pages turning, a corridor of doors) and a clear target age or period. Use present tense once arrived, and ask open sensory questions rather than supplying details. Always provide a matching return path and reorient to the present age before emergence. It fails or harms when the script supplies emotionally loaded details the listener may take as real memory.

> With each number I count, you go back one year younger... ten... nine... eight... and now you're small again.

> Notice how big the table looks from down here. What do you see?

> And now, coming back up through the years, all the way to today, your own age, here, now.

**Spot it by:** 'younger and younger', 'smaller', 'going back through the years'; counting backwards through years, ages, birthdays or school grades; a stated age or period as the present: 'you are seven now', 'it is your first day of school'; child's-eye details: furniture looking big, small hands, a childhood room; return passage naming the present age or date: 'back up to today', 'your own age'.

**Not to be confused with:** Revivification (the listener stays their present self and recalls one memory for its feeling; label age regression only when the text states or implies a different age, body or date); Suggested memory (supplies events that did not happen; regression moves the listener back without itself adding events); Future progression (moves forward to a future time, not back); Time confusion (scrambles days and tenses without sending the listener to any particular time; it may lead into regression but is only the scrambling).

**Evidence:** contested. Listeners report vivid regression, but controlled studies find adult, not child-like, cognition and no special accuracy of recovered details. Source: Nash, What, if anything, is regressed about hypnotic age regression? (1987).

**Why it works:** Sociocognitive theory of hypnosis, Trance logic, Imagination inflation, Abreaction, State-dependent memory.

**Consent:** Can surface distressing material and produce confident but inaccurate memories; tell the listener beforehand, give a clear return path and do not treat what emerges as fact.


### Revivification *(unit)*

Also called: reliving, re-experience a memory, resource recall.

A recall device aimed at re-entering a state: the listener picks or is led to a real memory and walks through its sights, sounds and body sensations until the feeling comes back. The target is the state (calm, confidence, absorption), and the listener stays their present self. This is the Ericksonian and NLP sense of the word; older hypnosis texts use 'revivification' for the complete form of age regression, in which the earlier time is relived as the present, and that sense is covered here by age regression. Label age regression when the text changes the listener's age or date, and revivification induction when the recalled memory is of trance and the passage is the induction.

**How:** Let the listener choose the memory ('a time when you felt completely calm') rather than supplying one. Move through senses one by one in present tense, then name the state as it returns. Often followed by anchoring the state. It fails when the memory is rushed or narrated in past tense from outside.

> Remember a time you felt completely sure of yourself. Be there now. What do you see around you?

> Notice the temperature of the air, the sounds nearby, and that feeling of being sure, coming back now.

> Go back to the last time you were truly rested, and let your body remember it.

**Spot it by:** remember a time when; go back to that moment / be there now; what do you see / hear / feel there; past memory narrated in present tense; that feeling coming back now.

**Not to be confused with:** Age regression (moves the listener's felt age back; revivification only re-enters one memory's state); Revivification induction (uses a memory of past trance to induce trance; revivification targets any resource state); Guided imagery (builds an imagined scene rather than recalling a lived one).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Standard in clinical hypnosis for accessing resource states; affect returns with vivid recall in ordinary memory research, but the hypnotic version is not separately validated.

**Why it works:** State-dependent memory, Utilization, Priming.


### Future progression *(unit)*

Also called: pseudo-orientation in time, future self, age progression, looking back from the future.

A time-orientation suggestion: the listener is told it is now a later date, the goal is achieved, and they recall how they got there. The defining feature is looking back on the change as finished. It differs from future pacing, which rehearses using a change in a future situation from the present, and from retroactive framing, which places the trait in the past rather than the listener in the future.

**How:** Name a concrete future point (next month, a year from now), then switch to past tense for the change: 'you remember how it started to get easier'. Ask the listener what helped, so they supply the path. Bring them back to the present before emergence. It is weaker if the script stays in future tense, which makes it ordinary rehearsal.

> It's a year from now. Look back at this past year and notice how easily the change happened.

> From here, six months on, you can remember the first day it got easier. What did you do differently?

> Now come back to today, bringing that finished feeling with you.

**Spot it by:** a later date asserted as now: 'it's a year from now', 'it is next spring'; 'look back on', 'looking back from here'; past tense about events that are still in the future; 'you remember how it changed', 'remember the day it got easier'; questions about the path from the future side: 'what did you do differently?'; return passage: 'come back to today'.

**Not to be confused with:** Future pacing (rehearses a future cue or response as it happens; progression places the listener after the change and looks back on it); Mental rehearsal (runs through the future behavior itself; progression looks back on it as completed); As-if frame (asks the listener to suppose an outcome is true; a hypothetical future scene can also be future progression when it places them at a later time looking back on a completed change); It was always so (places a new trait in the listener's past; progression places the listener at a future time); Already-happened framing (presupposes finished change without moving the listener to a later time).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. A standard clinical technique since Erickson; no controlled studies show it beats ordinary goal imagery. Source: Erickson, Pseudo-orientation in time as a hypnotherapeutic procedure (1954).

**Why it works:** Presupposition, Response expectancy theory, Imagination inflation.


### It was always so *(unit)*

Also called: retroactive framing, you've always been, retroactive continuity, retcon.

A framing move that backdates the suggestion: instead of 'you will become calm', the script says 'you've always been calm underneath'. The new trait is presented as rediscovered, not installed. It differs from an identity statement, which asserts the trait in the present with no claim about the past, and from suggested memory, which supplies specific false events.

**How:** Use perfect tense and continuity words: always, all along, never really stopped, remember. Present the session as noticing rather than changing. Works best with traits that plausibly have some past evidence, which the listener can then supply. Overreaching ('you have always obeyed') against clear contrary memory breaks belief.

> You've always been calmer than you thought. You're only noticing it now.

> This focus isn't new. It's been there all along, waiting to be used.

> Some part of you has always known how to rest like this.

**Spot it by:** always / all along / always have been; you've always (been / known / wanted); it was never new; you're only noticing / remembering it now; deep down you always.

**Not to be confused with:** Identity statement (asserts the trait now, with no claim it was always there); It's what you want (claims a wish the listener has now; label retroactive framing when a backdating word (always, all along, never new) is present, and both when a wish is backdated ('you've always wanted this')); Suggested memory (supplies specific past events rather than a timeless trait); Already-happened framing (presupposes a change has happened; retroactive framing denies there was a change); Gaslighting (tells the listener their own memory or perception is wrong; retroactive framing adds a claim about the past without disputing what the listener recalls).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Common in practitioner and community scripts; it relies on presupposition and self-perception, which are studied, but the device itself is not.

**Why it works:** Presupposition, Self-perception theory, Labeling effect, Belief perseverance.

**Consent:** Rewrites how the listener understands their own past and can persist after the session; the listener should know the script presents new traits as always present.


### Suggested memory *(unit)*

Also called: false memory play, implanted memory, memory implantation, pseudomemory suggestion.

A suggestion that supplies the content of a memory: an event, a conversation, a scene, presented as something the listener now recalls. It differs from retroactive framing, which backdates a trait without specific events, from revivification, which recalls a real memory, and from age regression, which moves the listener back without itself adding events.

**How:** Frame it explicitly as play or fiction in the pretalk if it is not meant to be believed. Inside the script, invite remembering rather than asserting ('you might remember the time...') and add sensory detail; detail and repetition make the image feel more like memory. Close by marking it as a story or a suggestion so the listener can file it correctly. Never use it on real-world history the listener cares about.

> You might remember the afternoon you first learned to float, the water holding you up, the sky so wide.

> Remember the first time you heard this voice, years ago, on a train, and how you leaned in to listen.

> And you can recall what you said that evening on the porch, the exact words, and how easy they were to say.

**Spot it by:** 'you remember the time when' followed by a specific event the speaker introduces as the listener's memory; 'remember when you ...' followed by a specific scene supplied by the speaker; past time or place details introduced as the listener's own recollection, without an established memory to elaborate; vividness instructions attached to a scene supplied as the listener's past experience; detailed past-tense scene presented as the listener's own recollection.

**Not to be confused with:** Revivification (invites recall of an experience the listener supplies; suggested memory supplies the event); It was always so (backdates a trait without supplying a specific event); Gaslighting (denies or rewrites a memory or perception the listener already has; a supplied past event can carry both labels if it also contradicts the listener's account); Memory enhancement (suggests clearer recall of established material; suggested memory supplies the event to be recalled); Positive hallucination (suggests perceiving something now rather than remembering a past event).

**Evidence:** experimental. False memories can be created by suggestion and imagination in a minority of participants, with or without hypnosis; hypnosis raises confidence more than accuracy. Source: Laurence & Perry, Hypnotically created memory among highly hypnotizable subjects, Science (1983).

**Why it works:** Misinformation effect, Imagination inflation, Source-monitoring error, Illusory truth effect.

**Consent:** Can produce memories the listener later believes are real; frame it as fiction, mark it at the end and never use it on real personal history.


### Dream suggestion *(unit)*

Also called: you'll dream of, dream incubation, posthypnotic dream suggestion, wet dreams.

A posthypnotic suggestion whose target is sleep: that a dream will occur, what it will contain, or that it will be remembered. It differs from sleep ending, which lets the listener fall asleep at the end of the session, and from a general posthypnotic suggestion, whose target is waking behavior.

**How:** Place it near the end, often just before a sleep ending. Keep the content open ('a dream about this feeling') rather than scripted scene by scene, and use permissive wording ('you may dream'), since dreams cannot be checked. Add recall support if wanted ('when you wake, the dream stays with you'). Overly specific content tends not to appear and can read as a failure.

> Tonight you may dream of water, slow and warm, carrying this calm into your sleep.

> Whatever you dream, some part of it will carry this feeling.

> And when you wake tomorrow, you'll remember your dream clearly.

**Spot it by:** 'tonight', 'as you sleep', 'when you go to bed' + a dream clause; 'you may dream of', 'you will dream about'; 'in your dreams' said of a later night, not as a simile ('like a dream' does not count); 'remember your dream when you wake', 'the dream stays with you'; future tense reaching into sleep after the session.

**Not to be confused with:** Drift into sleep (lets the listener fall asleep; it does not suggest dream content); Posthypnotic suggestion (the general label for a response after the session; use dream suggestion when that response is a dream during later sleep); Guided imagery (a dream or dreamlike scene the listener is led through now, in the session; dream suggestion points at sleep afterwards).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Presleep suggestion can modestly shift dream content in some studies; effects are small and inconsistent, and reports depend on what the dreamer recalls.

**Why it works:** Posthypnotic suggestion, Priming, Response expectancy theory.

**Consent:** Acts during sleep after the session ends; say in the pretalk that dream suggestions are included.


### Memory enhancement *(unit)*

Also called: hypermnesia, you'll remember every word, enhanced recall.

A suggestion of improved recall of named material: a past event, study material, or the session's own words. It is the opposite direction to amnesia suggestion. The mark is a recall verb (remember, recall, come back to you) with an object. It differs from sealing, which says the suggestions stay in effect without saying they will be remembered; from capacity suggestion, which claims better memory as a general ability with nothing in particular to recall; and from revivification, which re-enters a memory's state.

**How:** Say what will be remembered and when it will come back ('every word will be there when you need it'). Use it to keep key suggestions available or to support study recall; pair with a cue for retrieval. Do not use it to recover past events as evidence; it raises confidence more than accuracy.

> You'll remember every word I say tonight, clearly, whenever you want it.

> When you sit the exam, what you studied will come back to you, one fact after another.

> You'll remember this feeling exactly, whenever you choose to.

**Spot it by:** 'you'll remember every word', 'remember everything I say'; 'it will come back to you' when 'it' refers to named material; 'recall' or 'remember' + named material + 'clearly', 'perfectly', or 'in detail'; a retrieval moment tied to named material: 'when you sit the exam, what you studied will come back'; 'every detail' of a specified event or passage will be remembered.

**Not to be confused with:** Sealing suggestions before waking (says the suggestions stay in effect after waking; memory enhancement says named material will be recalled); Capacity suggestion (claims memory as an ability improves in general; memory enhancement names what will be recalled); Revivification (re-experiences a memory's state rather than suggesting clearer recall); Amnesia suggestion (the opposite direction: suggests forgetting).

**Evidence:** contested. Hypnotic recall enhancement produces more recalled items but also more errors, with confidence rising faster than accuracy; the popular claim of better memory outruns the evidence. Source: Dywan & Bowers, The use of hypnosis to enhance recall (1983).

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Placebo effect, Posthypnotic suggestion.

**Consent:** Hypnotic memory enhancement can increase confidence in inaccurate recollections; say beforehand if the script suggests clearer recall, and do not treat recalled material as verified.


## Identity and belief

Also called: identity work, self-concept suggestion, belief change.

This family groups moves aimed at the listener's self-description and standing beliefs rather than at a momentary state or action. Some state the new identity outright (identity statement, renaming, role assignment); some work through how the listener is referred to (pronoun shift, ownership and object language); some supply the reasoning that makes the new self feel earned (from act to trait, linking to values, it's what you want); some fix beliefs or the durability of the change (belief statement, permanence claim). It has no nested families. Close neighbours live elsewhere: labeling and your-actions-prove-it (compliance), persona/alter (dissociation), it-was-always-so (memory and time), first-person suggestion (suggestion forms) and using the listener's name (attention).

**Choosing:** Choose by what you need to change. To name the new self, use identity statement, renaming or role assignment; to make it feel earned, use from act to trait or linking to values; to change self-reference in the language itself, use pronoun shift or third-person self-reference; to change thinking habits, use inner-voice suggestion or thought replacement; to fix a rule or the durability of the change, use belief statement or permanence claim. Identity suggestions land best after the listener has already done something the identity can be built on, and they need a consent frame when they are meant to persist.

**Not to be confused with:** Labeling (labeling assigns a trait in order to ask for matching behavior; this family changes the self-description itself); Persona / alter (a persona is a separate switchable self; identity devices change the listener's one ongoing self).

**Why it works:** Labeling effect, Self-perception theory, Commitment and consistency, Self-reference effect.

**Consent:** Identity changes are meant to outlast the session, so the listener should know in advance what self-description is being installed and how to reverse it.


### Identity statement *(unit)*

Also called: you are, I am, identity suggestion, being statement.

A direct suggestion whose predicate is a standing trait or a kind of person: "you are a calm person", "you are a confident speaker". The move is the copular "you are X" (or first-person "I am X") said as settled fact about who the listener is. A passing condition in the same grammar ("you are relaxed", "you are ready") is an ordinary direct suggestion; label an identity statement only when X is offered as still true of the listener after the session. It differs from labeling, which assigns a trait in order to request behavior, and from it-was-always-so, which adds a claim about the past.

**How:** Place it in the suggestion section after the listener is absorbed, and phrase it in present tense as a description, not a wish. Pick a trait the listener can recognize in themselves at least a little, then widen it. Repetition across the session and pairing with a moment of felt success make it land; claims the listener can immediately disprove make it fail.

> You are someone who stays calm when others rush.

> You are a patient person. You are a steady person. You are a person who finishes things.

> I am a clear speaker, and I am someone people listen to.

**Spot it by:** 'you are' + kind-of-person noun phrase ('a calm person', 'a listener', 'a natural speaker'), said as fact; 'you're someone who ...' / 'you're the one who ...' / 'you're the kind of person who ...' with no request attached; 'I am' + trait or kind-of-person noun in a line for the listener to hear or repeat; 'that is who you are' / 'this is what you are'; series of short 'you are a/an X' sentences.

**Not to be confused with:** Direct suggestion ('you are relaxed' or 'you are ready' states a passing condition and is a plain direct suggestion; an identity statement names a standing trait or kind of person); Labeling (labeling attaches a trait to justify a requested behavior; an identity statement stops at the trait); It was always so (it-was-always-so adds the claim that the trait was always true); Affirmations (affirmations are first-person self-descriptions repeated as a practice; a single 'I am X' line is an identity statement, and a repeated block takes both labels); Naming the state (naming the state gives the present condition a name ('this is trance'); it says nothing about who the listener is).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Ego-strengthening identity statements are standard in clinical hypnosis texts; their specific contribution beyond the session as a whole is not well measured.

**Why it works:** Direct verbal suggestion, Labeling effect, Self-reference effect, Illusory truth effect.


### Renaming *(unit)*

Also called: new name, designation, title, assigned name.

The act of assigning a name, designation or title to the listener, usually with a statement of what it means. It differs from using the listener's name, which is the later act of addressing them by it, and from role assignment, which gives a role with expected behavior rather than a label.

**How:** Announce the name once, clearly, at a marked moment (often after deepening), and say what it stands for. Then use it consistently so it gathers meaning. A name that is easy to say and that fits the theme lands; changing it mid-script or never using it again wastes it.

> From now on, in this place, your name is Still.
