**Spot it by:** the last word of one clause repeated as the first word of the next; chains of 'X brings Y, Y brings Z'; a progression of three or more linked terms rising in intensity.

**Not to be confused with:** The more... the more (that ties two increases together in one comparison, without the linked chain); Contingent suggestion (contingent suggestion attaches a response to an ongoing event; gradatio is the repeated-word chain); Cause-effect link (cause-effect is the assertion that X makes or brings Y; gradatio is the carrying of the last term of one clause into the start of the next. A chain of 'X brings Y, Y brings Z' takes both labels); Parallelism (parallelism repeats the clause shape with new words; gradatio needs the end word of one clause repeated at the head of the next).

**Evidence:** rhetorical-tradition. A classical figure; no study of its effect in hypnosis.

**Why it works:** Processing fluency.


### Antithesis *(unit)*

Also called: contrast pair, balanced opposition.

Antithesis places contrasting ideas in parallel clauses so the contrast is sharpened by the matching form. It is a figure of phrasing. It differs from apposition of opposites, which pairs two opposed bodily experiences as a suggestion, and from chiasmus, which reverses word order.

**How:** Build two clauses with the same shape and swap in opposed terms (tense / loose, out there / in here, trying / allowing). Put the state you want second, so the contrast resolves into it. It fails when the two halves are unequal in length or the opposition is forced.

> You don't have to make it happen; you only have to let it happen.

> Out there, everything is noise; in here, everything is still.

**Spot it by:** two adjacent clauses of the same shape whose key words are opposites (tense / loose, out there / in here, make / let); 'not X but Y' / 'you don't have to X; you only have to Y'; 'out there... in here' / 'before... now' set in matching clauses; a semicolon or comma at the midpoint of a balanced contrast.

**Not to be confused with:** Apposition of opposites (apposition of opposites suggests two opposed experiences at once; antithesis is the balanced wording); The more... the more (that yokes two changing amounts with a correlative comparative, even when one rises and one falls; antithesis opposes two ideas without tying their amounts together); Old self / new self (old self / new self contrasts identities; antithesis is any balanced contrast); Chiasmus (chiasmus reverses the order of repeated terms).

**Evidence:** rhetorical-tradition. A classical figure; contrast effects on judgment are studied, but not this figure in hypnosis.

**Why it works:** Contrast effect, Processing fluency.


### Chiasmus *(unit)*

Also called: reversal, ABBA, antimetabole.

Chiasmus repeats key words or ideas in mirrored order, so the second clause turns the first around. The reversal invites a moment of working-out and tends to sound like a closed, quotable truth. It differs from antithesis, which opposes ideas without reversing word order.

**How:** Take two terms and put them in A-B order, then B-A in the next clause. Use it for a line you want remembered or for a gentle twist that slows evaluation. Keep it to one or two in a script; more becomes a puzzle.

> You don't need to go into trance; trance can come into you.

> Let your breath follow my voice, and let my voice follow your breath.

**Spot it by:** two terms appearing A...B in one clause and B...A in the next; 'not X into Y, but Y into X'; mirrored phrase pairs separated by a semicolon or 'and'.

**Not to be confused with:** Antithesis (antithesis opposes ideas in parallel order; chiasmus mirrors the order); Self-reinforcing loop (the loop also runs A-B then B-A, but it states that each term increases the other; label the loop when the clauses are 'the more... the more' links, and chiasmus when the reversal makes a turn of phrase with no claim that the terms feed each other); Circular wordplay (circular wordplay loops sound-alikes to confuse; chiasmus is a single clean reversal).

**Evidence:** rhetorical-tradition. A classical figure; its memorability is widely claimed but untested in hypnotic scripts.

**Why it works:** Processing fluency.


### Rhyme *(unit)*

Also called: rhyming, verse, rhymed suggestion.

Rhyme matches the final stressed vowel and following sounds of two or more words, usually at line ends. It makes a line easier to process and remember, and rhymed sayings are judged more accurate than unrhymed ones with the same meaning. It differs from alliteration, which repeats initial consonants.

**How:** Put the suggestion into a short rhymed couplet or a rhyming pair inside a sentence, keeping the wording natural. Reserve it for lines meant to be remembered or repeated, such as triggers, mantras and closing lines. Forced rhyme that bends the grammar draws attention to itself and breaks the mood.

> Sink and rest, you're doing your best.

> Down you go, soft and slow.

**Spot it by:** line-final or phrase-final words sharing end sounds; short couplets; rhyming pairs inside one sentence ('slow... go', 'deep... sleep').

**Not to be confused with:** Alliteration and sibilance (alliteration repeats initial consonants, not end sounds); Rhythm and meter (meter is a regular beat, which can exist without rhyme).

**Evidence:** experimental. Rhymed aphorisms were rated more accurate than unrhymed equivalents in controlled studies; that this deepens trance or strengthens suggestions is not tested. Source: McGlone & Tofighbakhsh, Birds of a feather flock conjointly (?): Rhyme as reason in aphorisms (2000).

**Why it works:** Cognitive fluency of rhyme (rhyme-as-reason), Processing fluency.


### Rhythm and meter *(unit)*

Also called: cadence, metrical pacing, rhythmic language.

Meter is a regular beat built into the wording itself, through syllable count and stress placement. In scripts it gives a rocking, predictable cadence that a reader falls into. It differs from a metronome or music bed, which supply the beat as audio, and from breath-synced delivery, which is timing in performance.

**How:** Write short lines with a similar count of stresses, often two or three, and keep the pattern steady through a passage. Read it aloud and fix any line that trips. Shift the meter, or break it, when you want to wake attention.

> Slowly drifting, softly sinking, gently letting go.

> Down and down and deeper still, resting, resting, as you will.

**Spot it by:** consecutive lines or phrases with the same number of stressed syllables; a run of same-shaped feet, such as stressed-unstressed pairs ('slowly drifting, softly sinking'); verse-like lineation with lines of near-equal syllable count; word order bent or filler words added ('and down and down') to keep the beat.

**Not to be confused with:** Metronome / steady beat (a metronome is an audio beat under the voice, not a beat in the words); Breath-synced pacing (breath-synced pacing is how the lines are timed in performance); Parallelism (parallelism matches grammar; meter matches stress pattern).

**Evidence:** rhetorical-tradition. Rhythm aids fluency and memory in general; claims that metrical language entrains trance are practitioner belief.

**Why it works:** Processing fluency, Habituation.


### Alliteration and sibilance *(unit)*

Also called: soft sounds, s sounds, sibilance, consonance.

Alliteration repeats a consonant sound at the start of nearby words; sibilance fills a line with s, sh and z sounds. In scripts the choice is usually soft sounds (s, sh, m, l) for a lulling surface, or hard stops (d, k) for a firmer edge. It is a figure of sound, separate from rhyme (end sounds) and meter (beat).

**How:** Pick the sound to match the state: s, sh, m and l for drifting and softness; d and k for firm commands. Cluster three or more in a phrase, on the words that carry the meaning. It fails when it becomes a tongue-twister.

> So soft, so still, so sleepy.

> Slipping slowly into silence.

> Mellow, melting, more and more.

**Spot it by:** three or more nearby words starting with the same consonant; dense s / sh / z sounds in a short span; repeated m or l sounds in a soothing phrase.

**Not to be confused with:** Rhyme (rhyme repeats end sounds); Whisper (whisper is a voice choice; sibilance is written into the words).

**Evidence:** rhetorical-tradition. A classical sound figure; sound symbolism is studied in linguistics, but the claim that soft consonants relax listeners is untested.

**Why it works:** Processing fluency.


### Rhetorical question *(unit)*

Also called: question for effect, erotema.

A rhetorical question is phrased as a question but works as an assertion: the answer is taken for granted. It draws the listener into silently agreeing rather than being told. It differs from question as suggestion, where considering the question produces a response, and from hypophora, where the speaker answers out loud.

**How:** Use it where a plain claim might be doubted: frame the point so that the only sensible inner answer is the one you want ('Isn't it nice to stop trying?'). Leave no answer and move on. It fails if the listener could reasonably answer the other way, which invites counterargument.

> And why would you want to hold on, when letting go feels this good?

> Who doesn't enjoy a moment with nothing to do?

**Spot it by:** a question whose only sensible answer is built in ('Who doesn't...?', 'Why would you...?', 'What could be easier than...?'); a sentence-opening negative question that asserts its content ('Isn't it nice to...?', 'Wouldn't anyone...?'); the question makes a general claim or evaluation, not a request to check a present sensation; the speaker moves on without answering it and without leaving time for an answer.

**Not to be confused with:** Question as suggestion (there considering the question produces the response; a rhetorical question asserts a point); Ask and answer (hypophora answers its own question aloud); Tag question (a tag question is a short add-on to a statement).

**Evidence:** contested. Experiments find rhetorical questions can raise or lower persuasion depending on argument strength and listener involvement; there is no simple boost. Source: Petty, Cacioppo & Heesacker, Effects of rhetorical questions on persuasion: a cognitive response analysis (1981).

**Why it works:** Elaboration likelihood model, Conversational implicature.


### Ask and answer *(unit)*

Also called: hypophora, anthypophora, question and answer.

Hypophora raises a question and immediately supplies the answer. It lets the writer voice the listener's likely thought and then settle it, keeping control of where the thought goes. It differs from a rhetorical question, which leaves the answer unspoken.

**How:** Phrase the question in the listener's voice or as an open wonder, then answer it in one or two plain sentences that carry the suggestion. Use it to explain, reassure, or move to the next section. It fails if the answer is weaker than the question.

> What happens if a thought drifts in? Nothing at all. You let it pass and sink a little deeper.

> And where does that tension go? Down through your arms and out of your fingertips.

**Spot it by:** a question immediately followed by a declarative answer from the speaker; 'What happens if...? ...' / 'And where does it go? ...'; question-answer pairs in the pretalk.

**Not to be confused with:** Rhetorical question (a rhetorical question leaves its answer implied); Preempting objections (preemption names and answers an objection; hypophora is the question-answer form, used for any content).

**Evidence:** rhetorical-tradition. A classical figure; no direct study in hypnosis.

**Why it works:** Conversational framing.


### Refrain *(unit)*

Also called: recurring line, chorus, return line.

A refrain is a fixed line that recurs across a script, separated by other material, the way a chorus recurs in a song. Each return reconnects the listener to the state built the last time. It differs from anaphora (a consecutive run), from mantra (a phrase repeated many times in a row) and from repeating a suggestion in varied words.

**How:** Write one short, memorable line that sums up the state or suggestion, and return to it at section ends or after each deepener. Keep it verbatim so it can become a cue. Spacing matters: too often and it becomes a mantra; too rarely and it is not recognized.

> (after each section) "And it feels so good to let go."

> (recurring) "Just listen, and drift."

**Spot it by:** the same full sentence appearing three or more times, separated by other text; a line repeated at section boundaries; verbatim return of an earlier line after a gap.

**Not to be confused with:** Mantra (a mantra is repeated many times in a row; a refrain returns at intervals); Anaphora (anaphora repeats an opening across consecutive clauses); Suggestion repetition (that repeats the suggestion, possibly varied; a refrain is one fixed line).

**Evidence:** rhetorical-tradition. A poetic and musical form; spaced repetition aids memory in general, but its hypnotic effect is untested.

**Why it works:** Spacing effect, Illusory truth effect, Mere-exposure effect.


### Written pause *(unit)*

Also called: ellipsis, line break, beat, pause marker.

A written pause puts silence into the script itself, telling the reader or performer where to stop. It slows the reading pace, isolates words for emphasis, and leaves room for a response. It is the text-side marking; the actual silence in a recording belongs to the delivery family, and a pause given a depth instruction is a silence deepener.

**How:** Place pauses after suggestions, before key words, and between counts. Use ellipses or line breaks for short beats and an explicit note ('[pause]') for long ones. Pauses everywhere flatten the rhythm; place them where something should land.

> And now... just... let go.

> Breathe in.

And out.

[pause]

**Spot it by:** ellipses ('...') mid-sentence; dashes isolating a word; blank lines between short lines; bracketed stage notes like [pause], [beat], (wait).

**Not to be confused with:** Silence / pause deepener (a silence deepener gives the silence a job (going deeper); a written pause only marks timing); Silence (silence is the heard gap in the audio); Analog marking (marking sets selected words apart (by pause, capitals or italics) so that together they carry a separate message; a written pause only sets the timing of the line); Unfinished sentence (an unfinished sentence breaks off and never resumes).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Pause marking is standard in clinical and practitioner scripts; its specific effect is not measured.

**Why it works:** Attentional capture.


### Lengthening sentences *(unit)*

Also called: run-on sentences, long sentences, loosening syntax.

This is a trend across a passage or script: sentences start ordinary and become long, run-on and loosely joined as trance deepens. Long, loose syntax is hard to parse critically and invites the listener to float along. It is a pattern across many sentences, not a single linking device like polysyndeton.

**How:** Open with normal sentences, then join clauses with 'and', 'as', 'while' and commas, dropping full stops. Keep each clause simple so length does not become confusion. Reverse the trend, back to short clear sentences, for emergence.

> You sit down. You get comfortable. And as you settle, and your breathing slows, and the room seems to drift further and further away while my voice stays right here with you, you find there is less and less to hold on to...

**Spot it by:** average sentence length rising across the passage; late-script sentences of 40+ words with few full stops; clauses joined by 'and', 'as', 'while' in long chains.

**Not to be confused with:** And... and... and (polysyndeton is the 'and' linking inside a run; lengthening is the trend across the script); Cognitive overload (overload piles up simultaneous demands; lengthening only loosens syntax); Shortening sentences (the opposite trend).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Common in Ericksonian-style writing; no study shows that longer sentences deepen trance.

**Why it works:** Cognitive load.


### Shortening sentences *(unit)*

Also called: fragments, one-word lines, stripping down.

This is a trend across a passage: full sentences give way to phrases, then to single words. The reduction mirrors a quieting mind and leaves little to evaluate. It is the opposite trend to lengthening sentences and is distinct from epizeuxis, which is one burst of repetition.

**How:** Build normal sentences, then drop subjects and verbs, leaving the state words alone on their lines. End the passage on one or two words with pauses between. Return to full sentences when you need the listener to follow detailed instructions.

> You can let your mind go quiet now. Quieter. Still. Empty. Gone.

**Spot it by:** average sentence length falling across a passage; a run of one- to three-word lines or fragments; verbless lines near the end of a deepener.

**Not to be confused with:** Lengthening sentences (the opposite trend); Immediate repetition (epizeuxis repeats one word back to back; shortening reduces length over a run); Mind-blanking (cognitive quieting suggests thoughts stopping; shortening is the stylistic reduction that can accompany it).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. A common stylistic choice in recorded scripts; no study of its effect.


### Euphemism *(unit)*

Also called: soft wording, softening term.

A euphemism substitutes a gentle term for a harsh, explicit or alarming one ('let go' for 'give up control', 'quiet' for 'unable to think'). It lowers the listener's reaction to what is being suggested. It differs from redefinition, which openly gives a word a new meaning, and from loaded language, which carries a group's judgment.

**How:** Choose a term that is accurate but soft, and use it consistently. Use it for comfort, not concealment: the listener should still be able to tell what is meant. It fails, ethically and practically, when it hides what the suggestion does.

> Just let me take care of the deciding for a while.

> In a moment you'll take a little rest, and when you come back you won't mind what you missed.

**Spot it by:** a mild expression in place of a blunter referent recoverable from the script's context; the same act or effect named plainly in one place and softly in another; an indirect phrase for bodily, sexual or control content whose direct referent is clear in context.

**Not to be confused with:** Unspecified verb (a vague process verb ('let go', 'allow', 'drift') leaves out how; it is a euphemism only when the script shows a blunter thing it is standing in for); Surrender as freedom (that reframe claims that giving up control is a gain; euphemism makes no claim and only substitutes a gentler word); Redefinition (redefinition openly assigns a new meaning to a word); Loaded language (loaded language is a standing vocabulary that carries a group's judgment; euphemism softens one expression); Nominalization (nominalization turns a process into an abstract noun; euphemism swaps a harsh word for a soft one).

**Evidence:** rhetorical-tradition. A recognized figure; framing effects of word choice are well studied, but not euphemism in hypnosis specifically.

**Why it works:** Framing effect.

**Consent:** When a euphemism disguises what a suggestion actually changes, the listener cannot consent to it; content notes should state effects plainly.


### Hyperbole *(unit)*

Also called: exaggeration, overstatement.

Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration ('a thousand times deeper', 'heavier than stone'). It is not meant to be checked; it signals intensity and gives the imagination a large target. It differs from a reference point, where a number sets a scale for later judgments, and from a potency claim about the recording itself.

**How:** Exaggerate the felt quality, not a checkable fact. Keep it occasional so ordinary statements stay believable. It fails when it sounds like hype or when the listener's experience is obviously smaller.

> Your arms feel as heavy as mountains.

> So relaxed you could melt straight through the chair.

**Spot it by:** large round multipliers ('a thousand times', 'a million miles'); superlatives about felt states ('the deepest you've ever been'); impossible comparisons ('heavier than stone').

**Not to be confused with:** Stepwise doubling (a multiplier or increment tied to each count, breath or repetition is stepwise doubling, even when the number is exaggerated); Reference point (a number offered as a reference point for later depth or judgment is anchoring; hyperbole is an obvious overstatement for emphasis, and a numeric phrase may do both); Comparative deletion (a bare comparative with no stated standard ('deeper', 'more relaxed') is not itself an overstatement); Potency claim (a potency claim describes the recording or technique in advance; hyperbole overstates a sensation, depth or effect).

**Evidence:** rhetorical-tradition. A classical figure; its effect on suggestion response is unstudied.


### Sense crossing *(unit)*

Also called: synesthesia, synaesthetic metaphor, feel my voice, words as touch.

Sense crossing describes a perception in one modality using words from another ('my voice wraps around you', 'a warm color of calm'). It makes the speaker's words seem physically present and blends attention across senses. It differs from sensory overlap, which leads step by step from one active sense into another, and from plain sensory language, which stays within each sense.

**How:** Pick the sense the listener is receiving (usually hearing) and describe it with touch, temperature or weight words. Use it to make the voice tangible or a state visible. It fails when mixed so densely that nothing is concrete.

> Feel my voice settle over your shoulders like a warm blanket.

> Notice how bright that tingling is in your fingertips, so bright it almost hums.

**Spot it by:** a sound, voice or silence described with touch, temperature or weight words ('warm voice wrapping', 'heavy silence'); 'feel my words' / 'feel my voice' / 'taste the sound'; a sound or touch given a colour or brightness ('a soft blue hush', 'a bright tingle'); a perception verb paired with the wrong sense's object ('hear the warmth', 'see how quiet it is').

**Not to be confused with:** Sensory overlap (sensory overlap leads the listener in steps from a sense already active into another; sense crossing is a single phrase that describes one sense in another's words); State-as-substance (state-as-substance turns a state (calm, blankness) into a material that moves through the body; sense crossing starts from an actual perception (a voice, a touch) and borrows another sense's vocabulary for it); Sensory language (sensory language describes each sense in its own terms).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Synaesthetic metaphor is a known literary figure; its use to deepen absorption is practitioner lore.

**Why it works:** Absorption (trait).


### Present tense and progressive *(unit)*

Also called: ing-forms, happening now, present progressive.

Present-tense and progressive phrasing ('you are relaxing', 'your arm is lifting') describes the response as under way rather than requested or in the future. It lets the listener find the effect as current experience. It differs from already-happened framing, which presents the effect as complete, and from change-of-state verbs, which presuppose an ongoing process by verb choice.

**How:** Prefer 'you are drifting' to 'you will drift', and 'noticing' to 'you will notice'. Use the progressive for gradual effects and the simple present for steady states. Keep future tense for posthypnotic suggestions, where the timing is the point.

> You're sinking, softening, letting go.

> Your hand is getting lighter, lifting now, all by itself.

**Spot it by:** a run of two or more progressive verbs describing a response that is not yet verifiable ('you are sinking, softening, letting go'); bare -ing participles stacked without a subject ('drifting... floating... sinking'); 'now' attached to a present-tense description of the suggested response ('lifting now'); a visible switch from future or modal phrasing ('you will', 'you can') to the present for the same response; label once per passage, not per sentence.

**Not to be confused with:** Pacing (pacing describes in the present what the listener can verify now; this entry is the present tense used for a response that is being suggested); Direct suggestion (direct suggestion is the open statement or command of the response in any tense; this label marks the tense choice and sits on top of it); Already-happened framing (already-happened framing speaks of the effect as done; present tense has it under way); Change-of-state verb (that relies on verbs like 'continue' to presuppose the process).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Present-tense phrasing is standard advice in clinical suggestion writing; its advantage over other tenses is not experimentally shown.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory.


### Counted passage *(unit)*

Also called: count as scaffold, numbered beats, counted pacing.

A counted passage uses numbers as a scaffold: each count marks a beat, and material sits between counts. The numbers set rhythm and progress and signal an end point. It differs from a countdown deepener or counting induction, where each number is itself tied to going deeper, and from losing the numbers, where the count is meant to vanish.

**How:** Choose a range that suits the passage length (often ten to one, or one to five), and put one sentence or image between each number. Make the gaps grow or the content change as the count advances. Mark the final number clearly so the end lands.

> Ten. Notice your feet on the floor. Nine. Your legs grow still. Eight. Your hands rest easily...

> One, the room is behind you. Two, only my voice. Three, nothing else matters right now.

**Spot it by:** numbers in sequence as their own sentences or line openings; sentences of content between consecutive numbers; 'ten... nine... eight' or 'one... two... three' spread over a passage.

**Not to be confused with:** Countdown deepener (label the deepener when a rule is stated or plain that each number means deeper ('with each number, deeper'); label counted passage when the numbers only mark off the content and nothing is said to happen because of the number); Counting induction (counting induction ties each number to going into trance); Count-up wake (a count upward in which each number restores alertness is the wake-up); Countdown finale (the finale is the session's closing count toward a release on the last number); Losing the numbers (losing the numbers makes the count disappear).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Counting is a long-standing clinical pacing tool; its role as pure scaffold, apart from depth suggestion, is not separately studied.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory.


## Coercive-control patterns

Also called: coercive control, thought-reform patterns, undue influence patterns, cult techniques.

Devices named by researchers of thought reform, high-control groups and coercive relationships, written here as things a script can say. Each one shifts power toward the speaker by controlling the listener's perception, information, relationships, attachment, self-judgment or freedom to leave. In consensual erotic hypnosis they appear as agreed fantasy with exits kept open; used on someone who has not agreed, or with no exit, they are abuse. Related devices that are not coercive by themselves sit elsewhere: intermittent reinforcement and deprivation under operant conditioning, fear then relief and the craving frame under motivation and emotion, exclusivity and in-group language under social influence, the money ask and recruiting others under task assignment.

**Choosing:** Pick the child by what the line controls: perception or memory (gaslighting), relationships (isolation), information (controlling the inputs), vocabulary (loaded language), thinking (thought-terminating cliche), disclosure (confession), needs (sole-source claim; create the need, sell the cure), exit (fear of leaving), blame (blame reversal), attachment (affection flooding, hot and cold), standards (impossible standard), self-monitoring (self-policing). Label the most specific control target. An instruction to pay the speaker or to bring in other people is a task assignment variant (money ask, recruiting others); label it there, alongside whichever device in this family carries it. If the line only rewards or withholds without targeting one of these, use the operant-conditioning entries instead. Any script using these needs a visible fiction frame, a working exit, and nothing that persists past the session without explicit agreement.

**Not to be confused with:** Operant conditioning (conditioning shapes behavior with consequences; coercive patterns target the listener's perception, ties, money or exit); Motivation and emotion (emotion levers raise or release feeling; coercive patterns use feeling to narrow the listener's options).

**Why it works:** Conditional regard, Intermittent reinforcement, Epistemic trust, Cognitive dissonance, Commitment and consistency.

**Consent:** Every device in this family is abuse when used on someone who has not agreed to it as fantasy, and should never be aimed at real money, relationships or self-trust outside an explicit, revocable agreement.


### Affection flooding *(unit)*

Also called: love bombing, overwhelming warmth, approval flooding.

A dense, unearned stream of warmth, praise and closeness at the start of a session or relationship. Its effect comes from volume and timing: the listener receives much more approval than the situation warrants. It differs from praise, which rewards a specific response, and from liking, which builds affection gradually through similarity and warmth.

**How:** Stack several statements of affection, admiration and special worth in a short span, early, with nothing asked of the listener and no response being rewarded. The statements are about the listener as a person, not about anything they just did. If the warmth is later withdrawn, the pair becomes hot and cold. In agreed fantasy, present it openly as play; for ordinary rapport, warmth and praise for specific responses do the work without the flood.

> You're wonderful. You're so special to me. I knew the moment you started listening how perfect you are.

> So good, so lovely, so precious. I adore how you listen.

> No one has ever listened the way you do. You're everything.

**Spot it by:** several affection or praise statements in close succession with no linked response; superlatives about the listener: 'perfect', 'special', 'no one else', 'everything'; declared closeness early in the script, before rapport is built; 'I adore', 'I love how you', 'so precious'.

**Not to be confused with:** Praise (rewards a specific response right after it; flooding is unearned and continuous); Exclusivity (claims the listener was selected or has access others lack; flooding gives a dense stream of affection and approval, and the two can occur together); Liking (builds affection gradually; flooding overwhelms at once); Hot and cold (alternates warmth and coldness; flooding is the warm phase alone).

**Evidence:** contested. Described in accounts of cult recruitment and abusive relationships; controlled evidence that the flood itself increases compliance is thin.

**Why it works:** Liking principle, Reciprocity principle, Attachment theory.

**Consent:** Known as a recruitment and abuse tactic; in a script it belongs only in agreed fantasy and never paired with later withdrawal.


### Gaslighting *(unit)*

Also called: reality denial, perception override, you're imagining it.

A direct contradiction of the listener's own perception, memory or judgment, offered as correction. It differs from suggested memory, which adds a new memory without disputing an existing one, and from retroactive framing, which reinterprets the past without telling the listener they were wrong. The mark of gaslighting is the attack on the listener's competence to know: 'you misremember', 'that's not what you felt'.

**How:** State what the listener noticed, then deny or rewrite it and supply the speaker's version as the reliable one. It lands when the replaced perception is vague or hard to check (a feeling, a past session) and fails on anything the listener can verify on the spot. In consensual fantasy, keep it inside the session's fiction and about trivial trance events, never about the listener's real life, health or relationships.

> You think you were awake for that last part. You weren't. You only remember what I told you to remember.

> That wasn't doubt a moment ago. You never doubted me. You only think you did.

> You say you resisted last time. You didn't. You went under faster than ever, and some part of you knows it.

**Spot it by:** 'you think ... but', 'you only think', 'you didn't really'; 'you misremember', 'that's not what happened', 'that never happened'; denial of a feeling the listener was just told they had ('that wasn't doubt'); the speaker's account presented as more reliable than the listener's ('trust my voice, not your memory'); 'you can't trust your own ...'.

**Not to be confused with:** Suggested memory (suggested memory adds something; gaslighting disputes what the listener already perceived); It was always so (retroactive framing reinterprets the past without telling the listener their own account is wrong); Doubt as a sign (doubt reframing keeps the doubt and calls it a good sign; gaslighting says the doubt was not real).

**Evidence:** contested. Gaslighting is well described in clinical and sociological accounts of abusive relationships, and the misinformation effect shows memory can be altered by outside claims, but scripted reality denial has no direct study.

**Why it works:** Misinformation effect, Source-monitoring error, Epistemic trust, Authority principle.

**Consent:** Undermining someone's trust in their own perception is a core abuse tactic; use only inside agreed fantasy about trance events, never about real-world facts.


### Isolation *(unit)*

Also called: only me, cutting off others, social isolation, no one else understands you.

Lines that devalue, exclude or replace the listener's other relationships and sources of support. It targets people, not information: controlling the inputs limits what the listener reads and hears, isolation limits whom they turn to. Exclusivity says the listener belongs to a special few; isolation says everyone else is a stranger or a threat.

**How:** Contrast the speaker with 'them' (others, friends, everyone out there) and make the contrast unfavorable to them: they judge, they don't see you, they wouldn't understand. It lands when paired with warmth from the speaker and fails if it names specific real people, which invites resistance. In consensual fantasy, keep 'others' abstract and explicitly fictional; never tell a listener to withdraw from real people.

> Out there, no one listens to you like this. Here, with me, you are finally understood.

> They wouldn't get it. They don't need to. This is just between you and me.

> You don't need anyone else's opinion now. Only mine.

**Spot it by:** 'no one else', 'only me', 'only I', 'just between you and me'; 'they wouldn't understand', 'they don't see you', 'out there'; unfavorable contrast between the speaker and other people; instructions to keep the experience secret from others; 'you don't need anyone else'.

**Not to be confused with:** Controlling the inputs (milieu control limits information sources; isolation limits relationships); Exclusivity (exclusivity flatters membership in a select group; isolation devalues everyone outside the speaker); Parasocial intimacy (parasocial intimacy builds closeness to the speaker without running down anyone else).

**Evidence:** contested. Isolation is a consistently reported feature of coercive relationships and high-control groups, but the effect of scripted isolation talk on a listener's real relationships is unstudied. Source: Evan Stark, Coercive Control (2007).

**Why it works:** Attachment theory, Epistemic trust, Normative social influence, Investment model of commitment.

**Consent:** Encouraging real withdrawal from friends or family is abuse; keep 'others' fictional and never suggest it persists after the session.


### Loaded language *(unit)*

Also called: loading the language, group jargon, thought-reform vocabulary.

A private vocabulary in which words come pre-loaded with approval or condemnation, so that describing an experience in the group's terms already evaluates it. Lifton's term for the compressed jargon of thought-reform settings. It differs from in-group language, which signals belonging without fixing judgments, and from redefinition, which changes one word's meaning once; loaded language is a standing lexicon used throughout.

**How:** Coin or adopt a small set of terms for the listener's states, the speaker, doubt and compliance, each with its value built in (for example 'clean' for compliant, 'noise' for questioning). Use them consistently across sessions and ask the listener to use them too. It lands through repetition and fails if the terms are explained or argued for, which exposes the judgment. Mark consensual use as fantasy vocabulary that the listener can drop.

> When the noise comes back, you go quiet. Good pets don't make noise.

> That was a clean drop. Clean, empty, good. Anything else is just static.

> Say it the right way: not 'I gave in', but 'I came home'.

**Spot it by:** recurring coined terms with built-in value ('clean', 'noise', 'static', 'pure', 'good girl/boy' used as a category); correction of the listener's word choice ('say it the right way'); a negative coined term for doubt or questioning; terms used without definition, as if already shared; the same evaluative label applied to many different states.

**Not to be confused with:** In-group language (in-group language marks belonging; loaded language carries a fixed judgment in each term); Redefinition (redefinition changes one word's meaning; loaded language is a standing vocabulary); Euphemism (euphemism softens one expression; loaded language evaluates the listener's whole experience).

**Evidence:** contested. Framing effects of word choice are experimental, but Lifton's claim that loaded vocabulary constricts thought rests on interviews and case material. Source: Robert Jay Lifton, Thought Reform and the Psychology of Totalism (1961).

**Why it works:** Framing effect, Labeling effect, Moralization, Illusory truth effect.

**Consent:** A loaded vocabulary can outlast the session and shape how the listener judges themselves; keep it inside agreed fantasy and let the listener drop it.


### Thought-terminating cliche *(unit)*

Also called: thought stopper, semantic stop sign, conversation stopper.

A brief, memorable, repeatable phrase deployed at the moment of doubt to end inquiry, such as 'it is what it is' or 'don't think, just obey'. Lifton named it as part of loaded language. It differs from doubt reframing, which answers the doubt by giving it a new meaning, and from a mantra, which is repeated for absorption rather than at the point of questioning.

**How:** Mention or anticipate a doubt, then cut it off with a fixed phrase, and reuse the same phrase every time doubt appears so it becomes the reflex. Short, rhythmic, self-evident phrases work best. It fails if followed by an argument, which reopens the question. In consensual play, pair it with a stated exit so the listener's real doubts still have a route.

> A question starts to form. Let it go. Thinking is not your job.

> Why? There is no why. There is only deeper.

> Whenever you wonder, remember: good subjects don't wonder.

**Spot it by:** a short fixed phrase placed right after a mentioned doubt or question; 'there is no why', 'don't think', 'thinking is not your job', 'it is what it is'; the same stopper phrase recurring at each point of doubt; dismissal of the listener's question without an answer.

**Not to be confused with:** Doubt as a sign (doubt reframing answers the doubt with a new meaning; the cliche ends it with no answer); Mantra (a mantra is repeated for absorption; a stopper is placed at the point of doubt); Setting doubt aside (setting doubt aside asks the listener to park it for later; a stopper dismisses it).

**Evidence:** contested. Widely cited from Lifton's interviews and cult-recovery literature; the stopping effect of the phrases themselves has not been tested. Source: Robert Jay Lifton, Thought Reform and the Psychology of Totalism (1961).

**Why it works:** Processing fluency, Cognitive ease, Epistemic vigilance.

**Consent:** Training the listener to shut down their own questions works by the listener not noticing; keep real doubts answerable outside the fantasy.


### Confession *(unit)*

Also called: public confession, tell me your secrets, cult of confession, admission.

A demand or invitation to reveal something the listener would normally keep private: secrets, failings, desires, fears. In Lifton's account the confession is both a bonding ritual and a source of leverage. It differs from self-policing, which reports ongoing lapses against a rule, and from repeat after me, which has the listener say the speaker's words rather than their own material.

**How:** Frame disclosure as relief or proof of trust, then ask for something specific and private, spoken aloud or written down. It lands when the speaker responds with acceptance, which binds the listener closer; it fails if the request comes before rapport. In audio, the listener's answer is unseen, so the device is the instruction itself. Never ask for identifying information or anything that could be recorded and used.

> Say it out loud now, the thing you've never told anyone. It's safe here. Say it.

> Whisper the thing you hide from everyone else. I'll keep it for you.

> Tell me one thing you're ashamed of, and feel how good it is to have no secrets from me.

**Spot it by:** 'tell me', 'admit', 'confess', 'say it out loud'; 'what you've never told anyone', 'your secret', 'what you're ashamed of'; disclosure framed as relief or cleansing ('no secrets from me'); an instruction to write down or speak private material.

**Not to be confused with:** Self-persuasion (self-persuasion asks for the listener's reasons for wanting the change; confession asks for a secret, a failing or something shameful); Self-policing (self-policing reports lapses against a rule; confession reveals private material); Repeat after me (repeat after me supplies the words; confession asks for the listener's own); Stated commitment (a stated commitment promises future behavior; confession discloses the past or inner life).

**Evidence:** contested. Disclosure is known to increase closeness, and coerced confession is well documented in thought-reform settings, but the effect of scripted confession prompts is unstudied. Source: Robert Jay Lifton, Thought Reform and the Psychology of Totalism (1961).

**Why it works:** Commitment and consistency, Self-perception theory, Investment model of commitment.

**Consent:** Disclosed material creates leverage; never request identifying or recordable personal information, and keep any disclosure private to the listener.


### Sole-source claim *(unit)*

Also called: relief monopoly, only I can, need for the speaker, dependence induction.

Claims that place the speaker as the sole source of something the listener wants: calm, sleep, pleasure, approval, the trance itself. It differs from create the need sell the cure, which first tells the listener they have a lack; a sole-source claim asserts a monopoly over a need that may already exist. It differs from the craving frame, which says the need is strong without saying nothing else can meet it. Isolation removes other people; this removes other sources, including the listener's own ability.

**How:** Name a need, then state that only the speaker or only this voice or file can meet it, and that self-sourced or other-sourced versions do not work. Pair it with real relief delivered in the session so the claim feels confirmed. It fails if stated before the listener has felt any relief. In consensual use, make the monopoly explicitly fictional and keep the listener's own coping skills intact.

> No one else can bring you down like this. Only my voice can.

> You'll find you can't quite relax on your own anymore. You'll need to come back to me.

> This calm belongs to my voice. When you want it, you'll press play.

**Spot it by:** 'only I', 'only my voice', 'no one else can'; 'you'll need me', 'you'll need to come back'; claims that the listener cannot reach a state on their own; a feeling described as owned by the speaker or the file.

**Not to be confused with:** Create the need, sell the cure (create the need sell the cure manufactures the lack first; dependency claims sole access to a need); Isolation (isolation devalues other people; dependency devalues other sources of relief); Next-time-deeper suggestion (next-time-deeper invites return without claiming the listener cannot do without it).

**Evidence:** contested. Dependency is a common theme in coercive-control and cult accounts, but whether scripted monopoly claims create real dependence is unstudied.

**Why it works:** Motivating operations, Attachment theory, Response expectancy theory, Epistemic trust.

**Consent:** Dependency claims are meant to persist after the session; state them only inside agreed fantasy and never undermine the listener's own ways of coping.


### Create the need, sell the cure *(unit)*

Also called: manufactured deficit, problem-agitate-solve, invented lack.

A two-beat move: first the script asserts or amplifies a deficit the listener had not named (restlessness, emptiness, not being good enough), then it offers the speaker as the fix. It is one move because the deficit exists only to be cured. It differs from a sole-source claim, which asserts a monopoly on an existing need, from fear of leaving, which predicts harm only if the listener stops, and from fear then relief, which raises and resolves an emotion within the session rather than selling a remedy.

**How:** Describe the lack in vague, relatable terms so most listeners recognize it, make it slightly uncomfortable, then immediately name the cure and where to get it. Vague deficits ('something missing') land better than specific claims the listener can reject. It fails when the cure is offered before the lack feels real. Avoid inventing deficits about health, body or worth outside an agreed fantasy.

> You've felt it for a while now, that restless empty feeling. That's the part of you that's been waiting for this. Only this fills it.

> You never quite feel finished, do you? Always a little behind, a little short. That's what these sessions are for.

> Something has been missing. You know what it is now. It's my voice.

**Spot it by:** a vague standing deficit attributed to the listener ('something missing', 'that empty feeling', 'never quite enough'); the deficit said to predate the speaker ('you've felt it for a while', 'long before you found this'); the deficit followed closely by the speaker, file or session named as what fills or fixes it; 'that's what was missing', 'that's why you're here', 'this is what you were looking for'.

**Not to be confused with:** Sole-source claim (a sole-source claim asserts a monopoly on a need; this move first tells the listener they have the need); Fear of leaving (fear of leaving predicts harm if the listener stops; this asserts a lack the listener has now, whatever they do, and names the cure); Craving frame (the craving frame describes wanting the content itself; this describes a lack in the listener's life and offers the content as its fix); Fear then relief (fear then relief resolves a feeling in the session; this sells the speaker as an ongoing remedy); Mind reading (mind reading asserts a thought or feeling; this asserts a lack and pairs it with a cure).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Problem-agitate-solve is standard copywriting practice and appears in accounts of cult recruitment, but its effect has not been tested as such.

**Why it works:** Motivating operations, Framing effect, Contrast effect.

**Consent:** Inventing a deficit to sell a remedy is manipulation when the listener has not agreed to the fantasy; never apply it to real health, body or self-worth.


### Fear of leaving *(unit)*

Also called: phobia indoctrination, exit cost, exit fear, you'll lose everything.

Suggestions that make the act of quitting feel dangerous or unbearable: the listener will fall apart, lose what they gained, feel empty, or be unable to stop. Hassan calls the cult version phobia indoctrination. It differs from punishment, which follows a specific act, and from a permanence claim, which says a change stays; fear of leaving targets the exit itself.

**How:** Describe the listener imagining stopping, then attach a specific bad feeling or loss to that image, often contrasted with the comfort of staying. It works best phrased as prediction ('you'll find') rather than threat. It fails, and turns frightening, when stated as fact about real life. In consensual use keep it explicitly fictional and pair it with a real, stated way to stop that carries no penalty.

> Imagine deleting these files. Feel how empty and cold that thought is. Now come back to my voice, and feel warm again.

> If you ever tried to stop listening, you'd only find yourself pressing play again, more desperate than before.

> Walking away would undo everything we've built. You don't want that, do you?

**Spot it by:** 'if you ever stop', 'if you tried to leave', 'imagine deleting'; a bad feeling or loss attached to quitting ('empty', 'cold', 'undo everything'); contrast between the discomfort of leaving and the comfort of staying; 'you'll always come back', 'you can't stop'.

**Not to be confused with:** Punishment (punishment follows a specific act; fear of leaving targets the exit itself); Permanence claim (a permanence claim says a change stays; fear of leaving makes stopping feel dangerous); Sunk-cost appeal (a sunk-cost appeal cites what has been invested; fear of leaving attaches dread to quitting).

**Evidence:** contested. Fear of leaving is consistently reported by former members of high-control groups, but whether scripted exit fear produces it is unstudied. Source: Steven Hassan, Combating Cult Mind Control (1988).

**Why it works:** Classical conditioning, Sunk-cost effect, Investment model of commitment, Framing effect.

**Consent:** Dread attached to stopping is designed to outlast the session; never use it outside explicit fantasy, and always keep a penalty-free real exit.


### Blame reversal *(unit)*

Also called: DARVO, it's your fault, victim-offender reversal, turning it around.

A response to a complaint, objection or failure that denies the speaker's part and shifts responsibility onto the listener, often with the speaker presented as hurt. Freyd's DARVO names the full pattern: deny, attack, reverse victim and offender. It differs from no-fail framing, which says every outcome is success, and from resistance reframing, which treats resistance as participation; blame reversal says the problem is the listener's fault.

**How:** Anticipate the complaint ('if this doesn't work', 'if you feel uneasy'), deny the speaker's role, and attribute the cause to the listener's effort, attitude or character. Adding the speaker's disappointment makes it sharper. It fails if the listener's complaint is plainly valid. In hypnosis scripts, blaming failure on the subject is common and corrosive; in consensual play keep it in clearly fictional character and never apply it to real discomfort or a safety concern.

> If it isn't working, that's because you're holding back. The voice is doing its part.

> You want to blame me for how you feel? After everything I've given you?

> When you don't drop, it's your resistance, not my words. Try harder.

**Spot it by:** 'that's because you', 'it's your fault', 'you're holding back'; the speaker's role denied while failure is attributed to the listener; the speaker presented as hurt or wronged ('after everything I've given you'); 'try harder' following a reported failure or complaint.

**Not to be confused with:** No-fail framing (no-fail framing calls every outcome success; blame reversal calls failure the listener's fault); Resistance as participation (resistance reframing makes resistance part of trance; blame reversal makes it a failing); Gaslighting (gaslighting denies what the listener perceived; blame reversal accepts it and assigns the fault).

**Evidence:** contested. DARVO has survey support as a pattern abusers use and as a factor in victim self-blame; scripted blame reversal has not been studied. Source: Jennifer Freyd, Violations of power, adaptive blindness, and betrayal trauma theory, Feminism & Psychology (1997).

**Why it works:** Conditional regard, Cognitive dissonance, Moralization.

**Consent:** Blaming the listener for discomfort or failure can suppress real safety concerns; never apply it to unease, pain or a request to stop.


### Hot and cold *(unit)*

Also called: trauma bonding, push-pull, intermittent warmth, traumatic bonding.

A pattern in which the speaker's affection, approval or attention is given and then withdrawn, with the switches not tied to anything the listener did. Dutton and Painter described the bond it produces in abusive relationships as traumatic bonding. It differs from intermittent reinforcement, which rewards a behavior on a schedule; hot and cold varies the relationship itself. Love bombing is a single flood of warmth; hot and cold is the alternation.

**How:** Write passages of open warmth and praise, then a sudden cool or distant passage with no stated reason, then return to warmth as relief. Keep the timing irregular. The cold phase must be withdrawal of the speaker, not punishment for an act, or it becomes ordinary punishment. It fails if the cold phases are too long or harsh, which provokes leaving. In consensual play, keep the coldness theatrical and close the session warm.

> You're doing so well. I'm so proud of you. ... Hm. That's enough. I'm not sure you deserve that yet.

> Maybe I'll be kind to you today. Maybe I won't. You'll just have to wait and see.

> There. Now you have my warmth back. Don't you want to keep it this time?

**Spot it by:** abrupt shift from praise or affection to distance without a stated cause; 'maybe I will, maybe I won't', 'you'll have to wait and see'; warmth returned on the speaker's whim, not for anything the listener did ('because I felt like it'); speaker approval described as unpredictable or revocable.

**Not to be confused with:** Intermittent reinforcement (intermittent reinforcement schedules rewards for a behavior; hot and cold switches the speaker's warmth regardless of behavior); Deprivation (deprivation withholds a known reward in advance to raise its value; hot and cold alternates the speaker's warmth without tying the shifts to the listener's behavior); Affection flooding (love bombing floods warmth; hot and cold alternates it with withdrawal); Tease and denial (tease and denial withholds pleasure or release; hot and cold withholds the speaker's affection).

**Evidence:** contested. Intermittent reinforcement is experimental and traumatic bonding has observational support in abusive relationships, but scripted hot-and-cold alternation has no direct study. Source: Donald Dutton and Susan Painter, Traumatic bonding, Victimology (1981).

**Why it works:** Intermittent reinforcement, Variable-ratio schedules, Attachment theory, Conditional regard, Rejection sensitivity.

**Consent:** Unpredictable withdrawal of affection is a core abuse pattern and works on attachment; use only in clearly agreed role-play and end warm.


### Controlling the inputs *(unit)*

Also called: milieu control, information control, only listen to me, media restriction.

Instructions or suggestions that narrow what else the listener reads, hears or considers: other creators, criticism, outside opinions, the listener's own research. Lifton's milieu control covers the whole environment of a thought-reform setting; in a script it appears as rules about inputs. It differs from isolation, which targets relationships, and from narrowing attention, which focuses attention within the session rather than restricting outside sources.

**How:** Frame other sources as noise, confusing or harmful to progress, then give a rule: listen only to these files, don't read what others say, other voices will slip off. It lands when tied to the listener's goal ('to go deeper you need focus'). It fails if it names specific critics. In consensual use, limit the rule to the session itself; never tell a listener to avoid safety information or criticism.

> Other voices just confuse you. From now on, my voice is the only one that gets in.

> You don't need to read what anyone else says about this. It's only noise.

> Other files will feel flat and wrong now. Only mine will work.

**Spot it by:** 'only my voice', 'the only one that gets in', 'other voices'; other sources described as noise, confusing or harmful; 'don't read', 'don't listen to', 'you don't need to look it up'; claims that other creators' content will not work.

**Not to be confused with:** Isolation (isolation targets relationships; controlling the inputs targets information sources); Narrowing attention (narrowing attention focuses within the session; this restricts sources outside it); Exclusivity (exclusivity flatters the listener's access; this forbids alternatives).

**Evidence:** contested. Information control is central to accounts of thought reform and cult membership, but scripted input restriction has not been studied. Source: Robert Jay Lifton, Thought Reform and the Psychology of Totalism (1961).

**Why it works:** Agenda-setting, Mere-exposure effect, Confirmation bias, Epistemic trust.

**Consent:** Restricting what else a listener hears cuts them off from correction and safety information; never extend it beyond the session.


### Impossible standard *(unit)*

Also called: demand for purity, never enough, perfectionism demand, moving goalposts.

A goal stated as total (perfectly empty, completely obedient, never doubting) and paired with the message that the listener has not yet reached it. Lifton called the cult form the demand for purity. It differs from shaping, which moves the target in reachable steps and rewards each one, and from escalation, which raises requests; the impossible standard keeps the final target out of reach on purpose.

**How:** State an absolute ideal, praise progress toward it, then point out that the listener still falls short and must do better. Reset the bar whenever it is reached. It lands when the listener is invested; it fails quickly in a first session. In consensual play, keep the standard about trance performance in the fiction, not about the listener's real worth or body.

> Good. Deeper than before. But not perfect. Not yet. You can always go deeper.

> A perfect subject has no thoughts at all. You still have a few, don't you?

> You're close. You're always close. That's why you keep coming back.

**Spot it by:** absolute ideals ('perfect', 'completely', 'no thoughts at all', 'never'); 'not yet', 'not quite', 'never enough', 'always deeper'; praise immediately followed by a remaining shortfall; the bar raised as soon as it is reached.

**Not to be confused with:** Shaping (shaping rewards reachable approximations; an impossible standard keeps the target out of reach); Graded escalation (graded escalation raises requests; an impossible standard keeps the same request unmeetable); Deeper and deeper (deeper and deeper invites more depth without telling the listener they fall short).

**Evidence:** contested. Conditional regard and unmeetable standards are linked to guilt and compliance in developmental research, but the scripted form has not been studied. Source: Robert Jay Lifton, Thought Reform and the Psychology of Totalism (1961).

**Why it works:** Conditional regard, Cognitive dissonance, Effort justification, Zeigarnik effect.

**Consent:** A standard built to be failed produces guilt that can persist; keep it about the fiction and never about the listener's real worth.


### Self-policing *(unit)*

Also called: self-monitoring, report yourself, self-reporting, internal monitor.

An instruction to install an internal monitor that checks the listener against rules and flags lapses, often with a duty to report them or apply a correction. It moves the speaker's control inside the listener so it runs without the speaker present. It differs from confession, which discloses private material once, and from self-administered reinforcement, which rewards good behavior rather than watching for bad.

**How:** Describe a part of the listener that notices every lapse, say what counts as a lapse, and say what happens when one is noticed: report it, correct it, or feel it. Tie it to a rule set the script has already given. It fails if the rules are vague. In consensual use, scope the monitor to the session or an agreed time and include how it switches off.

> A small part of you is always watching now. Each time you slip, it notices, and you'll tell me.

> Every time you break a rule, you'll feel it, and you'll correct yourself before I have to.

> Keep a count of your mistakes today. You'll report them next time.

**Spot it by:** 'a part of you is always watching', 'you'll notice every time'; 'you'll tell me', 'report', 'keep a count', 'confess it next time'; 'correct yourself', 'before I have to'; monitoring framed as continuous or extending past the session.

**Not to be confused with:** Confession (confession discloses private material; self-policing reports lapses against a rule); Self-administered reinforcement (self-administered reinforcement rewards good behavior; self-policing watches for bad); Parts (parts work addresses a part for therapy or role; self-policing installs a part as monitor).

**Evidence:** contested. Self-monitoring changes behavior in behavioral studies, and self-surveillance is described in thought-reform accounts, but scripted self-policing has not been studied.

**Why it works:** Operant conditioning, Ironic process theory, Self-perception theory, Posthypnotic suggestion.

**Consent:** An internal monitor is meant to run after the session ends; scope it in time, give it an off switch, and keep it out of the listener's real life without agreement.


## Safety and consent

Also called: safety framing, consent framing, safety clauses.

The safety and consent family holds the statements a script makes to protect the listener rather than to deepen or install anything: warnings, opt-in points, stop words, limits on where and when suggestions apply, emergency waking, the line between fantasy and life, and settling afterward. They are judged by whether they give the listener real information and a real exit. Related limiting devices live elsewhere: trigger conditions, expiry clauses and trigger removal sit under Triggers and anchors, and reorientation sits under Emergence.

**Choosing:** Pick by when the risk arises. Before the audio: content note and listening conditions. Before the induction: consent check, safeword and emergency wake. Around anything that persists: scope limits and, for roleplay, the fantasy boundary. At the end: wellbeing suggestions and aftercare, then a full reorientation. Intense, persistent or identity-level content needs more of these, not fewer.

**Not to be confused with:** Protected core (a protective-sounding claim used to lower vigilance, not a working safeguard); But you are free (a freedom statement used as a compliance lever rather than as a real exit).


### Scope limits *(unit)*

Also called: boundaries, only while, context limits, limiting clause.

A scope limit bounds the whole session's suggestions to stated contexts: only while listening, only at home, only with a named partner, never at work or while driving. It differs from trigger conditions, which bound one installed cue, and from discrimination, which trains a response to one cue rather than telling the listener a rule. Its job is protection, not conditioning.

**How:** Put it before the main suggestions and repeat it in the sealing passage before waking. Name concrete contexts, not vague ones: "only while you are listening to this file, in a safe place" beats "only when appropriate". Include an exclusion for situations needing full attention. It fails when it is buried, vague, or contradicted later by a permanence claim.

> Everything you feel here applies only while you are listening to this recording, somewhere safe and comfortable.

> Outside this session, none of these suggestions has any effect at work, in traffic, or anywhere you need your full attention.

> These feelings belong to this room and this voice, and nowhere else.

**Spot it by:** 'only while you are listening'; 'only when ... and never when'; 'outside this session ... no effect'; naming excluded settings (work, driving, in public); 'these suggestions apply only'.

**Not to be confused with:** Trigger conditions (bounds one named trigger (who may fire it, where); scope limits bound the session's suggestions as a whole); Discrimination (narrows one conditioned response to one cue against look-alikes ('this word from this voice, not when you hear it elsewhere'); scope limits name the contexts in which any of the session's suggestions apply); Expiry clause (sets how long a suggestion lasts (a date, a duration, a number of uses); scope limits set the contexts in which it applies while it lasts); Fantasy boundary (declares a roleplay's claims about the listener to be fiction that ends with the session; scope limits bound where responses occur).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Limiting posthypnotic suggestions to intended contexts is standard clinical advice; whether a spoken limit reliably confines effects has little direct study.

**Why it works:** Posthypnotic suggestion.


### Emergency wake *(unit)*

Also called: safety suggestion, emergency awakening, if you need to, you'll wake, safety clause.

An emergency wake is a standing suggestion that real-world need overrides the session: an alarm, a voice, a child, a physical problem or real distress brings the listener fully alert, clear-headed and able to act. It differs from a safeword, which needs the listener to act, and from a count-up wake, which is the planned ending. It overrides any locked or conditional trance.

**How:** Give it before or right after the induction, before anything intense or anything that limits movement or waking. Name concrete triggers (an emergency, someone needing you, any real discomfort) and the result (eyes open, fully alert, thinking clearly). Make it explicit that it beats any later suggestion, including suggestions that the listener cannot wake. Keep it short and in a plain voice so it is not heard as part of the play.

> If anything ever needs your attention, a sound, a person, anything at all, you will open your eyes at once, fully awake and clear-headed.

> Nothing in this session can stop you from waking if you need to. That always comes first.

> Should you feel any real discomfort, you simply wake up, alert and comfortable, right away.

**Spot it by:** 'if anything needs your attention'; 'you will wake immediately / at once'; 'fully alert and clear-headed'; 'nothing in this session can stop you'; 'in an emergency'.

**Not to be confused with:** Safeword (the listener speaks or thinks a word to stop; the emergency wake fires on outside need without any act); Count-up wake (the planned ending of the session, not an override); Conditional wake (its opposite: restricts waking, which the emergency wake must override).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Standard in clinical and recorded hypnosis practice; hypnotized people retain the ability to respond to real events, so the clause mainly reassures rather than creates the ability.

**Why it works:** Posthypnotic suggestion, Response expectancy theory.


### Consent check *(unit)*

Also called: opt-in, if you agree, continue, check-in, consent point.

A consent check is an explicit opt-in point: the script names what is about to happen and offers a genuine exit (stop the file, skip a section, wake now) for anyone who does not agree. It differs from asking for a yes, which harvests agreement as a compliance step, and from "but you are free", which mentions freedom to raise compliance. The test is whether declining is described as fine and given a concrete route.

**How:** Place one before the induction and another before any section that escalates, persists or changes identity. Say what is coming in plain terms, then give the exit and make it neutral: no guilt, no "good listeners stay". Leave a pause or a stated point to stop. It fails when the next lines treat continuing as proof of wanting it, or when it comes after the content it asks about.

> The next part installs a trigger that lasts after this session. If you don't want that, stop the recording now; that's completely fine.

> Before we go on, check in with yourself. If any part of you says no, open your eyes and come back up, and nothing is lost.

> Only continue if this is something you want. If not, this is a good place to stop.

**Spot it by:** 'only continue if'; 'if you don't want ..., stop the recording now'; 'that's completely fine' attached to stopping; description of the next section followed by an exit; 'check in with yourself'.

**Not to be confused with:** Asking for a yes (prompts the listener to say or nod yes and names no way to stop; a consent check names the exit and treats taking it as fine); But you are free (a clause tacked onto a request ('but you are free to say no') with no stopping point and no exit action; a consent check says what comes next and names what to do to stop (stop the file, open your eyes)); You chose this (cites the decision to continue as proof of desire; a consent check leaves the decision neutral).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Informed consent is an ethical standard in clinical hypnosis; in-recording opt-in points are community practice with no study of how often listeners actually use them.

**Why it works:** Self-determination theory, Psychological reactance.

**Consent:** An opt-in asked during trance is weaker than one asked before the induction. Everything a later check covers should already be in the content note; the in-trance check is an extra exit, not the consent itself.


### Content note *(unit)*

Also called: content warning, warning, description of contents, what this file does.

A content note is an up-front, factual description of a recording's themes, installed triggers, persistent effects and intensity, given so the listener can decide before any induction. It differs from a potency claim and from a warning used as a lure, which use warning language to raise expectation or desire. A real content note is specific and flat in tone.

**How:** Put it in the description and say it again at the very start of the audio, before the induction. List themes, any triggers and how to remove them, anything meant to persist, and any amnesia. Use neutral words; drop hype like "dangerously strong". It fails when it is vague ("intense content"), hidden after the induction, or written to tempt.

> This recording contains relaxation and a confidence trigger, the word 'steady', which lasts until you choose to remove it. There is no amnesia.

> Before we begin: this file includes light dominance and a suggestion to listen again tomorrow. Nothing in it is permanent.

> Here is exactly what this session does, so you can decide whether you want it.

**Spot it by:** 'this recording contains'; 'this file includes'; list of themes or triggers before the induction; 'nothing in it is permanent' / 'lasts until'; 'so you can decide'.

**Not to be confused with:** Expectation setting (predicts what the listener will feel so they look for it; a content note lists what the file contains, installs and leaves behind so they can decline); Warning as lure (a warning with a dare or prohibition in it and no specifics; a content note is a flat, specific list); Potency claim (asserts that the file is strong without saying what is in it); Title and description priming (title, tags and description wording that builds expectation; label a content note only where themes, triggers or lasting effects are actually listed).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Standard community practice; research on trigger warnings in general shows little protective effect on distress, and none has studied hypnosis files specifically.

**Why it works:** Forewarning effect, Response expectancy theory.


### Aftercare *(unit)*

Also called: post-session care, settling, comedown care.

Aftercare is the passage that follows intense, humiliating, dominant or emotional content and returns the listener to a settled, valued state: warmth, reassurance that they are fine, permission to feel whatever they feel, and practical care (water, rest, a moment before standing). It differs from reorientation, which restores alertness and body awareness, and from wellbeing suggestions, which install lasting positive change. It often includes the speaker stepping out of role.

**How:** Place it after the intense section and before or around the wake-up; it can continue after eyes open. Drop the dominant or charged voice, use a warm plain one, and say the listener is respected outside the scene. Give one or two concrete care steps. Scale it to the intensity of what came before. It fails when it is a single line tacked on after heavy content.

> That was a lot, and you did well. Take a slow breath. Whatever you're feeling right now is okay.

> Stepping out of the role for a moment: you are respected, you are safe, and you can let all of that go now.

> When you're ready, have some water, and give yourself a minute before you stand up.

**Spot it by:** 'stepping out of the role'; 'whatever you're feeling is okay'; 'have some water' / 'take a minute before you stand'; reassurance after intense content; 'you did well' followed by settling.

**Not to be confused with:** Reorientation check (restores body feeling, orientation and alertness; aftercare settles feelings and reassures); Wellbeing suggestions (general suggestions for the hours and days ahead (sleep, calm, confidence); aftercare addresses how the listener feels right now, after what just happened); Safety and comfort (reassurance of safety before or during the work, so vigilance drops; aftercare comes after intense content and refers back to it); Self-disclosure (the speaker leaves the role to reveal something about themselves; in aftercare the speaker leaves the role to reassure the listener); Affection flooding (heavy unearned warmth at the start; aftercare follows intense content and is scaled to it).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Borrowed from BDSM practice and widely recommended; there is no controlled study of scripted aftercare in recordings.

**Why it works:** Attachment theory.


### Safeword *(unit)*

Also called: stop signal, stop word, cancel word, out word.

A safeword is a listener-controlled stop: a named word or signal that, when the listener uses it, ends trance, cancels a suggestion or switches off an installed effect. It differs from the emergency wake, which fires on outside need with no act from the listener, and from trigger removal, which is the writer's cancellation of a trigger. It must work regardless of anything else the script says.

**How:** Install it before the induction, in plain words, and say what it does and that nothing can override it. Choose a word unlikely to come up by accident and unrelated to the play. Rehearse it once if the script installs anything persistent. It fails when it is introduced after the intense part, when it is ambiguous whether it ends everything or one effect, or when later lines play at overriding it.

> Your safeword is 'lantern'. Say it or think it, and you wake fully, at once, and every suggestion in this file switches off.

> If you ever want to stop, just think the word 'red', and you come all the way back up, clear and comfortable.

> Nothing in this session can override your safeword.

**Spot it by:** 'your safeword is'; 'say it or think it'; 'nothing can override'; a named word paired with waking or cancelling; 'stop word'.

**Not to be confused with:** Emergency wake (fires on outside need without any act by the listener); Trigger removal (the writer cancels a trigger; a safeword is the listener's tool); Trigger word / phrase (a cue that produces a response the writer wants, not an exit).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Borrowed from BDSM practice; whether a recorded safeword works better than simply stopping the file has not been studied.

**Why it works:** Posthypnotic suggestion.


### Fantasy boundary *(unit)*

Also called: only in this fantasy, stays in the session, out-of-scene disclaimer, ends with the session.

A fantasy boundary marks the claims made inside a scene (ownership, identity, rules, dependency) as play that does not carry into the listener's life and has no hold on them afterward. It differs from the fiction frame, which presents content as fiction to lower evaluation during the session, and from scope limits, which bound where responses occur rather than whether the scene's claims are true. It is meant to limit carryover from identity and coercive content; whether it does has not been tested.

**How:** Say it before the scene starts and again on the way out, in a voice clearly outside the role. Name the specific claims it covers: "you belong to me", the new name, the rules. Pair it with aftercare after heavy roleplay. It fails when the fiction frame is used only to slip content past evaluation and is never closed at the end.

> Everything I say about you in this scene is part of the fantasy. When the session ends, it ends with it.

> Outside of this recording you are exactly who you were, free and your own, and none of tonight's rules apply.

> The name I gave you belongs to this game. When you wake, you leave it here.

**Spot it by:** 'part of the fantasy'; 'when the session ends, it ends'; 'outside of this recording you are'; 'leave it here'; out-of-role statement about scene claims.

**Not to be confused with:** Fiction frame (says the content is a story or game and stops there; the boundary says the scene's claims end, naming the session's end or life outside it); Scope limits (bounds where suggestions apply rather than declaring a scene's claims fictional); Reorientation check (cancels session-only sensations and states (heaviness, numbness, lost time); the boundary declares the scene's claims about the listener (a name, ownership, rules) to be fiction); Story frame (the session-scale scene itself, not the statement that bounds it).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Common community practice; no study shows whether an end-of-session disclaimer reduces carryover of identity suggestions.

**Why it works:** Cognitive decoupling, Suspension of disbelief.


### Listening conditions *(unit)*

Also called: don't listen while driving, listening instructions, safe listening setup.
