Listening conditions are practical instructions about the setting: never while driving or operating machinery, lie or sit somewhere safe, with time free afterward, not when unwell or impaired. They differ from a content note, which describes what the file does, and from scope limits, which bound where suggestions take effect after listening.

**How:** Put them in the description and at the start of the audio, before the induction. Be concrete: driving, machinery, anything needing attention, and a few minutes free after waking. Add a medical caution for files with strong breath, arousal or regression content. Keep it brief and plain so it is not skipped as boilerplate.

> Never listen to this while driving or doing anything that needs your attention.

> Find somewhere comfortable where you can sit or lie down undisturbed for the next twenty minutes.

> Leave yourself a few minutes after waking before you get up and go about your day.

**Spot it by:** 'never listen while driving'; 'operating machinery'; 'somewhere comfortable where you won't be disturbed'; 'leave yourself a few minutes'; medical caution before the induction.

**Not to be confused with:** Content note (describes what the file contains rather than the setting to listen in); Scope limits (bounds where suggestions apply after the session, not where to listen).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. A standard disclaimer on recorded hypnosis and relaxation audio; it is common sense rather than a tested effect.


## Session structure

Also called: script structure, session architecture, script anatomy, session shape.

Session structure names the places where devices go, not devices. It holds two kinds of entry: sections (pre-talk, induction, deepener, suggestion, convincer, emergence, recap), which are spans of a script defined by their job, and shapes (loop, series, story frame, call and response, multi-drop, lesson, branching, countdown finale), which describe how a whole session or set of sessions is laid out. Labels from this family attach to sections or whole files; the devices inside each section are labelled from the other families.

**Choosing:** Start every script from the standard section order: pre-talk, induction, deepener, suggestion, optional convincer, emergence. Then choose one shape for the whole file by how it will be used: a loop for repeat play, a series for multi-week training, a lesson for practice drills, a story frame when the content is roleplay, multi-drop when depth matters more than content. Add a recap before the emergence when the suggestion section is long. Pick shapes deliberately; most files need only one, and stacking several (a branching loop inside a story frame) makes the script hard to follow and hard to end safely.

**Not to be confused with:** Induction (the induction family lists ways to start trance; the induction section is the span where one of them sits); Emergence (emergence devices are the moves; the emergence section is their place in the script); Delivery and production (delivery is how the script is voiced and mixed, not how its parts are ordered).

**Why it works:** Event segmentation theory, Response expectancy theory.


### Pre-talk *(structure)*

Also called: intro, preamble, pre-induction talk, pre-hypnosis talk, opening.

The pre-talk is the span of the script that comes before any attempt to start trance. Its job is framing: what will happen, what hypnosis is and is not, what the file contains, how to sit or lie, and how to stop. It ends where the induction begins, usually at the first instruction to close the eyes, fix the gaze or breathe in a particular way.

**How:** Keep it short in audio files; one to three minutes is typical. Cover, in order: what the file is for, what the listener will notice, one or two corrections of common fears, listening conditions and how to stop, then a physical set-up instruction that hands off to the induction. Speak in an ordinary waking register here and save trance pacing for after the handoff. A pre-talk that runs long or already contains deepening language blurs the boundary the listener uses to know trance has started.

> Before we begin, find somewhere you can sit or lie comfortably for the next twenty minutes, somewhere you won't need to drive or be alert.

> Hypnosis isn't sleep. You'll hear everything, and you can open your eyes and stop whenever you choose.

> In this session you'll relax, practice a simple focus exercise, and wake up feeling clear. When you're ready, let's start.

**Spot it by:** opening span before the first eye-closure, fixation or breathing instruction; 'before we begin', 'in this session', 'what you'll experience'; statements about what hypnosis is or is not ('it isn't sleep', 'you stay in control'); listening-condition and stopping instructions ('don't listen while driving', 'you can stop any time'); set-up instructions ('get comfortable', 'headphones on', 'find a quiet place').

**Not to be confused with:** Expectation setting (a device that can appear anywhere; the pre-talk is the opening span where it usually sits); Induction section (starts at the first instruction that aims to produce trance); Content note (one statement about contents, often placed in the pre-talk or the description).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Preparatory information that corrects misconceptions is standard clinical practice and studies of pre-hypnotic information suggest it can raise responsiveness modestly; the best content and length are not settled.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Sociocognitive theory of hypnosis, Forewarning effect.

**Consent:** The pre-talk is the natural place to state what the file installs and how to stop; leaving that out removes the listener's chance to decline.


### Induction section *(structure)*

Also called: induction phase, trance entry.

The induction section is the part of a script that moves the listener from ordinary attention into trance. It contains one or more induction devices (eye fixation, progressive relaxation, confusion, counting and so on). It is labelled as a span; the devices inside it are labelled separately from the induction family. Its end is often blurred into the deepener, and a labeler marks the boundary at the first passage whose job is intensifying rather than starting.

**How:** Choose one main induction method and run it to a clear marker of entry, such as eyes closing, an arm dropping or a stated 'now you are in trance'. Keep it focused; mixing three induction styles in one section usually reads as padding. Open with a clean handoff from the pre-talk and close with a short ratification before the deepener starts, so both edges are visible.

> Now let your eyes rest on one spot in front of you. Keep them there as I talk.

> Your eyelids are getting heavier, blinking more slowly, and when they want to close, let them close.

> That's right. Eyes closed, breathing slow, and already beginning to drift.

**Spot it by:** first sustained instruction to fix the gaze, close the eyes, breathe in a set rhythm or relax the body; shift into slow, repetitive, present-tense language after the pre-talk; an entry marker: 'eyes closed', 'that's right', 'now you're beginning to go into trance'; the span ends where depth words ('deeper', 'further down', countdowns to depth) take over.

**Not to be confused with:** Induction (the family of techniques; this is the span of the script where they are used); Deepener section (intensifies a trance already begun); Pre-talk (talks about trance without yet trying to produce it).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Research scales and clinical texts treat the induction as a distinct phase; studies find the specific induction method matters less than expectation and the listener's hypnotizability.

**Why it works:** Hypnotic induction, Response expectancy theory, Hypnotizability.


### Deepener section *(structure)*

Also called: deepening phase, deepening section.

The deepener section is the part of a script between the induction and the suggestion section, built from deepening devices such as countdowns, descent imagery, fractionation or breath-linked deepening. It is labelled as a span; the devices inside are labelled from the deepening family. It differs from the induction section by assuming trance has begun and from the suggestion section by carrying no change-work content of its own.

**How:** Use one or two deepeners that fit the induction (a staircase after a visualization induction, a countdown after a counting one). End with a stated arrival point ('at the bottom now', 'deeply relaxed') so the suggestion section has a clear start. Keep it proportionate: in a twenty-minute file a few minutes is typical. If the file needs much more depth, use a multi-drop structure rather than an ever-longer deepener.

> Now I'm going to count from ten down to one. Let each number take you twice as deep.

> Ten, drifting down. Nine, deeper still. Eight, every muscle letting go.

> One. All the way down now, resting here, ready to listen.

**Spot it by:** dense depth vocabulary: 'deeper', 'further down', 'sinking', 'twice as deep'; countdown or descent imagery (stairs, elevator) immediately after the induction; an arrival line: 'all the way down', 'at the bottom', 'deeper than before'; absence of change-work content (no new habits, traits or triggers yet).

**Not to be confused with:** Deepening (the family of techniques; this is the span where they are used); Induction section (starts trance rather than intensifying it); Multi-drop session (repeated wake-and-drop cycles as the skeleton of the whole session, not one span).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Deepening is a standard phase in clinical scripts; there is little controlled evidence that deepeners change responsiveness beyond the listener's own expectation of depth.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Sociocognitive theory of hypnosis.


### Suggestion section *(structure)*

Also called: body, change work, programming, therapeutic section, suggestion phase, work section.

The suggestion section is the part of a script, after deepening and before emergence, that carries the file's main content. Everything before it prepares; everything after it seals and exits. It is the span where triggers are installed, beliefs stated, imagery for change is run and posthypnotic suggestions are given. A labeler marks it from the first content suggestion after the deepener's arrival line to the start of the recap or emergence.

**How:** Open with a short transition that signals the work is starting ('and now, while you rest here...'). Deliver a small number of suggestions, each stated more than once in varied form, and group related ones together. Order them from easy to accept toward the harder ones, and keep a light thread of depth language running through so the trance holds. Close with a recap or a sealing line before the count-up so the section has a visible end.

> And now, resting here, your mind is open to ideas that help you.

> Each time you sit down to work, focus comes easily, the way it does right now.

> You'll notice it tomorrow, and the day after, a little more each time.

**Spot it by:** transition line after the deepener: 'and now', 'while you rest here', 'your mind is open'; future-tense or posthypnotic language: 'from now on', 'each time you', 'whenever'; dense identity, trigger or belief statements on the file's topic; span ends at a recap, sealing passage or count-up.

**Not to be confused with:** Deepener section (builds depth without delivering the file's content); Recap (restates suggestions already given rather than giving them); Convincer section (stages proof of trance or control, not the change itself).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Clinical scripts and research scales place the targeted suggestions after the induction, though suggestions also work with no induction; the ordering and number of suggestions within the section is convention, not tested.

**Why it works:** Direct verbal suggestion, Posthypnotic suggestion, Hypnotic suggestibility.

**Consent:** This is where anything that persists after the session is installed; the listener should have been told what it contains before the file started.


### Convincer section *(structure)*

Also called: test phase, proof section, convincer phase.

The convincer section is a bounded part of a script given over to suggested phenomena used as proof: eyelid lock, rigid arm, stuck hand, number amnesia, a trigger test. It is labelled as a span; the convincers inside are labelled from the convincers family. It usually sits between the deepener and the suggestion section, or after the suggestion section to prove a new trigger works.

**How:** Pick convincers that are very likely to succeed for the depth reached; a failed test does more harm than no test. Set up the suggestion, invite the attempt with permission to fail framed in advance, ratify the result, then cancel it explicitly before moving on. Keep the section short, and follow it with a line that links the proof to what comes next ('and because that worked, the rest will too').

> Your eyelids are so relaxed now that they simply won't open. Go ahead and try, and find they stay closed.

> That's right. Now stop trying, let it go, and relax even deeper.

> Your mind just showed you how well it responds. Everything that follows will work just as easily.

**Spot it by:** 'go ahead and try', 'try to', 'you'll find you can't'; a lock, stuck, rigid or forgotten phenomenon followed by a test; explicit cancellation: 'stop trying', 'let it go', 'back to normal'; a bridge line using the success as evidence for later suggestions.

**Not to be confused with:** Convincer (the single device; this is the span that stages one or more of them); Suggestibility test (done before induction, in waking state, to show responsiveness); Suggestion section (delivers the file's content rather than proof of trance).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Challenge items are standard in research scales and stage practice; that passing one raises later responsiveness is widely taught but not well tested.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Self-perception theory, Ideomotor effect.


### Emergence section *(structure)*

Also called: wakener, awakener, exit, termination, closing.

The emergence section is the last part of a script, from the end of the suggestion work (or recap) to the end of the file. It contains emergence devices: sealing, count-up wake, reorientation, or a deliberate non-wake such as drift into sleep or loop back. It is labelled as a span; its devices are labelled from the emergence family.

**How:** Mark the start clearly ('in a moment I'll bring you back'). Seal what should stay, cancel anything temporary (heaviness, numbness, locks, amnesia that should lift), then run the exit. Give the wake its own space and do not slip new content into it. If the file ends in sleep or a loop, say so in the pre-talk or description, since the listener then has no explicit wake.

> In a moment I'm going to bring you back up, and everything useful from today comes with you.

> Any heaviness in your arms and legs is gone now, completely back to normal.

> One, two, three, four, five. Eyes open, wide awake.

**Spot it by:** 'in a moment I'll bring you back', 'it's time to return', 'coming back up'; cancellation of temporary effects: 'back to normal', 'all sensation returns'; ascending count or 'wide awake', 'eyes open' near the end of the file; alternatively, 'drift into sleep' or a return to the opening lines.

**Not to be confused with:** Emergence (the family of exit devices; this is the span where they sit); Multi-drop session (a mid-session wake followed by another drop is not the exit); Recap (restates suggestions before the exit begins).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. An explicit termination is standard in clinical texts and research scales; reports of lingering after-effects make it a safety norm, but no wording has been shown superior.

**Why it works:** Event segmentation theory, Response expectancy theory.

**Consent:** An emergence that leaves trance, amnesia or a locked state in place should be disclosed before the session starts.


### Loop *(structure)*

Also called: loopable file, loop file, endless loop, repeat file.

A loop is a whole-file shape: the script has no wake, and its last lines lead into its first so that repeat playback continues the trance. It usually carries a short core of repeated suggestions and mantra-like lines in place of a full arc. It differs from the loop-back ending, which is the join at the close of the file; the loop structure is the decision to build the entire file for repetition, and a looped file normally takes both labels.

**How:** Drop the pre-talk and wake from the looped file and put them in a separate intro and outro file or in the description. Write the opening as if the listener is already in trance, and make the last line grammatically lead into the first. Keep the content short and highly repetitive, with no counted arc that would restart awkwardly. State the intended listening length and how to stop, because nothing in the file ends it.

> ...and drifting down again, back to the beginning, where my voice says...

> Listening, relaxing, focusing. Listening, relaxing, focusing.

> Each time this plays, you settle in more easily, and it plays again.

**Spot it by:** no count-up, wake instruction or 'eyes open' anywhere in the file; final line ends on a connective ('and', 'again', 'back to') that leads into the opening line; short repeated core suggestions or mantra lines; 'loop', 'on repeat', 'as many times as you like' in the title or description.

**Not to be confused with:** Loop back (the single closing device; this is the whole-file design); Repetition induction (an induction using a repeated phrase, inside a normal session); Series / curriculum (several distinct files heard in order, not one file repeated).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Loop files are common in online audio communities; that repeated exposure raises familiarity and acceptance is supported in general, but no study has examined looped hypnosis files.

**Why it works:** Mere-exposure effect, Illusory truth effect, Habituation.

**Consent:** A loop has no built-in end or wake; listeners should be told how long it is meant to run and how to stop it.


### Series / curriculum *(structure)*

Also called: training program, levels, curriculum, multi-part series, program.

A series is a multi-file shape: each file is a complete session, but the set is designed as a sequence, with later files reusing triggers, names or states installed earlier. A series often carries graded escalation, each file asking a little more, but the label marks the ordered layout whether or not the asks grow. It differs from a repeat-listening schedule, which prescribes playing the same file again, and from a single file with multiple drops.

**How:** Plan the endpoint first, then divide it into steps that each work on their own. Open each later file by recalling and firing what the earlier file installed, so the listener feels continuity. Number the files and say in each description which must come first. Include a removal or reset file, or removal lines, for anything that persists across the series.

> Welcome to part three. Last time you learned the word that relaxes you. Let's use it now.

> You've practiced this twice already, so today it happens faster.

> In the next session we'll build on what you learned today.

**Spot it by:** 'part two', 'level three', 'session 4 of 6' in title or opening; references to earlier sessions: 'last time', 'as you learned before', 'the word I gave you'; forward references: 'next session', 'in the next part'; triggers fired without being installed in this file.

**Not to be confused with:** Graded escalation (the device of asking a bit more each time; the series is the multi-file layout that carries it); Repeat listening (repeat listening of the same file, not a sequence of different ones); Instructional / practice session (a single file framed as a lesson; a series may or may not be lessons).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Multi-session protocols are standard in clinical hypnosis and spaced practice improves learning in general; no study compares series designs for hypnosis files.

**Why it works:** Spacing effect, Foot-in-the-door, Commitment and consistency.

**Consent:** Effects build across files, so the listener should be told where the series ends up before starting it, and how to undo it.


### Story frame *(structure)*

Also called: roleplay scene, scenario, narrative frame, fictional setting.

A story frame is a whole-file shape in which the session is narrated as a scene: a visit, a lesson in a fictional place, an encounter with a character. The standard sections are still present but disguised as plot events (the induction is sitting down in the chair, the wake is leaving the room). It differs from guided imagery and story absorption, which are devices used within a section; here the fiction contains the session itself.

**How:** Establish the setting and the listener's role in the first minute. Map each section onto a scene beat: arrival for the induction, moving further in for the deepener, the main encounter for suggestions, leaving for emergence. Keep the frame consistent; a shift out of the fiction mid-session reads as an error unless it is a deliberate wake. Close the fiction explicitly at the end so the listener knows the scene is over.

> You're walking into a quiet library. The door closes softly behind you.

> The librarian nods to the chair by the window, and as you sit, your eyes grow heavy.

> When you're ready, you stand, walk back to the door, and as it opens you wake, fully alert.

**Spot it by:** scene-setting opening: place, time, who 'you' are; induction and wake described as story actions (sitting, entering, leaving, a door); a consistent fictional setting or character across the whole file; 'roleplay', 'scenario', 'story' in title or description.

**Not to be confused with:** Guided imagery (an imagined scene used inside one section; here the scene contains the whole session); Fiction frame (a framing statement that the content is play; the story frame is the layout of the file); Story absorption (the absorption device; a story frame relies on it but is a structural choice).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. In persuasion research, readers absorbed in a story tend to counterargue less, though results vary across studies; whether framing a whole hypnosis session as a story changes outcomes has not been studied.

**Why it works:** Narrative transportation, Transportation-induced counterarguing reduction, Character identification.

**Consent:** Suggestions delivered as plot can persist outside the story; say in the description what is meant to stay after the fiction ends.


### Call and response *(structure)*

Also called: call-and-response, responsive session, repeat-after-me session, interactive session.

Call and response is a whole-session shape in which the speaker's lines are interleaved with listener replies on a regular pattern: the listener repeats phrases, answers yes, counts aloud or recites rules. A single repeat-after-me moment is a device; call and response is when that exchange becomes the session's rhythm. The listener's voice becomes a continuous part of the script.

**How:** Tell the listener at the start how and when to answer, and keep the cue for a reply consistent (a pause, 'say it', a tone). Make the replies short and easy at first and let them grow. Leave real silence for each reply. Decide whether replies are aloud or inward and keep to it, since mixing the two confuses the listener about when to speak.

> Each time I pause, repeat my words. I am calm.

> [pause] I am focused. [pause] I am ready.

> Every answer you give takes you a little deeper. Say yes. [pause]

**Spot it by:** regular reply prompts: 'repeat after me', 'say it', 'answer me', 'say yes'; short quoted first-person lines followed by marked pauses; stage directions such as [pause], [listener repeats] at regular intervals; an opening instruction explaining how the listener should respond.

**Not to be confused with:** Repeat after me (label the unit on each prompt to say supplied words; add this structure label when listener replies recur in a regular pattern through most of the session); Asking for a yes (one requested yes at a chosen moment does not make listener replies the session rhythm); Instructional / practice session (practice rounds teach a skill; call and response uses recurring listener replies as the session rhythm).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Self-generated and spoken statements are remembered better and can shift attitudes in lab studies; call-and-response hypnosis sessions themselves have not been studied.

**Why it works:** Generation effect, Self-perception theory, Commitment and consistency.


### Countdown finale *(structure)*

Also called: JOI countdown, final countdown, counted climax, climax countdown.

A countdown finale is a session shape in which the main build of the file resolves in a counted sequence ending on a release: a burst of pleasure, a trigger firing, a let-go of tension that has been built up on purpose. The count is the climax of the content, and what happens on the last number is the payoff the file has been building toward. The test against a countdown deepener or count-up wake is what follows the last number: if further suggestions follow that rely on the depth reached, the count was a deepener; if the last number brings alertness, it was a wake; if the last number is itself the payoff and only settling or the wake follows, it is a finale. It is common in erotic audio, where the release is often permission to climax.

**How:** Build anticipation through the session so the count lands on something the listener wants. Announce the count and what happens at zero before starting. Let the gaps between numbers lengthen toward the end, and allow pauses, holds or restarts if the file uses denial. Put the release on the final number exactly, then give a short settling passage before any wake.

> When I reach zero, all of that built-up tension lets go at once.

> Five. Four. Holding it. Three...

> Two. One. Zero. Let it all go, now.

**Spot it by:** a descending or ascending count in the last part of the file, after the main build; 'when I reach zero', 'on one', 'at the end of the count' tied to a release; lengthening gaps, holds or restarts between numbers; 'now' or 'let go' on the final number, followed by settling language.

**Not to be confused with:** Countdown deepener (counts toward depth, and suggestions that use that depth follow; after a finale's last number only settling or the wake follows); Count-up wake (the last number brings alertness; a finale's last number brings a release inside trance, and any wake comes separately afterward); Counted passage (numbers used to pace any passage; label both when the paced passage is the end-of-session climax).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. A community convention from erotic audio; anticipation and delayed release raise arousal in general, but no study has examined counted finales.

**Why it works:** Prediction error, Motivating operations.

**Consent:** If the finale ends in sexual release or fires a trigger installed earlier, that should be in the file's content note.


### Multi-drop session *(structure)*

Also called: multiple inductions, fractionated session, drop cycles, wake and drop.

A multi-drop session uses fractionation as its skeleton: the file repeatedly brings the listener partway up, then re-induces, often with a trigger, and each cycle is framed as deeper than the last. Content may be placed in the drops or the session may be mostly drops. It differs from fractionation the device, which can be one short cycle inside a deepener, by organizing the whole file around the cycles.

**How:** Decide the number of cycles in advance; three to five is common. Make each wake partial and brief, with a clear re-drop cue, and say each drop goes deeper than the last. Vary the wording of the drops slightly so they do not blur. End with a full emergence that clearly differs from the partial wakes, so the listener knows the final wake is real.

> Coming up now, eyes opening a little, just enough to notice the room.

> And drop. All the way down, deeper than the last time.

> Once more up, and once more down, twice as deep.

**Spot it by:** repeated partial wakes ('eyes opening', 'coming up a little') followed by 'drop', 'sleep', 'down'; 'deeper than last time', 'each time deeper' across several cycles; a re-induction trigger fired several times in one file; three or more induction-like passages in one session.

**Not to be confused with:** Fractionation (label the unit on each passage of repeated up-and-down cycles; add this structure label when those cycles organize the session rather than forming one bounded deepener, whether or not other material comes between them); Partial wake (a partial wake restores some faculties while declaring trance ongoing; it does not itself include a return to deeper trance); Drill (repeated firing and resetting of a specific response trains fluency; multi-drop cycles repeatedly interrupt and resume trance with a suggested increase in depth).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Fractionation is a long-standing clinical and stage technique attributed to Vogt; claims that each cycle measurably deepens trance lack controlled support.

**Why it works:** Response expectancy theory, Habituation.


### Instructional / practice session *(structure)*

Also called: lesson, practice session, training session, skill session.

An instructional session presents its content as a skill being taught: the speaker explains what will be learned, demonstrates or describes it, runs practice rounds, and praises progress. Each round is short and similar to the last. It differs from a series, which spreads learning across files, and from drill, which is repeated firing of one response with less teaching around it.

**How:** State the skill and the goal at the start. Explain each step before asking for it, then run several rounds, marking each with a number or a reset ('and again'). Give feedback after each round and make later rounds slightly harder or faster. End with a summary of what was learned and how to practice on one's own.

> Today you're learning to relax your shoulders on a single breath. Let's practice.

> Round one: breathe in, and as you breathe out, shoulders drop. Good.

> Round two, a little faster this time. That's it, you're getting better at this.

**Spot it by:** an opening statement of the skill to be learned: 'today you'll learn', 'this lesson', 'in this session you'll practice'; an explanation or demonstration of the step before the listener is asked to do it: 'here is how it works', 'first I'll show you'; practice rounds separated by feedback on progress: 'good, that was quicker', 'better than the last one'; a closing summary of the skill and how to practice it alone: 'now you know how to', 'practice this each day'; teacher and student wording throughout: 'lesson', 'exercise', 'you're learning', 'well done'.

**Not to be confused with:** Drill (label drill on a block of repeated cue-response-reset rounds; add this structure label when a teaching frame explains a skill and uses practice with feedback across the session, even if the skill is not named at the start or summarized at the end); Series / curriculum (a series orders several files; a lesson is a shape within one file); Call and response (recurring listener replies set the session rhythm there; this structure teaches and practices a skill).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Teaching self-hypnosis and skills through practice rounds is standard clinical practice and practice with feedback improves learning generally; lesson-framed hypnosis files are not separately studied.

**Why it works:** Operant conditioning, Automaticity.


### Recap *(structure)*

Also called: summary of suggestions, review, restatement, summary passage.

A recap is a section near the end of a script that restates, compactly, the suggestions delivered in the suggestion section. It adds no new content. It differs from sealing, which declares that the suggestions will stay, and from a refrain, which is one line returning throughout; a recap lists the session's content once more as a block.

**How:** Place it between the suggestion section and the emergence. Restate each main suggestion in one short line, in the same order and with the same key words used earlier. Keep it brief; a long recap becomes a second suggestion section. Follow it with a sealing line and then the wake.

> So, before you come back: you relax more easily, you focus when you sit down to work, and you sleep well.

> Calm when you begin. Clear while you work. Rested when you're done.

> Once more, the three things from today: easy breathing, steady attention, deep sleep at night.

**Spot it by:** 'before you come back', 'so remember', 'to summarize', 'everything you've learned'; a block of short lines repeating key words from earlier suggestions; position directly before the count-up or sealing passage; no new suggestions introduced.

**Not to be confused with:** Sealing suggestions before waking (states that suggestions stay, without listing them); Refrain (one line repeated at intervals through the file); Suggestion repetition (repeating a suggestion where it is given, not summarizing them all at the end).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Repetition aids recall and raises perceived truth in general; there is no specific evidence that a recap before waking improves hypnotic outcomes.

**Why it works:** Illusory truth effect, Spacing effect.


### Branching *(structure)*

Also called: choose your own adventure, branching session, interactive branching, multiple paths.

A branching session offers the listener real choices that select different continuations: different files, tracks, or passages to skip to. The branch points are structural, not rhetorical. It differs from illusion of choice and double binds, where every option leads to the same response; here the options lead to different content, though the writer usually ensures all branches serve the file's aim.

**How:** Keep branch points few and clear, and describe each option in a sentence so the choice is informed. Tell the listener exactly how to take each path (which track, which timestamp, which file). Make every branch complete on its own, with its own emergence or a rejoin point. Check that no branch skips safety content such as the wake.

> If you'd like to go deeper first, continue to track two. If you're ready for the main session, skip to track three.

> Choose now: the beach or the forest. Whichever you pick, follow that file next.

> Both paths meet again at the same quiet room.

**Spot it by:** 'if you'd like... go to', 'skip to', 'choose now', 'track two'; named options with different continuations; file or track references in the script or description; a rejoin point where branches meet.

**Not to be confused with:** Illusion of choice (options differ only in detail and lead to the same response); Forced choice (a choice inside the script's content, not one that selects the next section); Series / curriculum (files in a fixed order, not chosen).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Perceived choice can raise engagement and commitment in general; branching hypnosis files have not been studied.

**Why it works:** Self-determination theory, Commitment and consistency.


## Delivery and production

Also called: production, audio production, voice work.

The family groups choices that live in the recording, not in the words: pace, tone, whisper, silence, extra voice tracks, music, tones, effects and visuals. They are heard or seen, not read, so a labeler can mark them only where a script carries stage directions or production notes. Written devices that imitate delivery (ellipsis pauses, monotony, rapid wording) belong to other families.

**Choosing:** Choose by job. To slow the listener, use slowing pace, breath-synced pacing and silence. To change the feel of a whole passage, use tone shift or whisper. To make chosen words linger, use echo; marking chosen words with the voice itself is analog marking, in the suggestion-form family. To load or split attention, use layered voices or panning. For a steady carrier under the session, use a music bed or metronome. For cues the listener should learn, use sound effects. Treat binaural tones and subliminal tracks as optional extras with weak evidence, and disclose a subliminal track.

**Spot it by:** stage directions in brackets or parentheses: [whisper], (pause), [music fades]; production notes: 'pan left', 'layer under', 'add reverb'.

**Not to be confused with:** Rhetoric, rhythm and sound (rhetoric and sound devices are in the wording itself; delivery is in the recording); Written pause (a written pause marks rhythm in text; delivery is the realized audio).

**Why it works:** Analog marking, Attentional capture.


### Analog marking *(delivery)*

Also called: marking out, tonal marking, vocal marking, analogue marking.

Analog marking is a consistent non-verbal signal applied to selected words: a drop in pitch, a pause before and after, a change of volume, a gesture or a turn of the head. The marked words, heard together, form a message separate from the sentence they sit in. It is a delivery choice; in a written script it shows only as typography or a stage direction.

**How:** Decide which words carry the message, then give all of them the same marker and nothing else that marker. A slight downward inflection and a short pause either side is the usual choice; keep it subtle enough to pass as natural emphasis. In a script, mark the words with italics, capitals or a bracketed direction so the reader knows what to do. Marking with nothing worth marking, or marking inconsistently, does nothing.

> You don't have to [lower, slower] go deeper [normal] until you're ready.

> And somewhere in all of that you can... FEEL SAFE... while I keep talking.

> I wonder whether you'll *close your eyes* before or after the next breath.

**Spot it by:** italics, bold or capitals on a short phrase inside a sentence; stage directions: '[lower tone]', '[pause]', '[slower]' around specific words; ellipses or dashes fencing off a phrase mid-sentence; the marked phrases, read alone in order, form instructions; production notes telling the reader to emphasize listed words.

**Not to be confused with:** Embedded command (the embedded command is the wording; marking is how it is voiced); Tone shift (tone shift is a marked change of voice for a whole passage, not a signal on selected words); Interspersal (interspersal is the scattering of suggestion words in a narrative; marking is one way of making them stand out).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Vocal emphasis plainly changes what listeners attend to and remember, but the claim that marked words act as a separate message outside awareness is untested. Source: Bandler & Grinder, Patterns of the Hypnotic Techniques of Milton H. Erickson, M.D., Vol. 1 (1975).

**Why it works:** Analog marking, Attentional capture, Milton Model, Embedded commands.

**Consent:** It is meant to pass unnoticed, so the listener should know in advance that the session contains suggestions.


### Matching *(delivery)*

Also called: mirroring, rapport matching, breath matching, matching and mirroring, predicate matching, nonverbal pacing.

Matching is copying a feature of how this listener is behaving: speech rate, breathing rhythm, posture, or register (formality, sentence length, energy). It is pacing done through form instead of statements. Reusing the listener's words or topics is using their material, not matching. In live work it is mostly nonverbal. In a written script it is visible in stage directions that tell the speaker to follow the listener's observed breathing, tempo, posture, or way of speaking.

**How:** Begin at the listener's likely state, not the target state: a first line delivered at ordinary speaking pace and energy, then slow gradually. Time phrases to a natural breath cycle, with the downward or releasing words on the out-breath. Use the audience's own register and terms. Once matched, change your tempo a little and let the listener follow; that is the lead. Do not rely on choosing visual, auditory or feeling words to fit a listener 'type'; that claim has not held up.

> [listener is speaking quickly; begin at that rate] We can start right where you are. [as their speech slows, slow with them] And take a little more time.

> [watch the listener's breathing; speak only on their out-breath] ...and letting go... [wait for the next out-breath] ...a little more.

> [listener has been answering in short, flat sentences; match that] Long day. Lots in your head. Fine. We start there.

**Spot it by:** stage directions that refer to the listener's observed behavior: '[match their breathing]', '[at their pace]', '[mirror posture]'; a direction to change tempo as the listener's observed tempo changes; a direction to copy the listener's register or sentence length, without reusing their words; live-session notes that link the speaker's posture or speech rate to the listener's.

**Not to be confused with:** Pacing (pacing states what is true of the listener; matching copies how the listener is behaving without stating it); Breath-synced pacing (phrases timed to a fixed or typical breathing rhythm, as in any recording, are breath-synced delivery; label matching only when the direction is to follow this listener's observed breathing, tempo or posture); Using the listener's own material (repeating the listener's own words, interests or complaint is that variant; matching copies only how they speak and move (rate, rhythm, register), never what they said); Slowing pace (slowing pace is the delivery choice of getting slower through the session; matching starts at the listener's tempo, whatever it is).

**Evidence:** contested. Behavioral mimicry has experimental support for increasing liking (Chartrand & Bargh 1999), but NLP claims about matching sensory predicates to a preferred representational system failed controlled tests, and no study shows matching raises hypnotic response.

**Why it works:** Rapport matching, Liking principle, Pacing and leading, Processing fluency.


### Rapid delivery *(delivery)*

Also called: fast speech, rapid-fire, speed talking, rapid patter.

Overload by rate: a single stream delivered so quickly that the listener can follow or evaluate but not both. In hypnosis it appears as rapid patter in stage and street inductions and as bursts of fast commands. It is a delivery choice more than a wording choice; on the page it shows only as stage directions or as runs of very short clauses with no pauses.

**How:** Use it in short bursts, usually after rapport is set, and keep each item simple enough to act on without thought. Give no gaps between items. Then stop or slow sharply; the contrast is where the main suggestion goes. Sustained speed tires and irritates listeners and undercuts a relaxed state, so most of a script should not be fast.

> [fast] Eyes closed, breathe in, shoulders down, jaw loose, hands heavy, breathe out, again, deeper, again, deeper. [slow] And rest.

> [rapid, no pauses] Don't think just follow look here now there now here close them open them close them and sleep.

> [quickly] Yes to this, yes to that, yes to the next thing, yes before you've thought about it. [pause] Good.

**Spot it by:** stage directions: [fast], [rapid], [no pauses], [quickly]; run of five or more clauses of one to three words; commas or nothing where full stops would normally go; 'don't think, just', 'quickly now', 'keep up'; marked slowdown or pause directly after the run.

**Not to be confused with:** Small physical tasks (trivial bodily instructions mark micro-compliance; add rapid delivery only when speed is heard or explicitly directed); Shortening sentences (shortening sentences changes their length; rapid delivery requires audible speed or an explicit speed direction); And... and... and (repeated conjunctions can be delivered at any speed); Cognitive overload (overload presents multiple things to track; rapid delivery names the speed of one stream, though both may occur together).

**Evidence:** contested. Faster speech raised persuasion and perceived credibility in some studies (Miller et al. 1976) and later work found it mainly cuts scrutiny, helping weak arguments and hurting strong ones; there is no controlled evidence for its use in hypnosis.

**Why it works:** Cognitive load, Counterarguing, Elaboration likelihood model, Distraction-induced persuasion.

**Consent:** Speed removes the time to refuse, so restrict fast passages to simple acts the listener has agreed to.


### Slowing pace *(delivery)*

Also called: slow speech, slow delivery, progressive slowing, decelerating delivery.

Speech that is slower than conversation, usually slowing further by degrees across a section or the whole session, with pauses between phrases growing longer. A direction for a steady slow rate and a direction to keep slowing both belong here. It is the spoken tempo: its written counterparts are lengthening sentences and written pauses, and a single timed gap is silence.

**How:** Start near the listener's ordinary speaking rate so the first lines pace them, then slow by degrees through the induction. Lengthen pauses after suggestions so they have room. Keep consonants clear as you slow, or words blur. Speed back up for emergence so the change in tempo signals waking.

> [normal pace] Just settle in and get comfortable. [slower] And as you... breathe... out... [slower still] deeper... now...

> (from here, each line slower than the last) Drifting. Down. Further.

**Spot it by:** stage directions: '[slower]', '(slowing)', '(pause longer)'; ellipses or line breaks between words growing across a passage; notes like 'read at half speed from here'.

**Not to be confused with:** Silence (silence is a deliberate gap; slowing pace is a falling tempo across many lines); Rapid delivery (the opposite tempo choice, used to overload); Lengthening sentences (a written rhythm choice in the text, not the spoken rate).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Slowed, paced delivery is standard in clinical hypnosis teaching; its separate contribution to depth has not been isolated in controlled work.

**Why it works:** Pacing and leading, Habituation.


### Tone shift *(delivery)*

Also called: voice change, change of register, command voice, trance voice.

A change of vocal register held over a passage or section: the voice turns lower, firmer, softer, flatter or warmer than in the lines before it, and stays there. It signals that the session has moved on, for example from friendly pre-talk to a slow trance voice, or from soothing description to commands. The unit is the passage, not the word. A tonal signal on a few selected words inside a line is analog marking, and a whispered passage is the whisper entry.

**How:** Decide which sections get which voice and note it at the head of each section. A common plan is a conversational voice for the pre-talk, a lower and slower voice from the induction on, a firmer voice for direct commands, and a brighter voice for the wake. Make the change at a section boundary and hold it; a voice that keeps changing stops signalling anything. Use the same voice for the same job across a series so the listener learns what it means.

> [conversational] So that's all you need to know before we start. [lower, slower, from here on] Now let your eyes rest on one spot in front of you.

> [soft] You've done so well, and you can rest there. [firm voice for the next section] Listen. These are the three things you will do tomorrow.

> [brighter, normal speaking voice] And coming back up now, one, two, three.

**Spot it by:** a voice direction at the start of a section or paragraph: '[lower voice]', '[firm]', '[command voice]', '[soft]', '[flat]'; directions that give a duration: 'from here on', 'for this section', 'until the count'; a direction to return: '[back to normal voice]', '[brighter]' at the wake; production notes assigning a named voice to each section ('trance voice', 'command voice').

**Not to be confused with:** Analog marking (analog marking changes the voice on selected words or phrases to set them apart; tone shift holds a changed register across a passage or section); Whisper (when the direction names a whisper or close-mic voice, label whisper; tone shift covers other sustained changes of register); Attention call (an orienting cue is a change used to pull attention back just before a key line; tone shift is a sustained change of voice, which may also serve that purpose); Slowing pace (slowing pace changes tempo; tone shift changes pitch, firmness or quality of the voice).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Using a distinct lower or firmer voice for trance and for commands is widely taught; no controlled studies isolate the effect of the change of voice on hypnotic response.

**Why it works:** Orienting response.


### Whisper *(delivery)*

Also called: close-mic, whispered delivery, whispering.

Whispered or close-miked delivery held over a passage or a whole track. It creates a sense of physical closeness and, for some listeners, an ASMR response. It is one specific register: where a direction names a whisper or a close microphone, label whisper, and use tone shift for any other change of voice. Layered voices may use whispers as one of several tracks; a whisper alone is a single track.

**How:** Use it for intimate or soothing passages, or for a few lines that should feel like a secret. Record close to the microphone with pop protection, and check that sibilants are not harsh. Keep key suggestions intelligible; a whisper too faint to follow loses the words. A switch from normal voice into whisper can itself mark depth or closeness.

> [whisper, close] Just you and my voice now... nothing else matters.

> [close-mic, soft] Shh. Let it go. Right here, right next to your ear.

**Spot it by:** stage directions: '[whisper]', '[close-mic]', '(softly, right in the ear)'; ASMR in the title or tags; phrases like 'right next to your ear', 'so close' with production notes.

**Not to be confused with:** Tone shift (tone shift is any other change of register (lower, firmer, flatter); label whisper when the direction names a whisper or close-mic voice); Layered voices (layering stacks several tracks; a whisper alone is one track); Parasocial intimacy (parasocial intimacy is a relational framing in the words; whisper is the vocal choice that often carries it).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. ASMR responses to whispering are reported and have some survey and physiological study, but whether whisper deepens hypnotic response is untested.

**Why it works:** Attentional capture, Parasocial interaction.


### Layered voices *(delivery)*

Also called: multitrack, overlapping voices, background whispers, voice stacking.

Several recorded voice tracks overlap: a main voice with background whispers, two voices in different ears, or a chorus of repeated phrases. It loads attention and lets some lines arrive without being followed. It differs from double induction, the recipe built from two simultaneous inductions, and from a subliminal track, which is mixed below easy audibility.

**How:** Keep one track clearly dominant so the listener has something to hold. Put short, repeated phrases on the secondary tracks; long sentences become noise. Separate tracks by ear or by volume so the layering is heard as voices, not mud. Write each track as its own column or block so the editor can align them.

> [main] Just listen to my voice... [layer, left, whisper] deeper... deeper... [layer, right] let go...

> [track A] You can relax your hands. [track B, overlapping] sinking down, sinking down.

**Spot it by:** track labels: '[track A]', '[layer]', left/right channel columns; notes: 'overlapping', 'under the main voice', 'background whispers'; two scripts set side by side for simultaneous reading.

**Not to be confused with:** Double induction (double induction is a named recipe of two full inductions; layering is any multitrack voice); Subliminal track (a subliminal track is mixed to be barely audible; layered voices are audible); Concurrent task (dual task gives the listener a task; layering only presents competing input).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Overlapping speech raises cognitive load, which is well studied; its effect on hypnotic depth or suggestion uptake in recordings is untested.

**Why it works:** Cognitive load, Working-memory interference.

**Consent:** Secondary tracks are designed to be heard but not followed; the listener should be able to read what they say.


### Subliminal track *(delivery)*

Also called: subliminals, masked audio, hidden affirmations, subs.

Speech recorded at very low volume, sped up, masked by noise or music, or otherwise hidden in the mix. Its premise is that suggestions take effect without being noticed. It differs from layered voices, which are audible, and from a music bed, which carries no hidden words.

**How:** If you use one, publish the full text of the hidden track and say it is there. Keep it to statements the listener has already heard in the main track. Do not rely on it for any effect the script needs; the evidence for subliminal audio is weak. Label the track in the script with its level and masking method.

> [subliminal, -30 dB under music] I relax easily. I sleep deeply.

> (hidden track text, looped under the whole session) Calm. Focused. Calm. Focused.

**Spot it by:** stage directions: '[subliminal]', '[masked]', '-NN dB under'; title or description words: 'subliminal', 'subs', 'hidden affirmations'; a separate list of affirmations marked as the hidden track.

**Not to be confused with:** Layered voices (layered voices are audible; a subliminal track is meant not to be); Music bed (a music bed has no hidden speech); Analog marking (marking sets words apart audibly within the main voice).

**Evidence:** contested. A double-blind test of commercial subliminal self-help tapes (Greenwald, Spangenberg, Pratkanis & Eskenazi, Psychological Science, 1991) found no effect of the hidden content; listeners improved according to what the label told them the tape was for. The popular claim far outruns the evidence.

**Why it works:** Placebo effect, Response expectancy theory, Priming.

**Consent:** Works only if unnoticed by design; always disclose that a hidden track exists and publish what it says.


### Binaural / isochronic tones *(delivery)*

Also called: binaural, brainwave entrainment, isochronic tones, monaural beats.

Binaural beats are two slightly different tones, one per ear, heard as a beat at the difference frequency. Monaural beats mix the two tones in one channel, and isochronic tones are one tone pulsed on and off. All three are offered as brainwave entrainment toward relaxed or trance-like states. They differ from a metronome, which is a slow beat the listener can count and the speaker can time words to, and from a music bed, which is not tuned to a target frequency.

**How:** Treat tones as background texture, not a mechanism the script depends on. Binaural beats need headphones; say so in the listening notes. Keep them quiet under the voice and avoid harsh carrier frequencies. Do not promise a specific brain state unless you mean it as expectation setting.

> [binaural bed, 200/206 Hz, fade in] Let your breathing slow now...

> (pretalk) Use headphones; there are tones under my voice that many people find relaxing.

**Spot it by:** stage directions: '[binaural]', '[isochronic]', 'Hz', 'theta', 'delta'; listening notes: 'headphones required'; titles or tags: 'brainwave', 'entrainment'.

**Not to be confused with:** Metronome / steady beat (a metronome is an audible beat the listener can count; tones are a carrier aimed at entrainment); Music bed (a music bed is ordinary music or drone, not tuned beat frequencies).

**Evidence:** contested. The beat percept is real, but studies of entrainment and of effects on mood, relaxation or hypnotic response are mixed and often small or null. Source: Oster, Auditory beats in the brain, Scientific American (1973).

**Why it works:** Placebo effect, Response expectancy theory.


### Panning *(delivery)*

Also called: ear to ear, surround, 3D audio, spatial audio.

A spatial placement choice: the voice sweeps from ear to ear, sits in one ear, or circles the head. It directs attention and can disorient. It differs from layered voices, which add tracks, though the two are often combined so each ear carries its own voice.

**How:** Use slow sweeps to absorb and lull, fast or unpredictable moves to disorient. Tie the movement to the words when you can, such as a voice moving 'all around you' as it says so. Require headphones in the listening notes. Avoid hard pans that leave one ear silent for long.

> [pan slowly left to right] My voice moves... from here... to here... and you follow it.

> [left ear] One part of you listens... [right ear] while another part simply drifts.

**Spot it by:** stage directions: '[pan left]', '[L]', '[R]', 'ear to ear', 'circling'; scripts in two channels labeled left and right; words about where the voice is: 'in this ear', 'all around you'.

**Not to be confused with:** Layered voices (layering stacks simultaneous voices; panning moves placement); Left-right confusion (left-right confusion is a verbal confusion device; panning is audio placement); Conscious / unconscious split (the split is a verbal frame; one voice per ear is one way to voice it).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Sound movement captures attention in general; no studies isolate its effect on trance.

**Why it works:** Attentional capture, Orienting response.


### Metronome / steady beat *(delivery)*

Also called: ticking, clock, pulse, steady beat.

An audible regular beat beneath speech: a clock tick, metronome or soft pulse. The speaker may time words to it or slow it to lead. It differs from binaural or isochronic tones, which aim at entrainment rather than an audible count, and from meter, which is rhythm in the wording.

**How:** Set the tempo near a resting pulse or breath rate, then slow it gradually if you want to lead. Time key words to the beat so voice and pulse agree. Keep it low in the mix; a loud tick grates. Stop or change it at emergence so the change signals waking.

> [metronome, 60 bpm, slowing to 40] With each tick... a little deeper... tick... deeper.

> [clock ticking under voice] Every tick is a moment of letting go.

**Spot it by:** stage directions: '[metronome]', '[tick]', 'bpm'; phrases like 'with each tick', 'every beat', 'the clock'; notes on beat tempo changes.

**Not to be confused with:** Binaural / isochronic tones (binaural, monaural or isochronic tones are specified for a target beat frequency and proposed brainwave entrainment; a metronome supplies a regular tick or pulse for audible pacing); Sound effects (an effect is a sound placed at one moment; a tick or pulse that runs on at a regular rate under the voice is a metronome); Rhythm and meter (meter is rhythm in the wording; a metronome is a separate sound); Countdown deepener (a countdown deepens by spoken numbers; a beat runs without numbers).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Metronome sounds have been used in hypnosis and relaxation settings; there is no clear evidence of an effect beyond focus and monotony.

**Why it works:** Habituation, Pacing and leading.


### Music bed *(delivery)*

Also called: drone, ambient, pad, soundscape, background music.

A continuous bed of music, drone, nature sound or ambient texture beneath speech. It masks room noise, sets mood and gives the session a consistent carrier. It differs from sound effects, which are discrete cues, and from binaural tones, which are tuned for entrainment.

**How:** Pick something without lyrics and without sudden changes, clearly quieter than the voice. Match the mood to the section and change or fade it at emergence. Reuse the same bed across a series so it becomes familiar. Avoid tracks the listener may know, which pull attention to the music.

> [ambient pad fades in] Let the sound carry you as you settle back.

> [music bed drops out] And now, just my voice.

**Spot it by:** stage directions: '[music]', '[bed fades in/out]', '[drone]', '[ambient]'; credits for music or soundscapes; words about the music: 'let the music carry you'.

**Not to be confused with:** Binaural / isochronic tones (tones are tuned to a beat frequency; a music bed is ordinary music or drone); Sound effects (effects are discrete cue sounds; a bed is continuous); Subliminal track (a subliminal track hides speech; a bed carries none).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Relaxing music has modest experimental support for lowering arousal and anxiety in general settings; its specific effect on hypnotic response is not established.

**Why it works:** Mere-exposure effect, State-dependent memory.


### Sound effects *(delivery)*

Also called: snap, bell, chime, click, SFX.

Discrete non-speech sounds placed at points in the recording to mark events: a snap at a drop, a bell at a wake, a chime after praise. This entry covers placing the sound. When the sound is deliberately trained to evoke a response it is also a sound trigger.

**How:** Use few sounds and give each one job. Put the sound exactly where the script says so the listener hears event and sound together. Keep levels even with the voice so the sound is clear but not startling, unless startle is the point. Repeat the same sound for the same event across a series.

> Three, two, one... [snap] drop.

> Good. [soft chime] That's exactly right.

**Spot it by:** stage directions: '[snap]', '[bell]', '[chime]', '[click]', '(SFX)'; references in the words: 'when you hear the bell'; production notes listing sound cues and timings.

**Not to be confused with:** Sound trigger (a sound trigger is a trained association; a sound effect is the sound itself, trained or not); Marker signal (a marker signal is a specific conditioning use of one sound); Music bed (music is continuous; effects are discrete).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Sounds can be conditioned as cues, which is well established in general; their use in recorded hypnosis is untested.

**Why it works:** Classical conditioning, Orienting response.


### Echo *(delivery)*

Also called: reverb, delay, echo effect.

An audio effect applied to selected words or passages: a delayed repeat of a word, or a reverb tail that makes the voice sound distant or vast. Echo on a few chosen words sets them apart, as analog marking does with the voice, and adds repetition without the speaker saying the words again. It differs from immediate repetition, where the words are spoken twice.

**How:** Apply it to a few key words, typically the last word of a suggestion or a trigger. Keep delay times long enough to be heard as echo, and fade the repeats. Use heavier reverb for imagery of space, depth or distance. Too much makes the voice unintelligible.

> And you sink... [echo] deeper... deeper... deeper.

> [heavy reverb] Far away now, in a great still space.

**Spot it by:** stage directions: '[echo]', '[reverb]', '[delay]'; a word written repeatedly with a fading or echo mark; notes on effect settings.

**Not to be confused with:** Immediate repetition (immediate repetition is spoken by the voice and written as repeated words; echo is a production effect named in a direction); Analog marking (analog marking sets words apart with the voice itself (pitch, pause, volume); echo does it with an added effect, so label echo only where an effect is named); Tone shift (tone shift changes the speaker's register for a passage; echo and reverb are processing added to the recording).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. There are no studies of echo effects in hypnosis recordings; the practice rests on community use.

**Why it works:** Analog marking, Attentional capture.


### Breath-synced pacing *(delivery)*

Also called: pacing to the breath, breath pacing, speaking on the exhale.

The speaker times phrases to breathing: live to the listener's breath in person, or to a typical resting rate in a recording. Suggestions of letting go fall on the exhale. It differs from a breath-focus induction, which tells the listener to attend to breathing, and from pacing, which describes in words what the listener is doing.

**How:** In recordings, assume a slow rate, roughly four to six seconds per breath, and leave room for the listener's own exhale after each phrase. Put 'relax', 'let go', 'deeper' on the exhale and neutral words on the inhale. Mark the rhythm in the script so the reader holds it. Slow it gradually to lead the breath down.

> (wait for the out-breath) ...and your shoulders drop. (let them breathe in; speak again on the next exhale) ...heavier now.

> (one phrase per breath, on the exhale only) The chair holds you. (breath) Your hands are still. (breath) Nothing to do.

**Spot it by:** timing directions tied to breath: '(on the exhale)', '(on the out-breath)', '(wait for the inhale)'; '(inhale)' / '(exhale)' marks placed before lines whose words are not about breathing; notes on breath timing: 'one phrase per breath', 'match their breathing', 'leave a breath between lines'.

**Not to be confused with:** Breathe in, breathe out (that entry is in the words: the inhale and exhale are each given content; breath-sync is a timing direction and the words can be about anything); Breath-focus induction (the induction tells the listener to attend to or change their breathing; this entry times the voice to breath without mentioning it); Matching (matching is the rapport move of copying any feature of the listener; use this label when the direction is specifically about timing phrases to the breath); Pacing (pacing states the listener's experience in words; breath-sync times delivery to it).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Speaking on the client's exhale is common clinical teaching; its separate effect has not been tested.

**Why it works:** Pacing and leading, Rapport matching.


### Visuals *(delivery)*

Also called: spiral video, text flashes, captions, on-screen visuals.

A video or visual track that runs with the session. Common forms are rotating spirals for fixation, captions of the spoken text, and words flashed briefly on screen. It differs from spiral fixation, the induction move of telling the listener to watch, and from a visual trigger, a trained association to an image.

**How:** Decide what the visual is for: fixation, reinforcing the words, or atmosphere. Keep it in step with the audio. Avoid rapid flashing; strobing and fast-alternating patterns can trigger seizures in photosensitive viewers, so include a warning. If words flash too fast to read, treat them as a subliminal track and disclose them.

> [spiral video begins, slow rotation] Just watch the center as it turns.

> [on screen: RELAX, held two seconds] Relax. Let the word sink in.

**Spot it by:** stage directions: '[on screen]', '[spiral]', '[caption]', '[flash]'; video production notes with frame or duration markings; listening notes mentioning photosensitivity.

**Not to be confused with:** Spiral fixation (spiral fixation is the spoken instruction to watch; visuals are the production track, labeled from the direction that calls for it); Visual trigger (a visual trigger is an image given a stated response; visuals may or may not train one); Subliminal track (a subliminal track is hidden speech in the audio; words flashed on screen too fast to read are labeled visuals and carry the same duty to disclose); Gaze capture (gaze capture is the instruction to fix on the speaker's eyes, imagined or shown; visuals is the direction that puts anything on screen).

**Evidence:** practitioner-lore. Visual fixation is part of standard induction practice, but spiral and flash videos are community practice without controlled study.

**Why it works:** Attentional capture, Attentional tunneling.

**Consent:** Text flashed too fast to read works unnoticed and should be disclosed; flashing visuals need a photosensitivity warning.


### Silence *(delivery)*

Also called: dead air, pause, gap.

A planned gap in the audio: no voice, and often no added sound. Short silences give a suggestion time to land; long ones let the listener drift or complete an imagined task. It differs from the silence deepener, which tells the listener the quiet will take them deeper, and from a written pause, which is punctuation in the text.

**How:** Place silence after a suggestion or an instruction to imagine, not before. If a gap runs longer than a few seconds, say what it is for ('take a moment...') so the listener does not think the track has stopped. Keep a music bed under long gaps if dead air would feel broken. Resume with a soft, low voice so the return does not startle.

> Take a moment to explore that feeling. [silence, 20 seconds] And now...

> Just let that settle. (pause, 5 seconds) Good.

**Spot it by:** a gap direction with a duration: '[silence, 20 seconds]', '(pause, 5 seconds)', '[30s]'; directions for an extended gap: '[long pause]', '[long silence]', '[no voice, music only]'; timed gaps listed in production notes.

**Not to be confused with:** Silence / pause deepener (if the words before the gap say that depth grows during the quiet, label the silence deepener; a gap with any other job, or none stated, is silence); Written pause (an ellipsis, dash, line break or untimed '[pause]' or '[beat]' inside running speech is a written pause; label silence when the direction gives a duration or calls for a long gap); Slowing pace (slowing pace is a tempo held across many lines; silence is one discrete gap).

**Evidence:** clinical-tradition. Pauses for processing are standard clinical practice; their effect has not been measured separately.

**Why it works:** Cognitive load, Hypnotic induction.


## Theory


### Linguistic presupposition and pragmatics

**Presupposition** (empirical). Some sentences carry content they do not state: 'when you notice the heaviness' assumes the heaviness is there. Presupposed content is treated as already settled and survives negation and questioning ('do you notice the heaviness?' still assumes it). Listeners tend to evaluate the assertion and let the presupposition pass. A core, well-established notion in linguistics with several competing formal theories. Psycholinguistic work suggests presupposed content is checked less carefully than asserted content, though how much less varies with task and attention. *For writers:* Put what you want accepted in the background clause and make the foreground claim about something trivial or obviously true.

**Presuppositional framing** (theoretical). Beyond single sentences, a speaker can keep many presuppositions consistent so that a passage assumes one view of the situation. Responses then address details within that view. Questioning the frame itself means stepping outside the exchange, which feels effortful or rude. Built from well-supported parts (presupposition, framing), but there is little direct experimental work on frame-level stacking as such. *For writers:* Keep presuppositions consistent across a section so they reinforce one picture; a single contradiction invites the listener to examine the whole frame.

**Presupposition accommodation** (empirical). When a sentence presupposes something the listener did not already accept, the listener usually just updates their picture to include it. Objecting ('wait, what heaviness?') is possible but interrupts the flow and carries a social cost. Accommodation is what lets a presupposition introduce new content. Well established in formal pragmatics and supported by experimental work. Accommodation is easier for plausible, low-stakes content and harder for surprising or contested content. *For writers:* Presuppose things plausible enough to be accommodated without a jolt; save bolder content until smaller presuppositions have been accepted.

**Common ground** (empirical). Conversation builds a running record of mutually accepted information. Assertions propose additions to it; presuppositions assume content is already in it. What counts is what is treated as accepted, not what either party privately believes. A foundational, widely accepted construct in pragmatics, also studied experimentally in psycholinguistic work on grounding and audience design. *For writers:* Track what the script has actually established; refer back to it as shared only when it has been given, or when you deliberately mean to presuppose it.

**Common-ground manipulation** (theoretical). A speaker can add content to the common ground by acting as though it is already there, with phrasing like 'as we both know' or definite descriptions of things never introduced. The listener has to actively reject the content to keep it out. This is the mechanism behind many covert persuasion moves and some coercive ones. A framing from philosophy of language and rhetoric built on well-supported components (presupposition, accommodation); it has no separate experimental literature of its own. *For writers:* Recognize this as the engine of assumed-agreement lines; use it on content the listener has consented to, and treat it as a warning sign when it rewrites the listener's own experience.

**Pragmatic enrichment** (empirical). Literal meaning usually underdetermines what is communicated: 'you're ready' is heard as ready for something in particular, and 'something is beginning to change' as a specific change in the listener. Listeners supply the missing object, scope, time and reference from context. This happens quickly and mostly without awareness. Well supported in linguistics. Theorists disagree about how much enrichment belongs to 'what is said' versus implicature, but the phenomenon itself is not in dispute. *For writers:* Vague wording lets the listener enrich it with their own specifics, which then feel personal; be precise only where you need one specific reading.

**Conversational implicature** (empirical). Listeners assume speakers are informative, truthful, relevant and clear, and they draw inferences that keep that assumption intact. 'Some people notice their hands getting lighter' implies the listener might. Implicatures can be cancelled, which gives the speaker deniability. A foundational and well-supported account. Specific types, such as scalar implicatures, have large experimental literatures, with variation across contexts and listeners. *For writers:* Use implication when you want the listener to reach the conclusion themselves; what they infer feels like their own thought and is harder to argue with.

**Conventional implicature** (empirical). Some words add content that is not up for debate in the way the main claim is: 'even you can do this' asserts ability while implying low expectations. Unlike conversational implicature, this content is tied to the words and hard to cancel. It tends to survive negation and questioning. An established but contested category in semantics. Its boundary with presupposition and expressive meaning is debated: 'still', 'already' and 'finally' are usually treated as presupposition triggers, 'even' is analysed both ways, and some theorists argue the category should be dissolved. The observation that these words add content outside the main claim is not in dispute. *For writers:* Watch the small words; 'finally', 'still', 'already', 'even' and 'but' carry attitudes and assumptions the listener absorbs without examining.

**Factive presupposition** (empirical). Factive verbs take a clause whose truth is assumed: 'you may realize you are relaxing' presupposes that you are relaxing, whether or not you realize it. The open question becomes awareness, not truth. This is the linguistic basis of awareness predicates in hypnotic language. A classic, well-supported observation in semantics; factivity judgments are robust, though some verbs are borderline and context can weaken the inference. *For writers:* Wrap the content you want accepted inside 'notice', 'realize', 'discover' or 'become aware', and make the question about awareness.

**Projective content** (empirical). Presuppositions and some implications 'project': 'you don't have to go deeper just yet' still implies that you will. This makes such content resistant to the listener's usual ways of declining a suggestion. How strongly content projects varies by trigger and by what the speaker is taken to be addressing. A well-documented phenomenon with active experimental research; the projection strength of different triggers is still being mapped. *For writers:* Phrase permissive or negated lines so the suggestion projects through them; the negation softens the tone without removing the content.

**Loaded question** (empirical). 'How deep have you already gone?' cannot be answered directly without granting that you have gone deep. The listener can reject the premise only by refusing the question. Argumentation theory classes this as the fallacy of many questions; eyewitness research shows question wording shifts what people report. The logical point is uncontroversial. Experimental work on leading questions shows wording effects on answers and memory reports, with effect sizes that vary across studies. *For writers:* This construct duplicates the device of the same name; use the device where the presupposed content is something the listener has agreed to.

**Conversational framing** (theoretical). People interpret utterances through a shared definition of what kind of activity is going on. The same words mean different things under 'this is a game' and 'this is serious'. Cues that set or shift the frame change how everything after them is heard. An influential sociological framework that is descriptive and interpretive rather than a tested model; frame effects on interpretation are widely observed. *For writers:* Set the frame explicitly near the start (fiction, practice, play) and signal clearly when it changes, including on the way out.

**Metalinguistic negotiation** (theoretical). Speakers can push a definition by using a term as if the new meaning were standard, for example calling surrender 'freedom' or doubt 'a sign of trance'. A listener who goes along accepts the redefinition implicitly. Such disputes look factual but are really about word use. A recent, active topic in philosophy of language; a conceptual framework rather than an empirically tested model. *For writers:* When redefining a term, use it consistently in its new sense rather than arguing for it; repeated use does the work that argument would invite resistance to.

**Illocutionary force** (empirical). 'You might want to close your eyes' is grammatically a statement about possibility but functions as a request. Force can be direct or indirect, and listeners respond to the force rather than the grammar. Indirect forms soften directives while keeping their effect. A foundational concept in pragmatics; research on indirect requests supports that listeners readily recover the intended force. *For writers:* Choose the grammatical form for tone but keep the force clear; indirect phrasing lowers resistance only if the listener still knows what is being asked.

**Speech-act theory** (theoretical). Utterances perform acts: naming, declaring, promising, commanding.
